Vol.1 · 2026
What hundreds of agent sessions taught one team

How to run AI agents
you can trust.

One team ran AI agents at scale for months, watched them fail in ways that cost real time, and wrote down every pattern that turned an unreliable agent into one whose output could be trusted without re-checking it by hand.

The context. A human and an AI orchestrator build research tooling for a Princeton chemistry lab. The tooling gets one run at the real data — a professor’s environmental-contamination dataset that arrives once, with no second pass to fix a mistake — so every weakness gets hunted down first on stand-in data. Hundreds of sessions produced the patterns below. The chemistry does not matter here. The knowledge is about commanding agents, and it moves to any codebase.

  • 48 findings — the raw notes behind the method

§01 — The frame

Three questions,
asked once per decision.

Most decisions are not hard. When one feels heavy, these three questions resolve most of its weight before it reaches a person.

01

Blast radius

What breaks if this is wrong? The answer’s size sets how hard you check.

02

Right target

Fixing the tool, or fiddling with the test data?

03

Cheap probe

Could a thirty-second check settle this first?

What this project refuses to be

Scope drifts when no one writes the edges down. Each line below names a direction this project could have taken and deliberately refused.

Nota general-purpose AI. It serves one lab for one summer.
Notthe decision-maker. The human, Isaac, decides the science.
Nota finished product. It is an instrument being hardened for one critical run.
Notoptimized for cost or speed. It is optimized for trust on the day that matters.
Nota replacement for the professor. It gives him better evidence to judge.
Nota knowledge graph for its own sake. The graph exists to surface contradictions.
Nota referendum on the stand-in data. The data is a test track for the tooling.
§02 — The craft

The Method.

25 disciplines, stated as they were learned. Each one earned its place by preventing a specific failure that had already cost something, and they are grouped by the part of the work they govern.

Verify before you trust

00

Blast radius before verification

Every claim an agent makes about the system carries a cost if it is wrong. Rank that cost before checking it — cosmetic, degraded, corrupts downstream work, breaks the pipeline. The size of the consequence sets how hard the claim gets verified. A one-line check settles most of them in under a second; the expensive failures earn the deeper look.

01

Memory lies. Disk doesn't.

An agent's memory of a repository drifts the moment a file changes. Every factual claim about the current state earns one verifying command before it is spoken — grep, ls, wc -l. A re-read costs two hundred milliseconds. A stale claim costs a wrong decision a week later, traced back at ten times the price.

02

Discovery before verification

Verification is bounded by what someone thought to look for. The full surface comes first — git ls-files, a glob — and sampling comes second. The failure mode is confident wrongness: the sampled slice checked out while the answer sat in the slice no one opened.

03

I don't know

An agent that does not know says so, and names the one check that would resolve it. The agent admitting the gap three times an hour is the one that earns trust. A confident-sounding completion feels useful in the moment while it quietly hands over something false.

Prompting a single agent

04

Describe the risk, not the task

Pointing an agent at a location (“look in the memory folder”) yields a shallow inventory. Naming the failure to hunt (“find where this breaks once real data arrives”) forces it to reason toward real problems. The prompter becomes the director describing risk rather than a tour guide pointing at rooms.

05

The five-component prompt

A prompt precise enough that low-effort output is impossible carries five parts, each narrowing the agent: objective, severity filter, trigger condition, failure definition, and exclusions. Most prompts have one or two. The trigger condition is the strongest of them — it names the event the failure hides behind, which turns auditing into simulation.

06

Tighten the failure, never widen the scope

When results come back mixed, the instinct is to append “analyze all aspects.” That reverts to breadth and returns a blend of real problems and surface noise no one can sort. The fix runs the other direction: sharpen the failure definition until it is a net that catches everything relevant on its own.

07

Name the type, never the examples

Listing the specific failures to look for makes an agent anchor on exactly those and miss the rest. Naming the broad type — “hunt for index-file failures” — lets it surface failures no one anticipated. Prescription caps discovery at the prompter's own prior knowledge.

08

Negative identity first

The sharpest role prompts open with what the agent is not, before any positive instruction. “What You Are Not — Read This First” carves a role more reliably than a description of the job. Telling an agent the postures to refuse is what stops a synthesis role from quietly widening its own scope.

Designing the instructions

09

Attention budget is not token budget

A prompt has two budgets. The token budget is a hard wall. The attention budget is a soft gradient where quality silently decays as critical instructions land in low-attention zones. Large models read roughly uniformly; small ones have a pronounced middle-sag, so the same prompt that works on the big model degrades on the small one with no error. A fifty-token primer near the top recovers most of it.

10

Worked examples beat specifications

Handed a specification, an agent builds the blandest version that satisfies the words — the median-aesthetic version, indistinguishable from what any decent agent would produce. Two or three examples that vary along the axis that matters teach the standard prose cannot carry. More words only add text to compress past. Variation across the examples is the whole lesson; a single example just gets copied.

11

Narrative beats a bullet list

An instruction file written as the agent's own self-talk — “when I don't know, I say so” — propagates without enforcement. The same content as third-person rules requires policing every time. Identity-shaping has a lower cognitive floor than rule-application, so it holds even on weaker models. Files meant for grep stay as lists; files meant to shape behavior become story.

Running many agents

12

Subagents are blank slates

A subagent reads only the prompt it is handed. It holds none of the conversation, none of the memory, none of the project files unless they are pasted in. The prompt is the entire surface of its behavior. Ten vague prompts return ten vague answers that all get redone; one sharp prompt returns one usable result.

13

Firepower modes

Effort gets matched to the task by name. Shotgun fires eight to fifteen light parallel agents for breadth. Default runs three to five at medium depth. .50 cal is one heavy agent going deep. Stand down halts everything. The question that selects the mode is where attention buys the most, and a broad search and a subtle bug want opposite answers.

14

Coordinate through files, not chat

Let parallel agents talk to each other and coordination cost explodes with the square of their number. Route every handoff through typed files on disk instead, and the control graph collapses to near-linear. Pre-assign each agent its own output path before spawning so two writers never collide, and the filesystem layout becomes the concurrency control.

15

Verify the gate, not the artifact

“The file exists” is not “the file is correct.” A downstream stage that trusts the mere presence of an upstream output inherits every silent failure above it. Promotion waits on a verification record — a checker that confirms the artifact, captured with its hash and freshness — so a leftover file from a failed attempt can never masquerade as this attempt's work.

16

At scale, failure moves into the control plane

More agents do not remove failure; they relocate it. Two new failure modes appear and both scale: a bad task spec makes a hundred agents produce a hundred wrong answers fast, and weak checking certifies bad work with false confidence. These are more dangerous than slow execution because the error multiplies. The bottleneck stops being model capacity and becomes the quality of tasks and checks.

17

Cheap scan, expensive synthesis

Scanning and inventorying is a different job from connecting and reasoning, so they go to different models. Many cheap agents read in parallel and report facts; one expensive agent synthesizes across all of it at once. Reading sequentially loses precision by the tenth file; holding every pre-digested summary in one context at once is where the cross-cutting pattern surfaces. The synthesizer never touches raw files.

Keeping agents honest

18

Blind audits at high-stakes moments

A high-stakes write — a memory file, a ranked list of takeaways, a final artifact — gets a second reader who has never seen the conclusion, handed only the raw materials. Naming the sources it must not read is what makes the audit blind, and that is harder than naming the inputs it should use. A primed auditor is a mirror; the value is the asymmetry.

19

The cold-reader test

Parallel agents preserve structure and lose specificity, so an assembled deliverable often looks uniform where it should vary. The finished artifact goes to a reader with zero context. A cold reader judges shape rather than truth, and shape is exactly where templated, collapsed, look-alike output reveals itself.

20

Count cross-confirmations, not findings

When an artifact passes its own validation gate but a structural flaw is suspected, the cheapest credible test is six or more independent agents with overlapping-but-distinct scopes. Five converging on the same finding without being primed makes it real; one or two surfacing it makes it a hypothesis. The catch: the repetition only counts if the agents truly vary in scope, because a pipeline that cannot disconfirm itself will manufacture the same false certainty every run.

Memory and measurement

21

Retrieval beats summary-of-summaries

Summarizing summaries destroys information geometrically — a hundred thousand tokens become ten thousand, then one thousand, then noise — and still blows the budget eventually. An orchestrator does not need the full history; it needs answers to specific questions about it. Keep the record structured on disk and pull a small, query-relevant slice on demand.

22

Store the claim, point to the evidence

The durable unit of agent memory is a one-line claim with a confidence and a pointer to its evidence — a commit hash, a file, a test result — held in place of the evidence itself. The tiny claim lives in working memory; the proof is fetched only when the claim is challenged. That keeps memory cheap to carry and every conclusion traceable back to what produced it.

23

Calibration over catch-rate

Whether an agent got the answer right stops being measurable the moment real work has no answer key. Whether its stated confidence tracks its actual error rate transfers to any deployment. A calibrated agent at ninety percent beats an overconfident one at ninety-five, because buckets of “sure, unsure, treat as a lead” let a human scale judgment across the output. Flat all-certain confidence is the same warning as nothing flagged at all.

24

The self-improvement arc

The loop for fixing the tooling itself: spot the drift, write the guess at its cause down first, verify with blind agents, build the fix, cold-read it, record the lesson, ship. A guess committed before the build surfaces as a failed check instead of shipped bad code. Compute multiplies by running more of these loops, not bigger ones.

Real Data Migration Guide

When real data arrives from the Princeton lab, follow this guide.

Last updated: 2025-03-23 Context: System was built and tested on synthetic data (5 sites, 238 samples, 48 columns). This guide covers what to keep, what to swap, and what to rebuild.

Quick Checklist

[ ] 1. Drop new CSV in data/raw/ (never modify it)
[ ] 2. Read column headers — what do you actually have?
[ ] 3. Update DATA_COLUMNS in scripts/assemble-prompts.py
[ ] 4. Update SITES dict in scripts/assemble-prompts.py
[ ] 5. Decide VARIABLES — what varies enough to study?
[ ] 6. Keep seed findings F001-F012 (literature still applies)
[ ] 7. Delete site-specific findings from Batch 1 (they're synthetic artifacts)
[ ] 8. Delete site-specific constraints (C001, C006, C007) — keep physics ones (C002-C005)
[ ] 9. Reset status board: phase=planning, progress=0%, clear entity_coverage
[ ] 10. Update column interpretation warnings in assembly script
[ ] 11. Run scripts/assemble-prompts.py
[ ] 12. Spawn first batch on real data

Steps 2-5 are the only hard ones. Everything else is config swaps.

Variables: What Happens When Data Changes

The 8 variables we defined are hypotheses about what matters, derived from literature + synthetic data design:

gac_dosage_optimization
doc_interference_quantification
iron_speciation_impact
pre_treatment_requirements
seasonal_flow_effects
co_contaminant_competition
ph_adjustment_benefit
short_chain_pfas_removal

Some Variables Become Irrelevant

  • If real site has no iron problem → iron_speciation_impact is wasted
  • If real site has no co-contaminants → co_contaminant_competition is wasted
  • If pH is always ~7.0 → ph_adjustment_benefit is trivial
  • If no seasonal data → seasonal_flow_effects impossible

New Variables Emerge

  • Real data might show alkalinity matters (we don't measure it)
  • Real data might show specific PFAS congener ratios matter (we only have PFOS/PFOA/Other)
  • Real data might reveal biofilm effects, carbon age, or backwash frequency
  • Real data might have time-series structure (same contactor over weeks) vs our cross-sectional snapshot

What To Do

The variable sweep plan must be regenerated from real data, not carried over. The orchestrator should:

  1. Look at actual columns
  2. Identify which vary enough to study (sufficient range + enough samples)
  3. Propose variables from what's there
  4. Score each with ESIG

Three Tiers of Reusability

Tier 1: The Framework (100% Reusable)

Everything in this list transfers to ANY dataset, ANY project:

  • Agent architecture (orchestrator → scientist → memory)
  • Wave model (spawn all scientists, wait, spawn all memory)
  • File system layout (data/raw, agent-work, agent-summaries, memory/)
  • Schema formats (analysis schema, summary schema)
  • Prohibitions and negative-tone guardrails
  • Calibration loop mechanism
  • Prompt assembly script structure (not specific configs)
  • Finding/constraint registry format
  • Quality grading methodology (schema compliance, data accuracy, calibration specificity)

Tier 2: Domain Knowledge (Mostly Reusable If Still PFAS + GAC)

  • Seed findings F001-F012 (established literature — valid for any PFAS+GAC project)
  • Physical constraints C002-C005 (GAC capacity, C-F bond, EPA MCLs, EBCT range)
  • Scientist manual section guidance (adsorption kinetics, interference analysis framing)
  • Research goal (if still "optimize GAC for PFAS across water types")
  • Princeton research context (Jaffe lab, Feammox, biological destruction as alternative)

Tier 3: Site-Specific Configs (Rebuild Every Time)

  • SITES dict in assembly script
  • VARIABLES dict (derived from actual data columns)
  • Data column list and interpretation warnings
  • ESIG narratives
  • Site-specific findings from analysis runs
  • Site-specific constraints
  • Water type classification
  • Experimentor brief
  • All analysis/summary files from previous runs

Step-by-Step Migration Procedure

Phase 1: Receive Data (30 min)

# 1. Drop file in raw folder, never modify
cp /path/to/real-data.csv data/raw/YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM_real-pfas-data.csv

# 2. Inspect columns
head -1 data/raw/YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM_real-pfas-data.csv

# 3. Count rows/sites
python3 -c "
import csv
with open('data/raw/YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM_real-pfas-data.csv') as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
print(f'Rows: {len(rows)}')
print(f'Columns: {list(rows[0].keys())}')
# Check for site identifiers
sites = set(r.get('Site_ID', r.get('site', r.get('Location', 'unknown'))) for r in rows)
print(f'Sites: {sites}')
"

Phase 2: Update Configs (30 min)

# In scripts/assemble-prompts.py, update:

# 1. DATA path
DATA = PROJECT / "data" / "raw" / "YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM_real-pfas-data.csv"

# 2. DATA_COLUMNS — match real CSV headers exactly
DATA_COLUMNS = [
    # ... list every column from the real data
]

# 3. SITES — real site(s)
SITES = {
    "REAL-001": {
        "name": "Actual site name from data",
        "scenario": "Describe based on what you see in the data",
        "water_type": "classify from pH, DOC, conductivity, etc.",
    },
    # ... more sites if multiple
}

# 4. VARIABLES — what varies enough to study?
# Look at the data. Which columns have meaningful range?
# Don't carry over variables that don't exist in real data.
VARIABLES = {
    # ... derive from actual column variability
}

Phase 3: Reset Memory (15 min)

# Keep literature findings
# F001-F012 are from published science — they're still valid

# Delete synthetic-data findings (anything from Batch 1)
# If you added F013+ from synthetic runs, remove them

# Delete site-specific constraints
rm memory/constraint-registry/C001.yaml  # Fe(OH)3 at specific pH
rm memory/constraint-registry/C006.yaml  # anoxic peat chelation
rm memory/constraint-registry/C007.yaml  # SS fouling threshold

# Keep universal constraints
# C002 (GAC capacity), C003 (C-F bond), C004 (EPA MCL), C005 (EBCT range)

# Reset status board
# Edit memory/status-board.yaml:
#   phase: planning
#   overall_progress: 0%
#   entities: [new sites from real data]
#   variables_remaining: [new variables from real data]
#   sessions: empty
#   cross_session_patterns: empty

# Reset task counter
# Edit memory/task-counter.yaml:
#   next_task_id: 1

Phase 4: Clear Synthetic Artifacts (5 min)

# Archive (don't delete) synthetic runs for reference
mkdir -p data/archive/synthetic-backtest-2025-03-23
mv data/agent-work/2025-03-23/ data/archive/synthetic-backtest-2025-03-23/agent-work/
mv data/agent-summaries/2025-03-23/ data/archive/synthetic-backtest-2025-03-23/agent-summaries/
mv sessions/2025-03-23/ data/archive/synthetic-backtest-2025-03-23/sessions/

# Keep the synthetic dataset for reference (it's in data/raw/, never deleted)

Phase 5: Rebuild and Run (20 min)

# Generate new prompts
python3 scripts/assemble-prompts.py

# Verify prompts look correct
head -5 /tmp/prompts/scientist-task-0002.txt
grep "Distance" /tmp/prompts/scientist-task-0002.txt  # or whatever real column names are

# Spawn first batch
# Start with 1 test agent, verify output, then scale up

What NOT To Do

  • Do not modify the real data file. Ever. Drop it in data/raw/ as-is.
  • Do not rename columns in the real data to match our synthetic names. Update the script to match the real names.
  • Do not carry over Batch 1 findings as if they're real. They're synthetic backtest results.
  • Do not assume the same 8 variables apply. Derive variables from what the real data actually contains.
  • Do not keep the experimentor brief. Write a new one based on real findings.
  • Do not delete the synthetic data or backtest results. Archive them — they prove the system works.

Rebuild prompts and test20 minEasy
Total~1.5 hours

The framework took a full day to build. Migration takes 90 minutes.

Princeton Intern AI Project — Memory-Aware Agent Framework
Summarizing summaries destroys information geometrically — replace it with retrieval that pulls a small, query-relevant slice on demand.
2026-03-22

Princeton Intern AI Project — Memory-Aware Agent Framework

Problem Statement

Build a framework where autonomous agent swarms can:

  1. Remember — a memory agent tracks, summarizes, and indexes all work
  2. Orchestrate — an orchestrator agent makes decisions with full context awareness, without access to conversation history

The hard unsolved problem: How does the orchestrator get the right context when summaries-of-summaries eventually blow up to 1M tokens too?

Architecture Overview

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   USER CONVERSATION                  │
│                                                      │
│  Every 10 prompts → Memory Agent triggers            │
│  Every agent spawn → Memory Sidecar attaches         │
└──────────┬───────────────────────────────┬───────────┘
           │                               │
           v                               v
┌─────────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────────┐
│    MEMORY SYSTEM     │     │   ORCHESTRATOR AGENT     │
│                      │     │                          │
│  - Conversation Log  │────>│  Reads memory via        │
│  - Agent Index Files │     │  RETRIEVAL, not linear   │
│  - Master Timeline   │     │  summarization           │
│  - Semantic Index    │     │                          │
└─────────────────────┘     └─────────────────────────┘

Part 1: Memory Agent System

1.1 Conversation Memory Agent

Trigger: Every 10 user prompts (configurable)

What it captures:

  • Decisions made (what was chosen and what was rejected)
  • Files created/modified/deleted (paths + one-line description of change)
  • Errors encountered and how they were resolved
  • User intent/goal shifts
  • Key artifacts produced (test results, build outputs, URLs)

Output format: A structured memory entry, NOT prose

# memory/conversation/2026-03-22T14-30.yaml
timestamp: "2026-03-22T14:30:00Z"
prompt_range: [41, 50]
session_id: "abc123"

decisions:
  - chose: "SQLite for local memory store"
    over: "flat JSON files"
    reason: "concurrent write safety from multiple agents"

files_touched:
  - path: "src/memory/store.py"
    action: created
    summary: "SQLite-backed memory store with WAL mode"
  - path: "tests/test_store.py"
    action: created
    summary: "Basic CRUD tests for memory store"

errors_resolved:
  - error: "WAL mode not available on NFS"
    fix: "Added fallback to journal_mode=DELETE"

goals:
  - active: "Build memory persistence layer"
  - completed: "Design schema for memory entries"
  - deferred: "Distributed memory across machines"

key_facts:
  - "Memory entries use YAML not JSON for readability"
  - "Each agent gets its own SQLite connection"

Why structured, not prose: Structured entries are queryable. Prose summaries are not. This is the key insight that prevents the "summary of summaries" explosion.

1.2 Agent Sidecar Memory

Trigger: Spawned automatically alongside every subagent or agent team

What it tracks:

  • Every file the subagent reads/writes (intercepted at the tool level)
  • The subagent's assigned task and completion status
  • Duration, token usage, model used
  • Output artifacts

Output: An index file per agent spawn

# memory/agents/2026-03-22T14-35-agent-07.yaml
agent_id: "agent-07"
team: "refactor-auth"
spawned_at: "2026-03-22T14:35:12Z"
completed_at: "2026-03-22T14:35:48Z"
model: "haiku"
tokens: { input: 3200, output: 1100 }

task: "Refactor auth middleware to use new session store"
status: completed
result_summary: "Replaced in-memory session dict with SQLite-backed store in 3 files"

files_read: ["src/auth/middleware.py", "src/auth/session.py"]
files_written:
  - path: "src/auth/middleware.py"
    diff_summary: "Swapped SessionDict for SQLiteSession, added async init"
  - path: "src/auth/session.py"
    diff_summary: "New file, SQLiteSession class with get/set/delete"

dependencies: ["agent-03"]  # waited on agent-03's schema work

1.3 Master Timeline

What it is: An append-only log that all memory agents write to. The single source of truth for "what happened when."

Concurrency solution: Each writer appends to its own shard file. A merge process combines shards periodically.

memory/
  timeline/
    shard-conversation-abc123.jsonl    # conversation memory agent writes here
    shard-agent-07.jsonl               # agent-07's sidecar writes here
    shard-agent-08.jsonl               # agent-08's sidecar writes here
    merged.jsonl                       # periodic merge of all shards
    merged.index                       # offset index for fast lookups

Each line in the JSONL is a timestamped event:

{"ts": "2026-03-22T14:35:48Z", "type": "agent_complete", "agent": "agent-07", "team": "refactor-auth", "summary": "Refactored auth middleware", "files": ["src/auth/middleware.py", "src/auth/session.py"]}
{"ts": "2026-03-22T14:36:01Z", "type": "decision", "chose": "SQLite WAL mode", "context": "memory store concurrency"}
{"ts": "2026-03-22T14:40:00Z", "type": "conversation_summary", "prompt_range": [41,50], "ref": "memory/conversation/2026-03-22T14-30.yaml"}

Part 2: The Orchestrator Problem (The Hard Part)

The Core Challenge

The orchestrator needs to make decisions like:

  • "Which agents should I spawn next?"
  • "Is this task already done?"
  • "What's blocking progress?"
  • "Should I change the plan?"

Without conversation history, it needs sufficient context. But context grows unboundedly.

Why "Summary of Summaries" Fails

Summary Level 0: Raw conversation (100k tokens)
Summary Level 1: Summarize to 10k tokens (lose 90% detail)
Summary Level 2: Summarize to 1k tokens (lose 99% detail)
Summary Level 3: Summarize to 100 tokens (useless)

Each level destroys information. After 3 levels, you've lost the ability to answer specific questions. And eventually even Level 1 grows to 1M tokens.

The Solution: Retrieval, Not Summarization

Don't give the orchestrator everything. Give it a way to ASK for what it needs.

2.1 The Orchestrator's Context Budget

The orchestrator gets a fixed context budget (e.g., 50k tokens) composed of:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           ORCHESTRATOR CONTEXT (50k)         │
│                                              │
│  [5k]  Project Goals & Current Plan          │
│  [5k]  Active/Recent Agent Status Board      │
│  [5k]  Recent Timeline (last 30 min)         │
│  [10k] Retrieved Memory (query-relevant)     │
│  [25k] Working space for reasoning           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The key: the "Retrieved Memory" slot is filled by semantic search over the structured memory entries, not by linear summarization.

2.2 Memory Retrieval System

Orchestrator asks: "What do we know about the auth system?"
    │
    v
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│     MEMORY RETRIEVAL AGENT    │
│                               │
│  1. Search timeline for       │
│     "auth" related events     │
│  2. Find relevant agent       │
│     index files               │
│  3. Pull structured entries   │
│  4. Compose a focused brief   │
│     (bounded to 10k tokens)   │
└──────────────────────────────┘
    │
    v
  Orchestrator gets a targeted brief,
  not a full history dump

This is the breakthrough: the orchestrator never needs the full history. It needs answers to specific questions about the history.

2.3 The Three-Layer Memory Architecture

Layer 1: HOT MEMORY (always loaded, <5k tokens)
  - Current project goals
  - Active plan with checkboxes
  - Currently running agents and their tasks
  - Last 5 decisions made
  - Known blockers

Layer 2: WARM MEMORY (indexed, retrieved on demand, ~100k total)
  - All structured memory entries (YAML files)
  - Agent index files
  - Decision log with reasoning
  - Searchable by: time range, topic, file path, agent ID

Layer 3: COLD MEMORY (archived, rarely accessed)
  - Raw conversation logs
  - Full diffs
  - Complete agent outputs
  - Only accessed when Layer 2 retrieval is insufficient

The orchestrator ALWAYS gets Layer 1. It gets Layer 2 via retrieval. It almost never needs Layer 3.

2.4 The Status Board Pattern

Instead of summarizing history, maintain a living document that reflects current state:

# memory/status_board.yaml (HOT MEMORY - always loaded)

project: "Auth System Rewrite"
started: "2026-03-22T10:00:00Z"
overall_progress: "65%"

current_phase: "Implementation"
next_milestone: "All endpoints using new auth by EOD"

active_agents:
  - id: agent-12
    task: "Migrate /api/users endpoint"
    status: running
    started: "2026-03-22T14:40:00Z"
  - id: agent-13
    task: "Migrate /api/teams endpoint"
    status: running
    started: "2026-03-22T14:40:05Z"

completed_today:
  - "Designed new session schema" (agent-03, 10:30)
  - "Built SQLite memory store" (agent-05, 11:15)
  - "Refactored auth middleware" (agent-07, 14:35)
  - "Added migration script" (agent-09, 13:20)

blockers: []

recent_decisions:
  - what: "Use SQLite WAL mode for concurrent access"
    when: "14:30"
  - what: "Skip Redis caching for MVP"
    when: "12:00"

files_most_changed:
  - src/auth/middleware.py (4 agents, 7 edits)
  - src/auth/session.py (2 agents, 3 edits)

This is constantly updated by memory sidecars — not generated from scratch each time. The orchestrator reads this ONE file and knows the project state.

2.5 Handling the 1M Token Ceiling

When warm memory grows past retrieval capacity:

Strategy 1: Temporal Decay

  • Last hour: full detail entries
  • Last day: compressed entries (merge related events)
  • Last week: daily summaries only
  • Older: weekly summaries + key decisions only

Strategy 2: Relevance Pruning

  • Memory entries about completed, non-referenced work get archived
  • If no agent or decision has referenced a memory entry in 24h, compress it
  • Keep decisions and errors forever (they're small and high-value)

Strategy 3: Hierarchical Indexes Instead of one big index, maintain topic-specific indexes:

memory/indexes/
  by-file.yaml        # "Which agents touched which files?"
  by-topic.yaml       # "What decisions were made about auth?"
  by-agent.yaml       # "What did agent-07 do?"
  by-time.yaml        # "What happened between 2-3pm?"

Each index is small. The retrieval agent picks the right index for the query.

Part 3: The Full Framework

3.1 Agent Types

Agent TypeRoleMemory Access
WorkerExecutes a specific task (write code, run tests)Read-only via sidecar
Memory SidecarTracks a worker's actions, writes to timelineWrite to timeline + indexes
Conversation SummarizerEvery 10 prompts, creates structured entryWrite to conversation memory
Memory RetrievalAnswers queries about historyRead all memory layers
OrchestratorPlans, spawns agents, makes decisionsReads hot memory + queries retrieval
Index MergerPeriodically merges timeline shardsRead/write timeline
CompactorApplies temporal decay to old memoriesRead/write all memory

3.2 Spawn Flow

User sends prompt #10
    │
    ├─> Conversation Summarizer activates
    │     └─> Writes structured entry → timeline shard
    │
    ├─> Orchestrator reads status_board.yaml
    │     ├─> Queries Memory Retrieval for relevant context
    │     ├─> Decides to spawn 3 workers
    │     │
    │     ├─> Worker A + Memory Sidecar A
    │     ├─> Worker B + Memory Sidecar B
    │     └─> Worker C + Memory Sidecar C
    │
    └─> Each sidecar writes to its own timeline shard
          └─> Index Merger combines shards periodically

3.3 Concurrency: The Append-Only + Merge Pattern

Multiple agents writing to the same file = corruption. Solution:

  1. Each agent writes to its own shard file (no locks needed)
  2. A merger agent periodically combines shards into merged.jsonl
  3. The status board uses atomic file writes (write to tmp, then rename)
  4. Indexes are rebuilt from merged timeline (idempotent)

This is the same pattern as LSM-trees in databases (LevelDB, RocksDB).

Part 4: Solving "Infinite Context" — The Research Question

This is the genuinely hard/novel part worth a paper:

4.1 The Forgetting Curve Hypothesis

Not all information needs to be remembered equally. Inspired by human memory:

  • Episodic memory (what happened) decays quickly → aggressive compression
  • Semantic memory (what we learned) persists → keep indefinitely
  • Procedural memory (how to do things) is most valuable → keep forever

Applied to agents:

  • "Agent-07 started at 14:35 and took 36 seconds" → decay after 1 hour
  • "SQLite WAL mode works for our concurrency needs" → keep
  • "To migrate an endpoint: copy template from /api/users, swap model" → keep forever

4.2 The Context Distillation Problem

Key insight: The orchestrator doesn't need to remember everything. It needs to be able to RECONSTRUCT any decision it might need to revisit.

Store memories as claims + evidence pointers:

claim: "The auth middleware is fully migrated to SQLite sessions"
confidence: high
evidence:
  - ref: "data/agent-summaries/2026-03-22/task-0007_agent-07_summary.md"
  - ref: "git:abc123f"  # commit hash
  - ref: "tests/test_auth.py:passed_at:2026-03-22T14:40"
last_verified: "2026-03-22T14:40:00Z"

The claim is tiny (fits in hot memory). The evidence is only fetched if the claim is questioned.

4.3 What Happens at True Scale (Weeks/Months of Work)

Even with all the above, a month-long project will generate millions of memory entries. The final safety valve:

Memory Consolidation Runs (like human sleep):

  • Nightly: merge all day's memories into a daily digest
  • Weekly: merge daily digests into weekly themes
  • Monthly: extract only decisions, learnings, and procedural knowledge

The consolidation produces a new "era summary" that becomes the historical record. Raw data is archived to cold storage (disk) and only accessed if a specific question can't be answered from the consolidated record.

4.4 Open Questions for Research

  1. What's the optimal compression ratio at each temporal level? Too aggressive = lost context. Too conservative = blown budget.
  2. Can we learn which memories matter? Track which memories the orchestrator actually retrieves. Memories never retrieved can be compressed more aggressively.
  3. Is semantic search sufficient, or do we need causal chains? "A happened because B happened" is lost in flat search. Do we need a causal graph?
  4. Multi-agent memory conflicts: What if two sidecars report contradictory facts about the same file? Need a conflict resolution strategy.
  5. Memory-aware planning: Can the orchestrator factor in "what I'll forget" when planning? ("Do this task now because the relevant context is still in hot memory")

Next Steps

  1. Prototype the structured memory format — YAML entries, timeline shards
  2. Build the memory sidecar — hook into tool calls to track file operations
  3. Build the status board — living document updated by sidecars
  4. Build the retrieval agent — query memory by topic/time/file
  5. Build the orchestrator — reads status board + queries retrieval
  6. Stress test — spawn 50 agents and see if memory stays coherent
  7. Measure — what's the minimum context the orchestrator needs to make good decisions?
Framework
PFAS Wetlab Agentic Prediction Framework — Brainstorm
A wave-based agent swarm that explores a combinatorial hypothesis space, scoring each branch by expected information gain.
2026-03-22

PFAS Wetlab Agentic Prediction Framework — Brainstorm

Date: 2026-03-22 Context: Princeton internship, PFAS water contamination filtration wet lab Core Goal: Given proprietary wetlab data, maximize the probability of high-value scientific insight per experiment run — using agentic AI to reason through the combinatorial space of conditions, variables, and biological entities.

The Scientific Problem Being Solved

PFAS filtration research involves testing how biological/chemical entities (microbes, plants, reactive agents) interact with contaminants under varying conditions. For any given entity-variable pair, there's a massive hypothesis space:

Example: "pH-raising biological entity needs iron as food source"
  → What form of iron? Fe²⁺ (ferrous) vs Fe³⁺ (ferric)?
  → What phase? Dissolved, particulate, colloidal?
  → What will happen at varying pH? Fe(OH)₃ precipitation at pH > 3?
  → Competing reactions? PFAS chelation vs iron complexation?
  → Temperature sensitivity? Redox potential shifts?
  → Will it oxidize and become unavailable?
  → Interaction with other media components?

A human researcher can intuit maybe 5-10 of these branches. An agent swarm can explore 200+ simultaneously and rank them by scientific plausibility.

The Combinatorial Structure

One Variable, One Entity

Biological Entity: [e.g., iron-reducing bacteria strain X]
Variable: [e.g., iron bioavailability]

Brainstorming Agent generates hypothesis space:
  ├── Condition A: Ferrous iron (Fe²⁺), pH 6.5
  │     ├── Scenario 1: Standard anaerobic
  │     ├── Scenario 2: With PFAS present
  │     ├── Scenario 3: Competing sulfate reducers
  │     ├── Scenario 4: Temperature-stressed (35°C)
  │     └── Scenario 5: Low phosphate starvation
  ├── Condition B: Ferric iron (Fe³⁺), pH 6.5
  │     └── [5 scenarios]
  ├── Condition C: Iron nanoparticles, pH 6.5
  │     └── [5 scenarios]
  ├── Condition D: Ferrous iron, pH 7.5
  │     └── [5 scenarios]
  └── Condition E: Ferric iron, pH 5.0
        └── [5 scenarios]

= 5 conditions × 5 scenarios = 25 agent reasoning tasks

Scaling to N Variables × M Entities

Variables: [iron form, pH, temp, competing ions, PFAS concentration, media composition, ...]
Entities:  [bacteria A, bacteria B, algae C, reactive filter D, biofilm E, ...]

Each (entity, variable) pair → 25-agent team
N variables × M entities = N×M teams × 25 agents each

Example: 10 variables × 8 entities = 80 teams = 2,000 agent reasoning tasks
+ memory sidecars = ~2,200 total agent invocations per full analysis cycle

This is the computational scale we're designing for.

Framework Architecture

Layer 0: Input Processing

RAW WETLAB DATA (proprietary)
  → Data Intake Agent
    - Parses lab measurements, formats, headers
    - Normalizes units (µg/L, mg/kg, mM, etc.)
    - Flags anomalies and outliers
    - Outputs: structured data schema in JSON/CSV
    - Writes: 2026-03-22_HHMM_intake-report-[run-id].yaml

Layer 1: Hypothesis Space Generation

BRAINSTORMING AGENT (1 per entity-variable pair)
  Input: entity description, variable, wetlab data, domain knowledge brief

  Task: Generate a structured hypothesis matrix
    - Enumerate scientifically plausible conditions
    - For each condition, enumerate testable scenarios
    - Assign initial prior probabilities (literature-based or heuristic)
    - Flag known failure modes ("iron precipitates above pH 7, avoid")
    - Flag knowledge gaps ("no data on nanoparticle uptake at this scale")

  Output: hypothesis_matrix.yaml
    conditions: [A, B, C, D, E]
    scenarios_per_condition: [s1, s2, s3, s4, s5]
    prior_probabilities: {A-s1: 0.73, A-s2: 0.41, ...}
    known_constraints: [...]
    knowledge_gaps: [...]

Layer 2: The 25-Agent Reasoning Swarm

Each agent gets ONE (condition, scenario) cell from the hypothesis matrix.

AGENT TASK STRUCTURE:
  Input:
    - Entity profile (what is this biological entity, what do we know)
    - Specific condition (e.g., "Fe²⁺ at pH 6.5")
    - Specific scenario (e.g., "with competing sulfate reducers")
    - Relevant wetlab data slice
    - Literature priors (optional context)
    - Domain constraints from brainstorming agent

  Reasoning tasks:
    1. Mechanistic plausibility — does this chemistry/biology make sense?
    2. Kinetic feasibility — will the reaction proceed fast enough to matter?
    3. Thermodynamic favorability — ΔG sign, equilibrium position
    4. Interference analysis — what other reactions compete or interfere?
    5. Measurability — can this outcome actually be detected in a wetlab?
    6. Risk assessment — what could go wrong, false positives, contamination risks
    7. Expected information gain — if we run this experiment, what will we learn?
    8. Confidence score — 0-1, how sure are we about this analysis?

  Output: structured reasoning report (see schema below)

Agent Output Schema (agent-report.yaml):

run_id: "2026-03-22T16:00:00Z-team03-agent12"
entity: "iron-reducing bacteria strain X"
variable: "iron bioavailability"
condition: "Fe²⁺ at pH 6.5"
scenario: "with competing sulfate reducers"

mechanistic_plausibility:
  score: 0.82
  reasoning: "Fe²⁺ is the preferred electron acceptor for this strain. At pH 6.5, it remains soluble..."
  citations: ["Lovley 1993", "Weber et al 2006"]

kinetic_feasibility:
  score: 0.71
  reasoning: "Reduction rate ~0.5 µmol/hr/g based on literature analogs..."
  bottleneck: "Sulfate reducers may outcompete under sulfate-rich conditions"

thermodynamic_favorability:
  delta_g_estimate: "-24.3 kJ/mol"
  score: 0.88
  note: "Favorable but margin shrinks at pH > 7.5"

interference_analysis:
  competitors: ["sulfate reduction (ΔG = -25.1 kJ/mol, slightly more favorable)"]
  synergists: ["PFAS surfactant may enhance iron solubility at low concentrations"]
  risks: ["Fe(OH)₃ precipitation if pH drifts above 7.2 during experiment"]

measurability:
  score: 0.90
  method: "ICP-MS for Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ ratio, fluorescence for PFAS"
  detection_limit: "0.1 µg/L PFAS, 0.01 mM Fe"

expected_information_gain:
  score: 0.79
  reasoning: "High novelty — sulfate competition under PFAS conditions poorly studied"
  what_we_learn_if_positive: "Sulfate suppression of iron reduction → PFAS accumulation mechanism"
  what_we_learn_if_negative: "Iron reduction is robust to sulfate competition at this pH"

overall_priority_score: 0.81
confidence: 0.74
recommend_run: true
suggested_experiment_protocol: "Batch microcosm, 7-day incubation, 3 replicates..."

Layer 3: Team Synthesis (Per Entity-Variable Pair)

After 25 agents complete, a Synthesis Agent reads all 25 reports and produces:

# 2026-03-22_HHMM_synthesis-entity-X-iron-bioavailability.yaml
entity: "iron-reducing bacteria strain X"
variable: "iron bioavailability"

top_priority_experiments:
  1. condition: "Fe²⁺ pH 6.5" / scenario: "competing sulfate"
     priority_score: 0.81
     rationale: "Highest novelty + measurability + thermodynamic margin"
  2. condition: "Fe³⁺ pH 5.0" / scenario: "PFAS present"
     priority_score: 0.77
     ...

cross_cutting_findings:
  - "Across all iron forms: pH stability window is 5.5-7.2. Outside this, Fe precipitation dominates."
  - "PFAS presence appears to enhance iron solubility in 18/25 scenarios — unexpected finding."
  - "Nanoparticle iron (Condition C) consistently lowest priority — uptake kinetics too slow."

knowledge_gaps_identified:
  - "No literature on this strain + sulfate competition at PFAS > 50 µg/L"
  - "Redox potential data missing for nanoparticle scenarios"

recommended_experiment_sequence: [E1, E3, E7, E2, E12]
estimated_lab_hours: 84

Layer 4: Cross-Team Master Report (Python Merge)

The Python merge step is critical — it combines ALL synthesis reports across all (entity, variable) pairs into a unified master report.

# report_merger.py
# Reads all synthesis YAML files, merges, deduplicates, ranks globally

def merge_reports(synthesis_dir: Path) -> MasterReport:
    all_syntheses = load_all_yamls(synthesis_dir)

    # Global priority ranking across all entity-variable pairs
    all_experiments = flatten([s.top_priority_experiments for s in all_syntheses])
    globally_ranked = rank_by_priority(all_experiments)

    # Cross-entity pattern detection
    cross_entity_patterns = detect_patterns(all_syntheses)
    # e.g., "pH 6.5 Fe²⁺ appears in top-3 for 7/8 entities — may be universal condition"

    # Knowledge gap aggregation
    all_gaps = aggregate_gaps(all_syntheses)
    critical_gaps = [g for g in all_gaps if gap_frequency(g) > threshold]

    # Resource optimization — minimize lab hours while maximizing insight
    optimal_experiment_plan = optimize_experiment_sequence(
        experiments=globally_ranked,
        constraints={"max_lab_hours": 200, "available_equipment": [...]}
    )

    return MasterReport(
        ranked_experiments=globally_ranked,
        cross_entity_patterns=cross_entity_patterns,
        critical_gaps=critical_gaps,
        recommended_plan=optimal_experiment_plan,
        generated_at=datetime.utcnow()
    )

Master Report outputs:

reports/
  2026-03-22_HHMM_master-report-[run-id].md        ← Human-readable for researchers
  2026-03-22_HHMM_master-report-[run-id].json      ← Machine-readable for downstream
  2026-03-22_HHMM_experiment-plan-[run-id].csv     ← Lab scheduling table
  2026-03-22_HHMM_cross-patterns-[run-id].yaml     ← Cross-entity discoveries

Memory System (Scientific Version)

The general memory system from the previous brainstorm applies, but needs scientific-specific layers.

Scientific Hot Memory (always in orchestrator context)

# memory/pfas-status-board.yaml
project: "PFAS Filtration Agentic Analysis"
current_run_id: "run-2026-03-22-001"
phase: "Variable analysis sweep"

entities_analyzed: 3/8
variables_per_entity: 10
agent_teams_complete: 28/80
agent_teams_running: 4
agent_teams_queued: 48

emerging_cross_entity_patterns:
  - "Fe²⁺ at pH 6.5 consistently high priority across 3/3 analyzed entities"
  - "Nanoparticle iron universally deprioritized — update brainstorming priors"

active_knowledge_gaps:
  - "Redox potential data needed for Fe³⁺/PFAS interaction at scale"
  - "Strain-specific sulfate tolerance unknown for entities 4-8"

lab_data_freshness: "2026-03-21 — request updated measurements before entity 5+"

Scientific Warm Memory

Unlike software dev memory (which tracks decisions and file changes), scientific memory tracks:

  • Finding registry: Every novel finding, with confidence score and evidence chain
  • Constraint registry: Physical/chemical constraints that rule out hypotheses ("Fe precipitates > pH 7.2")
  • Literature index: Which papers were cited, how frequently, by which agents
  • Falsified hypotheses: What was explored and ruled out (critical — prevents re-exploring dead ends)
# memory/finding-registry.yaml
findings:
  - id: F001
    claim: "PFAS surfactant enhances iron solubility at low concentrations"
    confidence: 0.71
    observed_in: [team03, team07, team12, team15]
    consistency: "18/25 scenarios across team03"
    evidence_refs: ["data/agent-summaries/2026-03-22/task-0003_fe2-team03-agent07_summary.md"]
    status: "hypothesis — needs wetlab confirmation"

  - id: F002
    claim: "Iron nanoparticle uptake kinetics too slow for batch microcosm timescales"
    confidence: 0.88
    observed_in: [team03, team05, team08]
    status: "high confidence — recommend removing nanoparticle conditions from future runs"

falsified:
  - hypothesis: "Fe³⁺ at pH 5.0 sufficient for aerobic PFAS degradation"
    falsified_by: team04
    reason: "Thermodynamic analysis: ΔG positive under aerobic conditions"
    date: "2026-03-22T14:22:00Z"

The Orchestrator's Decision Problem

What the Orchestrator Needs to Decide

  1. Which (entity, variable) pairs to prioritize next?
  2. Are there cross-entity patterns emerging that should reshape the hypothesis matrix?
  3. Are there data gaps that should trigger a lab data request before continuing?
  4. Should the brainstorming agent's priors be updated based on findings so far?
  5. Is the current experiment plan still optimal, or should it be revised?

How It Gets Context (Without Conversation History)

The orchestrator reads, in order:

  1. memory/pfas-status-board.yaml → current run state, emerging patterns
  2. memory/finding-registry.yaml → what we've discovered and ruled out
  3. Query to Memory Retrieval: "What are the top 3 cross-entity patterns so far?"
  4. Query to Memory Retrieval: "Which variables have the highest variance in priority scores across entities?"

From these 4 inputs (~15k tokens), the orchestrator can make high-quality decisions.

The Priority Scoring Function

The orchestrator's core job is to maximize Expected Scientific Information Gain (ESIG):

ESIG(experiment) =
  P(novel_finding) × information_value(finding)
  + P(confirms_cross_pattern) × pattern_confidence_boost
  + P(falsifies_hypothesis) × hypotheses_eliminated
  - cost(lab_hours, reagents, equipment_time)
  + urgency_weight × (is_blocking_other_experiments)

This isn't just "highest priority score" — it factors in:

  • What other experiments depend on this result
  • Whether the result would update our priors significantly
  • Diminishing returns (if 18/25 scenarios already confirm PFAS iron enhancement, the 19th adds less)

The Exponential Growth Problem

The Math

Entities: M
Variables per entity: V
Conditions per variable: C = 5
Scenarios per condition: S = 5
Agents per team: C × S = 25
Memory sidecars: 1 per agent = 25  # NOTE: simplified model removes sidecars — 1 memory agent per task instead of 25 sidecars
Synthesis agents: 1 per team
Memory mergers: ~1 per 10 teams

Total agents per full run:
  = M × V × (25 workers + 25 sidecars + 1 synthesis)
  = M × V × 51 agents

For M=8 entities, V=10 variables:
  = 8 × 10 × 51 = 4,080 agents per full run

At 100 concurrent agents (tested, confirmed working), a full run takes:

  • 4,080 ÷ 100 = ~41 batches
  • At ~30 seconds per batch = ~20 minutes total wall clock time

Handling the Concurrency

Wave-based execution:

Wave 1: 80 brainstorming agents (1 per entity-variable pair)
         → All run concurrently, output hypothesis matrices
Wave 2: 2,000 reasoning agents (25 per team × 80 teams)
         → Run in batches of 100, ~20 batches
Wave 3: 80 synthesis agents (1 per team)
         → Run concurrently as their team's wave-2 completes
Wave 4: 1 master report merger
         → Runs after all synthesis complete

Memory sidecars run alongside their worker in the same wave.

Preventing Memory Explosion

With 4,000+ agent outputs, memory can't store everything in retrieval range. Apply:

  1. Immediate compression: Each sidecar writes a structured 5-field summary, not the full agent output
  2. Finding deduplication: If 50 agents all find "Fe precipitates > pH 7.2", that's ONE finding entry, not 50
  3. Falsification pruning: Once a hypothesis class is falsified, all related agent outputs are archived to cold storage
  4. Priority cascade: Low-priority findings (score < 0.3) are summarized to one line and archived immediately
  5. Cross-team pattern aggregation: The finding registry stores the pattern, not the individual observations

    raw/                            ← Proprietary wetlab data
    agent-summaries/                ← ALL memory agent summary docs, organized by date
      YYYY-MM-DD/
        task-NNNN_[name]_summary.md
    processed/                      ← Normalized, intake-processed
    schemas/                        ← Data format specs

  runs/

      status.yaml                   ← Live run progress
      log.jsonl                     ← Event timeline

Open Research Questions (Princeton-Level)

  1. Prior Learning: Can the system learn better initial priors from previous runs? After 10 runs, the brainstorming agent should know that "nanoparticle iron" is almost always low priority — and stop allocating 5 agents to it.
  1. Adaptive Hypothesis Pruning: Rather than generating all 25 (condition × scenario) cells upfront, can the first 5 agents inform which of the remaining 20 are worth running? Sequential Bayesian experimental design.
  1. Wetlab Feedback Loop: As real experiments are run, results feed back in to update agent priors. This is the closed loop that transforms this from a prediction system to a learning system.
  1. Cross-Domain Transfer: Knowledge gained from one PFAS compound (e.g., PFOA) — how much transfers to another (e.g., PFOS)? Agent-synthesized transfer learning.
  1. Contradictory Findings: What happens when two agents in the same team reach opposite conclusions? Need a debate/adjudication protocol, not just score averaging.
  1. Experiment Sequencing: The order of wetlab experiments matters (early results inform later ones). This is a bandit problem — optimize the sequence, don't just rank.
  1. Resource-Aware Planning: Given real constraints (2 centrifuges, 1 mass spec, 3 available hours of researcher time), what's the optimal experiment schedule?

Immediate Next Steps

  1. Define the data schema for wetlab inputs — what does the proprietary data look like?
  2. Build the brainstorming agent — scientific hypothesis matrix generator
  3. Build the reasoning agent — single (condition, scenario) analyzer with the 8-field output schema
  4. Build the Python merger — combine synthesis reports into master report
  5. Wire in the memory sidecar — attach to each reasoning agent
  6. Build the orchestrator — reads status board + finding registry + dispatches waves
  7. Test with synthetic data — mock wetlab data, verify agent reasoning quality
  8. Calibrate priority scores — work with wetlab researchers to weight the ESIG components correctly

Deduplication Framework + ESIG Scoring — Brainstorm

Date: 2026-03-22 Context: Sub-component design for the PFAS Wetlab Agentic Framework Depends on: 2026-03-22_1600_pfas-wetlab-agentic-framework-brainstorm.md

Part 1: The Deduplication Problem

Why It's Hard

4,080 agents per run all write findings. Without deduplication:

Agent 07 writes:  "Fe precipitates above pH 7.2"
Agent 11 writes:  "Iron precipitation occurs at pH > 7.2"
Agent 19 writes:  "Fe(OH)₃ forms when pH exceeds 7.2"
Agent 23 writes:  "Iron becomes unavailable above neutral pH (~7.2)"
Agent 31 writes:  "pH 7.2 is the solubility limit for ferric iron"
...
× 50 more agents

These are all the same finding. If stored separately:

  • Memory bloats to millions of entries
  • The orchestrator retrieves 50 near-identical findings and wastes context budget
  • Cross-pattern detection sees 50 "votes" for one thing and 1 vote for something novel — distorts priority scoring
  • The master report becomes unreadable

The challenge is that agents express findings in different words, at different granularities, with different confidence levels. Simple string matching fails. You need semantic deduplication.

The Deduplication Architecture

3 Levels of Deduplication

Level 1: SYNTACTIC  — exact string / hash match (free, instant)
Level 2: SEMANTIC   — embedding similarity (cheap, fast)
Level 3: REASONED   — LLM adjudication for ambiguous cases (expensive, only for conflicts)

Only escalate to the next level if the previous one doesn't resolve.

Level 1: Syntactic Deduplication

Before writing to the finding registry, every finding gets normalized:

def normalize_finding(raw_text: str) -> str:
    text = raw_text.lower().strip()
    text = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text)
    # Normalize chemical notation
    text = text.replace('fe(oh)₃', 'iron hydroxide')
    text = text.replace('fe³⁺', 'ferric iron')
    text = text.replace('fe²⁺', 'ferrous iron')
    text = text.replace('pfas', 'pfas')  # already normalized
    # Normalize numeric ranges
    text = re.sub(r'ph\s*[>≥]\s*7\.2', 'ph_above_7.2', text)
    text = re.sub(r'ph\s*[<≤]\s*7\.2', 'ph_below_7.2', text)
    return text

def syntactic_hash(normalized: str) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(normalized.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]

Hash lookup table (in SQLite, O(1) lookup):

CREATE TABLE finding_hashes (
    hash TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    finding_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    first_seen_at TIMESTAMP,
    observation_count INTEGER DEFAULT 1
);

If hash exists → increment observation_count, skip write. Done. Estimated dedup rate at Level 1: ~15-25% of findings (exact repeats).

Level 2: Semantic Deduplication

For findings that pass Level 1 (unique hash), check semantic similarity against existing findings.

Embedding approach:

  • Each finding is embedded with a lightweight model (e.g., text-embedding-3-small or a local sentence-transformers model)
  • Store embeddings in a vector index (FAISS or SQLite-vec)
  • On new finding: query top-5 nearest neighbors
  • If cosine similarity > threshold → candidate duplicate
SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD = 0.88  # tunable
AMBIGUOUS_BAND = (0.82, 0.88)  # escalate to Level 3

def semantic_dedup(new_finding: Finding, vector_index: VectorIndex) -> DedupResult:
    embedding = embed(new_finding.claim_text)
    neighbors = vector_index.query(embedding, k=5)

    for neighbor in neighbors:
        sim = cosine_similarity(embedding, neighbor.embedding)

        if sim > SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD:
            return DedupResult.DUPLICATE(existing_id=neighbor.finding_id, similarity=sim)

        if sim > AMBIGUOUS_BAND[0]:
            return DedupResult.AMBIGUOUS(candidate_id=neighbor.finding_id, similarity=sim)

    return DedupResult.NOVEL

For DUPLICATES: merge into existing finding

def merge_into_existing(existing: Finding, new: Finding):
    existing.observation_count += 1
    existing.confidence = update_confidence_bayesian(existing.confidence, new.confidence)
    existing.observed_in.append(new.agent_id)
    existing.last_confirmed = new.timestamp
    # If new has higher-quality evidence, upgrade
    if new.evidence_quality > existing.evidence_quality:
        existing.best_evidence_ref = new.evidence_ref
    # Never overwrite, only append

For NOVEL: write new finding entry.

Estimated dedup rate at Level 2: ~55-70% of remaining findings.

Level 3: LLM Adjudication (Ambiguous Cases Only)

When similarity is in the AMBIGUOUS_BAND (0.82-0.88), two findings are probably related but not clearly duplicates. Examples:

Finding A: "Fe²⁺ bioavailability drops sharply above pH 7.2"
Finding B: "Fe³⁺ precipitation begins at pH 7.0-7.5 depending on concentration"

Similarity: 0.84 — related but NOT the same finding.
A is about Fe²⁺ bioavailability; B is about Fe³⁺ precipitation threshold.
Finding A: "PFAS surfactant increases iron solubility at low concentrations"
Finding B: "At PFAS < 10 µg/L, iron solubility is enhanced by surfactant effect"

Similarity: 0.85 — SAME finding, just more specific in B.
Should MERGE (B refines A).

Adjudicator Agent prompt (minimal, fast, cheap — Haiku):

You are a scientific finding deduplicator.

Finding A: {finding_a.claim_text}
Context A: {finding_a.entity}, {finding_a.variable}, {finding_a.condition}
Confidence A: {finding_a.confidence}

Finding B: {finding_b.claim_text}
Context B: {finding_b.entity}, {finding_b.variable}, {finding_b.condition}
Confidence B: {finding_b.confidence}

Options:
1. DUPLICATE — same claim, same scope, merge B into A
2. REFINEMENT — B is a more specific version of A, merge and update A's claim
3. RELATED — same topic but different claims, keep both, link them
4. INDEPENDENT — different claims, no relationship

Reply with ONLY: {option_number} | {one_sentence_reason}

Adjudicator output processing:

DUPLICATE   → merge_into_existing(A, B)
REFINEMENT  → upgrade_claim(A, B.claim_text), merge_into_existing(A, B)
RELATED     → write B as new finding, add link: B.related_to = [A.id]
INDEPENDENT → write B as new finding

Estimated dedup rate at Level 3: resolves ~90% of ambiguous cases correctly. Cost: 1 Haiku call per ambiguous pair, ~100-200 tokens. Negligible.

The Finding Registry Schema (Full)

Deduplication Pipeline Flow

Agent completes reasoning task
    │
    v
Sidecar extracts findings from agent report
(typically 3-8 findings per agent report)
    │
    v
For each finding:
    │
    ├─[1]─> Normalize + hash
    │           │
    │           ├─ Hash EXISTS in DB → increment count, DONE (Level 1 dedup)
    │           │
    │           └─ Hash NEW → continue to Level 2
    │
    ├─[2]─> Embed + vector search (top-5 neighbors)
    │           │
    │           ├─ sim > 0.88 → DUPLICATE → merge, DONE (Level 2 dedup)
    │           ├─ sim 0.82-0.88 → AMBIGUOUS → queue for Level 3
    │           └─ sim < 0.82 → NOVEL → write new finding entry
    │
    └─[3]─> Adjudicator Agent (async, low priority)
                │
                ├─ DUPLICATE or REFINEMENT → merge
                └─ RELATED or INDEPENDENT → write new finding

Async adjudication: Level 3 doesn't block the pipeline. Ambiguous cases are queued and resolved in the background. In the meantime, the ambiguous finding is written with status: "pending_adjudication" and excluded from the orchestrator's active finding set until resolved.

Confidence Update: Bayesian Model

Each new observation of a finding updates its confidence score:

def bayesian_confidence_update(
    prior: float,           # current confidence
    new_confidence: float,  # new agent's confidence for this finding
    agent_quality: float,   # 0-1, how reliable is this agent (model, prompt quality)
    novelty_weight: float   # diminishing returns: 10th observation adds less than 2nd
) -> float:

    # Weight the new observation
    effective_weight = agent_quality * novelty_weight

    # Bayesian update (Beta distribution approximation)
    # prior represents α/(α+β) where α = confirmations, β = doubts
    alpha = prior * 10          # pseudo-count
    beta = (1 - prior) * 10

    if new_confidence > 0.5:    # agent supports the finding
        alpha += effective_weight
    else:                       # agent has doubts
        beta += effective_weight * (1 - new_confidence)

    return alpha / (alpha + beta)


def novelty_weight(observation_count: int) -> float:
    # Log-diminishing returns: 1st obs = 1.0, 10th = 0.5, 100th = 0.25
    return 1.0 / (1 + math.log(observation_count))

This means:

  • A finding seen by 1 agent at confidence 0.7 → stored confidence: 0.7
  • Same finding confirmed by 5 more agents → confidence rises to ~0.85
  • Finding confirmed 50 times → confidence plateaus, additional observations add little
  • ONE strong contradiction → confidence drops significantly (beta increases)

Part 2: ESIG — Expected Scientific Information Gain

Motivation

Naive priority scoring just asks: "how promising does this experiment look?" ESIG asks: "if we run this experiment, how much will we actually learn — relative to what we already know and what else we could run instead?"

This is a decision-theoretic quantity, not a quality score.

The Full ESIG Formula

ESIG(e) = P(novel_finding | e) × V(finding)
         + P(confirms_pattern | e) × ΔConfidence(pattern)
         + P(falsifies_hypothesis | e) × V(falsification)
         + P(enables_downstream | e) × Σ ESIG(blocked_experiments)
         - Cost(e)
         + Urgency(e)
         - Redundancy(e)

Each term explained below.

Term 1: Novel Finding Value

P(novel_finding | e) × V(finding)

P(novel_finding | e): How likely is this experiment to produce a finding NOT already in the finding registry?

def p_novel(experiment: Experiment, finding_registry: FindingRegistry) -> float:
    # Check if experiments in the same (entity, variable, condition) space
    # have already saturated the finding space
    related_findings = finding_registry.query(
        entity=experiment.entity,
        variable=experiment.variable,
        condition=experiment.condition
    )

    if len(related_findings) == 0:
        return 0.85  # high novelty — unexplored space

    # Saturation model: novelty decreases as related findings accumulate
    saturation = 1 - math.exp(-len(related_findings) / SATURATION_CONSTANT)
    novelty_gap = finding_registry.knowledge_gap_score(experiment.scope)

    return (1 - saturation) * 0.85 + novelty_gap * 0.15

V(finding): How valuable is a novel finding in this area?

def finding_value(experiment: Experiment) -> float:
    # Factors:
    # 1. How central is this variable to PFAS filtration mechanism?
    centrality = variable_centrality_scores[experiment.variable]  # researcher-defined priors

    # 2. How much does the community not know this? (literature gap)
    literature_gap = query_literature_gap(experiment.entity, experiment.variable)

    # 3. How actionable is a finding here?
    # (some findings are interesting but don't change what experiments to run)
    actionability = experiment.actionability_score  # from brainstorming agent

    return (centrality * 0.4) + (literature_gap * 0.35) + (actionability * 0.25)

Term 2: Pattern Confirmation Value

P(confirms_pattern | e) × ΔConfidence(pattern)

When a cross-entity pattern is emerging but not yet confirmed, experiments that would confirm it are high value because they boost confidence in a large claim.

def pattern_confirmation_value(experiment: Experiment, findings: FindingRegistry) -> float:
    # Find cross-entity patterns that this experiment could confirm
    relevant_patterns = findings.get_emerging_patterns(
        variable=experiment.variable,
        condition=experiment.condition,
        min_entity_count=2,
        max_confidence=0.80  # not yet confirmed
    )

    total = 0.0
    for pattern in relevant_patterns:
        # How likely is this experiment to observe this pattern?
        p_confirm = estimate_p_confirm(experiment, pattern)

        # How much would confirmation increase confidence?
        # More valuable if pattern is currently 0.60 vs already 0.78
        delta_confidence = expected_confidence_boost(pattern.confidence, p_confirm)

        # How many experiments would this pattern unlock or settle?
        pattern_scope_multiplier = len(pattern.observed_in_entities) / total_entities

        total += p_confirm * delta_confidence * pattern_scope_multiplier

    return total

Why this matters: If 3/8 entities show "PFAS enhances iron solubility", running the 4th entity's experiment is highly valuable — it's approaching the threshold for a universal claim. Running the 8th entity's experiment after 7 already confirmed adds much less.

Term 3: Falsification Value

P(falsifies_hypothesis | e) × V(falsification)

Falsifying a hypothesis is often MORE valuable than confirming one. A falsified hypothesis:

  • Eliminates an entire branch of the hypothesis tree
  • Prevents future agents from spending compute on it
  • Often reveals something unexpected about the mechanism
def falsification_value(experiment: Experiment, hypotheses: HypothesisRegistry) -> float:
    # Find active hypotheses that this experiment could falsify
    falsifiable = hypotheses.get_falsifiable_by(experiment)

    total = 0.0
    for hypothesis in falsifiable:
        p_falsify = estimate_p_falsify(experiment, hypothesis)

        # Value of falsification = number of downstream experiments it eliminates
        # × confidence those experiments would have been run
        downstream_eliminated = count_dependent_experiments(hypothesis)
        compute_saved = downstream_eliminated * AVG_AGENT_COST

        # Also: falsification often reveals the TRUE mechanism
        # Weight this by how "surprising" the falsification would be
        surprise_multiplier = 1 + hypothesis.current_confidence  # high confidence → more valuable to falsify

        total += p_falsify * compute_saved * surprise_multiplier

    return total

Example: If we currently believe "nanoparticle iron works for entity X", but an experiment falsifies it, we eliminate ~25 future agent tasks (5 conditions × 5 scenarios) from the queue. That falsification is worth the compute of 25 agents.

Term 4: Downstream Enablement

P(enables_downstream | e) × Σ ESIG(blocked_experiments)

Some experiments are prerequisites — their results must be known before other experiments can be designed meaningfully.

def downstream_enablement_value(
    experiment: Experiment,
    experiment_dag: ExperimentDAG
) -> float:
    # Get all experiments that are blocked on this one
    blocked = experiment_dag.get_blocked_by(experiment.id)

    if not blocked:
        return 0.0

    # Probability this experiment actually unblocks them
    p_unblocks = estimate_p_success(experiment)

    # Recursive: the value of unblocking = their ESIG
    # But use a discount factor to prevent infinite recursion
    downstream_value = sum(
        esig(blocked_exp, depth=depth+1) * DISCOUNT_FACTOR
        for blocked_exp in blocked
    )

    return p_unblocks * downstream_value

Example: "Determine whether entity X can survive in high-PFAS conditions" is a prerequisite for all 50 experiments involving entity X under PFAS conditions. Its ESIG is enormous because failing to run it means 50 other experiments are poorly designed.

ExperimentDAG is built by the brainstorming agent — it explicitly marks which experiments depend on which. This is a directed acyclic graph of scientific prerequisites.

# experiment_dag.yaml
nodes:
  E001:
    description: "Test entity X survival in PFAS at 10 µg/L"
    blocks: [E002, E003, E004, ..., E050]

  E002:
    description: "Fe²⁺ bioavailability for entity X with PFAS at 10 µg/L"
    requires: [E001]
    blocks: []

Term 5: Cost

- Cost(e)
@dataclass
class ExperimentCost:
    lab_hours: float          # researcher time
    equipment_hours: float    # centrifuge, mass spec, etc.
    reagent_cost_usd: float   # actual dollar cost
    opportunity_cost: float   # equipment unavailable for other experiments

def compute_cost(experiment: Experiment, resources: LabResources) -> float:
    # Normalize everything to a 0-1 scale relative to the most expensive experiment
    raw_cost = (
        experiment.lab_hours / MAX_LAB_HOURS * 0.35 +
        experiment.equipment_hours / MAX_EQUIPMENT_HOURS * 0.30 +
        experiment.reagent_cost_usd / MAX_REAGENT_COST * 0.20 +
        opportunity_cost(experiment, resources) * 0.15
    )
    return raw_cost  # 0-1, higher = more expensive

Cost is subtracted from ESIG. A high-ESIG experiment that takes 40 lab hours might be outranked by a slightly lower-ESIG experiment that takes 2 hours and uses a different instrument.

Term 6: Urgency

+ Urgency(e)

Some experiments have time pressure:

  • Biological entities degrade over time (run these first)
  • Reagent batches expire
  • Seasonal or environmental conditions affect results
  • The lab is sharing equipment on a schedule
def urgency(experiment: Experiment, current_time: datetime) -> float:
    factors = []

    # Biological entity viability window
    if experiment.entity.viability_deadline:
        days_remaining = (experiment.entity.viability_deadline - current_time).days
        if days_remaining < 7:
            factors.append(0.9 - (days_remaining / 7) * 0.5)

    # Reagent expiry
    if experiment.reagent_expiry:
        days_until_expiry = (experiment.reagent_expiry - current_time).days
        if days_until_expiry < 14:
            factors.append(0.7 - (days_until_expiry / 14) * 0.4)

    # Equipment window (shared booking)
    if experiment.requires_equipment:
        next_available = lab_schedule.next_window(experiment.required_equipment)
        if next_available == current_time:  # available NOW
            factors.append(0.3)

    return max(factors, default=0.0)

Term 7: Redundancy Penalty

- Redundancy(e)

If 5 similar experiments are already queued or running, running a 6th provides diminishing marginal value.

def redundancy_penalty(experiment: Experiment, queue: ExperimentQueue) -> float:
    # How many experiments in the queue are highly similar?
    similar_in_queue = queue.count_similar(
        entity=experiment.entity,
        variable=experiment.variable,
        similarity_threshold=0.85
    )

    # Diminishing returns penalty
    # 0 similar → 0 penalty
    # 1 similar → small penalty (maybe intentional replication)
    # 5+ similar → large penalty
    penalty = 1 - math.exp(-similar_in_queue / 2)
    return penalty * 0.3  # max 0.3 penalty

Full ESIG Computation

def esig(
    experiment: Experiment,
    finding_registry: FindingRegistry,
    hypothesis_registry: HypothesisRegistry,
    experiment_dag: ExperimentDAG,
    lab_resources: LabResources,
    queue: ExperimentQueue,
    current_time: datetime,
    depth: int = 0
) -> float:

    if depth > 2:  # prevent deep recursion
        return 0.0

    # Term 1: Novel finding
    t1 = p_novel(experiment, finding_registry) * finding_value(experiment)

    # Term 2: Pattern confirmation
    t2 = pattern_confirmation_value(experiment, finding_registry)

    # Term 3: Falsification
    t3 = falsification_value(experiment, hypothesis_registry)

    # Term 4: Downstream enablement
    t4 = downstream_enablement_value(experiment, experiment_dag)

    # Terms 5-7: Adjustments
    cost    = compute_cost(experiment, lab_resources)
    urgency = urgency(experiment, current_time)
    redund  = redundancy_penalty(experiment, queue)

    raw_esig = t1 + t2 + t3 + t4 - cost + urgency - redund

    # Normalize to 0-1
    return sigmoid(raw_esig)

ESIG in the Master Report

The master report ranks experiments by ESIG score and explains the breakdown:

Rank  Experiment                              ESIG   Novel  Pattern  Falsify  Unlock  Cost
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1   Entity-X, Fe²⁺ pH6.5, PFAS present     0.91   0.72    0.61     0.12    0.89   0.18
  2   Entity-Y, Fe³⁺ pH5.0, sulfate comp.     0.84   0.58    0.45     0.71    0.12   0.22
  3   Entity-X, survival in PFAS 10µg/L       0.83   0.31    0.10     0.05    0.95   0.08
  4   Entity-Z, Fe²⁺ pH6.5, standard          0.78   0.45    0.81     0.08    0.14   0.30
  ...

Experiment #3 has low novelty/pattern/falsify scores but ranks high because it UNLOCKS 50 downstream experiments (t4 = 0.95). The system correctly identifies prerequisite experiments.

Experiment #2 ranks high because it has a high falsification score (0.71) — falsifying "Fe³⁺ + sulfate competition is viable" eliminates a large branch of future work.

Calibration Strategy

ESIG is only as good as its weights. How to calibrate:

Phase 1 — Prior calibration (before first run):

  • Wetlab researchers assign centrality scores to each variable
  • Researchers mark prerequisite relationships in the experiment DAG
  • Cost estimates from historical lab records

Phase 2 — Posterior calibration (after first 20 real experiments):

  • Compare predicted ESIG to actual information gained
  • Track: did high-ESIG experiments actually yield novel findings?
  • Did low-ESIG experiments produce anything surprising?
  • Use regression to adjust term weights

Phase 3 — Online learning (production):

  • Each completed experiment updates the model
  • The system gets smarter every run
  • Track calibration error over time: good calibration = high-ESIG experiments consistently outperform low-ESIG ones
class ESIGCalibrator:
    def update(self, experiment: Experiment, actual_outcome: ExperimentOutcome):
        predicted = self.esig_at_time_of_prediction[experiment.id]
        actual_gain = self.compute_actual_information_gain(actual_outcome)

        error = predicted - actual_gain
        self.error_history.append(error)

        # Which terms were most wrong?
        term_errors = self.decompose_error(predicted, actual_gain, experiment)
        self.term_calibration.update(term_errors)

        # Adjust weights via gradient descent
        self.weights = self.weights - LEARNING_RATE * self.term_calibration.gradient()

How Deduplication and ESIG Interact

These two systems are deeply coupled:

  1. Deduplication feeds ESIG novelty scoring: p_novel() queries the finding registry, which deduplication maintains. Accurate dedup → accurate novelty estimates.
  1. ESIG drives deduplication priority: High-ESIG experiments get their findings adjudicated first (Level 3 queue is prioritized by experiment ESIG). Low-ESIG experiment findings can wait.
  1. Confidence updates from dedup change ESIG pattern terms: When dedup merges a new observation into finding F001 and its confidence rises from 0.70 to 0.79, the pattern_confirmation_value() of related experiments drops (less marginal gain from further confirmation).
  1. Falsification interacts with dedup constraint registry: When a hypothesis is falsified, the constraint registry is updated, which affects p_novel() for related experiments (they're now exploring a known-invalid space → lower novelty).
Finding Registry ←──── Deduplication Pipeline
       │
       ▼
ESIG Scorer
  ├── p_novel()         reads finding registry
  ├── pattern_value()   reads finding registry confidence
  ├── falsify_value()   reads hypothesis registry
  └── redundancy()      reads experiment queue + finding registry
       │
       ▼
Master Report → Ranked Experiment Plan → Orchestrator Dispatches Next Wave

Summary: What This Buys You

Without Dedup + ESIGWith Dedup + ESIG
4,080 agent outputs, mostly duplicate findings~400-800 unique, high-confidence findings
Orchestrator overwhelmed by finding volumeOrchestrator reads a compact finding registry
Experiments ranked by naive "looks promising" scoreExperiments ranked by actual expected learning value
Prerequisite experiments missedPrerequisite chain explicitly modeled in DAG
System gets dumber over time (more noise)System gets smarter over time (calibrated weights)
1M token memory explosionMemory plateaus as dedup absorbs repeats

The combination of semantic deduplication + ESIG transforms a brute-force agent swarm into a system that actually reasons about what to do next — not just what looks good in isolation.

Data pipeline
Deep Folder & Index Data Organization System — Brainstorm
The filesystem layout itself becomes the concurrency control: every folder a unit of work, every index a contract, no shared write targets.
2026-03-22

Deep Folder & Index Data Organization System — Brainstorm

Date: 2026-03-22 Context: How do we organize the outputs of 25-agent swarm sessions so nothing is lost, everything is findable, and memory agents can summarize without blowing their context windows?

Core Philosophy

Every folder is a unit of work. Every index is a contract.

  • Folders are named by timestamp → sessions are self-ordering chronologically
  • Every folder has exactly one INDEX.md → you never have to open a file to know what's inside
  • Agent outputs are raw and never modified → memory agents summarize but originals persist
  • Summaries live ABOVE their sources → you read up, not down, to get the picture (in the simplified model, summaries live in data/agent-summaries/ — a dedicated data folder separate from the session hierarchy, not nested above the task folder)

The Folder Hierarchy

Level 0 — Project Root

princeton-intern-ai-project/
  INDEX.md                ← what this project is, links to all sessions
  README.md               ← human-readable intro
  brainstorm/             ← design docs (not session data)
  data/                   ← wetlab inputs
  sessions/               ← ALL session work lives here
  memory/                 ← cross-session memory: findings, patterns, status board
  reports/                ← final merged reports per run
  src/                    ← code

Level 1 — Session Folder

sessions/
  2026-03-22_1400_iron-bioavailability-sweep/
  2026-03-22_1600_pfas-concentration-series/
  2026-03-23_0900_ph-sensitivity-analysis/
  ...

Naming: YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM_short-descriptor/

Each session = one targeted analysis run. Could be:

  • A full 25-agent sweep of one (entity, variable) pair
  • A follow-up session drilling into one condition
  • A cross-entity pattern validation run
  • A literature gap analysis
