# Agent-03 Reasoning Report
**Run ID**: run-2026-03-22-001
**Team**: team-01_fe2-standard
**Scenario**: Competing sulfate reducers
**Model**: claude-haiku-4-5
**Tokens**: in=3,240 out=1,180
**Duration**: 34s

## Mechanistic Plausibility (0.82)
Fe²⁺ is the preferred electron acceptor for this strain.
At pH 6.5, ferrous iron remains soluble (below Fe(OH)₂ precipitation threshold ~pH 8.5).
Sulfate reducers compete for electron donors (H₂, acetate) but not directly for Fe²⁺...

## Kinetic Feasibility (0.71)
Fe reduction rate estimated at ~0.5 µmol/hr/g biomass from literature analogs.
Sulfate reduction rate typically 0.3-0.8 µmol/hr/g — similar range.
Competition is real but not decisive at pH 6.5...

## Thermodynamic Favorability
ΔG Fe reduction: -24.3 kJ/mol
ΔG sulfate reduction: -25.1 kJ/mol
Sulfate slightly more favorable but margin is small...

## Interference Analysis
- Sulfate reducers produce H₂S — may complex with Fe²⁺ to form FeS
- FeS precipitation could sequester iron — WATCH THIS
- PFAS surfactants may partially inhibit sulfate reducers (literature: Xiao et al 2020)

## Expected Information Gain (0.79)
Novel angle: sulfate competition under PFAS conditions is poorly studied.
If positive: reveals sulfate suppression of iron reduction → PFAS accumulation mechanism
If negative: confirms robustness of iron reduction under mixed conditions

## Overall ESIG: 0.91
## Recommend Run: YES
## Suggested Protocol
Batch microcosm, 7-day incubation, 3 replicates.
Controls: no sulfate, no PFAS, both, neither.
Measure: Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ ratio (ICP-MS), sulfate (IC), PFAS (LC-MS/MS)...

Level 3 — Memory Agents

Each team has a dedicated memory agent that runs AFTER the 5 worker agents complete.

What the team memory agent does:

  1. Reads all 5 agent markdown files (fits in one context window — ~5 × 2k = 10k tokens)
  2. Extracts structured findings with deduplication
  3. Writes a compact team summary YAML
  4. Updates the finding registry
  5. Writes sidecar files for each agent

Level 2 — Session Synthesis

After all 5 teams complete, a synthesis agent reads the 5 team memory summaries (not the raw agent files) and produces the session-level synthesis.

Context budget: 5 team summaries × ~3k tokens each = ~15k tokens. Fits comfortably.

sessions/2026-03-22_1400_iron-bioavailability-sweep/

    2026-03-22_1445_follow-up-sessions.yaml   ← what to run next

Memory Reading Strategy — Context Window Management

This is the key design decision. Memory agents NEVER read raw agent files if a summary exists.

Level 4 agent files:     ~2k tokens each × 5 = 10k   → team memory agent reads these
Level 3 team summaries:  ~3k tokens each × 5 = 15k   → session synthesis agent reads these
Level 2 session summary: ~5k tokens each × N = Nk    → cross-session orchestrator reads these
Level 1 master status:   ~5k tokens always loaded     → orchestrator always has this

At each level, the memory agent COMPRESSES the level below. The output is always smaller than the input. This is the pyramid:

                    ┌─────────────────────┐
Level 0             │   Master Status     │  5k tokens (always loaded)
                    │   Finding Registry  │
                    └──────────┬──────────┘
                               │ reads
                    ┌──────────▼──────────┐
Level 1             │  Session Summaries  │  ~5k each, N sessions
                    └──────────┬──────────┘
                               │ reads
                    ┌──────────▼──────────┐
Level 2             │   Team Summaries    │  ~3k each, 5 per session
                    └──────────┬──────────┘
                               │ reads
                    ┌──────────▼──────────┐
Level 3             │  Agent Raw Output   │  ~2k each, 25 per session
                    └─────────────────────┘

Each level is 3-5× smaller than the level below. A session with 25 agents produces ~50k tokens of raw output that compresses to a ~5k session summary. The orchestrator only ever reads session summaries.

Deep Nesting — Recursive Sessions

Sessions can spawn sub-sessions. Example:

sessions/
  2026-03-22_1400_iron-bioavailability-sweep/
    synthesis/
      2026-03-22_1445_follow-up-sessions.yaml
        → "Fe²⁺ + PFAS interaction needs deeper drill-down"
        → spawns: sessions/2026-03-22_1500_fe2-pfas-interaction-drill/

  2026-03-22_1500_fe2-pfas-interaction-drill/
    INDEX.md
      parent_session: 2026-03-22_1400_iron-bioavailability-sweep
      reason_spawned: "Investigate PFAS surfactant effect on Fe²⁺ solubility"

The INDEX.md always tracks parent_session and child_sessions. This creates a navigable session tree.

Session tree structure (stored in master INDEX):

Rules for Agents Writing to This Structure

The 4 Laws

  1. Never modify raw agent output — agents/ is append-only. Memory agents read but never write there.
  2. Always write an INDEX.md when creating a folder — no folder exists without a contract.
  3. Summaries live above their sources — team memory summary lives in team-XX/memory/, not inside agents/. Session synthesis lives in synthesis/, not in teams/. In the simplified model, task summaries live in data/agent-summaries/YYYY-MM-DD/ — a dedicated data folder separate from the session hierarchy entirely.
  4. Date-time every file — YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM_descriptor.ext. No exceptions.

Agent Write Targets

Agent TypeWrites To
Brainstorming agentsession/brainstorm-agent/
Reasoning agentsession/teams/team-XX/agents/
Memory sidecarsession/teams/team-XX/sidecars/
Team memory agentdata/agent-summaries/YYYY-MM-DD/ + memory/finding-registry/
Session synthesis agentsession/synthesis/ + updates session/INDEX.md
Cross-session orchestratormemory/status-board.yaml + memory/session-tree.yaml
Report mergerreports/[run-id]/

INDEX.md Update Protocol

When any agent writes a new file to a folder, it ALSO updates that folder's INDEX.md:

  1. Add a row to the file table with: filename, date, one-line description
  2. Update the folder status field if applicable
  3. Never rewrite the whole INDEX — append to the table

Why This Works at Scale

ProblemSolution
4,000 agent outputs unnavigableHierarchy: always read summaries, never raw files
Memory agents blow context windowEach level summarizes only ONE level below (~10-15k tokens max input)
Concurrent agents clobber same fileEach agent has its own folder + own file. No shared write targets.
Hard to find what session produced finding XFinding registry entry has agent_source, team, session — navigate up the tree
Cross-session patterns invisiblememory/finding-registry/ aggregates across sessions. Orchestrator reads this, not individual sessions.
Folder gets stale/confusingINDEX.md is the contract — you know what's there without opening anything
Infinite recursion of sub-sessionssession-tree.yaml tracks parent/child relationships. Depth limit enforced by orchestrator (e.g., max depth 3).

2026-03-22

Agent Bootstrap & Context Design — Brainstorm

Date: 2026-03-22 Question: How do we make subagents file-aware and framework-aware without complex infrastructure? Core Idea Being Evaluated: Bootstrap brainstorm docs directly into agent context → agent does work → context abandoned.

What's Right About This Approach

1. Context Abandonment Is Correct

Subagent context is ephemeral. The ONLY thing that persists is what gets written to disk. This is a feature, not a bug — it forces a discipline:

"If it's not written, it doesn't exist."

Every piece of reasoning an agent does must be externalized. This gives you:

  • Full audit trail of how conclusions were reached
  • Re-runnable analysis (same inputs → reproduce outputs)
  • Memory agents can actually summarize because everything is explicit

Agents must be explicitly told this in their prompt: "Your context will be destroyed when you finish. Write everything that matters."

2. ESIG Score as Semantic Frame

Giving each agent its ESIG breakdown isn't just metadata — it's a reasoning directive.

Instead of: "Analyze Fe²⁺ at pH 6.5 with competing sulfate"

Do: "Analyze Fe²⁺ at pH 6.5 with competing sulfate. Your novelty score is 0.85 because this scenario is understudied. Your pattern confirmation score is 0.61 because 2 other entities show PFAS-iron interaction. Lean into the novelty angle — the community doesn't know this."

The ESIG breakdown tells the agent WHERE to spend its reasoning budget.

3. Direct File Bootstrap Works — For Now

The current brainstorm docs are ~100k tokens combined. A 200k context window can hold them. Simple, zero infrastructure, agents know exactly where to write and how to format.

What's Wrong / Needs Fixing

Problem 1: Bootstrap Files Will Grow

Right now: ~100k tokens across 4 brainstorm docs. Manageable. In 3 months: 40 brainstorm docs, spec files, updated schemas, lessons learned. Easily 500k+ tokens.

If you inject everything into every agent:

  • Expensive (input tokens × 4,000 agents per run = massive cost)
  • Agents get confused by irrelevant content
  • You hit the same context explosion problem you were designing against

Fix: The Agent Operating Manual

Don't inject brainstorm docs. Distill them into a single, dense, role-specific bootstrap file:

agent-prompts/
  base-operating-manual.md        ← 3k tokens: file naming, folder structure, INDEX rules
  reasoning-agent-manual.md       ← 2k tokens: output schema, what fields to fill, where to write
  memory-agent-manual.md          ← 2k tokens: dedup rules, finding registry format, write targets
  synthesis-agent-manual.md       ← 2k tokens: how to read team summaries, session synthesis format
  brainstorm-agent-manual.md      ← 2k tokens: hypothesis matrix format, prior probability rules

Total per agent: base (3k) + role-specific (2k) = 5k tokens — not 100k.

The brainstorm docs stay as the human/orchestrator source of truth. The manuals are the distilled agent-facing contracts. When brainstorm docs change, you update the manual — one place.

Problem 2: Different Agents Need Different Context

A reasoning agent analyzing Fe²⁺ + sulfate doesn't need to know:

  • How the report merger works in Python
  • The full deduplication algorithm
  • Other teams' results (until synthesis)

Injecting everything wastes context budget and creates noise. Agents perform better with focused context.

Fix: Role-Specific Bootstrap Packages

The orchestrator assembles a custom context package for each agent spawn:

def build_agent_context(agent_type, task, session_context):

    if agent_type == "reasoning":
        return [
            load("agent-prompts/base-operating-manual.md"),         # 3k
            load("agent-prompts/reasoning-agent-manual.md"),        # 2k
            task.esig_breakdown,                                     # 1k
            task.relevant_findings_snippet,  # from finding registry # 2k
            task.constraints_snippet,        # relevant constraints  # 1k
            task.wetlab_data_slice,          # only their entity     # varies
        ]
        # Total: ~10-15k tokens overhead. Rest of context = actual reasoning.

    if agent_type == "memory":
        return [
            load("agent-prompts/base-operating-manual.md"),
            load("agent-prompts/memory-agent-manual.md"),
            task.agent_file_to_summarize,  # the single raw analysis file for this task
        ]

    if agent_type == "synthesis":
        return [
            load("agent-prompts/base-operating-manual.md"),
            load("agent-prompts/synthesis-agent-manual.md"),
            task.relevant_task_summaries,          # summaries from data/agent-summaries/ relevant to this synthesis
            load("memory/finding-registry-snapshot.yaml"),  # current findings
        ]

Problem 3: Finding Registry Injection

You can't inject the whole finding registry — it grows unboundedly. But agents need to know what's already known to avoid re-discovering and wasting ESIG on low-novelty work.

Fix: Pre-Query the Registry Before Spawning

Before spawning a reasoning agent, the orchestrator queries the finding registry:

# Orchestrator pre-spawn step
relevant_findings = finding_registry.query(
    entity=task.entity,
    variable=task.variable,
    condition=task.condition,
    max_results=10
)

# Inject the snippet, not the full registry
task.relevant_findings_snippet = format_findings_for_agent(relevant_findings)

The agent gets: "Here's what we already know about Fe²⁺ + sulfate. Don't re-derive these. Look for what's NOT here."

This keeps injection bounded regardless of registry size.

Problem 4: Agents Writing INDEX.md Updates

If 25 agents all try to update the same teams/INDEX.md simultaneously — race condition, corruption.

Fix: INDEX updates are the memory sidecar's job, not the worker's

Workers write ONLY to their own files:

agent-03 writes: teams/team-01/agents/2026-03-22_1411_agent-03_....md
                 (that's it. nothing else.)

The memory sidecar, running AFTER all workers complete, writes:

sidecar writes:  teams/team-01/sidecars/2026-03-22_1415_sidecar-03.yaml
                 teams/team-01/INDEX.md  (appends agent-03's row)
                 teams/team-01/memory/2026-03-22_1415_team-summary.yaml

No worker ever touches an INDEX. Only memory/synthesis agents do. No race conditions.

The Full Bootstrap Package Design

What Goes In Each Agent's Context

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    REASONING AGENT CONTEXT                       │
│                                                                  │
│  [3k]  Base Operating Manual                                     │
│         - folder structure, naming conventions                   │
│         - INDEX.md format                                        │
│         - "your context is abandoned — write everything"         │
│                                                                  │
│  [2k]  Reasoning Agent Manual                                    │
│         - output schema (8 fields)                               │
│         - where to write your output file                        │
│         - what makes a good confidence score                     │
│                                                                  │
│  [1k]  Your Task Assignment                                      │
│         - entity, variable, condition, scenario                  │
│         - output file path (pre-assigned, no decisions needed)   │
│         - session folder path                                     │
│                                                                  │
│  [1k]  Your ESIG Breakdown                                       │
│         - overall: 0.91                                          │
│         - novelty: 0.85 (why), pattern: 0.61 (why), ...         │
│         - "focus your reasoning on the novelty angle"            │
│                                                                  │
│  [2k]  Relevant Prior Findings (pre-queried)                     │
│         - top 10 findings relevant to your (entity, variable)    │
│         - constraints registry snippet                           │
│         - "don't re-derive these — look for what's missing"      │
│                                                                  │
│  [Xk]  Wetlab Data Slice                                         │
│         - only measurements relevant to this entity              │
│                                                                  │
│  [remaining]  Your actual reasoning work                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Total overhead: ~10-15k tokens

Base Operating Manual (the only thing every agent shares)

This is the most important file. Keep it TIGHT. ~3k tokens.

# Agent Operating Manual

## Your Context Will Be Destroyed
When you finish, your context is gone. Everything you think must be written to disk.
If it's not in your output file, it doesn't exist.

## File Naming
ALL files you create: YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM_descriptor.ext
Use current UTC time. No exceptions.

## Your Output Location
You will be given an exact output path. Write there. Do not create other files unless
your role-specific manual says to.

## Folder Rules
- Never modify files in agents/ folders — those are raw outputs, read-only
- Never write to another agent's assigned path
- If you create a subfolder, create INDEX.md in it immediately

## INDEX.md Updates
YOU do not update INDEX.md files. The memory agent does that after you complete.
Your only job is to write your output file cleanly.

## Format Discipline
- Use the schema in your role-specific manual exactly
- Do not omit fields — write "N/A" or "unknown" if you don't have data
- Confidence scores: 0.0-1.0, be honest, explain your reasoning
- Citations: always include when available, even if uncertain

## Prior Findings
You will receive relevant prior findings. Do not re-derive them.
Your job is to find what's NOT in that list — novel angles, gaps, contradictions.

The Orchestrator's Assembly Line

The orchestrator's job before spawning any agent is to build their context package. This is the critical path.

class AgentContextBuilder:

    def build_reasoning_agent(self, task: ReasoningTask) -> AgentContext:
        # Step 1: Load static manuals (cached, not re-read each time)
        base = self.cache.get("base-operating-manual")
        role = self.cache.get("reasoning-agent-manual")

        # Step 2: Build ESIG breakdown narrative
        esig_narrative = self.esig_scorer.build_narrative(task)
        # "Your novelty score is 0.85. This is high because no published
        #  work covers Fe²⁺ + sulfate competition under PFAS conditions
        #  at this pH. Lean into this angle."

        # Step 3: Pre-query finding registry
        prior_findings = self.finding_registry.query_relevant(
            entity=task.entity,
            variable=task.variable,
            condition=task.condition,
            max_tokens=2000
        )

        # Step 4: Slice wetlab data
        data_slice = self.data_store.slice(
            entity=task.entity,
            variable=task.variable
        )

        # Step 5: Pre-assign output path (agent doesn't decide this)
        output_path = self.path_allocator.assign(task)
        # e.g., sessions/2026-03-22_1400_.../teams/team-01/agents/
        #         2026-03-22_1410_agent-03_scenario-competing-sulfate.md

        return AgentContext(
            system_prompt=base + role,
            task_block=format_task(task, output_path),
            esig_block=esig_narrative,
            findings_block=prior_findings,
            data_block=data_slice
        )

Key point: the agent is told its output path upfront. It doesn't decide where to write. The orchestrator pre-assigns paths for all 25 agents before spawning any of them. No coordination needed between agents.

Path Pre-Assignment Pattern

Before spawning a session's 25 agents, the orchestrator generates ALL paths:

def pre_assign_paths(session: Session) -> Dict[AgentID, Path]:
    paths = {}
    ts = session.start_time  # 2026-03-22T14:10:00Z

    for team_idx, condition in enumerate(session.conditions):
        for agent_idx, scenario in enumerate(condition.scenarios):
            agent_id = f"agent-{team_idx*5 + agent_idx + 1:02d}"
            team_folder = f"team-{team_idx+1:02d}_{condition.slug}"
            scenario_slug = scenario.name.lower().replace(' ', '-')
            filename = f"{fmt_ts(ts)}_{agent_id}_{scenario_slug}.md"

            paths[agent_id] = (
                session.path / "teams" / team_folder / "agents" / filename
            )
            ts += timedelta(seconds=1)  # stagger timestamps

    return paths

Now all 25 agents can run fully concurrently — no path collisions, no coordination, no locks.

Summary: The Clean Model

Orchestrator
  │
  ├─ Pre-queries finding registry for each task
  ├─ Builds ESIG narratives
  ├─ Pre-assigns all output paths
  ├─ Assembles role-specific context packages (~10-15k tokens each)
  │
  └─ Spawns 25 agents concurrently
       │
       Each agent receives:
         base manual (3k) + role manual (2k) + task (1k) +
         esig breakdown (1k) + prior findings (2k) + data slice (Xk)
       │
       Each agent writes ONE file to its pre-assigned path
       Context abandoned on completion
       │
  Memory agent runs after each task's scientist completes
  Reads task analysis file → dedup → update finding registry → writes ONE summary to data/agent-summaries/YYYY-MM-DD/task-NNNN_[name]_summary.md
  (no team summaries step — simplified model: 1 memory agent per task, writes directly to data/agent-summaries/)
  │
  Orchestrator reads daily INDEX + status board → plans next task
  │
  Orchestrator reads session summary → updates status board → plans next session

Total context overhead per agent: ~10-15k tokens (framework awareness) Remaining context per agent: ~185k tokens (actual scientific reasoning) What persists: only what's written to disk What's ephemeral: everything else

This is the right model. Cheap, parallel, file-safe, and scales to 4,000 agents per run without any coordination infrastructure.

The Summary Doc — Full Schema

The summary doc is the memory agent's only output. It must be self-contained and redundant enough that the full task can be understood, located, and reconstructed from this file alone — even if everything else is lost.

Why This Many Redundancy Fields

The Problem Being Prevented

Without redundancy, a summary doc is only as good as its context. If:

  • The daily INDEX is deleted → you can't find the task
  • The task folder name is wrong → you can't match it to the summary
  • The raw analysis is corrupted → you lose the source
  • The finding registry entry is missing → you lose the cross-session link

Each redundancy field is a recovery path:

FieldWhat it recovers
full_path in the bodyRelocate the file if moved or mis-indexed
task_id repeated in header + bodyMatch to daily INDEX even if folder renamed
raw_analysis_pathJump directly to source without navigating folders
analysis_sha256_prefixDetect if raw analysis was corrupted or swapped
unblocks_tasksDownstream tasks can find this summary by searching for their own ID
finding_registry_updateRe-link to cross-session memory if registry entry goes missing
reconstruction_inputs_neededRe-run the task from scratch if needed
enough_to_rerun: true/falseOrchestrator knows whether to trust this summary or re-run

Redundancy Is Cheap

A summary doc is ~500-800 tokens. Redundancy adds ~100 tokens. Compared to the cost of a lost finding or an un-runnable task, this is free insurance.

Calibration & bench
The Calibration Loop — Brainstorm
An agent's raw confidence is meaningless until measured against its hit rate — lock predictions at spawn and calibrate against outcomes.
2026-03-22

The Calibration Loop — Brainstorm

Date: 2026-03-22 Core idea: The system makes predictions. The lab runs experiments. Results come back. The system compares what it predicted to what actually happened. It updates its weights. It gets smarter. Repeat forever.

This is what separates a prediction system from a learning system.

The Problem Without Calibration

Right now the scientist agent reasons from:

  1. General chemistry/biology training (generic)
  2. Published literature (may not apply to this lab)
  3. The wetlab data slice (most valuable but limited)

It produces a confidence score of 0.78 and says "recommend run: yes."

But 0.78 means nothing unless we know: when this agent says 0.78, how often is it actually right?

If 0.78 predictions are right 40% of the time, the system is overconfident and wasting lab hours. If 0.78 predictions are right 95% of the time, the system is underconfident and underselling its own recommendations.

Without measuring this, you're flying blind. With it, every experiment the lab runs makes the system more accurate for the next one.

What a Calibration Event Is

A calibration event is a structured record created when a real lab result comes back for an experiment the system recommended.

# memory/calibration/2026-04-15_calibration-event-0047.yaml

event_id: cal-0047
created_at: 2026-04-15T10:30:00Z
experiment_run_date: 2026-04-14

## The Prediction (written at task spawn time, locked — never modified)
task_ref: data/agent-summaries/2026-03-22/task-0001_fe2-sulfate-competition_summary.md
predicted_esig: 0.91
predicted_recommend: yes
predicted_finding_type: novel
predicted_confidence: 0.78
predicted_measurement:
  metric: Fe²⁺ concentration
  expected_range: [0.3, 0.8]  # mM at day 5
  units: mM
  timepoint: day_5
predicted_failure_modes:
  - "FeS precipitation if H₂S builds up"
  - "Fe oxidation if headspace not controlled"

## The Reality (filled in when lab result arrives)
actual_outcome: success       # success | partial | failure | inconclusive
actual_measurement:
  metric: Fe²⁺ concentration
  value: 0.52
  units: mM
  timepoint: day_5
actual_finding_type: novel    # matches prediction → good calibration
lab_notes: "Clean reduction curve, no visible precipitation. Sulfate did not interfere."
protocol_modifications_needed: none   # did our suggested protocol work?
researcher_rating: high       # researcher's subjective assessment: low | medium | high | breakthrough

## The Delta (computed by calibration agent)
esig_accuracy: hit            # hit | miss | partial (did high ESIG → high value?)
measurement_accuracy: within_range   # within_range | close | off | completely_wrong
confidence_accuracy: well_calibrated # well_calibrated | overconfident | underconfident
protocol_validity: valid      # valid | needed_minor_mod | needed_major_mod | failed

## Error Analysis
prediction_error_type: none   # none | systematic | random | domain_specific | data_gap
error_explanation: >
  Prediction was accurate. Fe²⁺ reduction proceeded as expected.
  Sulfate competition hypothesis (from prior literature) did not materialize
  at this pH — which itself is a novel finding worth noting.

## What This Updates
updates_finding: F003         # finding confidence goes up
updates_esig_component: novelty   # novelty scoring was accurate here
updates_constraint: none
calibration_weight: 1.0       # how much to weight this event (0-1, lower if noisy experiment)

The Two Types of Predictions Being Calibrated

Type 1 — ESIG Calibration

Did high-ESIG experiments actually produce high scientific value?

Prediction: ESIG 0.91 → this experiment will produce novel, high-value finding
Reality:    researcher rated it "high" → ESIG was well-calibrated

Prediction: ESIG 0.82 → high value
Reality:    researcher rated it "low," result was already known → ESIG overconfident

Over 50 calibration events you can plot the ESIG calibration curve:

  • X axis: predicted ESIG bucket (0.0–0.2, 0.2–0.4, ... 0.8–1.0)
  • Y axis: actual researcher rating (converted to 0–1)
  • Perfect calibration = straight diagonal line
  • Overconfident system = curve bends below diagonal
  • Underconfident = curve bends above

This curve tells you exactly how much to trust the ESIG score at any given level.

Type 2 — Confidence Score Calibration

When the scientist agent says confidence 0.78, is it right 78% of the time?

Collect all predictions with confidence 0.75–0.85
Count: how many were confirmed by real experiments?
If 60% confirmed → agent is systematically overconfident in this range → deflate by 0.15
If 90% confirmed → agent is underconfident → inflate by 0.10

This is standard probabilistic calibration (Platt scaling / temperature scaling applied to LLM outputs). The calibration agent applies a correction factor to raw confidence scores before they go into the finding registry.

# Calibration correction (learned from events)
calibration_map = {
    (0.9, 1.0): 0.82,   # agent says 0.9+ → actually right 82% of the time
    (0.8, 0.9): 0.74,
    (0.7, 0.8): 0.61,
    (0.6, 0.7): 0.49,
    (0.5, 0.6): 0.38,
}

def calibrated_confidence(raw: float) -> float:
    for (low, high), correction in calibration_map.items():
        if low <= raw < high:
            return correction
    return raw

The finding registry stores CALIBRATED confidence, not raw agent confidence. This is the number researchers should trust.

The Retroactive Bootstrap — Using 5 Years of Historical Data

This is the cold start solution. The lab has 5 years of experiment results. You don't have to wait for new experiments to start calibrating.

Step 1: Get the historical experiment log (what they ran + what happened).

Step 2: For each historical experiment, ask the scientist agent: "if you had been asked to analyze this experiment before it was run, what would you have predicted?"

Step 3: Compare that retroactive prediction to what actually happened. Log as a calibration event.

Step 4: Run the calibration agent on all 5 years at once. You now have a calibrated system from day one.

5 years × ~50 experiments/year = ~250 calibration events
That's enough to fit a reliable calibration curve before you run a single new experiment.

This is the single highest-leverage thing to do when the data arrives. Don't build the agent swarm first — build the retroactive calibration pipeline first. It makes every subsequent agent call more accurate.

The Weekly Recalibration Agent

Runs every Sunday night. Reads all new calibration events from the past week. Updates the calibration map.

INPUT:
  - All calibration events from the past 7 days
  - Current calibration_map.yaml
  - Current ESIG weight config

PROCESS:
  1. Compute prediction error for each new event
  2. Update calibration map (rolling window — recent events weighted more)
  3. Identify systematic errors: is one ESIG component consistently wrong?
     - "novelty scores are consistently overestimated for Fe³⁺ conditions"
     - "falsification value is underestimated — we keep not running things we should"
  4. Update ESIG component weights
  5. Flag any anomalies for orchestrator attention

OUTPUT:
  - Updated calibration_map.yaml
  - Updated esig_weights.yaml
  - Weekly calibration report: YYYY-MM-DD_calibration-weekly-report.md
  - Anomaly flags if any

Rolling window weighting: recent calibration events count more than old ones. The lab's conditions change over time — a calibration from 3 years ago may not apply today.

def event_weight(event_age_days: int) -> float:
    # Half-life of 90 days — event 90 days old counts half as much
    return 0.5 ** (event_age_days / 90)

What the Calibration Agent Detects

Systematic Overconfidence

"The scientist agent consistently rates Fe³⁺ scenarios at 0.85+ confidence but they're only right 55% of the time."

Fix: add a domain-specific deflation factor for Fe³⁺ conditions. Embed in scientist prompt: "Note: Fe³⁺ scenarios have historically been overestimated — apply extra skepticism to your confidence score."

Systematic ESIG Miscalibration

"High-ESIG experiments are being rated low value by researchers."

Diagnose: which ESIG term is wrong? Is novelty being overweighted? Is cost being underweighted?

Fix: adjust ESIG component weights in esig_weights.yaml.

Protocol Failure Patterns

"3/5 experiments involving nanoparticle iron required major protocol modification."

Fix: add to constraint registry: "Nanoparticle iron protocols require modification — flag for manual review before running." This flows into the brainstorm agent's constraints and reduces future nanoparticle iron ESIG scores.

Paradigm Shift Detection

"Error rate spiked from 15% to 60% over the last 4 weeks."

This is the "something changed" signal. Could be:

  • Reagent batch changed
  • Lab equipment recalibrated
  • A foundational assumption was wrong
def detect_paradigm_shift(recent_events: list, baseline_error_rate: float) -> bool:
    recent_error_rate = compute_error_rate(recent_events[-20:])  # last 20 events
    return recent_error_rate > baseline_error_rate * 2.5

When detected: freeze new task spawning, alert orchestrator, flag all findings from the affected period as "under review." This is the recovery mechanism for catastrophic failures.

The Selection Bias Problem

This is the hardest problem in the calibration loop. You only observe calibration events for experiments the lab actually ran. The lab mostly runs experiments the system recommended. So you never see the counterfactual: "what would have happened if we'd run the low-ESIG experiment instead?"

This creates selection bias — the system appears better calibrated than it is because its predictions are only tested on the experiments it was already confident about.

Partial Solutions

1. Mandatory exploration budget: Force the lab to occasionally run a randomly selected low-ESIG experiment (say, 1 in 10). This gives you counterfactual data.

2. Natural experiments: Sometimes the lab runs experiments for non-AI reasons (advisor request, reagent expiry, equipment availability). Treat these as random — log calibration events for them even if the system would have deprioritized them.

3. Counterfactual reasoning agent: Monthly, spawn an agent that asks: "For all the experiments we did NOT run in the last 30 days, what would we have expected? And based on the findings from experiments we DID run, can we infer whether the skipped ones would have been positive or negative?" This is imperfect but better than nothing.

4. Track disagreement: When the orchestrator overrides the ESIG ranking (researcher insists on running something the system rated low), log this as a "human override event" and treat the outcome as especially valuable calibration data — these are the cases most likely to reveal systematic errors.

What Gets Better Over Time

System ComponentYear 1Year 3Year 5
ESIG accuracy~60%~78%~88%
Confidence calibrationGeneric literatureLab-specificCondition-specific
Brainstorm hypothesis qualityMany dead endsFew dead endsTargeted
Protocol validity~70% usable as-is~85%~92%
Experiment prioritizationGuessingInformedPredictive
Context per decisionHigh (lots of exploration)MediumLow (mostly confirming)

The system gets cheaper to run AND more accurate over time. That's the compounding return.

Open Questions

  1. How do you get lab results back into the system? The researcher needs a simple way to log "experiment X ran, here's what happened." A form? A CLI command? A Slack bot? The calibration loop is only as good as the feedback channel.
  1. What's the minimum viable calibration dataset? How many events do you need before the calibration map is trustworthy enough to act on? Probably 30–50 events minimum.
  1. Can you calibrate at the variable level? "Fe²⁺ predictions are well-calibrated but Fe³⁺ predictions are systematically off" — this is more useful than a global calibration map but requires more data.
  1. Should the scientist agent KNOW its own calibration history? You could inject: "historically, your analyses of nanoparticle iron have been 40% accurate — apply extra skepticism." This is meta-learning — the agent learns from its own track record.
  1. What happens at year 5 when the lab has solved the core problem? The experiment space narrows. ESIG novelty scores collapse toward zero because everything interesting has been tried. The system needs to recognize when it's done and shift from exploration to confirmation mode.
Orchestration
Three-Wave Batch Architecture
Keep parallel workers blind to each other, then add one synthesis pass that reads them all — contradictions are invisible to any single worker.
2026-03-27

Three-Wave Batch Architecture

The Problem

In the original design, every agent worked in isolation. 10 scientists each analyzed one variable at one site. They never read each other's work. A pre-treatment agent at PBNJ-002 might discover coagulation reduces DOC by 50%, but the co-contaminant agent at the same site designed its protocol for raw water DOC. Nobody connected the dots.

The orchestrator (Isaac + Claude in conversation) connected them manually. That doesn't scale for a 10-week internship with 2 real sites and dozens of tasks.

The Architecture

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WAVE 1: Scientists (Sonnet 4.6, parallel)      │
│  10 agents, each analyzes one (site × variable) │
│  ~3 min wall clock                               │
│  Output: data/agent-work/YYYY-MM-DD/task-NNNN/  │
└──────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                   │ all 10 outputs
                   ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WAVE 2: Cross-Pollinator (Opus 4.6, single)   │
│  1 agent reads ALL scientist outputs + goal     │
│  Finds contradictions, connections, next steps  │
│  ~5-10 min                                       │
│  Output: sessions/YYYY-MM-DD/synthesis.md       │
└──────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                   │ synthesis complete
                   ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WAVE 3: Memory Agents (Haiku 4.5, parallel)   │
│  10 agents, each compresses one scientist output│
│  ~1 min wall clock                               │
│  Output: data/agent-summaries/YYYY-MM-DD/       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Total wall clock per batch: ~15 minutes for 10 tasks fully analyzed, cross-referenced, and compressed.

What Each Wave Does

Wave 1: Scientists

Same as before. Each agent:

  • Reads the full scientist manual (prohibition-first, 39KB prompt)
  • Receives the goal config (overarching research goal, decision sequence)
  • Receives the site contamination profile (compliance gap)
  • Receives one site's data slice (25 PFAS analytes, water quality, treatment data)
  • Produces a structured analysis with experiment protocol

What they DON'T do: talk to each other or read other scientists' work.

Wave 2: Cross-Pollinator (THE NEW PIECE)

One Opus agent that:

  • Reads ALL scientist outputs from Wave 1 in a single context window (~200KB fits in 1M)
  • Reads the goal config (decision sequence, constraints, current status)
  • Reads the framework learnings (SYS findings from past batches)
  • Finds what NO individual scientist could find:
  • Contradictions — where agents disagree or assume different conditions
  • Connections — where one agent's finding changes another's conclusion
  • Decision sequence progress — maps batch results to goal config steps
  • Next batch recommendation — what to run tomorrow and why
  • Proposed goal config updates — keeps the goal current

This is the orchestrator intelligence that was previously manual (Isaac + Claude in conversation).

Wave 3: Memory Agents

Same as before. Each agent compresses one scientist output into a structured summary with:

  • Key finding (one line)
  • Calibration predictions (copied verbatim)
  • Finding registry updates (max 2 new per task)
  • Reconstruction info (enough to re-run the task if the analysis is lost)

Why This Order

Scientists first because they need raw data, not other agents' opinions. Parallel because they're independent.

Cross-pollinator second because it needs ALL scientist outputs to find cross-connections. Sequential because there's only one and it needs the full picture.

Memory agents last because they compress individual scientist outputs. They don't need the cross-pollinator's synthesis — they summarize the raw analyses. Parallel because they're independent.

The Cross-Pollinator as Session Bridge

The synthesis document is the most important file for context persistence:

Session N:  Run batch → Cross-pollinator writes synthesis
                         ↓
Session N+1: New Claude reads synthesis → knows what happened, what to run next
                         ↓
            Runs next batch → Cross-pollinator writes new synthesis
                         ↓
Session N+2: ...

Without the cross-pollinator, every new session starts from scratch and has to re-derive what batches have run and what to do next. With it, context restoration is: read goal config + read latest synthesis = full operating context.

Scripts

WaveScriptCommand
1 + 3scripts/assemble-prompts.pypython3 scripts/assemble-prompts.py --tasks task-0009,task-0013
2scripts/spawn-cross-pollinator.pypython3 scripts/spawn-cross-pollinator.py --date 2026-03-26

The assembly script generates both scientist AND memory prompts in one run. The cross-pollinator script generates its prompt separately because it needs scientist outputs that don't exist until Wave 1 completes.

Inputs and Outputs Per Wave

Wave 1 Inputs

  • data/goal-config.yaml — research goal, targets, constraints
  • data/raw/*.csv — the dataset (synthetic or real)
  • brainstorm/agent-manuals/02_*_scientist-agent-manual.md — scientist schema
  • memory/finding-registry/F001-F012.yaml — literature findings
  • data/task_manifest.json — which tasks to run

Wave 1 Outputs

  • data/agent-work/YYYY-MM-DD/task-NNNN/YYYY-MM-DD_1200_analysis.md (one per task)

Wave 2 Inputs

  • All Wave 1 outputs
  • data/goal-config.yaml
  • brainstorm/agent-manuals/05_*_cross-pollinator-manual.md
  • memory/finding-registry/INDEX.md — framework learnings

Wave 2 Outputs

  • sessions/YYYY-MM-DD/YYYY-MM-DD_cross-pollinator-synthesis.md

Wave 3 Inputs

  • Individual Wave 1 outputs (one per memory agent)
  • brainstorm/agent-manuals/03_*_memory-agent-manual.md

Wave 3 Outputs

  • data/agent-summaries/YYYY-MM-DD/task-NNNN_*_summary.md (one per task)

Agents Per Batch

WaveModelAgentsRole
1Sonnet 4.610Individual site × variable analysis
2Opus 4.61Cross-pollination, synthesis, next batch planning
3Haiku 4.510Compression and structured summary
Total21 agents

What This Replaces

Before: Isaac and Claude manually read outputs, discuss contradictions, decide next batch in conversation. Knowledge lost when session ends.

After: Opus cross-pollinator does the synthesis automatically. Its output persists to disk. Next session reads it and picks up where we left off. Isaac still grades manually and makes final decisions — but the analysis connecting 10 independent analyses is automated.

Open Questions

  • Should the cross-pollinator get previous batch syntheses as input? (Adds context about what's already been tried, but increases prompt size)
  • Should Wave 3 memory agents also get the cross-pollinator synthesis? (Would let them annotate their summaries with cross-connections, but adds complexity)
  • At what batch count does the cross-pollinator benefit from reading previous batch syntheses as additional input?
Prompting
Massive Data Digestion Architecture
Feed gigabyte-scale data to context-limited agents by progressive disclosure: schema, chunk summaries, a reasoned index, then targeted reads.
2026-03-28

Massive Data Digestion Architecture

The Problem

Isaac's professor has ~10 years of wetlab data for contaminated sites. This could be 100,000+ rows × 200+ columns — gigabytes of CSV. Our current system injects ~25 rows into a 43KB prompt. That's a 4,000x scale gap.

No single agent can read this. No context window fits it. The data has to be chunked, summarized, indexed, and then targeted slices fed to scientists.

The Pipeline

Massive CSV (possibly GB-scale)
    ↓
STEP 1: Schema Agent (1 agent, reads headers + samples)
    ↓ outputs: data dictionary (~20KB)
STEP 2: Slicing Script (Python, no AI)
    ↓ outputs: 50-200 chunk files (~100K tokens each)
STEP 3: Chunk Summarizers (100 Haiku agents, parallel)
    ↓ outputs: 100 structured summaries (~5-10KB each)
STEP 4: Master Index Agent (1 Opus, reads all summaries)
    ↓ outputs: master index (~200KB) — the map of everything
STEP 5: Scientist Agents (Sonnet × N, each gets index + relevant chunks)
    ↓ outputs: targeted analyses
STEP 6: Cross-Pollinator (1 Opus, reads all scientists)
    ↓ outputs: synthesis + next steps

Step 1: Schema Agent

Model: Sonnet or Haiku Input: Header row + first 100 rows + last 100 rows + 100 random rows from the CSV Job: Produce a data dictionary. Not analysis — just "here's what's in this data." Output (~20KB):

  • Every column name, data type, range (min/max/mean), units
  • Date range covered (earliest to latest experiment)
  • How many unique experiments/treatments/sites
  • Whether the schema changed over time (column additions, name changes)
  • Missing data patterns (which columns have gaps, which years)
  • Obvious grouping variables (experiment ID, site, treatment type, date)

Why: You can't slice what you don't understand. The schema agent maps the terrain before anything else happens.

Step 2: Slicing Script

Model: None — this is pure Python Input: The massive CSV + the data dictionary from Step 1 Job: Split the CSV into chunks sized to fit ~100K tokens when converted to text Slicing strategy (in priority order):

  1. By experiment group / treatment type (if the data has an experiment ID column)
  2. By year (if experiments span 10 years)
  3. By row count (fallback: every ~2,000-5,000 rows becomes a chunk)

Output: 50-200 CSV chunk files in data/chunks/chunk-001.csv through chunk-NNN.csv Also outputs: data/chunks/chunk-manifest.json — which rows are in which chunk, what date range, what variables

Why: AI is expensive for slicing. A Python script does it in seconds.

Step 3: Chunk Summarizers

Model: Haiku 4.5 (cheap, parallel) Input per agent: One chunk file (~100K tokens) + the data dictionary from Step 1 Job: Read every row in the chunk and produce a structured summary Output per agent (~5-10KB):

chunk_id: chunk-037
rows: 2,401-4,800
date_range: 2018-03-01 to 2019-08-15
experiments_in_chunk: 47
treatments_tested:
  - GAC (bituminous, EBCT 10-20 min): 23 experiments
  - Ion exchange (Purolite A694E): 12 experiments
  - Coagulation pre-treatment (ferric sulfate): 8 experiments
  - Control (no treatment): 4 experiments
pfas_compounds_measured: [PFOS, PFOA, PFHxS, PFNA, PFBA, PFPeA, GenX, ...]
concentration_ranges:
  PFOS: 12-340 ng/L
  PFOA: 8-180 ng/L
key_results:
  - GAC bed life averaged 18,000 BV in this period (DOC 2.1 mg/L)
  - IX resin showed no PFOS breakthrough through 45,000 BV
  - Ferric coag reduced DOC by 40% and extended GAC bed life 2.2x
anomalies:
  - Row 3,247: PFOS spike to 1,200 ng/L (10x normal) — possible contamination event
  - Rows 4,100-4,200: all iron measurements missing (instrument downtime?)
relevant_for: [gac_dosage, pre_treatment, iron_speciation, short_chain]

Scale: 100 agents × ~40 seconds each = ~1 minute wall clock (all parallel) Total data processed: 100 chunks × 100K tokens = 10 MILLION tokens of raw data read by AI

Step 4: Master Index Agent

Model: Opus 4.6 (needs the intelligence to reason across 100 summaries) Input: All 100 chunk summaries (~500KB-1MB) + data dictionary + goal config Job: Produce the master index — the map of everything. Not raw data. The REASONED overview. Output (~100-200KB):

# Master Data Index

## Dataset Overview
- Total: 98,432 rows, 187 columns, 2016-01-15 to 2025-11-30
- Sites: 2 (Assunpink Wetland, JBMDL groundwater)
- Total experiments: 1,247
- Treatments tested: GAC (412), IX resin (198), Feammox (87), coag/floc (156), ...

## What Has Been Tried (organized by treatment)
### GAC Experiments (412 total, chunks 3,7,12,14,22,37,41,55,62,78,89)
- Carbon types: bituminous (267), coconut (98), wood-based (47)
- EBCT range tested: 5-45 min
- Bed volumes tracked: up to 65,000 BV
- Best result: PFOS <4 ng/L through 32,000 BV (chunk-037, bituminous, DOC 1.8 mg/L)
- Worst result: PFOS breakthrough at 800 BV (chunk-078, coconut, DOC 12 mg/L)
- Key finding: bed life correlates R²=0.84 with SUVA (chunks 37, 55, 89)

### Feammox Experiments (87 total, chunks 28,29,44,45,67,68)
- A6 inoculum source: lab culture (67), field-enriched (20)
- pH range tested: 3.5-7.0
- Iron sources: ferrihydrite (45), goethite (22), site sediment (20)
- Best result: 78% PFOA destruction in 14 days (chunk-045, MEC reactor, pH 4.0)
- Key gap: no experiments at pH >6.5 (site water is pH 6.8)

## Where To Find Specific Data
[chunk pointers organized by topic — "if you need iron speciation data, read chunks 14, 37, 82"]

## What Has NOT Been Tried
[gaps identified by comparing what exists against the goal config decision sequence]

## Recommended Reading Order for Scientists
[which chunks to read first for each variable in the task manifest]

Why this is the key document: Every scientist agent gets this index. It tells them: "the answer to your question might already be in chunk 37 and chunk 82." They don't read the raw data — they read the index + the specific chunks the index points them to.

Step 5: Scientist Agents (Modified)

Model: Sonnet 4.6 Input per agent: Master index (~200KB) + 3-5 relevant chunks (~50-80K tokens each) + goal config + scientist manual Total context: ~400-600K tokens (fits in Sonnet's window)

Key change from current system: Scientists don't get a pre-sliced data table anymore. They get the index (which tells them the big picture) + the raw chunk data (which gives them the detail). They decide what to focus on within their chunks.

Output: Same schema as now — analysis with protocol, predictions, connections.

Step 6: Cross-Pollinator (Same as Now)

Model: Opus 4.6 Input: All scientist outputs + master index + goal config Output: Synthesis, contradictions, connections, next batch plan

Context Window Budget Per Agent

AgentIndexChunksInstructionsTotal
Schema-~50K (sampled rows)~5K~55K
Chunk Summarizer~20K (data dict)~100K (one chunk)~5K~125K
Master Index~500K (all summaries)-~20K~520K
Scientist~200K (master index)~300K (3-5 chunks)~40K (manual + goal)~540K
Cross-Pollinator~200K (master index)- (reads scientists instead)~120K (scientist outputs)~320K

Everything fits. No agent exceeds 600K tokens. The 1M context windows have room to spare.

What This Preserves

  • Detail: 100 Haiku agents each read 100K tokens. Nothing is skipped. Every row is seen by at least one AI.
  • Cross-references: The master index connects chunks. "Chunk 37's GAC result contradicts chunk 78 — different carbon type explains the discrepancy."
  • Progressive disclosure: Schema → summaries → index → targeted deep reads. Each layer adds detail without overwhelming.
  • The existing framework: Scientists, cross-pollinator, and memory agents work exactly as built. Only the DATA INPUT layer changes.

What's New to Build

ComponentExists?Effort
Schema agent promptNoSmall — one prompt, runs once
Slicing scriptNoMedium — Python, reads CSV, splits by natural groupings
Chunk summarizer promptNoSmall — similar to memory agent manual
Master index agent promptNoMedium — new manual, similar to cross-pollinator
Modified assembly scriptPartially — needs to inject index + chunks instead of raw CSVMedium
Scientist/cross-pollinator/memory agentsYes — unchangedZero

Open Questions

  • What if the data isn't one CSV but a folder of mixed formats (Excel, PDF lab reports, handwritten notes scanned to images)?
  • What if 10 years of data means 10 different schemas? Column names may have changed, units may have changed, instruments may have changed.
  • Should chunk summaries be stored permanently (like memory agent summaries) or regenerated each time?
  • At what point does the master index itself become too large for a scientist's context window? (Current estimate: 200KB for 100 chunks. If 500 chunks, that's 1MB — too big for Sonnet, would need compression.)
  • Should there be a "chunk retrieval" step where scientists REQUEST specific chunks based on the index, rather than receiving pre-assigned chunks? More flexible but adds a tool-use round trip.

How Context Restoration Works With This

New session chain becomes:

  1. MEMORY.md → project_princeton_internship.md (auto-loaded)
  2. data/goal-config.yaml (current goal)
  3. data/chunks/master-index.md (the map of all data — this replaces reading raw data)
  4. Latest cross-pollinator synthesis (what was found last, what's next)

The master index IS the context. A new session reads it and knows everything the data contains without reading any raw data files.

Data pipeline
Scientist Agent & Goal Revamp for Massive Data
Reframe the goal and the output schema follows — forbid proposing what the existing data already answers, and make-work becomes structurally impossible.
2026-03-28
SUPERSEDED 2026-04-26. The scientist-goal revamp described here was the design predecessor to v3. v3 corpus generation + 6 new biological-destruction VARIABLES in assemble-prompts.py + scientist manual updates 2026-04-26 implemented the revamp's intent.
