  2. Verifies memory/knowledge-graph/graph-stats.yaml was updated (check generated_at timestamp)
  3. Updates CANONICAL.md — finds the Knowledge Graph Stats freshness table row and updates generated_at
  4. Prints a freshness report: node count, orphan count, edge count, epistemic stability distribution

Interface reads: memory/knowledge-graph/nodes/*.yaml (via graph-stats.py), CANONICAL.md Interface writes: memory/knowledge-graph/graph-stats.yaml (via graph-stats.py), CANONICAL.md (freshness row) Uses: subprocess or direct import, pyyaml, pathlib, re (for CANONICAL.md update)

Agent 05 — scripts/check-l2-trigger.py

Why this file exists: The L2 CP is the most expensive agent in the pipeline (Opus 4.6, 100k+ context). Running it every batch would waste significant compute and produce low-signal output before enough batches accumulate. This guard script is the only thing preventing redundant L2 runs — without it, the orchestrator has no programmatic way to know whether Wave 4 should fire. Where: princeton-intern-ai-project/scripts/check-l2-trigger.py (new file) Scope boundary: Read-only. Writes to stdout only — no files modified, no side effects. Does NOT spawn the L2 CP itself. Does NOT check whether the L2 CP previously ran for this batch (that's the orchestrator's responsibility). Returns exit code 0 for "trigger" and 1 for "skip." Failure trigger: Breaks when runtime-state.yaml's completed_batches list has an unexpected structure — script may count incorrectly and trigger L2 CP on the wrong batches (e.g., batch 4 instead of batch 3, batch 6 instead of batch 9). Confirm it works by: python3 check-l2-trigger.py --batch-id 3 must exit 0; python3 check-l2-trigger.py --batch-id 4 must exit 1; python3 check-l2-trigger.py --batch-id 6 must exit 0.

Task: Write a Python script that:

  1. Reads data/runtime-state.yaml
  2. Counts completed_batches entries
  3. Returns 0 (trigger L2) if batch count % 3 == 0 and batch count > 0, else returns 1 (skip)
  4. Prints human-readable: "L2 CP trigger: YES — batch N is a multiple of 3" or "NO"
  5. Accepts optional --batch-id N flag to check a specific batch number

Interface reads: data/runtime-state.yaml Interface writes: stdout only Uses: pyyaml, argparse, sys

Agent 06 — scripts/validate-proposed-edges.py

Why this file exists: Merge failures are silent data corruption. If Wave 2b writes a proposed edge referencing "N099" (nonexistent) or "superseded" (invalid type), and the merge script doesn't catch it, bad edges silently enter node files — poisoning blast-radius and epistemic stability computations. This validator runs as a hard gate between Wave 2b output and merge, so merge-graph-proposals.py can trust its inputs are clean. Where: princeton-intern-ai-project/scripts/validate-proposed-edges.py (new file) Scope boundary: Read-only. Takes a single proposed-edges.yaml path as a CLI argument. Does NOT modify any file. Does NOT run the merge — that's merge-graph-proposals.py's job. Exits 0 (all valid) or 1 (any invalid). Reports specific reasons for each failure to stdout. Failure trigger: Breaks when "NEW:some-claim" source_nodes are accepted as valid (because they start with a recognized prefix) but downstream merge fails on them. Confirm it works by: passing a proposed-edges.yaml with one NEW: source_node and verifying it produces exit 1 with a specific "NEW: prefix not allowed" message — not just "node not found."

Task: Write a Python script that:

  1. Reads a proposed-edges.yaml file (path passed as CLI argument)
  2. Validates each edge:
  • source_node exists in nodes/ OR is prefixed with "NEW:"
  • target_node exists in nodes/
  • edge_type is one of the 5 valid types
  • reasoning is non-empty
  • breaks_if is non-empty
  • confidence_weight is 0.0–1.0
  • No self-referential edges (source == target)
  • No duplicate edges (same source+target+type)
  1. Checks for circular superseded_by chains
  2. Prints validation report: N valid, N invalid, with reasons for failures
  3. Exit 0 if all valid, exit 1 if any invalid

Interface reads: proposed-edges.yaml (arg), memory/knowledge-graph/nodes/*.yaml Interface writes: stdout only Uses: pyyaml, argparse, pathlib, sys

Agent 07 — scripts/check-preflight.py (full rewrite)

Why this file exists: The existing check-preflight.py has 5 gates that guard the original 3-wave pipeline. It knows nothing about the knowledge graph pipeline: it won't catch a missing proposals/ folder, stale graph-stats.yaml, or absent graph-updater-manual. Running Batch 7 without these gates means Wave 2b could fire into a broken environment with no pre-run warning. The 3 new gates (6-8) close this gap. ALL existing code — functions, constants, gate logic, update_gate_in_file(), the no-PyYAML constraint — must survive exactly. Gates 6 AND 7 are both WARN (not FAIL) — see C5 fix above for critical reasoning. No new external dependencies. Confirm it works by: running check-preflight.py on a fresh repo (no proposals/ folder, no graph-stats.yaml) and verifying all 5 original gates pass AND Gates 6+7 produce WARN (yellow) not FAIL (red) with the message "will be created by first Wave 2b run."

Group B — New Agent Manuals (3 agents)

Agent 09 — brainstorm/agent-manuals/07_2026-04-02_1022_graph-updater-manual.md

Why this file exists: Wave 2b is a new agent role with no prior precedent in this framework. Without an authoritative manual defining what it reads, how it evaluates edge validity, what it writes, and what it must NOT do, the Opus graph updater will hallucinate its own output format — producing proposals that merge-graph-proposals.py cannot parse. This manual is the behavioral contract for Wave 2b. Where: princeton-intern-ai-project/brainstorm/agent-manuals/07_2026-04-02_1022_graph-updater-manual.md (new file) Scope boundary: Covers Wave 2b ONLY. Does NOT define L2 CP behavior (that's Agent 10). Does NOT define the merge script logic (that's Agent 01). The manual tells the agent how to produce proposed-edges.yaml and graph-delta.md — not how to modify node files directly (the agent must not do that). Failure trigger: Breaks when the graph updater proposes "NEW:some-claim" source_nodes (because the manual doesn't explicitly forbid this format) — merge-graph-proposals.py rejects all such edges and the graph never grows from novel batch findings. Confirm the manual works by: checking that it explicitly says "All proposed edges must reference existing node_ids. NEW: prefix is forbidden in proposed-edges.yaml. Novel claims belong in graph-delta.md only."

Task: Write the Wave 2b Opus graph updater agent manual. This agent:

  • Is Opus 4.6
  • Runs after all scientist outputs for a batch are complete
  • Reads all scientist analysis files from the batch
  • Reads the current graph-stats.yaml and all node files
  • Reads the goal config
  • Does NOT write to any node files directly — it writes to memory/knowledge-graph/proposals/batch-NN_YYYY-MM-DD/proposed-edges.yaml
  • Also adds a ## Graph Delta section to its output (written to sessions/batch-NN_YYYY-MM-DD/graph-delta.md)

The manual must specify:

  1. What You Are Not (like all other manuals — prohibition-first design)
  2. What You Receive (list exactly: scientist files, graph-stats, node files, goal config)
  3. How to evaluate a proposed edge (when to declare contradicts vs. supports vs. derived_from)
  4. How to handle proposed edges from scientist metadata — validate them, then either accept or modify and explain why
  5. Output schema: proposed-edges.yaml + graph-delta.md (both required)
  6. Hard limits: do not modify node files directly, do not write to sessions/ (only the graph delta md)

CRITICAL: All proposed edges in proposed-edges.yaml MUST use existing node_ids (N001–N013, H001, G001–G003, etc.) as both source_node and target_node. Do NOT use "NEW:some-claim" prefix — merge-graph-proposals.py has no handler for new node creation and will reject all NEW: edges. If this batch produces a claim that deserves a new node, declare it in graph-delta.md as a NEW action entry (for human review) but do NOT include it in proposed-edges.yaml as an edge.

Agent 21 — scripts/graph-stats.py (targeted modification)

Haiku → Opus Planning Pattern
Split agent labor by cognitive task, not capability tier: cheap models scan in parallel, one expensive model synthesizes across all of it at once.
2026-04-03

Haiku → Opus Planning Pattern

date: 2026-04-03 status: brainstorm — active conversation

The Pattern (as described by Isaac)

Phase 1: Haiku breadth scan Launch 5-15 Haiku agents in parallel. Each one gets a narrow, specific file or subsystem to scan. They run fast, cheap, and write structured outputs to files. They don't synthesize — they inventory, describe, and flag.

Phase 2: Opus deep synthesis One Opus agent reads ALL Haiku outputs in its full context window (1M tokens). It has the full picture from every corner of the codebase at once. It synthesizes connections, spots patterns, and produces a high-quality plan or analysis.

Why This Works

The Haiku→Opus split maps directly to two different cognitive tasks:

PhaseModelJobFailure mode if wrong model
ScanHaikuRead, describe, extractDoesn't need to reason — just inventory
SynthesizeOpusConnect, plan, reason deeplyShallow synthesis misses cross-cutting patterns

Using Sonnet for Phase 1 is wasteful — you're paying for reasoning you don't need. Using Haiku for Phase 2 is a mistake — you're skimping on the most critical step.

The Meta-Observation

This is the same architecture as the project itself:

  • Wave 1 Sonnet scientists = Phase 1 (but scientists need reasoning, so Haiku isn't quite right there)
  • Wave 2 Opus CP = Phase 2

For pure file scanning tasks (not scientific reasoning), you can drop Wave 1 to Haiku and get the same information faster and cheaper.

The project already does this implicitly in Wave 3 (Haiku memory agents compress individual files). The planning pattern extends it to analysis and planning tasks, not just memory compression.

Applied to Memory Agent Reanalysis

What the Haiku agents should each scan (proposed):

  1. Memory agent manual (brainstorm/agent-manuals/03_*_memory-agent-manual.md) — what does the manual currently say the memory agent should do?
  2. CP prompt assembly (scripts/spawn-cross-pollinator.py) — does the CP read summaries or analyses? What files does it actually pull?
  3. A sample summary file (e.g., data/agent-summaries/batch-62_2026-04-02/task-0043_*_summary.md) — what fields are actually being produced?
  4. A sample analysis file (the same task) — what fields exist in the source that may or may not be in the summary?
  5. Finding registry snapshot (memory/finding-registry-snapshot.yaml) — what does the compact memory surface look like vs. what the summary produces?
  6. Goal config + decision sequence (data/goal-config.yaml) — what does the research goal actually need from memory agents?
  7. Runtime state + recent session bridge — what context does the CP actually have access to today?
  8. Scientist manual's proposed_edges schema — does the summary capture proposed edges? Should it?
  9. Graph updater manual — does the graph updater read summaries? What does it need?
  10. Agent summaries INDEX.md — what's the documented purpose vs. actual use?

What Opus synthesizes:

  • Does anyone actually read the summaries? Trace the full read path.
  • What is the memory agent's job REALLY (vs. what the manual says)?
  • What fields are missing from summaries that downstream agents need?
  • What fields exist in summaries that nobody reads?
  • Redesign recommendation: new memory agent output schema + updated manual structure

Open Questions Before Planning

  1. Does the CP read summaries or analyses? This is the key question from our conversation. If CP reads analyses, summaries are orphaned output. If CP reads summaries, their structure matters enormously.
  1. Does the graph updater read summaries? The graph updater extracts proposed_edges — but do those come from the analysis file or the summary?
  1. How stale is the memory agent manual? Has it been updated since the 5-wave architecture was added? Does it know about proposed_edges, graph delta, Wave 2b?
  1. What fields does the finding registry update process actually consume? The memory agent produces finding registry update blocks — but what script or agent reads those?

Prompting
Haiku Context Consolidation for Planning
The output of a scan swarm is a fully loaded synthesizer context window, not a report — and you give agents the type of failure to hunt, never examples.
2026-04-03

Haiku Context Consolidation for Planning

date: 2026-04-03 status: active brainstorm depends_on: brainstorm/2026-03-30_1028_prompting-strategy-and-session-learnings.md

What This Is

A planning pattern for tasks where the relevant context is scattered across many files and folders. Instead of feeding a single agent a massive prompt with everything, or doing sequential file reads that burn the main context window, you deploy parallel Haiku agents as context consolidators. Each one starts from MEMORY.md, follows path traces outward into the filesystem, explores freely, and hunts for a typed class of failure. One Opus agent then reads all outputs in a single context window and produces the plan.

The output of this pattern is not a plan. The output is a fully loaded Opus context window — one agent that simultaneously knows every relevant failure across the whole codebase, ready to reason across all of it at once.

This matters because planning quality degrades when the planner has to read files sequentially. By the time it reads file 10, it has lost precision on file 1. The Haiku→Opus pattern eliminates that degradation: Opus receives everything pre-digested and simultaneously present.

The Two Jobs — Do Not Mix Them

AgentModelJobWhat it does NOT do
Context consolidatorHaikuStart from MEMORY.md, follow traces, explore filesystem, surface failures of its assigned typeReason, interpret, synthesize, plan
PlannerOpusRead all Haiku outputs, reason across them, produce the planRead raw source files

Haiku explores and surfaces. Opus reasons and plans. Opus never touches raw files.

Mixing these jobs wastes both models:

  • Haiku reasoning is shallow — asking it to interpret produces low-quality conclusions

that Opus then has to second-guess

  • Opus file-scanning is expensive and slow — it costs full Opus tokens to do work

that Haiku could do in parallel at a fraction of the cost

The split is not about model capability. It is about task type. Exploring and extracting is a different cognitive job than reasoning and planning. Haiku is fast and cheap at the first job. Opus is deep and expensive at the second. Use each for exactly its job.

The Core Principle: Give the Type, Not the Failure

This is the most important rule in the pattern.

Do not tell Haiku what specific failure to find. Tell it the type of failure to hunt.

The type is the instruction. The specific failures are what Haiku discovers.

WrongRight
"Find broken references in index files""Hunt for index file failures"
"Check if MEMORY.md has stale paths""Hunt for organization failures"
"Find folders missing an INDEX.md""Hunt for structure failures"

Why this matters:

  • Prescribing specific failures constrains Haiku to only finding what you already knew to look for
  • Type-based hunting lets Haiku surface failures you didn't anticipate
  • The type is broad enough to catch edge cases that no checklist would include
  • Haiku decides what counts as a failure within its type — this produces richer findings

The three failure types that cover organizational and structural problems in any codebase:

Type 1: Organization failures

Is the project organized correctly? Haiku explores the filesystem and surfaces anything that is in the wrong place, named incorrectly, or structurally inconsistent with the rest of the project's organizational conventions.

Examples of what Haiku might find (Haiku discovers these, they are NOT prescribed):

  • Files in the wrong folder for their type
  • Naming convention violations
  • Duplicate files serving the same role in different locations
  • Files that belong to a subsystem but live outside it

Type 2: Structure failures

Is the structure of the project intact? Haiku follows path traces from MEMORY.md and index files, verifies that referenced structures exist, and flags anything broken, missing, or inconsistent with what the index claims exists.

Examples of what Haiku might find:

  • Folders that exist but have no documented purpose
  • Referenced paths that don't exist on disk
  • Files that exist on disk but are referenced nowhere
  • Directory hierarchies that don't match the documented structure

Type 3: Index file failures

Are the index files (MEMORY.md, INDEX.md files, CANONICAL.md) accurate, complete, and internally consistent? Haiku reads every index file it can find from MEMORY.md traces and hunts for anything wrong with them.

Examples of what Haiku might find:

  • Index entry descriptions that don't match the file's actual content
  • Paths referenced in an index that don't exist
  • Files that exist but appear in no index
  • Two index files that contradict each other about the same file's role
  • Index files that are stale (describe an old state of the system)
  • Folders with no INDEX.md that clearly need one

How Haiku Explores: Start from MEMORY.md

MEMORY.md is the project's navigation index. Every Haiku agent starts there.

The exploration pattern:

  1. Read MEMORY.md — get the full map of what the project claims exists and where
  2. Follow path traces outward — every file and folder reference in MEMORY.md is

a trace to follow. Each trace leads to more files, more index entries, more paths.

  1. Recurse into index files — every INDEX.md found along a trace is itself a map.

Read it, follow its traces. Go as deep as the failure type warrants.

  1. Hunt for the assigned failure type — as you explore, apply one question to

everything you encounter: "does this represent a [type] failure?"

  1. Report what you find — structured output to a file. Facts only, no interpretation.

The exploration is not bounded by a file list. It is bounded by the failure type. Haiku explores as far as it needs to find failures of its type, and stops when the traces run out or the failures become repetitive.

What Makes a Good Haiku Consolidator Prompt

Built directly on the five-component prompting framework from: brainstorm/2026-03-30_1028_prompting-strategy-and-session-learnings.md

The framework says: don't tell the agent where to look. Tell it what failure to find. Applied here: don't prescribe specific failures. Assign a failure type and let Haiku discover what it finds.

The five components applied to a type-based consolidator:

1. Objective

What type of failure is this agent hunting? State the type clearly. Do not list specific failures to look for.

Weak: "Check if MEMORY.md has any broken paths" Strong: "Hunt for index file failures throughout the project"

2. Starting point

Where does Haiku begin its exploration? Always MEMORY.md unless there is a specific reason to start elsewhere.

"Start from MEMORY.md at [absolute path]. Follow all path traces outward."

3. Exploration instruction

How deep should Haiku explore? Give permission to follow traces recursively. Don't constrain the path.

"Follow path traces into every index file, folder, and subsystem you encounter. Explore as far as the traces lead."

4. Failure definition

What counts as a failure of this type? Give the type, then give one sentence defining what a failure looks like within it. Do not give examples — Haiku will anchor on examples and miss everything else.

"An index file failure is any case where an index file's claims about the filesystem do not match what the filesystem actually contains, or where the filesystem contains things the index files don't account for."

5. Exclusions

What is out of scope for this agent's failure type? Without this, agents overlap and Opus gets duplicate reports.

"Do not flag content quality issues — only organizational and structural facts. Do not flag issues covered by the structure or organization agents."

Full Haiku Prompt Template

You are a context consolidator for a planning agent (Opus).
Your job: explore the project filesystem and surface failures of one type.
Do not reason about what failures mean. Do not recommend fixes.
Report what you find. Opus will reason about it.

Read ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and the project CLAUDE.md before starting.
Use the conventions, file naming rules, and structural expectations defined there
as your baseline for what "correct" looks like. Any deviation from those conventions
is a candidate failure.

FAILURE TYPE: [organization | structure | index files]

FAILURE DEFINITION:
[one sentence defining what counts as a failure of this type]

STARTING POINT:
Read MEMORY.md at: [absolute path to MEMORY.md]
Follow all path traces outward from there.
Read every index file (MEMORY.md, INDEX.md, CANONICAL.md) you encounter.
Explore as far as the traces lead.

EXPLORATION INSTRUCTION:
As you explore, apply one question to everything you encounter:
"Does this represent a [type] failure?"
If yes, record it. If no, continue exploring.

SEVERITY: Only flag failures that would matter to a planner redesigning this system.
Ignore cosmetic issues (typos, formatting, whitespace).

EXCLUSIONS:
[what the other Haiku agents are covering — don't duplicate]

FAILURE CHECK before writing:
- Have you followed traces at least 3 levels deep from MEMORY.md?
- Have you checked both directions: index→filesystem AND filesystem→index?
- Have you written facts only, no interpretations or fix recommendations?

OUTPUT FILE: [absolute path]

OUTPUT FORMAT — use exactly these headers:

## Exploration Path
[what you read, in order — file paths only, no descriptions]

## Failures Found
[each failure as: TYPE | LOCATION | WHAT IS WRONG]
[no prose — one line per failure]

## Gaps in Coverage
[parts of the filesystem you could not fully explore and why]

## Count
failures_found: N
files_explored: N

Output Format Rules for Haiku Agents

The Haiku output is Opus's raw material. Every formatting decision should make Opus's job easier, not the human reader's job easier.

Structured over prose. Opus processes structured data faster than narrative. The Failures Found section should be a clean list — one line per failure, consistent format.

Both directions always. Index failures are bidirectional: an index can reference something that doesn't exist, AND something can exist that no index references. Haiku must check both. An agent that only checks index→filesystem misses half the failures.

File paths everywhere. Every failure entry must include the exact file path (and line number if relevant) where the failure was found. "MEMORY.md line 43 references sessions/batch-07_2026-04-02/ which does not exist on disk" is useful. "MEMORY.md has a broken path" is not.

Flag gaps explicitly. If Haiku cannot follow a trace (file is missing, permission denied, folder is empty), say so in Gaps. Opus needs to know what was not explored.

No interpretation. Ever. "This is stale" = interpretation. "Index says file was last updated 2026-03-22, file header says 2026-04-01" = fact. "This will probably cause problems" = interpretation. "File is referenced in MEMORY.md but does not exist at the referenced path" = fact.

Consistent format across all agents. Every Haiku output uses the same four headers: Exploration Path, Failures Found, Gaps in Coverage, Count. Opus scans all outputs without reorienting.

Sizing the Haiku Swarm

One agent per failure type for organizational/structural audits.

Three failure types = three Haiku agents, always run in parallel:

  1. Organization agent
  2. Structure agent
  3. Index files agent

All three start from MEMORY.md. Their failure types are distinct enough that overlap is minimal. If failures appear in multiple agents' reports, Opus treats that as a signal the failure is severe — it was caught from multiple angles.

For larger tasks that go beyond organizational audits, add agents for content-specific failure types (e.g., "schema failures", "path reference failures", "manual staleness"). Still one agent per type. Still all start from MEMORY.md.

Target swarm size: 3–10 agents for organizational tasks. The three organizational types above cover most planning scenarios. Add more only when the task requires content analysis beyond organization and structure.

Opus Synthesis Prompt Structure

The Opus agent receives all Haiku outputs. Its prompt should be minimal — Opus has the full picture from the Haiku outputs. The prompt frames the planning goal and specifies the output format.

Five elements:

1. State the planning goal precisely

What is Opus building or deciding?

"Produce a plan to rebuild the memory agent prompt — what it should produce, what schema it should follow, and what it is missing."

2. List every Haiku output file explicitly

Read these files:
- tasks/[name]/haiku-01_organization.md
- tasks/[name]/haiku-02_structure.md
- tasks/[name]/haiku-03_index-files.md

3. State the failure Opus is preventing

Apply trigger + failure definition from the prompting strategy.

"Failure: a Batch 8 memory agent runs, produces a summary, and the downstream agents that consume it cannot extract what they need. Trigger: Batch 8 runs with an unrebuilt memory agent prompt."

4. Specify the exact output format

What is Opus producing? Be exact — format, structure, file location.

5. Explicit scope exclusions

What adjacent problems should Opus ignore?

Full Opus template:

You are the planner. All context has been pre-extracted by Haiku agents.
Do not read any files except those listed below.

READ:
[list all Haiku output files]

PLANNING GOAL: [precise statement]

FAILURE YOU ARE PREVENTING:
Trigger: [when it surfaces]
Failure: [concrete definition]

PRODUCE EXACTLY:
[artifact 1 — format, path, structure]
[artifact 2 — format, path, structure]

DO NOT PRODUCE: [scope exclusions]

Write output to: [paths]

Common Failure Modes of This Pattern

Haiku gets prescriptive failure examples and anchors on them. Symptom: Haiku only finds the failures you listed as examples, misses everything else. Fix: Remove examples from the prompt. State the type and one-sentence definition only.

Haiku explores too shallowly. Symptom: Haiku only reads MEMORY.md and one level of files, misses deeply nested issues. Fix: Add "follow traces at least 3 levels deep" to the exploration instruction. Add a failure check: "have you followed traces at least 3 levels deep?"

Haiku output sections are inconsistent across agents. Symptom: Opus has to reorient every file — different section names, different formats. Fix: Mandate the four standard headers in every Haiku prompt. No deviations.

Agents overlap — same failure appears in multiple outputs. Symptom: Opus sees the same failure reported three times with slightly different framing. Fix: Add explicit exclusions to each agent's prompt stating what the other agents cover. Treat overlap as a severity signal, not a problem — severe failures appear from multiple angles.

Opus reads Haiku outputs and then reads raw files anyway. Symptom: Opus says "let me also check the script directly." Fix: Explicitly instruct Opus: "do not read any files other than those listed." If Opus goes back to raw files, a Haiku agent missed something — fix the Haiku prompt.

Gaps section empty or missing. Symptom: Opus builds a plan that references unexplored territory without flagging assumptions. Fix: Require Gaps section. Treat empty Gaps as a Haiku prompt failure.

When to Use This Pattern

Use it when:

  • The project has index files (MEMORY.md, INDEX.md) that can serve as exploration maps
  • Context spans 5+ files and organizational/structural correctness matters
  • You need a plan before building — this is pre-execution only
  • You have time to run parallel Haiku agents before needing the plan

Do not use it when:

  • The answer is in 1-2 files — read them directly
  • The task is execution, not planning
  • The project has no index files — there is no starting map for exploration

Connection to the Wave Architecture

This pattern is isomorphic to the research pipeline's Wave 1→Wave 2 structure:

Research pipelinePlanning pattern
Wave 1 Sonnet scientistsHaiku context consolidators
Wave 2 Opus CPOpus planner
Scientist output filesHaiku output files
CP synthesisPlan artifact

Wave 1 scientists need Sonnet because scientific reasoning is required. Haiku consolidators only explore and extract — no reasoning required. For pure filesystem exploration and failure surfacing, Haiku is always the right model.

Honesty & audit

This log records every editing pass made to the Haiku context consolidator manual, what Isaac identified at each pass, and what was changed.

Pass 1 — Initial Write

Isaac asked for the Haiku context consolidator pattern to be formalized as an agent manual and added to brainstorm/agent-manuals/. The manual was written from scratch based on the brainstorm in file 18.

Pass 2 — More Detail

Isaac: "can you make it more detailed" Added: full Haiku prompt template, output format rules, sizing guidance, Opus synthesis prompt structure, common failure modes, when-to-use section, two-layer variant, full worked example of one Haiku prompt.

Pass 3 — CLAUDE.md Injection

Isaac: "tell them to look at and use them" Added: instruction at top of Haiku prompt template to read ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and project CLAUDE.md before starting, and use conventions as baseline for "correct."

Pass 4 — Dual Purpose Reframe

Isaac described the dual-purpose mechanism: failure-finding is the forcing function, the paper trail is the real artifact. An orchestrator can pick up the trail itself. "you're using it to find something else." Changed: "What You Are" reframed around dual purpose. Exploration Path replaced with Exploration Trail. Every hop now requires why, learned, connects to, failure found. Added: "the trail IS the deliverable" as explicit principle.

Pass 5 — Failure Types Corrected

Isaac: "the failures are supposed to be organization, structure, index files" Changed: removed prescriptive specific-failure lists. Replaced with three type-based failure categories (organization, structure, index files). Added core principle: "give the type, not the failure." Haiku discovers specific failures within its type.

Pass 6 — Scan for Ambiguity

Isaac: "i need you to scan that prompt to find ambiguity" Found 11 ambiguities. Isaac: "fix" Fixed:

  • "assigned" type with no source → now says look in spawning prompt for FAILURE TYPE:
  • "five headers" but four listed → corrected to four
  • "3 levels deep" undefined → depth now defined with MEMORY.md=0
  • "follow all traces" unbounded → capped at 10 most significant
  • failure found TYPE undefined → matched to Failures Found schema
  • "document as you go" incoherent → "compose at the end"
  • output file path location unspecified → "given in spawning prompt"
  • project CLAUDE.md no path → absolute path added
  • "pick up from any node" vague → removed, replaced with hop block field requirements
  • trail vs failure tension → explicit: produce both, neither sacrifices the other
  • filesystem→index method unspecified → specific folders + ls/glob instruction added

Pass 7 — Fix Incoherencies

Isaac: "find incoherency now" → "fix" Found 7 incoherencies. Fixed:

  • MEMORY.md read twice (Before You Start + Step 2) → removed from Before You Start
  • 10 traces (bounded) vs every index file (unbounded) → Step 4 bounded to index files along those 10 traces, up to depth 5
  • "write as you go" incoherent with agent output model → "compose at the end"
  • Gaps section defined differently in two places → single definition with two labeled entry types
  • LOCATION redundant in trail failure field → removed LOCATION, file path already in hop header
  • "Are all facts" sentence fragment → complete sentence
  • Step 1 cross-reference + repeated path → clean split: Step 1 = CLAUDE.md, Step 2 = MEMORY.md

Pass 8 — Fix Direction and Process

Isaac: "check for direction and process now" → "fix" Found 6 process issues. Fixed:

  • Step 6 (failure filter) positioned after exploration → integrated into Steps 3 and 4
  • No Step 7 handoff from exploration to writing → Step 6 renamed "Compose and Write Output"
  • Failure type check buried in section 2 → moved to Step 0, first action before any file read
  • Self-check had no recovery process → "return to the relevant step and fix it"
  • Rules positioned after Output Format → moved to top, before all steps
  • Step 5 scope "every path an index file claims" undefined → specified as "all index files read in Steps 2–4"

Pass 9 — Tone, Voice, and Implicit Instructions

Isaac: "tone and voice check for it and implicit instructions" → "fix" Found 6 tone/voice issues and 7 implicit instructions. Fixed:

Tone/voice:

  • "What You Are" philosophical/narrative → stripped to four directive sentences
  • "Both matter / A good output has both" pep talk language → "Produce both. A trail with no failures is acceptable. A failure list with a thin trail is not."
  • Rules inconsistent depth → every rule has one example or one clarifying sentence
  • "now", "silently", "hit" informal language → formal imperative throughout
  • Self-check mixed tenses → all present tense "Did you"
  • Rules section inconsistent justification depth → normalized

Implicit instructions:

  • Unreadable file fallback missing → defined in Steps 3 and 4 with exact hop block format
  • Step 3 significance ranking subjective → explicit 4-tier priority list
  • Step 5 why here and depth undefined for enumerated files → depth: 5+, cite enumeration method
  • Step 0 "spawning prompt" vs manual context boundary ambiguous → "search your full context"
  • Self-check recovery implicit → "fix the relevant step first" before writing
  • MEMORY.md missing handler absent → hard stop with error message in Step 2
  • Depth range "at least 3, stop at 5" ambiguous → "do not stop at depth 3, depth 5 is the target"

Parallel Agent Wave Orchestration
Kill the N-squared communication graph: forbid worker-to-worker chat and route every handoff through typed files on disk.
2026-04-05

Parallel Agent Wave Orchestration

date: 2026-04-05 20:40 status: brainstorm - active conversation depends_on:

  • brainstorm/05_2026-03-22_1635_agent-bootstrap-and-context-design-brainstorm.md
  • brainstorm/12_2026-04-01_knowledge-graph-and-l2-cross-pollinator.md
  • brainstorm/17_2026-04-03_0946_haiku-opus-planning-pattern.md
  • brainstorm/18_2026-04-03_0950_haiku-context-consolidation-for-planning.md

The Problem

Current planning is still too conversational and too manual for large parallel swarms. Even when subagents exist, the human and the orchestrator still carry too much scheduler state in their heads:

  • what can run now
  • what must wait
  • which outputs unlock the next wave
  • which tasks overlap
  • which tasks need checking before downstream work can trust them

This does not scale to 50-100 concurrent workers. The bottleneck stops being raw model capacity and becomes coordination load.

The human constraint matters:

A strong engineer may only have a few hours of peak planning energy per day. The system should minimize prompt count and maximize parallel useful work.

The target is not "more agents" in the abstract. The target is:

one high-leverage planning action from the human -> many bounded agents execute in parallel -> structured outputs unlock the next wave automatically

Core Idea

Treat planning as compilation into a dependency graph.

The human gives a high-level goal. The planner does not just make a 5-10 step checklist. It compiles that goal into:

  • task contracts
  • dependency edges
  • file ownership
  • acceptance checks
  • wave triggers

Then the system runs in waves:

  1. launch all tasks with satisfied dependencies
  2. collect outputs into structured artifacts
  3. run checker agents and deterministic validators
  4. unlock the next set of tasks
  5. repeat until the graph is exhausted

This is closer to a build system or workflow engine than a normal chat plan.

Scope And Interfaces

This orchestrator owns:

  • task decomposition into bounded parallel units
  • dependency tracking and unlock decisions
  • worker/checker/reducer/adjudicator prompt assembly
  • artifact validation and state transitions
  • retry, blocking, and escalation decisions

This orchestrator does not own:

  • the scientific content of individual task manuals
  • canonical project truth in data/*.yaml
  • long-term memory structures like the knowledge graph
  • direct editing outside a task's owned write scope

Existing project surfaces it is expected to read:

  • CANONICAL.md
  • MEMORY.md
  • data/goal-config.yaml
  • data/runtime-state.yaml
  • data/live-baseline.yaml
  • data/next-batch.yaml
  • role manuals under brainstorm/agent-manuals/

Expected artifact location for this orchestrator layer:

  • tasks/<project-name>/task-manifest.json
  • tasks/<project-name>/contracts/<task-id>.json
  • tasks/<project-name>/results/<task-id>.json
  • tasks/<project-name>/checks/<task-id>.json
  • tasks/<project-name>/reductions/<wave-id>.json
  • tasks/<project-name>/index.md

Integration boundary:

  • planner reads existing canonical/runtime truth and writes orchestration artifacts
  • workers/checkers/reducers read orchestration artifacts and write only within owned paths
  • downstream wave unlocks read only artifact status, not chat history or undocumented state

Why This Is Different From Normal Planning

Normal planner behavior:

  • explore codebase
  • make a small step list
  • maybe parallelize a few subtasks
  • revisit plan as work completes

Wave orchestrator behavior:

  • create many task contracts at once
  • assign tasks to parallel workers with disjoint ownership
  • define what evidence unlocks later waves
  • insert checking/reduction/adjudication waves between worker waves
  • keep the human out of the loop unless a gate fails or a strategic decision is needed

The difference is not "more detail." The difference is that the planner is now a control-plane compiler.

The Desired Human Experience

The human should not have to manage 100 independent prompts.

The human should be able to do something like:

Plan this project for aggressive parallel execution. Isolate tasks that can run now, stage dependent work behind them, and keep going wave by wave until blocked.

From that, the system should generate:

  • a manifest of tasks
  • prompts derived from contracts
  • output paths
  • checking tasks
  • retry/escalation paths

The human's job becomes:

  • set the objective
  • inspect strategic pivots
  • approve changes when the scheduler hits ambiguity

Not:

  • manually babysit every subagent
  • remember what depends on what
  • reread 100 outputs to know what to do next

The Critical Insight: Kill the N^2 Communication Graph

The company analogy is correct if every worker talks to every other worker. That creates exponential coordination pain.

The fix is to forbid open-ended peer coordination.

Workers do not talk to each other. They communicate through structured artifacts:

  • task-manifest.json
  • task-contract.json
  • task-result.json
  • check-result.json
  • reduction-summary.json

This forces the graph closer to:

  • human -> planner
  • planner -> workers
  • workers -> files
  • checkers -> files
  • reducers -> files
  • planner/adjudicator -> next wave

That is much closer to linear control than free-form swarm chatter.

Artifact Schemas

These are the minimum interfaces needed so an implementer does not have to invent the control plane from scratch.

task-manifest.json

Purpose:

  • defines the full task set for one orchestration run
  • append-only for task history, replace-in-place for status updates

Required fields:

  • run_id
  • goal
  • created_at
  • planner_version
  • tasks

Each tasks[] entry must include:

  • task_id
  • title
  • wave
  • contract_path
  • result_path
  • check_path
  • status

Invariants:

  • every task_id is unique within the manifest
  • every path is absolute or rooted to the run folder
  • status enum is one of pending|ready|running|passed|failed|blocked|needs-adjudication

task-contract.json

Required fields:

  • task_id
  • goal
  • dependencies
  • allowed_inputs
  • owned_files
  • forbidden_files
  • expected_outputs
  • acceptance_checks
  • escalation_conditions

Invariants:

  • dependencies reference other tasks by task_id, never by filename
  • owned_files must be disjoint across parallel workers in the same wave
  • expected_outputs must be a subset of owned_files

Typed shape:

  • dependencies: array of {"task_id": string, "type": "hard"|"soft"|"informational"}
  • acceptance_checks: array of {"check_id": string, "kind": "deterministic"|"judgment", "description": string, "blocking": boolean}
  • allowed_inputs|owned_files|forbidden_files|expected_outputs: array of repo-rooted path strings
  • all fields above are required unless explicitly documented as optional in a future revision

task-result.json

Required fields:

  • task_id
  • status
  • started_at
  • finished_at
  • output_files
  • summary
  • problems

Invariants:

  • output_files must exist on disk before status can be passed
  • status cannot be passed if problems contains any blocking item

Typed shape:

  • problems: array of {"code": string, "message": string, "blocking": boolean}
  • summary: short human-readable string, not the full artifact payload

check-result.json

Required fields:

  • task_id
  • checker_id
  • status
  • deterministic_checks
  • judgment_checks
  • blocking_findings
  • recommended_action

Invariants:

  • a checker may emit pass|fail|needs-adjudication
  • any blocking deterministic failure forces recommended_action != pass

Typed shape:

  • deterministic_checks: array of {"check_id": string, "status": "pass"|"fail", "evidence": string}
  • judgment_checks: array of {"check_id": string, "status": "pass"|"fail"|"uncertain", "reason": string}
  • blocking_findings: array of {"code": string, "message": string}
  • recommended_action: one of pass|retry|adjudicate|rewrite-contract

reduction-summary.json

Required fields:

  • wave_id
  • input_tasks
  • passed_tasks
  • failed_tasks
  • adjudication_tasks
  • new_ready_tasks
  • notes_for_next_wave

Invariants:

  • reducers do not change worker outputs
  • reducers only summarize state and unlock recommendations

Typed shape:

  • new_ready_tasks: array of task_id strings promoted by reducer output
  • reducers may persist readiness recommendations, but only the orchestrator mutates canonical task status in the manifest

Minimal Examples

{
  "task-manifest.json": {
    "run_id": "run-2026-04-05_2040",
    "goal": "Implement feature X with parallel execution",
    "created_at": "2026-04-05T20:40:00Z",
    "planner_version": "v1",
    "tasks": [
      {
        "task_id": "task-001",
        "title": "Add schema validator",
        "wave": 1,
        "contract_path": "tasks/feature-x/contracts/task-001.json",
        "result_path": "tasks/feature-x/results/task-001.json",
        "check_path": "tasks/feature-x/checks/task-001.json",
        "status": "ready"
      }
    ]
  },
  "task-contract.json": {
    "task_id": "task-001",
    "goal": "Add schema validator for worker outputs",
    "dependencies": [],
    "allowed_inputs": [

Proposed Wave Pattern

For a large project, the base loop looks like this:

Wave 0: Planning / compilation

One planner agent or planner stack reads the goal and produces:

  • task decomposition
  • dependency graph
  • owned file paths
  • required outputs
  • acceptance checks
  • checker assignments

Wave 1: Worker execution

Many worker agents run in parallel. Each worker gets:

  • one task contract
  • one write scope
  • one output path
  • explicit exclusions

Their job is execution, not coordination.

Wave 2: Checking

Checkers verify outputs against the same contract. This includes two kinds of checking:

  • deterministic checks
  • judgment checks

Deterministic checks should be preferred where possible:

  • file exists
  • schema valid
  • required sections present
  • forbidden files untouched
  • tests/lints pass

Judgment checks remain necessary for:

  • whether the task intent was actually satisfied
  • whether reasoning is coherent
  • whether obvious edge cases were missed

Wave 3: Reduction / adjudication

Reducers summarize completed work for the next wave. Adjudicators only read failures, conflicts, or disputed checks.

Wave 4+: Repeat

Any tasks whose dependencies are now satisfied become eligible for execution. The cycle repeats until the whole dependency graph is complete.

Scheduler State Machine

Task states:

  • pending = known to the planner but not yet dependency-satisfied
  • ready = all hard dependencies passed; safe to launch
  • running = worker currently executing
  • passed = worker finished and checker passed
  • failed = worker or checker produced a blocking failure
  • blocked = cannot run because a dependency failed or artifact is missing
  • needs-adjudication = conflicting or ambiguous result requires a higher-order decision

Dependency types:

  • hard = downstream task cannot start until upstream passed
  • soft = downstream may start, but checker should note upstream failure or absence
  • informational = included for context only; does not affect readiness

Unlock rule:

  • a task enters ready only when all hard dependencies are in passed
  • if any hard dependency is failed, downstream task becomes blocked
  • if any hard dependency is needs-adjudication, downstream task remains pending
  • soft dependency failure does not block launch but is recorded in downstream context

Wave advancement rule:

  • a wave is complete when every task in that wave is in passed, failed, or needs-adjudication
  • blocked tasks count as not-finished for the current wave until the orchestrator records the upstream cause and converts them to terminal blocked
  • reducer runs after wave completion
  • next wave launch set is the subset of pending tasks promoted to ready by reducer + state rules

Retry exhaustion rule:

  • if a worker retry budget is exhausted and the artifact is still invalid, task becomes failed
  • if two independent failures point to contract ambiguity rather than worker execution, task becomes needs-adjudication with recommended_action = rewrite-contract

Reducer authority rule:

  • reducers recommend promotions and summarize state
  • only the orchestrator writes status transitions back into task-manifest.json

Threshold definitions for this draft:

  • repeated failure = two failed executions of the same contract with materially similar blocking findings
  • fixable by rewrite = failure mode limited to missing sections, malformed schema, or incomplete artifact with no forbidden-file writes

The Two New Loopholes Introduced By Scale

Scaling to 100 workers does not remove failure. It moves failure into the control plane.

Loophole 1: Bad task generation

If the planner or task generator makes bad contracts, 100 agents can produce 100 wrong results very quickly.

This is the "fast wrong answer" failure mode.

Loophole 2: Bad checking

If the checker is weak, superficial, or poorly scoped, the system can certify bad work as complete.

This is the "false confidence" failure mode.

These are more dangerous than slow execution because they scale error.

Failure Policy

Failure caseDetection methodRetry countDownstream effectResolver
Worker timeoutwall-clock exceeds task budget1 automatic retryblocks hard dependentsorchestrator
Missing artifactexpected output file absent0task = failed, hard dependents blockedworker or orchestrator
Schema-invalid outputdeterministic validator fail1 if fixable by rewritetask = failed until passing result existschecker then worker
Forbidden-file writeowned-path validator or diff check0immediate needs-adjudicationadjudicator + human if risky
Partial task completionrequired sections/checks missing1hard dependents remain pendingworker
Checker disagreementtwo checkers disagree on pass/fail0task = needs-adjudicationadjudicator
Bad planner contractrepeated worker/checker inability tied to contract ambiguity0all dependents remain pendingplanner/human

Policy notes:

  • no downstream hard-dependent task should run after a blocking checker failure
  • repeated failure on the same contract is evidence of a contract problem, not just a worker problem
  • adjudication should read artifacts and checks, not restart the whole wave by default

Implication: Prompts Cannot Be The Source Of Truth

Prompt quality still matters, but prompts should be generated from contracts rather than serving as the source of truth themselves.

The source of truth should be a task contract with fields like:

  • task_id
  • goal
  • dependencies
  • allowed_inputs
  • owned_files
  • forbidden_files
  • expected_outputs
  • acceptance_checks
  • escalation_conditions

Then:

  • worker prompts are compiled from the contract
  • checker prompts are compiled from the same contract
  • reducers read contract + outputs, not oral history

This reduces drift between what was asked, what was built, and what was checked.

Model Specialization Still Matters

The repo already contains a strong pattern here:

  • cheap/faster agents for scanning, extraction, and bounded transformation
  • stronger/slower agents for synthesis, planning, and adjudication

The orchestration layer should preserve that split.

A likely pattern:

  • cheap workers for narrow independent tasks
  • stronger planner for task compilation
  • stronger reducer for strategic synthesis
  • checker mix depending on task type

This is not a commitment to specific model names. It is a role split.

Measurable Acceptance Criteria

The orchestrator is only successful if it can satisfy concrete checks:

  1. 0 worker writes occur outside declared owned_files.
  2. 100% of tasks that reach passed have a valid task-result.json and check-result.json.
  3. A failed checker on a hard dependency prevents downstream launch.
  4. The scheduler can execute a 10-task DAG with at least 3 dependency layers without manual state tracking.
  5. The reducer can produce a valid reduction-summary.json after each completed wave.
  6. Human intervention is required only for ambiguity, checker disagreement, forbidden-file writes, or repeated contract failure.
  7. A cold implementer can reconstruct task state from artifacts on disk without reading prior chat history.

Validation Fixtures

The first implementation should ship with explicit fixture scenarios so the orchestrator can be tested mechanically.

Fixture 1: Canonical 10-task DAG

  • 10 tasks
  • 3 dependency layers
  • mixed hard and informational dependencies
  • expected outcome: tasks unlock in topological order and all terminal artifacts are present

Fixture 2: Forbidden-write violation

  • worker writes outside owned_files
  • expected outcome: checker emits blocking finding, task enters needs-adjudication, no hard dependents launch

Fixture 3: Checker disagreement

  • checker A passes, checker B fails on the same artifact
  • expected outcome: task enters needs-adjudication, reducer does not promote dependents

Fixture 4: Contract ambiguity

  • two workers fail with similar blocking findings caused by vague acceptance criteria
  • expected outcome: task receives recommended_action = rewrite-contract, planner/human review required

Each fixture should define:

  • input manifest and contracts
  • expected task states after each wave
  • expected artifact files on disk
  • expected reducer output

What This Is Not Yet

This is not yet an implementation plan.

Open design questions remain:

  • When should the system use one checker vs. multiple independent checkers?
  • How much should be deterministic vs. LLM-based validation?
  • What is the first concurrency level worth benchmarking: 10, 20, or 40?
  • How much of the scheduler should live in code vs. in prompts + file conventions?

Most Important Takeaway

The scaling problem is not primarily "how many agents can run."

It is:

Can the system preserve coherence, trust, and low human mental load while many agents run in parallel?

If yes, high concurrency is useful. If no, a 100-agent swarm is just a faster way to create confusion.

Calibration & bench
Code Search Experiment: Grep vs Semantic vs Hybrid
An experiment: hybrid beat semantic beat grep for cold repo understanding — and all three agents reported 8/10 confidence regardless of actual quality.

Code Search Experiment: Grep vs Semantic vs Hybrid

date: 2026-04-05 20:47 status: experiment - completed depends_on:

  • brainstorm/05_2026-03-22_1635_agent-bootstrap-and-context-design-brainstorm.md
  • brainstorm/17_2026-04-03_0946_haiku-opus-planning-pattern.md
  • brainstorm/18_2026-04-03_0950_haiku-context-consolidation-for-planning.md

Why Run This

If future subagents need fast repo understanding, retrieval quality matters.

The practical question is not "is grep good?" or "is semantic search good?" The practical question is:

What search strategy best recovers the true control plane of this repo when an agent starts cold?

This matters because cold subagents are often asked to:

  • orient to an unfamiliar codebase
  • identify bootstrap files
  • explain the repo simply
  • avoid stale docs and outdated summaries

Experimental Setup

Three no-context explorer subagents were given the same task:

Understand the entire codebase well enough to answer: "What bootstraps this repo, how does it work, and how should a fresh agent orient quickly?"

Each run had a different retrieval constraint:

Condition A: grep-only

  • allowed: rg, rg --files, sed, ls, direct file reads
  • disallowed: semantic/codebase search

Condition B: semantic-only

  • allowed: semantic/codebase search plus targeted file reads
  • disallowed as the primary discovery method: broad rg, grep, find

Condition C: hybrid

  • allowed: semantic/codebase search for discovery
  • allowed: rg and direct reads for exact verification and drift checking

All three agents were asked to return:

  • bootstrap file list
  • simplest project explanation
  • method limitations and likely misses
  • confidence score

Run Protocol

This experiment was run under the following concrete conditions:

  • date: 2026-04-05
  • workspace: /Users/isaacchen/princeton-intern-ai-project
  • repo revision at run time: 969d3b73d33849a40b71b3ae011b45e1bcdae88f
  • repo cleanliness: dirty working tree; results therefore reflect the local working copy, not a pristine commit snapshot
  • subagent type: explorer
  • model for all three runs: gpt-5.4-mini
  • reasoning effort for all three runs: low
  • execution style: cold start, no prior repo context forked into the subagent
  • stopping condition: each subagent stops when it can answer the task with a bootstrap list, simple explanation, likely misses, and confidence score

Exact task prompt shared across all three runs:

Understand the entire codebase well enough to answer: "What bootstraps this repo, how does it work, and how should a fresh agent orient quickly?"

Condition-specific retrieval constraints:

  • grep-only:
  • allowed: rg, rg --files, sed, ls, direct file reads
  • disallowed: semantic/codebase search
  • semantic-only:
  • allowed: semantic/codebase search plus targeted file reads
  • disallowed as primary discovery method: broad rg, grep, find
  • hybrid:
  • allowed: semantic/codebase search for discovery
  • allowed: rg and direct reads for exact verification and drift checking

Subagent identities for traceability:

  • grep-only: 019d6042-76ce-7162-829f-c307fe8c9b8f
  • semantic-only: 019d6042-76f3-7631-819a-a4f646c40e94
  • hybrid: 019d6042-76fc-71f2-b5da-b93f81242a21

Known reproducibility caveat:

  • the semantic condition was constrained at the agent instruction layer, but the semantic subtool itself may still rely on literal mechanisms internally

Evaluation Criteria

Each run was judged on:

  1. Did it recover the true canonical bootstrap chain?
  2. Did it identify the actual runtime center of gravity?
  3. Did it distinguish current truth from stale repo surfaces?
  4. Did it over-promote support docs into bootstrap truth?
  5. Would its answer be safe to hand to a fresh agent?

For this repo, the authoritative baseline for comparison is:

  • CANONICAL.md
  • data/goal-config.yaml
  • data/runtime-state.yaml
  • data/live-baseline.yaml
  • data/next-batch.yaml
  • data/task_manifest.json

Scoring Rubric

Each run was judged by the primary agent against the canonical surfaces above.

Scoring dimensions:

  • 0-2 canonical bootstrap recovery
  • 0-2 runtime center-of-gravity recovery
  • 0-2 stale-surface and drift detection
  • 0-2 precision of bootstrap set
  • 0-2 safety for handing to a fresh agent

Interpretation:

  • 0 = failed badly on that dimension
  • 1 = partially correct / mixed
  • 2 = clearly correct and usable

Tie-break rule:

  • when total scores are close, prefer the method that better distinguishes canonical truth from stale supporting docs

False-positive rule:

  • a file counts as a false positive if it is elevated into the bootstrap/control-plane set even though it is better classified as support, validation, or historical context rather than canonical truth or primary runtime entry

Confidence-scale rule:

  • subagent-reported confidence was recorded, but ranking was based on judged retrieval quality rather than self-confidence

Results

A. grep-only

What it did well:

  • recovered the canonical read chain correctly
  • identified scripts/assemble-prompts.py as the executable center of gravity
  • caught important drift in README.md, .factory/services.yaml, and some INDEX.md files
  • produced a usable orientation answer without semantic help

What it got wrong or fuzzy:

  • still elevated some support/config surfaces like .factory/services.yaml into the bootstrap set
  • static reading of large scripts left some deeper helper behavior unverified
  • strong result here depends on this repo having unusually explicit canonical files

Assessment:

  • better than expected for a literal-only run
  • repo-specific success, not proof that grep is generally enough

B. semantic-only

What it did well:

  • found the correct control-plane surfaces quickly
  • recovered the canonical docs, YAMLs, orchestrator manual, and key scripts
  • explained the repo well as a file-driven orchestration framework
  • identified several stale surfaces and control-plane drifts

What it got wrong or fuzzy:

  • included some support materials (.factory/*) in the bootstrap set
  • semantic discovery was strong, but exact verification was still weaker than hybrid
  • the semantic tool itself may still rely on literal mechanisms internally, so this was semantically guided discovery rather than a purely non-literal pipeline

Assessment:

  • very good discovery
  • somewhat weaker than hybrid on exactness and drift verification

C. hybrid

What it did well:

  • recovered the canonical read chain and the actual runtime entrypoints
  • verified exact script ownership for Wave 1, 2a, 2b, 4, and 5
  • clearly distinguished canonical truth from stale summaries
  • found multiple live drifts:
  • stale current-bridge references in summaries
  • inconsistent preflight state in data/next-batch.yaml
  • old 3-wave validation in .factory/services.yaml

What it got wrong or fuzzy:

  • still did not execute a full batch, so runtime behavior remained inferred from scripts and files
  • large scripts were sampled in relevant sections rather than fully audited

Assessment:

  • best overall balance
  • safest result to hand to a fresh agent

Key evidence extracted from the three outputs:

  • all three runs recovered the canonical read chain unusually well
  • all three identified scripts/assemble-prompts.py as the main executable center of gravity
  • both semantic-only and hybrid explicitly identified stale or inconsistent repo surfaces
  • hybrid was the strongest at exact drift checking, especially around data/next-batch.yaml and .factory/services.yaml

Evidence limitation:

  • raw subagent outputs were not separately archived to disk during this run; the evidence preserved here is the summarized comparison plus the subagent IDs above

Ranking

For this repo, the ranking is:

  1. hybrid
  2. semantic-only
  3. grep-only

Important nuance:

grep-only performed unusually well because this repo has a strong literal control plane:

  • CANONICAL.md explicitly defines authority
  • canonical YAMLs are easy to find by name
  • script names map directly to waves

In a messier codebase with weaker naming and less explicit authority structure, the gap between grep-only and semantic-first would likely widen.

Main Lessons

Lesson 1: semantic search is best for discovery

Use semantic/codebase search when the agent knows the idea but not the exact word.

Examples:

  • "what bootstraps this repo?"
  • "what is the control plane?"
  • "where does orchestration live?"

Lesson 2: grep is best for exact verification

Use rg when the agent needs:

  • exact path
  • exact script name
  • exact string
  • exact count
  • exact drift verification

Lesson 3: hybrid is the default for cold subagents

The best pattern is:

  1. semantic search to locate the likely structure
  2. rg plus direct reads to verify exact files and current truth
  3. canonical files to arbitrate conflicts when summaries disagree

Recommended Rule For Future Subagents

If a subagent needs repo context and starts cold:

  1. start with semantic/codebase discovery
  2. immediately verify candidate bootstrap files and entrypoints with rg and direct reads
  3. trust canonical surfaces over summaries and indexes when they disagree

Suggested bootstrap sequence for this repo:

  1. CANONICAL.md
  2. data/goal-config.yaml
  3. data/runtime-state.yaml
  4. data/live-baseline.yaml
  5. data/next-batch.yaml
  6. current session bridge from runtime-state.yaml
  7. scripts/INDEX.md and brainstorm/agent-manuals/INDEX.md only after the canonical chain

Limitation Of This Experiment

This experiment tested repo understanding, not end-to-end execution.

It does not prove:

  • which method best debugs runtime failures
  • which method best edits code
  • which method best handles symbol-level refactors

It does show which retrieval strategy best recovers the repo's top-level operating model from a cold start.

Rerun Instructions

To rerun this experiment faithfully:

  1. Pin the repo to a specific commit and record whether the tree is dirty.
  2. Use three cold no-context explorer agents with the same model and reasoning effort.
  3. Reuse the exact shared task prompt and retrieval constraints above.
  4. Judge outputs against the same canonical surfaces and the same 0-2 rubric.
  5. Record for each run:
  • bootstrap files recovered
  • false positives
  • drift detections
  • self-confidence
  • elapsed time
  1. Preserve raw outputs to disk in a future rerun if stronger auditability is needed.

Bottom Line

For codebase understanding, grep and semantic search solve different problems.

  • grep gives exact text retrieval
  • semantic search gives meaning-based discovery
  • hybrid gives the best result because it combines structure discovery with exact verification

For this repo, the default should remain:

semantic discovery first, rg verification second, canonical files as tie-breaker

Mission-Controlled Workflow Atlas
Downstream agents depend on the upstream verification record, not on the artifact merely existing — failure becomes a controlled state, not improvisation.

Mission-Controlled Workflow Atlas

date: 2026-04-08 15:45 status: design spec - implementation target depends_on:

  • brainstorm/20_2026-04-05_2040_parallel-agent-wave-orchestration.md
  • brainstorm/05_2026-03-22_1635_agent-bootstrap-and-context-design-brainstorm.md
  • brainstorm/17_2026-04-03_0946_haiku-opus-planning-pattern.md
  • brainstorm/18_2026-04-03_0950_haiku-context-consolidation-for-planning.md

The Problem

The book/chapter metaphor is good for human orientation, but weak for agent execution. It implies a mostly linear narrative, soft closure, and a vague relationship between progress and proof.

Long-running multi-agent work needs four things at once:

  • a human-readable map
  • machine-readable execution state
  • strict handoff contracts
  • continuous verification and failure logging

No single simple metaphor covers all four well.

Core Conclusion

The most useful agent-translated metaphor is layered:

  • Atlas for human navigation
  • Workflow graph / leased jobs for execution
  • Sealed work packets for handoffs between agents and stations
  • Mission control for verification, anomaly tracking, and release decisions

This is better than a pure book metaphor because it preserves readability while making state, concurrency, retries, evidence, and publish gates explicit.

Short version:

humans read an atlas agents run leased jobs handoffs move as sealed packets verification is mission control

Production Mapping

The layered metaphor now maps to concrete repo surfaces.

ConceptRepo surface
atlastasks/<workspace>/index.md + task-manifest.json
routetasks/<workspace>/routes/<route-id>.json
execute stationtasks/<workspace>/jobs/<job-id>.json where station=execute
verify stationtasks/<workspace>/jobs/<job-id>.json where station=verify + checks/<job-id>.json
publish stationtasks/<workspace>/publishes/<route-id>.json
sealed packettasks/<workspace>/packets/<packet-id>.json
anomaly streamtasks/<workspace>/anomalies/<anomaly-id>.json
black box evidencetasks/<workspace>/evidence/<attempt-or-check-id>.json + stdout/stderr artifacts

This is the operational cutover:

  • lower waves (1 -> 2a -> 2b -> 3) use the route/station control plane now
  • higher waves (4 -> 5) remain wave-scoped until the same station model is extended upward
  • canonical runtime state still lives in data/*.yaml; task workspaces are operational control surfaces, not canonical truth

Route Lifecycle

The production lifecycle is:

  1. plan
  2. execute
  3. structural_check
  4. verify
  5. publish

In the current implementation:

  • plan is expressed by the workspace builder and packet contracts
  • execute is a route execute job
  • structural_check is deterministic output/path/shape checking recorded in checks/
  • verify is either a generic verifier job or a dedicated checker script
  • publish is a recorded clearance object in publishes/

Route state model:

  • blocked
  • ready
  • running
  • needs_verify
  • verified
  • published
  • failed_retryable
  • failed_terminal
  • superseded

Job state model:

  • blocked
  • ready
  • running
  • passed
  • failed
  • superseded

Promotion rule:

  • downstream execute jobs depend on upstream verify jobs, not just artifact existence
  • route publish records are the durable proof that a downstream route is allowed to trust the upstream route

Layer 1: Atlas For Human Navigation

The atlas is the human-facing surface. It answers:

  • what the project is trying to do
  • what major routes exist
  • what route depends on what
  • what is blocked, active, or done

Core units:

  • atlas
  • route
  • waypoint
  • gate
  • artifact

Suggested meanings:

  • atlas = whole project
  • route = major workstream or objective
  • waypoint = concrete step inside a route
  • gate = a required check before downstream trust
  • artifact = output or evidence object

Why this layer matters:

  • it is intuitive for humans
  • it supports lookup and branching better than a book
  • it makes prerequisites visible without implying everything is linear

Layer 2: Workflow Graph For Agent Execution

The atlas is not enough for orchestration. Underneath it, the system should run as a workflow graph of leased jobs.

Core units:

  • job
  • dependency edge
  • lease
  • attempt
  • checkpoint
  • merge/integration job

This layer answers:

  • what can run now
  • who owns it
  • what inputs are required
  • whether it may retry
  • what downstream work becomes ready when it passes

Minimum state model:

  • blocked
  • ready
  • leased
  • running
  • needs_verify
  • verified
  • failed_retryable
  • failed_terminal
  • superseded
  • published

Dependency types should be explicit:

  • requires
  • blocks
  • informs
  • soft_dep
  • parallel_ok

Why this layer matters:

  • it supports concurrency safely
  • it makes retries and resumability explicit
  • it prevents narrative structure from masquerading as a scheduler

Layer 3: Sealed Work Packets For Handoffs

Agents should not work from broad conversational context when a bounded packet will do.

A work packet is the contract that moves through stations such as:

  1. intake
  2. plan
  3. execute
  4. structural check
  5. verify
  6. publish or rework

Minimum packet objects:

  • WorkPacket
  • packet_id
  • route_id
  • job_id
  • goal
  • scope_in
  • scope_out
  • dependencies_required
  • inputs
  • deliverable
  • done_when
  • failure_if
  • PlanContract
  • substeps
  • ordering
  • parallelizable_steps
  • risk_points
  • evidence_required
  • ExecutionContract
  • allowed_surfaces
  • forbidden_surfaces
  • deliverable_shape
  • assumptions_to_log
  • stop_conditions
  • DefectReport
  • defect_id
  • failure_type
  • severity
  • evidence
  • contract_broken
  • rework_target
  • VerificationContract
  • claims_to_check
  • checks_required
  • downstream_compatibility_checks
  • pass_threshold
  • allowed_residual_risk
  • HandoffRecord
  • what_changed
  • artifacts_produced
  • evidence_attached
  • known_limits
  • next_station

Why this layer matters:

  • it gives each agent a bounded local truth
  • it makes executor/verifier separation natural
  • it turns rework into a controlled state transition instead of an ad hoc conversation

Layer 4: Mission Control For Verification

Mission control is the verification and monitoring layer. It should exist throughout the run, not only at publishing time.

Core units:

  • anomaly stream
  • incident log
  • black box record
  • clearance gate
  • rollback plan

This layer answers:

  • what is failing right now
  • what evidence exists
  • what was verified vs assumed
  • whether the current state is safe to promote
  • how to recover if a release goes bad

Error records should be first-class objects, not closure footnotes.

Minimum anomaly fields:

  • anomaly_id
  • route_id
  • job_id
  • attempt_id
  • timestamp
  • failure_type
  • severity
  • evidence_refs
  • repro_steps
  • status

Black box records should preserve:

  • diffs
  • logs
  • test outputs
  • traces
  • snapshots
  • commands run

Why this layer matters:

  • defects are discovered continuously, not only at the end
  • publish/release requires a stronger proof standard than build completion
  • replacement agents need replayable evidence, not oral history

Current Lower-Wave Cutover

The implemented lower-wave harness uses this mapping for each route:

  • scientist route:
  • execute = analysis generation
  • verify = contract/evidence check on the analysis
  • publish = route clearance for downstream L1 work
  • L1 route:
  • execute = session bridge synthesis
  • verify = contract/evidence check on the synthesis
  • publish = route clearance for downstream Wave 2b work
  • Wave 2b route:
  • execute = graph delta proposal generation
  • verify = dedicated proposal validator plus route check record
  • publish = route clearance for downstream Wave 3 work
  • memory route:
  • execute = durable summary generation
  • verify = contract/evidence check on the summary
  • publish = durable route clearance inside the workspace

This is the current production target because it breaks the old error chain:

  • artifact exists is no longer sufficient
  • downstream readiness comes from verified upstream state
  • publish records make replacement workers and reruns reconstructable from disk

What Publishing Becomes

Publishing should become launch clearance, not a vague final chapter.

Launch clearance means:

  • the promotable artifact matches the verified artifact
  • critical gates have passed
  • residual risks are explicit
  • rollback steps exist
  • release evidence is attached to the exact version being promoted

Publishing is still the same broad lifecycle:

  • plan the release
  • run the release checks
  • decide go / no-go

But it is verification-dominant rather than build-dominant.

Recommended Terminology Mapping

If the team wants to keep the original book language for readability, translate it like this:

  • book -> atlas
  • chapter -> route
  • section -> waypoint
  • chapter plan -> route brief plus PlanContract
  • build -> leased job execution
  • closure -> structural gate plus anomaly review
  • publish -> launch clearance

This preserves the human story while making the agent-facing layer operational.

Prompting Implications

Prompts should target station contracts, not broad route narratives.

Examples:

  • planner prompt:
  • write PlanContract for this WorkPacket
  • do not execute
  • optimize for minimal steps, explicit evidence, and verifier-ready outputs
  • executor prompt:
  • satisfy this ExecutionContract only
  • if blocked or contradicted, emit DefectReport instead of improvising
  • structural checker prompt:
  • identify failures that would break downstream route consumption
  • verifier prompt:
  • judge only against the VerificationContract
  • return pass, pass_with_risk, or fail
  • release prompt:
  • decide launch clearance from evidence, gates, and residual risk

The general rule is:

prompt by proof obligations and failure targets, not by activity

Bounded Exploration

The prompt should be strict about authority and outputs, but it should not force the agent into blind literalism.

Some tasks require bounded expansion:

  • following a suspected failure into adjacent files
  • reading one layer deeper to verify a contract mismatch
  • comparing a declared workflow against the actual runtime surface
  • widening from one artifact to a small local neighborhood when the task is explicitly failure-hunting

This should be explicit in the prompt instead of left to agent instinct.

Bad pattern:

  • find failures in these files

Good pattern:

  • find structural failures of type X in these files
  • you may expand to adjacent files only when needed to verify a concrete failure hypothesis
  • every expansion must be justified by the suspected failure class
  • every reported failure must cite the file and line evidence that made the expansion necessary

The rule is:

tight contracts for outputs, bounded freedom for investigation

Prompts should not ask agents to be open-ended general critics. They should ask agents to perform controlled exploration inside an explicit failure space.

Bounded exploration is opt-in by contract. No role receives it merely because the atlas describes it. If a role manual or station overlay does not explicitly grant an exploration envelope, that role remains closed execute.

Failure-Finding Is A Distinct Prompt Mode

find failures is not the same task as extract facts or execute contract.

Failure-finding prompts should change the agent's search posture in four ways:

  1. they permit wider local exploration than a normal extractor prompt
  2. they require explicit comparison against an intended contract, workflow, or design goal
  3. they require separating real failures from style differences, future work, and uncertainty
  4. they require a stronger evidence threshold before a claim is emitted

Failure-finding should therefore be treated as its own station/prompt mode, not as a casual instruction suffix.

Useful failure classes include:

  • structural_failure
  • parallelism_failure
  • handoff_failure
  • verification_gap
  • authority_drift
  • designed_vs_operational_drift
  • stale_surface
  • prompt_contract_gap

When the prompt names the failure class, the agent gets room to think without getting room to hallucinate.
