Role Posture Split

Use this split to decide whether a role should stay file-local, receive a bounded exploration envelope, or be allowed to hunt failures explicitly.

posturemeaningcurrent roles
closed executesatisfies a narrow assigned contract against injected materials only; no investigative widening unless a local contract says otherwisescientist, literature_synthesis, memory, base-manual inheritance by default
bounded investigativemay compare across injected materials or a locally granted neighborhood to satisfy a named contract; still not a verifier or publish gateplanner (future harness pattern), batch-scoped investigative roles such as l1_cross_pollinator once locally patched
audit / failure-huntexplicitly hunts named failure classes with bounded exploration, evidence thresholds, downgrade rules, and stop conditionshaiku_context_consolidator

This posture split is intentionally narrower than the full role list. A role is not investigative by default just because it performs synthesis. The local manual or station overlay must grant that posture explicitly.

Prompt Contract Stack

The repo already implies a standard compiled prompt order. The atlas should name it directly so future harness work does not rebuild it from scripts by inference.

Standard Order

  1. bootstrap authority
  • CANONICAL.md re-entry chain for orchestrator/planner roles
  • base manual first for roles whose manuals explicitly require it
  1. role manual
  • the role-specific contract, scope limits, schema, and completion signal
  1. station overlay
  • planner / executor / synthesis / graph / release framing for the current run
  1. WorkPacket or task block
  • exact scope, inputs, output path, decision step, rationale
  1. evidence surfaces
  • only the files, findings, graph context, or papers that the role is allowed to use
  1. verification / failure clause
  • failure definition, escalation rule, and exact return contract
  1. exploration envelope when the task is investigative rather than purely extractive
  • allowed expansion scope, evidence threshold, and stopping rules

Mandatory Steering Fields

Every compiled prompt should declare these steering fields explicitly, even if they are distributed across the manual and the task block. For closed execute roles, the exploration envelope should be explicit as none or equivalent local wording.

  • objective
  • severity filter
  • trigger condition
  • failure definition
  • exclusions
  • exploration envelope

This is the minimum prompt skeleton that keeps a role from drifting into prose, shallow work, or unauthorized inference.

Exploration Envelope

The exploration envelope is the part of the prompt that tells the agent how much legitimate investigation is allowed.

It should answer:

  • allowed_expansion_scope
  • what adjacent files, indexes, packets, or logs may be read beyond the initial target
  • failure_hypotheses
  • what kinds of issues justify leaving the initial file set
  • evidence_threshold
  • what level of proof is required before reporting a failure
  • non_failure_classes
  • what should be reported as style drift, uncertainty, or future work instead of failure
  • stop_conditions
  • when the agent must stop expanding and return with either findings or insufficiency

This is what turns intuition into a contract surface. Without it, open-ended prompts drift into either shallow literalism or confident nonsense.

Reusable Failure-Finding Pattern

For audit, checker, planner, and meta-intelligence roles, the prompt should include a compact failure-finding block like this:

  • failure_class
  • the exact category under review, such as structural_failure or parallelism_failure
  • comparison_target
  • the contract, design goal, or runtime invariant the files are being judged against
  • seed_surfaces
  • the initial files or artifacts to start from
  • allowed_expansion_scope
  • what additional files may be opened if a concrete failure hypothesis requires it
  • reporting_threshold
  • line-referenced evidence required for a real finding
  • downgrade_rules
  • when to emit style difference, uncertain, or future work instead of failure
  • termination_rule
  • stop when additional reads no longer produce new in-scope evidence

Short version:

explore more, but only for a reason

This pattern is especially important for:

  • repo audits
  • stale-surface passes
  • prompt audits
  • framework drift reviews
  • planner/adjudicator roles
  • any agent asked to find failures rather than merely summarize a file

Return Contracts

station typereturns
plannerPlanContract or task-manifest fragment

synthesis rolesynthesis artifact at pre-assigned path plus exact completion signal
graph roleproposed-edges.yaml + graph-delta.md

Existing Mismatches Worth Naming

  • literature_synthesis currently behaves like base -> literature conceptually, but the live builder injects only the literature manual
  • memory manuals require the standard Done ... Output: ... contract, but the live builder still emits summary: in the final instruction
  • l1_cross_pollinator and l2_cross_pollinator both have small live-builder/manual mismatches around what upstream context is explicitly injected

The harness should treat those as reconciliation tasks, not silent variance.

Hard rule:

create a new manual only when at least one of these changes: output schema, authority surface, or allowed write scope

If those stay the same, prefer a station overlay or a task-block variant.

Prompt Direction By Active Agent Role

The current manuals do not support one generic worker prompt. They imply a typed prompt object per manualized role.

Shared shape:

PromptObject:
  role:
  manual_stack:
  required_inputs:
  forbidden_scope:
  expected_completion_signal:
  escalation_or_failure_behavior:

Notes:

  • the base operating manual is a shared dependency for scientist, literature_synthesis, and memory, not a standalone agent role
  • only manualized roles belong in this map
  • the digestion schema/chunk/master-index agents should not get stable prompt objects until they have manuals

orchestrator

  • prompt_object: OrchestratorControlPrompt
  • manual_stack: CANONICAL.md re-entry chain -> 04_2026-03-22_1653_orchestrator-agent-manual.md
  • required_inputs:
  • data/goal-config.yaml
  • data/runtime-state.yaml
  • data/live-baseline.yaml
  • data/next-batch.yaml
  • memory/finding-registry-snapshot.yaml
  • memory/calibration/calibration-map.yaml
  • memory/calibration/esig-weights.yaml
  • forbidden_scope:
  • scientific reasoning or wetlab interpretation
  • reading scientist outputs for scientific content
  • skipping waves, bypassing trigger scripts, or reconstructing project state if data/runtime-state.yaml is missing
  • expected_completion_signal:
  • no freeform narrative completion
  • a spawn step is complete only when the five-condition spawn contract is satisfied
  • every spawned agent must return Done. [timestamp] Output: [file path]
  • escalation_or_failure_behavior:
  • halt and report if data/runtime-state.yaml is missing
  • halt and report if a script and the manual disagree
  • report and stop on failed preflight, failed proposal validation, or trigger-script error exit
  • treat any missing spawn contract field as a blocker
  • if one targeted retrieval still cannot resolve a decision, flag a blocker rather than loading more context

scientist

  • prompt_object: ScientistAnalysisPrompt
  • manual_stack: 01_2026-03-22_1650_base-operating-manual.md -> 02_2026-03-22_1651_scientist-agent-manual.md
  • required_inputs:
  • GOAL CONFIG
  • TASK BLOCK
  • MASTER DATA INDEX plus ASSIGNED CHUNKS, or DATA SLICE in pre-digestion mode
  • PRIOR FINDINGS BLOCK
  • FOCUS COLUMNS
  • YOUR SPECIFIC QUESTION
  • optional CP RATIONALE
  • forbidden_scope:
  • planning next work
  • writing shared state
  • reading beyond injected context
  • returning anything except one analysis file plus one completion line
  • expected_completion_signal: Done. [YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC] Output: [absolute path]
  • escalation_or_failure_behavior:
  • if a column meaning is unclear, write column interpretation uncertain instead of silently relabeling it
  • if the data cannot answer the question, say so explicitly in What The Data Cannot Answer
  • if the dataset already ran the proposed experiment, do not re-propose it; state what prior experiments showed and why any new proposal is different
  • if a schema field cannot be supported, write unknown rather than omit it

literature_synthesis

  • prompt_object: LiteratureSynthesisPrompt
  • manual_stack: 01_2026-03-22_1650_base-operating-manual.md -> 06_2026-04-01_1200_literature-synthesis-manual.md
  • required_inputs:
  • GOAL CONFIG
  • TASK BLOCK
  • PRIOR FINDINGS BLOCK
  • injected PAPER ABSTRACTS/METHODS
  • forbidden_scope:
  • inventing data or citing papers not injected
  • conflating enrichment results with pure A6 results
  • treating percent removal as defluorination without fluoride evidence
  • inventing a custom schema
  • expected_completion_signal: Done. [YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC] Output: [absolute path]
  • escalation_or_failure_behavior:
  • if a paper did not measure something, say so directly rather than speculate
  • if the literature does not test a mechanism, write not yet tested in published literature
  • every gap must be labeled confirmed_gap or unconfirmed_gap
  • if a numeric calibration range is unsupported, write predicted_range: "not_quantifiable_from_literature"

  • prompt_object: L2StrategicSynthesisPrompt
  • manual_stack: 08_2026-04-02_1022_l2-cross-pollinator-manual.md

  • forbidden_scope:
  • re-reading individual scientist outputs
  • proposing specific next-batch tasks

  • creating new graph nodes
  • expected_completion_signal: Done. [YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC] Output: [full file path]

  • if a claim would require surfaces that were not injected, say the evidence is unavailable in this run
  • if a section has nothing to report, write None identified plus the reason; do not omit the section
  • if a pattern is based on one batch or cannot survive a This pattern is wrong if ... sentence, cut it or downgrade it to an open hypothesis
  • keep the standing Feammox counter until real Feammox lab evidence exists

l3_cross_pollinator

  • prompt_object: L3ProgramReviewPrompt
  • manual_stack: 09_2026-04-02_2200_l3-cross-pollinator-manual.md
  • required_inputs:
  • GOAL CONFIG
  • GRAPH STATS SUMMARY
  • the last 5 L2 SYNTHESIS DOCUMENTS
  • forbidden_scope:
  • reading scientist outputs, L1 syntheses, or raw node files
  • specific next-batch task assignment
  • single-batch or single-L2-run evidence framed as program drift
  • fabricating unsupported fields
  • expected_completion_signal: Done. [YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC] Output: [full file path to l3-strategic-synthesis.md]
  • escalation_or_failure_behavior:
  • if fewer than 2 L2 syntheses were provided, return only ERROR: Insufficient L2 syntheses to produce L3 synthesis. [N] received, minimum 2 required.
  • if a requested field is unsupported, write not available in provided inputs or not assessable from provided inputs
  • only report blindspots or unknowns that persist across multiple L2 runs

haiku_context_consolidator

  • prompt_object: HaikuContextConsolidatorPrompt
  • manual_stack: 10_2026-04-03_1000_haiku-context-consolidator-manual.md
  • required_inputs:
  • a prompt-level FAILURE TYPE assignment
  • repo-root CLAUDE.md
  • repo-root or prompt-supplied MEMORY.md
  • 6 to 10 high-signal traces selected from MEMORY.md
  • bidirectional checks against explored INDEX.md and CANONICAL.md surfaces
  • an explicit output path from the spawning prompt
  • forbidden_scope:
  • planning or recommending fixes
  • impact speculation
  • flagging non-assigned failure types as primary findings
  • unbounded deep traversal after the trace stops yielding new evidence
  • expected_completion_signal: Done. Output: [full absolute path] | failures_found: N | files_explored: N | trail_depth: N
  • escalation_or_failure_behavior:
  • if no FAILURE TYPE is assigned, return ERROR: no failure type assigned.
  • if MEMORY.md is missing, return ERROR: MEMORY.md not found at expected path.
  • if a file cannot be read, record the hop block plus the appropriate gap/failure record instead of guessing
  • stop descending when deeper reads no longer produce new relevant facts or new in-scope failures

The prompt-direction consequence is simple:

  • route-level language is for humans
  • prompt objects must bind to manualized agent roles
  • missing-input behavior must be explicit in the prompt object, not left to agent judgment
  • non-manualized roles should stay unstable until the manuals exist

Boundary To Deeper Specs

This document should stop at the layer where a human can understand the operating model and an implementer can see how the current manuals plug into it.

It should not absorb every lower-level spec.

Ownership boundary:

  • this atlas owns the layered metaphor, live role inventory, prompt-contract stack, and manual reuse rules
  • 20_2026-04-05_2040_parallel-agent-wave-orchestration.md owns the deeper orchestration-state and artifact-schema design
  • contract-fixtures.md plus the manuals own exact output schemas
  • the spawn builders and prompt assemblers own the concrete prompt bodies actually emitted at runtime

That split keeps this file implementation-oriented without turning it into a duplicate of the manuals, fixtures, and script code.

Proposed Task-Workspace Surfaces

If this is implemented in tasks/, the workspace should likely separate navigation, execution state, handoffs, anomalies, and evidence:

  • tasks/<project>/index.md -> atlas view for humans
  • tasks/<project>/routes/<route-id>.md -> route summary and decisions
  • tasks/<project>/jobs/<job-id>.json -> machine execution state
  • tasks/<project>/packets/<packet-id>.json -> handoff contracts
  • tasks/<project>/anomalies/<anomaly-id>.json -> persistent error stream
  • tasks/<project>/evidence/<artifact-id>/... -> logs, traces, diffs, outputs
  • tasks/<project>/publish/<release-id>.md -> launch clearance record

This is more explicit than the current convention-driven tasks/ layer and better aligned with long-running multi-agent work.

Why This Is The Better Translation

The book metaphor was useful because it introduced pacing, closure, and the idea that each major unit of work should feel complete before the next one trusts it.

The layered metaphor keeps that strength while fixing the operational gaps:

  • atlas solves navigation
  • workflow graph solves scheduling
  • work packets solve bounded execution and handoffs
  • mission control solves verification and release rigor

That is a better fit for agents because it matches how they actually fail:

  • stale assumptions
  • weak handoffs
  • hidden verification gaps
  • race conditions
  • lost state after interruption

The right system is not one pretty metaphor. It is one readable metaphor on top of several explicit operating models.

Addition to Prompt Engine: Scientific Theory Steering
Force deeper reasoning through question shape — one compound question per surface, with an escape hatch placed before it, targeting 20-40% usage.
2026-04-10

Addition to Prompt Engine: Scientific Theory Steering

Why This Exists

The current prompt system already has better authority boundaries, bounded exploration, and failure-finding posture than it did before. What it still needs is a stronger way to make models think scientifically without introducing new role classes or new control-plane variables.

This document is an additive prompt-engine brainstorm. The idea is simple:

  • do not ask for summary first
  • ask questions that force mechanism, contrast, falsification, and experimental discrimination

The target is deeper scientific thinking from the existing prompt system by making the question itself more structurally demanding.

Position Relative to Existing Docs

This file extends, but does not replace:

  • brainstorm/22_2026-04-08_1545_mission-controlled-workflow-atlas.md
  • brainstorm/2026-03-30_1028_prompting-strategy-and-session-learnings.md

The atlas already improves prompt contracts, role posture, and bounded exploration. This addition focuses on a narrower question:

How do we ask questions inside prompts so the model reasons more like a scientist?

Core Claim

Models stay shallow when prompts ask for:

  • summary
  • takeaways
  • what the literature says
  • what the result means

Models become more scientifically useful when prompts ask for:

  • the best mechanistic explanation
  • the strongest competing explanation
  • the main confounder or artifact explanation
  • the evidence that distinguishes the explanations
  • the condition where the preferred explanation fails
  • the smallest decisive experiment or measurement

So the prompt-engine improvement is not “say think harder.”

It is:

make the model do harder scientific moves.

Prompt Principle

Prefer explanation, contrast, and falsification over recap.

The right question shape is:

  1. explain the pattern
  2. challenge the explanation
  3. identify what is missing
  4. name what would change the conclusion
  5. propose the cleanest next test

That sequence is what makes the model spend more reasoning effort in a useful way.

Scientific-Theory Steering Moves

1. Mechanism

Ask:

  • What causal process could produce this result?
  • What mechanism best fits the observed pattern?

Do not ask only:

  • What happened?

2. Rival Explanation

Ask:

  • What is the strongest competing explanation?
  • What else could explain the same pattern without the preferred mechanism being true?

This prevents a one-track answer.

3. Confounder / Artifact Check

Ask:

  • What measurement artifact, dataset artifact, or hidden confounder could mimic this result?
  • What non-causal explanation remains plausible?

This is especially important for synthetic data, partial literature, and mixed environmental datasets.

4. Boundary Condition

Ask:

  • Under what conditions would this explanation stop being true?
  • Where would this conclusion break?

This pushes the model out of generic confidence and into actual limits.

5. Falsification

Ask:

  • What observation would most strongly weaken this explanation?
  • What evidence would change your mind?

This is the move that prevents “confident but untestable” reasoning.

6. Decisive Next Experiment

Ask:

  • What is the smallest decisive experiment or measurement that would distinguish explanation A from explanation B?

This is better than:

  • What should we do next?

because it asks for discrimination, not generic productivity.

Prompt Shapes To Prefer

Weak

What does this result mean?

Stronger

What mechanism most plausibly explains this result, what rival mechanism remains plausible, and what evidence would distinguish them?

Weak

What does the literature say about Feammox here?

Stronger

Does the literature support true defluorination here, or could the apparent effect be better explained by favorable chemistry, indirect transformation, or measurement artifact? What would falsify the leading view?

Weak

What should the next experiment be?

Stronger

What is the smallest decisive experiment that would rule out the strongest competing explanation?

Long Compound Question Types To Prefer

These are useful when the task is not just to identify one explanation, but to force the model to keep multiple scientific obligations active at once inside a single response.

1. Mechanism + Rival + Falsifier

Use a compound question like:

What mechanism most plausibly explains the observed pattern, what rival mechanism remains genuinely plausible even if the leading view is attractive, and what observation or measurement would most directly falsify the current favorite explanation?

Why it works:

  • it prevents early closure
  • it forces the model to hold both belief and doubt in working memory
  • it ends with a scientific stress test rather than a recap

2. Effect + Artifact + Discrimination

Use a compound question like:

If this apparent effect is real, what causal process would produce it, but if it is not real, what measurement artifact, preprocessing distortion, sampling bias, or hidden confounder could create the same surface pattern, and what evidence would cleanly separate those two stories?

Why it works:

  • it treats artifact explanations as first-class competitors
  • it is well suited to noisy environmental, observational, and partially reduced datasets

3. Theory + Context Shift + Failure Boundary

Use a compound question like:

Assuming the leading theory is correct under the current conditions, which environmental, chemical, biological, or sampling changes would make that theory stop generalizing, and which of those failure boundaries is most likely to matter first here?

Why it works:

  • it forces the model to reason about transfer, not just local fit
  • it turns confidence into a conditional scientific claim

4. Literature Agreement + Literature Tension + Decisive Test

Use a compound question like:

Where do the papers genuinely agree on mechanism, where do they only appear to agree because they are measuring different proxies or operating under different conditions, and what experiment or measurement would best resolve the deepest disagreement?

Why it works:

  • it stops the model from flattening literature into fake consensus
  • it pushes the output toward useful synthesis rather than citation accumulation

5. Intervention + Competing Risk + Minimal Next Step

Use a compound question like:

If we act on the leading interpretation, what is the best intervention implied by that theory, what is the strongest reason that intervention could fail or backfire if the theory is wrong or incomplete, and what is the smallest next step that reduces that risk before committing to a larger experiment?

Why it works:

  • it ties theory to decision-making
  • it favors discriminating action over generic follow-up work

6. Signal + Missing Data + Ranking

Use a compound question like:

Given the evidence we do have, which explanation should rank first, which should rank second, what missing data most weakens the ranking, and how likely is it that the ordering would flip if that missing data were collected?

Why it works:

  • it makes the model rank instead of hand-wave
  • it introduces a reversible judgment rather than a rigid answer

Compound Question Dosage Rule

One compound question per prompt surface. No stacking.

Each synthesis surface should receive exactly one compound question type, chosen for that surface's epistemic job. Multiple compound questions on the same surface collapse the internal-tension mechanism — the model triages instead of reasoning deeply, and the whole point is lost.

If a surface doesn't have a clear epistemic job that maps to one of these types, it should not receive a compound question at all.

The reason is structural: a single compound question forces multi-pass reasoning because the model can't satisfy clause 2 without genuinely engaging clause 1. Two compound questions compete for working memory, and the model satisfices on the easier one while treating the other as a checklist.

Scientific Reasoning Add-Ons

When the task is especially theory-heavy, the prompt can also ask the model to make these distinctions explicitly:

  • observed pattern vs inferred mechanism
  • What is directly supported by the evidence, and what is still an inference?
  • supporting evidence vs damaging evidence
  • What is the strongest fact in favor of the leading theory, and what is the strongest fact against it?
  • local fit vs generalizable theory
  • Does this explanation only fit the current dataset, or does it plausibly generalize?
  • interesting experiment vs discriminating experiment
  • Which next step would actually separate competing explanations instead of just generating more data?
  • real uncertainty vs avoidable vagueness
  • What is inherently unresolved, and what is merely underspecified in the current analysis?

Scientific Reasoning Standard Block

This is a reusable additive block for scientific prompts:

Scientific reasoning standard:

Do not stop at summary. For each major claim:
1. State the leading mechanistic explanation.
2. State the strongest competing explanation.
3. State the strongest artifact, confounder, or non-causal explanation if one exists.
4. Compare the evidence for and against each explanation, including the strongest supporting fact and the strongest damaging fact.
5. Distinguish what is directly observed from what is inferred.
6. Identify the key uncertainty, hidden assumption, or missing evidence carrying the conclusion.
7. State the boundary condition where the claim may fail or stop generalizing.
8. Name the observation, measurement, or result that would most weaken the leading explanation.
9. Name the smallest decisive experiment or measurement that would distinguish the explanations.
10. If appropriate, rank the explanations and state what missing data is most likely to change the ranking.

Prefer causal explanation, falsification logic, confounder analysis, and discriminating experiments over descriptive recap.
If evidence is weak, state clearly what cannot yet be concluded.
Do not treat proxy agreement, correlation, or literature repetition as proof of mechanism without saying why the mechanism is justified.

Implementation rule: This block is a design-time reference library, not a runtime injection.

Never inject more than 3 items from this list into a single rendered prompt. Instead, select the 2-3 items most relevant to the specific task type and write them as compact, surface-specific variants:

  • Scientist variant (items 1-2, 5, 9): mechanism vs rival, observation vs inference, decisive experiment
  • Literature variant (items 1-2 adapted, 5 adapted, 6): false consensus detection, proxy vs mechanism agreement, what literature alone cannot decide
  • Synthesis variant (items 1-2 adapted, 8, 10): convergence vs repeated assumption, strongest rival to current direction, what would flip the ranking

Pasting all 10 items into a prompt is the "analyze all aspects" scope-expansion trap from the March 30 prompting strategy doc. The model will satisfice on 4-5 and phone in the rest. Focused variants produce deeper reasoning than the full block.

Sentence-Level Steering Tactics

The exact sentence shape matters. A good scientific prompt often has three clauses:

  • a clause that asks for the leading explanation
  • a clause that asks for the strongest competitor or confounder
  • a clause that asks for the decisive falsifier or discriminating next test

This is usually better than a series of short disconnected questions because the model is less able to answer one part shallowly and ignore the rest.

Good pattern:

What mechanism best explains X, what serious alternative still survives, and what observation would distinguish them?

Even stronger pattern:

If X reflects a real mechanistic change rather than an artifact of sampling, proxy choice, or preprocessing, what theory best explains it, what rival theory still deserves consideration, and what single result would force us to revise the current ranking of explanations?

The sentence stays long on purpose. It creates a constrained but intellectually demanding task.

Anti-Patterns To Avoid

These question styles usually flatten the reasoning:

  • Summarize the literature on...
  • What happened in this dataset?
  • What does this result mean?
  • What are the takeaways?
  • What should we do next?

These are not always wrong. They are wrong when the real need is theory discrimination rather than recap.

When Not To Force Theory Language

Everything above adds pressure — pressure to reason about mechanisms, rivals, falsifiers, confounders, boundary conditions, decisive experiments. That pressure is the whole point. But pressure only produces good results if the system has a release valve.

If the evidence does not support mechanism-level reasoning, the correct output is "insufficient evidence," not a fabricated mechanism.

The compound questions and reasoning variants create implicit social pressure to fill every slot. A three-clause question asking for mechanism + rival + falsifier makes an empty slot feel like a failure. The model will produce plausible-sounding but evidence-free language to fill the slots — "mechanism theater" — rather than say "I can't do this."

Mechanism theater is worse than no mechanism at all, because downstream consumers (cross-pollinator, calibration system, knowledge graph) treat it as real scientific judgment.

Implementation rule: Every prompt surface that receives a compound question or reasoning variant must also receive an escape hatch, positioned BEFORE the compound question, not after it. The escape hatch must:

  • come before the pressure source (so the model reads "you can skip" before it reads "fill these slots")
  • make insufficiency feel like a correct answer, not a cop-out
  • be louder than the compound question (short, direct, unambiguous)

Example wording:

If the evidence does not support mechanism-level reasoning for any part of the question below, say so in one sentence and move on. An honest "insufficient evidence" is more valuable than a fabricated mechanism. Do not fill a slot you cannot defend.

The positioning matters. If the escape hatch comes after the compound question, the model has already committed to filling the slots by the time it reads the permission to skip. Before = conditional framing ("do this IF you can"). After = afterthought ("do all this, but also you could skip it I guess").

Calibration target: If scientists never use the escape hatch, the compound questions are too demanding for the evidence level. If they always use it, the data is too thin for theory-level reasoning. The healthy range is ~20-40% escape usage, reflecting genuine variation in evidence quality across tasks.

Why This Should Make Models Think Longer

The reason this works is not magic phrasing. It works because the prompt creates internal tension:

  • preferred explanation vs competing explanation
  • signal vs confounder
  • current evidence vs missing evidence
  • confidence vs falsifier
  • conclusion vs decisive test

That tension forces multiple reasoning passes.

In other words:

  • not “be deep”
  • but “resolve a scientifically difficult structure”

Where To Apply This First — And How Much

Each surface gets a specific dosage. More is not better — the right amount is what that surface's job requires.

SurfaceWhat it getsWhy this much
Scientist promptsCompact reasoning variant (2-3 items) + escape hatchScientists analyze primary data. They need mechanism vs rival, observation vs inference, decisive experiment. Not synthesis-level compound questions.
Literature synthesisCompact reasoning variant (2-3 items) + escape hatchLiterature is vulnerable to fake consensus. Needs false consensus detection, proxy vs mechanism agreement, what literature can't decide.
Wave 2a (L1 cross-pollinator)One compound question (Type 1: Mechanism + Rival + Falsifier) + escape hatchThis is where conflicting scientist interpretations first collide. Needs the mechanism-discrimination question.
L2 (strategic synthesis)One compound question (Type 3: Theory + Context Shift + Failure Boundary) + escape hatchL2's job is cross-batch generalization. Needs the question about where the theory stops transferring.
L3 (program-level synthesis)One compound question (Type 5: Intervention + Competing Risk + Minimal Next Step) + escape hatchL3's job is program decisions. Needs the question that ties theory to action and risk.

Do not apply to:

  • graph-updater (structured extraction, not theory work)
  • narrow structural verifiers
  • deterministic checkers
  • publish gates
  • memory agents
  • digestion scripts

Those should remain tighter and less theory-heavy. If theory-steering leaks into structured surfaces, they become pseudo-scientific essay writers instead of disciplined extractors.

Structural prerequisites before any rollout:

These five fixes must land before or alongside this brainstorm's deployment (see tasks/2026-04-10_1910_prompt-integrity-fixes/):

  1. Escape hatches in scientist manual calibration predictions + gap-filling experiment
  2. Compact reasoning variants (not the full 10-item block)
  3. Post-digestion priority hierarchy in assemble-prompts.py
  4. One compound question per surface (not stacked)
  5. Pre-positioned escape hatch before each compound question

Without these, the brainstorm's pressure flows into the system's weakest points and produces mechanism theater, confounder theater, and fabricated predictions — the exact failure modes this brainstorm was designed to prevent.

What This Does Not Require

This addition does not require:

  • new agent roles
  • new prompt-mode fields
  • new control-plane variables
  • new schema objects

It is a prompt-engine improvement through better question design.

Practical Heuristic

If a prompt can be answered by summary alone, it is too weak for scientific theory work.

If a prompt forces the model to:

  • explain
  • contrast
  • check for artifact
  • falsify
  • bound
  • discriminate
  • rank
  • and design a decisive next test

then it is much closer to the kind of reasoning needed for real research support.

Next Design Question

~~The next implementation question is not whether this idea is good. It is: which live prompt surfaces should receive this question shape first, and how do we add it without making the prompts bloated or repetitive?~~

Answered 2026-04-10. The dosage table above defines which surfaces get what. The structural prerequisites are planned in tasks/2026-04-10_1910_prompt-integrity-fixes/. The six-scope rollout plan is in tasks/2026-04-10_1734_scientific-theory-steering-six-scope-plan/.

The remaining design question is:

After the first-slice rollout, does the escape hatch get used at the right rate (~20-40%), and does the compound question produce genuine discrimination or just longer output? That question can only be answered by running a batch with the fixes in place and evaluating with the rubric from the six-scope plan's scope 5.

Prompting
Attention-Aware Prompt Architecture
Section ordering is a tunable parameter: attention budget is separate from token budget, and small models have a measurable middle-sag.
2026-04-10

Attention-Aware Prompt Architecture

date: 2026-04-10 19:58 status: brainstorm — pre-implementation depends_on:

  • brainstorm/24_2026-04-10_1523_addition-to-prompt-engine-scientific-theory-steering.md
  • brainstorm/2026-03-30_1028_prompting-strategy-and-session-learnings.md
  • tasks/2026-04-10_1910_prompt-integrity-fixes/ (Haiku validation tests)

Origin

During Haiku validation testing of the prompt integrity fixes (2026-04-10), Haiku 4.5 self-reported that the scientific reasoning standard at line 139 of the rendered prompt was "buried in the middle" and might be skimmed rather than internalized. Haiku suggested moving it closer to the top.

This surfaced a deeper architectural question: the ordering of sections in a rendered prompt is a design parameter, not just a convenience choice. The current prompt builder assembles sections in a fixed order optimized for human readability. But models aren't humans, and different model sizes have different attention profiles.

The Core Claim

Every prompt has two budgets:

  1. Token budget — how many tokens fit in the context window. Visible, measurable, well-understood. Fix 3 (post-digestion priority hierarchy) already addresses this.
  1. Attention budget — how much weight the model gives to each section based on its position in the sequence. Invisible, unmeasured, currently ignored by the prompt builder.

Token budget is a hard limit — exceed it and the prompt fails. Attention budget is a soft gradient — nothing breaks, but quality silently degrades as critical instructions land in low-attention zones.

Attention Profile by Model Size

Large models (Opus)

  • Roughly uniform attention across the full context window
  • Primacy and recency effects exist but are small relative to context size
  • Can hold 200k tokens with minimal middle sag
  • Current prompt order (context first, task second) works fine

Medium models (Sonnet)

  • Good attention across context but measurable middle sag on long prompts
  • Primacy bias is real — the first 500 tokens set the reasoning frame
  • Recency bias helps — instructions near the task-specific content get extra weight
  • Current prompt order works adequately but isn't optimal

Small models (Haiku)

  • Faster and cheaper precisely because attention is less deep
  • Significant primacy bias — early tokens disproportionately shape the response
  • Middle sag is pronounced — content at position 5000-15000 in a 20000-token prompt carries noticeably less weight
  • Recency helps but can't recover what primacy bias missed
  • Current prompt order (goal config at line 1, reasoning standard at line 139) puts the reasoning standard in Haiku's weakest attention zone

Current Prompt Assembly Order

assemble-prompts.py renders in this order:

1. System instruction (1 line)
2. Goal config (~80 lines, ~5k tokens)
3. Compliance gap (~10 lines)
4. Site scenario (~5 lines)
5. CP rationale (~5 lines, if present)
6. Directed question (~5 lines)
7. Focus columns (~5 lines)
8. Finding snapshot (~30 lines, ~3k tokens)
9. INSTRUCTIONS block (~15 lines)          ← operational
10. Scientific reasoning standard (~8 lines) ← CRITICAL but buried
11. Base operating manual (~60 lines)
12. Scientist/literature manual (~300 lines)
13. Data slice or chunks (~variable)
14. Completion signal (~3 lines)

The scientific reasoning standard lands at position 10 — after ~150 lines of context. For Opus, this is fine. For Haiku, this is the attention sag zone.

Five Design Options

Option A: Reorder sections (instructions first)

Move the INSTRUCTIONS block and reasoning standard to position 2, right after the system instruction. Push goal config and context below.

1. System instruction
2. INSTRUCTIONS + reasoning standard    ← moved up
3. Goal config
4. Context, findings, data
5. Manual
6. Completion signal

Pro: Maximum primacy for critical instructions. Haiku reads the reasoning standard before anything else. Con: The model hasn't seen the context yet when it reads the instructions. Instructions reference concepts (compliance gap, site conditions) that haven't been introduced. May confuse smaller models more than it helps.

Option B: Compressed primer at the top (preview + detail)

Add a 50-100 token compressed primer at position 2 that previews the reasoning standard. Keep the full standard at its current position.

1. System instruction
2. REASONING PRIMER (50 tokens)          ← new
3. Goal config
4. Context, findings, data
5. INSTRUCTIONS + full reasoning standard ← unchanged
6. Manual
7. Completion signal

Pro: Smallest change. Primer sets the frame ("you will reason about mechanism, rival, falsifier"). Full standard delivers the details later. Works like a textbook introduction. Con: Adds ~50 tokens per prompt. Minor duplication. The primer might be too compressed to change behavior.

Option C: Model-adaptive ordering

Add a model_tier parameter to the prompt builder. Different tiers get different section ordering.

if model_tier == "small":  # Haiku
    order = [system, instructions, reasoning_standard, primer, goal_config, context, manual, data]
elif model_tier == "medium":  # Sonnet
    order = [system, primer, goal_config, context, instructions, reasoning_standard, manual, data]
else:  # Opus
    order = [system, goal_config, context, instructions, reasoning_standard, manual, data]

Pro: Optimal for each model class. No wasted tokens for capable models. Con: More complex builder. Three code paths to maintain. Risk of drift between orderings.

Option D: Anchor repetition

Repeat the most critical instructions at three positions: top (primer), middle (full standard), and bottom (compressed reminder before completion signal).

1. System instruction
2. REASONING PRIMER (50 tokens)           ← anchor 1
3. Goal config, context, findings
4. INSTRUCTIONS + full reasoning standard  ← anchor 2
5. Manual, data
6. REASONING REMINDER (30 tokens)          ← anchor 3
7. Completion signal

Pro: Covers primacy, middle, and recency. Works for all model sizes. No model-adaptive logic needed. Con: ~80 tokens of repetition per prompt. Could feel nagging. Might cause the model to over-index on the reasoning standard relative to other instructions.

Option E: Priority-weighted sections with explicit attention guidance

Tell the model which sections matter most, similar to Fix 3's priority tiers but for input rather than output.

ATTENTION PRIORITY:
- MUST FOLLOW: Scientific reasoning standard (below)
- MUST FOLLOW: Output schema (in the manual)
- CONTEXT: Goal config, site data, findings (use as reference)
- REFERENCE ONLY: Base operating manual (consult if unsure)

Pro: Makes the attention hierarchy explicit. The model can allocate its own attention. Con: Relies on the model being capable enough to follow meta-instructions about attention allocation. Haiku might not be.

Recommendation

Start with Option B (compressed primer). It's the smallest change, testable in one Haiku run, and doesn't require builder refactoring.

If Option B shows significant improvement, move to Option D (anchor repetition) — it's Option B plus a recency anchor, and the combined primacy + recency coverage should capture both attention biases.

If the project scales to routine Haiku use (e.g., context consolidation agents running on prompts assembled by this builder), invest in Option C (model-adaptive ordering) as a permanent solution.

Do not start with Option C. It's the right long-term architecture but premature optimization before Option B is tested.

The Primer

Draft primer (50 tokens, position 2 in rendered prompt):

REASONING FRAME: In this task, you must distinguish observation from inference, name competing explanations before committing to one, and identify what evidence would change your conclusion. If evidence is insufficient for mechanism-level reasoning, say so directly — do not fabricate.

This primer contains the four core moves from brainstorm 24 (observation/inference, competing explanations, falsification, honest insufficiency) in two sentences. It doesn't replace the full standard — it primes the model to pay attention to the standard when it appears later.

What This Does NOT Address

  • Whether attention profiles vary within a model family across different prompt lengths (a 5k-token Haiku prompt might have different attention characteristics than a 40k-token one)
  • Whether attention profiles are task-dependent (reasoning tasks vs extraction tasks may have different attention patterns)
  • Whether the primer effect is durable across the full generation or fades as the model produces more output
  • Whether Sonnet's attention profile is close enough to Opus that it needs no special treatment

These are empirical questions that can only be answered by testing.

Connection to Existing Architecture

This brainstorm extends the prompt integrity fix chain:

Fix 1: escape hatches          → content fix (what to say)
Fix 2: compact variants        → density fix (how much to say)
Fix 3: post-digestion priority → output budget fix (where to spend output tokens)
Fix 4: compound questions      → pressure fix (what reasoning to demand)
Fix 5: escape hatch positioning→ ordering fix (where to place content relative to pressure)
Fix 6: attention-aware ordering→ attention fix (where to place content relative to model attention)

Fix 5 already demonstrated that ordering matters — escape hatch before compound question, not after. Fix 6 extends the same principle from within-section ordering to cross-section ordering across the entire prompt.

Next Design Question

Does a 50-token primer at position 2 measurably improve Haiku's compliance with the scientific reasoning standard compared to the current ordering?

This is a single A/B test: render the same prompt with and without the primer, run both through Haiku, compare the output quality using the evaluation rubric from the six-scope plan's scope 5.

Multi-Branch Agent Workflow And Merge Conflicts
Semantic conflicts survive git's auto-merge — 'no merge conflict' does not mean 'safe merge' — so split parallel work by file ownership.
2026-04-11

Multi-Branch Agent Workflow And Merge Conflicts

date: 2026-04-11 09:19 EDT status: brainstorm / teaching note

Why This Exists

This note explains how branches, pull requests, rebases, merge conflicts, and integration branches should work when multiple agents or parallel workstreams are changing the same repository.

The core teaching goal is:

  • make branch workflow legible to a human who only knows commit, push, and pull request
  • explain how many branches can eventually become one repository again
  • define what should happen when parallel branches touch the same file or the same logic
  • define a low-chaos workflow for this repo specifically

Core Mental Model

A branch is an alternate line of history

main is the shared stable line.

A feature branch is a copy of that line where one person or one agent can make changes without touching main yet.

That means:

  • main = accepted shared state
  • feature branch = isolated proposed work

A pull request is a merge proposal

A pull request is not a separate kind of code.

It is simply:

  • "compare branch X against branch Y"
  • "show the diff"
  • "review it"
  • "merge it if accepted"

So a PR is a reviewable path from one branch into another, usually from a feature branch into main.

Merging means replaying accepted work into the shared line

When a branch is merged into main, Git tries to combine:

  • the changes already in main
  • the changes introduced on the feature branch

If the text changes do not collide, Git usually merges automatically. If they collide, you must resolve a conflict.

How Multiple Agent Branches Become One Repository Again

If you have multiple agents working on different branches, the normal pattern is:

  1. each agent starts from the same base branch, usually main
  2. each agent creates its own feature branch
  3. each branch changes a scoped slice of the project
  4. each branch gets reviewed separately
  5. the accepted branches merge back into main one by one

After that, main contains the combined accepted work.

There is nothing special about this being "agents" instead of humans. Git sees branches, commits, merges, and conflicts — not intent.

The Three Merge Cases

Case 1: Different files

Example:

  • Branch A edits scripts/assemble-prompts.py
  • Branch B edits README.md

These usually merge cleanly because the files do not overlap.

This is the easiest and safest parallelism.

Case 2: Same file, different regions

Example:

  • Branch A edits lines 40-60 of a file
  • Branch B edits lines 180-210 of the same file

Git often merges this automatically because the text changes do not overlap directly.

This is still safe enough, but it increases the chance of subtle semantic problems if the two edits affect the same logic from different directions.

Case 3: Same file, same region

Example:

  • Branch A rewrites the scientist reasoning block
  • Branch B rewrites the same scientist reasoning block differently

This creates a merge conflict.

Git stops and asks for human resolution because it cannot know which version is correct, or whether both should be combined.

What A Merge Conflict Actually Is

A merge conflict is not "Git is broken."

It means:

  • two branches changed overlapping text
  • Git cannot safely choose one version by itself

When that happens, Git inserts conflict markers into the file and waits for a resolution.

You then choose one of three outcomes:

  • keep branch A's version
  • keep branch B's version
  • write a third merged version that combines both correctly

The third option is common in real engineering work.

Textual Conflict vs Semantic Conflict

This distinction matters.

Textual conflict

Git sees overlapping edited lines and stops.

This is obvious because the merge fails immediately.

Semantic conflict

Git merges successfully because the lines do not overlap, but the resulting code or prompt is incoherent.

Example:

  • one branch adds a new prompt rule
  • another branch changes the surrounding prompt order
  • Git merges both
  • the final prompt technically merges, but the logic is now wrong or duplicated

This is why "no merge conflict" does not mean "safe merge."

The Safest Pattern For Multi-Agent Work

The safest pattern is:

  • one branch per scoped task
  • one owner per high-conflict file
  • merge small branches early
  • avoid long-lived branches that drift away from main

Good split:

  • branch A owns manuals
  • branch B owns builder scripts
  • branch C owns docs/indexes

Bad split:

  • branch A changes the top half of assemble-prompts.py
  • branch B changes the middle of assemble-prompts.py
  • branch C changes the same reasoning block in assemble-prompts.py

That bad split creates merge chaos because the same file becomes a shared battlefield.

Integration Branch Pattern

When many branches are all valid but you do not want to merge them directly into main one by one, use an integration branch.

Pattern:

  1. create an integration branch from fresh main
  2. merge feature branches into the integration branch
  3. resolve conflicts there
  4. test the integrated result
  5. open one PR from the integration branch into main

This is useful when:

  • several branches are part of one larger feature
  • the branches are individually incomplete
  • you expect interaction effects between them

This is often the cleanest approach for agent swarms building one feature in parallel.

Rebase vs Merge

Merge

git merge main

This pulls the latest main into your feature branch and creates a merge commit if needed.

Pros:

  • simpler mental model
  • preserves the real history of integration

Cons:

  • noisier history if overused

Rebase

git rebase main

This rewrites your branch so it appears to start from the newest main, replaying your commits on top.

Pros:

  • cleaner linear history
  • good before opening a PR

Cons:

  • can be confusing
  • rewrites history
  • more dangerous if you already shared the branch widely

Practical rule:

  • if the branch is local or lightly shared, rebase is fine
  • if the branch is already a shared collaboration branch, merge is safer

Recommended Workflow For This Repo

Default pattern

Use one branch per coherent slice, and split by file ownership when possible.

Good examples here:

  • one branch for assemble-prompts.py
  • one branch for scientist/literature manuals
  • one branch for synthesis manuals
  • one branch for bookkeeping/docs/indexes

High-conflict files

Treat these as high-conflict and prefer single-owner branches:

  • scripts/assemble-prompts.py
  • scripts/spawn-cross-pollinator.py
  • scripts/spawn-graph-updater.py
  • brainstorm/22_2026-04-08_1545_mission-controlled-workflow-atlas.md
  • large central manuals such as the scientist manual

If multiple agents need to affect one of these, do either:

  • one owner branch
  • or an integration branch after the parallel sub-branches finish

Low-conflict files

These are easier to split:

  • README.md
  • INDEX.md files
  • task workspaces under tasks/<timestamp>/
  • standalone brainstorm docs

A Concrete Multi-Agent Example

Suppose six agents are doing one project.

Use branches like:

  • codex/prompt-builders
  • codex/scientist-literature-manuals
  • codex/synthesis-manuals
  • codex/evaluation-rubric
  • codex/docs-and-indexes
  • codex/integration-scientific-theory-rollout

Recommended flow:

  1. agents do their work on the first five branches
  2. review each branch
  3. merge those branches into codex/integration-scientific-theory-rollout
  4. resolve any conflicts there
  5. run tests / render prompts / do review
  6. open one PR from the integration branch into main

This reduces the risk of merging half a feature into main while the rest is still unstable.

What Happens When Two Branches Change The Same Surface

When two branches change the same surface, ask two questions:

  1. Is the overlap only textual?
  2. Or do the branches make competing product/architecture decisions?

If it is only textual, resolve the file and continue.

If it is architectural, do not "just merge both." Stop and decide:

  • which decision is actually correct
  • whether one supersedes the other
  • whether a third combined design is needed

This is where conflict resolution becomes engineering, not version control.

What I Can Help With

I can help at three levels:

1. Before conflicts happen

  • split work into low-conflict branch scopes
  • identify high-conflict files
  • recommend merge order

2. When conflicts happen

  • read the conflict markers
  • understand both sides
  • produce the merged version
  • choose between keep-A, keep-B, or combine-both

3. After Git auto-merges

  • review for semantic conflicts
  • catch duplicated prompt rules, inconsistent contracts, broken ordering, or accidental regressions

This third category is important because Git only understands text, not system coherence.

Practical Rules

  • Prefer one branch per scoped change.
  • Prefer one owner for high-conflict files.
  • Keep branches short-lived.
  • Merge small, accepted branches quickly.
  • Use an integration branch when many related branches need to land together.
  • Treat "same file" as a risk signal even when Git can auto-merge it.
  • Treat "same logic, different files" as a semantic-risk signal even if there is no Git conflict.

Bottom Line

Multiple branches are not a problem.

Unclear ownership is the problem.

Git can merge many valid branches back into one repository just fine, but it cannot decide architectural intent when two branches overlap. That is where disciplined branch scope, integration branches, and deliberate conflict resolution matter.

The real goal is not "avoid every conflict."

The real goal is:

  • make conflicts small
  • make ownership clear
  • make merge order intentional
  • and have a clean place to integrate related parallel work before it hits main

Paradigm Shift Propagation System
The human states only the directional principle; the system traces its blast radius across every index file and proposes each edit.
2026-04-12

Paradigm Shift Propagation System

Brainstormed 2026-04-12 via Socratic method with Isaac

The Problem

1-2 times per summer, Isaac has a realization that changes how every agent should think. Example: "scientists mine existing data, they don't recommend new experiments." This principle touches 12+ files across manuals, prompts, schemas, validation, and task manifests. The system needs to propagate it completely and fast.

Design Decisions (from Socratic session)

QuestionAnswerImplication
What triggers adjustment?Isaac's realization, not automated detectionSystem is reactive to human insight, not eval metrics
How many shifts per summer?1-2Not a continuous loop — a paradigm propagator
What does Isaac say?One high-level directional principle, no technical detailsSystem must trace the blast radius itself
What approval model?Summary review for first shift, trust-and-execute afterTrust builds, then system runs autonomously
Where does the principle live?memory/improvement/paradigm-directives.yamlSingle canonical source, all modes read it
How does it find affected surfaces?Dynamic discovery — scan every folder and INDEX fileNo fixed registry, no missed surfaces

Three Execution Modes

Hot Mode (Isaac + Claude live)

  1. Isaac states the principle
  2. Claude records it in paradigm-directives.yaml
  3. Claude spawns N agents — each reads one INDEX.md, scans that subtree for content matching the old paradigm
  4. Agents report: file path, what's affected, proposed change, one-line rationale
  5. Claude produces a summary doc: every file, every change, every rationale
  6. Isaac reviews (first time) or Claude executes (after trust established)

Warm Mode (Isaac writes, Claude picks up next session)

  1. Isaac appends to paradigm-directives.yaml with status: pending
  2. Next session, Claude reads the directive during context restoration
  3. Same discovery + proposal + execution as Hot Mode
  4. Claude marks directive status: applied with date and surface count

Cold Mode (Automation)

  1. Scheduled sweep checks paradigm-directives.yaml for status: pending
  2. Spawns discovery agents across all INDEX files
  3. Produces change set in a task workspace: tasks/YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM_paradigm-shift-PD-NNN/
  4. Writes summary doc + diffs
  5. Stops at review gate (Cold Mode never auto-applies — only Hot/Warm auto-apply after trust)

The Directive File

# memory/improvement/paradigm-directives.yaml
# Canonical source for paradigm-level behavioral shifts.
# Each directive reshapes how agents think across all surfaces.

directives:
  - id: PD-001
    principle: "Scientists mine existing data for patterns and answers. They do not recommend new experiments unless they first prove the assigned question cannot be answered from existing data."
    issued: 2026-04-04
    status: applied
    applied_date: 2026-04-04
    surfaces_affected: 12
    trigger: "Realized Prof. Jaffe's data arrives as a 10-year dump, not a stream of new experiments"

  # Next directive goes here when the realization hits

Dynamic Discovery Protocol

When a new directive arrives, the system:

  1. Reads every INDEX.md in the repo (26 files as of 2026-04-12)
  2. For each INDEX.md, identifies files in that subtree that could encode agent behavior:
  • Agent manuals (brainstorm/agent-manuals/*.md)
  • Prompt assembly code (scripts/assemble-prompts.py, scripts/spawn-*.py)
  • Output schemas (sections in scientist/memory/CP manuals)
  • Validation lists (contract-fixtures, eval rubrics)
  • Task definitions (data/task_manifest.json — rationale, directed_question fields)
  • Configuration (data/goal-config.yaml — decision_sequence, key_unknowns)
  • Inline prompts (scripts/digest-*.py — prompt text inside scripts)
  • Design docs (brainstorm/*.md — only if they define active contracts)
  1. For each candidate file, an agent reads it and asks:
  • Does this file contain language or logic that contradicts the new principle?
  • Does this file contain language or logic that should be updated to reflect the new principle?
  • If neither: skip (no change needed)
  1. Each agent reports: file path, section/line affected, old behavior, proposed new behavior, one-line rationale
  2. A summarizer agent merges all reports into one change set document

What This System Does NOT Do

  • Does not auto-detect when a paradigm shift is needed (Isaac provides the principle)
  • Does not evaluate whether the shift improved outputs (that's the eval harness's job)
  • Does not modify canonical truth surfaces (goal-config, runtime-state) — only agent behavior surfaces
  • Does not apply changes in Cold Mode without human review
  • Does not handle incremental prompt tweaks (those go through the improvement event → candidate → decision loop)

Boundary With Existing Systems

SystemHandlesTrigger
Paradigm propagator (this)1-2 major behavioral shifts per summerIsaac's realization
Improvement loop (memory/improvement/)Incremental prompt/script fixesEval failure, calibration miss, user correction
Calibration system (memory/calibration/)Lab result → prediction comparisonNew lab data
Eval harness (digestion eval scripts)A/B testing prompt variantsProposed prompt change

The paradigm propagator is upstream of all others. A paradigm shift may invalidate existing improvement candidates, recalibrate what "good" means in the eval harness, and change what the calibration system considers a miss.

Implementation Scope

What to build

  1. memory/improvement/paradigm-directives.yaml — the directive file
  2. scripts/YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM_propagate-paradigm-shift.py — discovery + proposal script
  • Reads directives file for status: pending
  • Scans all INDEX.md files for subtree discovery
  • Spawns agents per subtree (or Claude does this manually in Hot Mode)
  • Writes change set to task workspace
  1. One-page summary template for the change set document

What already exists

  • memory/improvement/ stack — candidates and decisions can record paradigm-driven changes
  • paradigm-shift-log.yaml — historical log (can be linked to directives)
  • All INDEX.md files — the discovery substrate
  • Agent manuals — the primary target surfaces
  • The April 4 shift — a concrete worked example of the full lifecycle

What to defer

  • Cold Mode automation (build after Hot Mode proves the discovery protocol works)
  • Cross-directive conflict detection (not needed for 1-2 directives)
  • Rollback protocol (if a shift was wrong, Isaac will just issue a new directive)
