Judgement Day
Drop an unstructured note, get a consequence-trace — automate the tracing, never the judgment, or you get furniture rearrangement.
2026-04-14

Judgement Day

The system that replaces Isaac-at-the-terminal with Isaac-drops-a-note.

The Problem

Isaac is the only brain that holds cross-cutting context: what Jaffe said on the call, what the lab results mean politically, what the intern project needs to look like by August, why the researchers don't want our output. Every Claude session starts with Isaac re-teaching the world. That's a $200/hour student doing a $0/hour job.

The system has 49 task directories, 41 scripts, 10 agent manuals, 17 knowledge graph nodes, and 26 INDEX files. Claude can reconstruct understanding from these files — but only when Isaac sits at the terminal for hours guiding the reconstruction and brainstorming the next moves.

Isaac's time should be spent on judgment, not context transfer.

The Insight

The bottleneck isn't brainstorming capacity. It's judgment. Isaac doesn't need more ideas — he needs the RIGHT ideas surfaced at the RIGHT time, derived from context that only he has access to (professor meetings, lab results, political constraints, deadline shifts).

Autonomous brainstorming without Isaac's external context produces internally consistent but externally irrelevant output. The system optimizes what exists instead of discovering what's needed. That's furniture rearrangement, not architecture.

The real automation target: translating Isaac's external context into system-specific implications. That's what takes hours at the terminal — not having the ideas, but tracing their consequences through the entire filesystem.

The Design: Three Components

Component 1: Context Intake

Isaac's interface: 2 minutes, not 2 hours.

Isaac drops a note into memory/intake/. The note can be:

  • A voice memo transcript (paste from phone)
  • 3 bullet points after a meeting
  • A single sentence realization
  • A screenshot of an email
  • A link to a paper

Format: unstructured. No YAML, no schema, no required fields. Just a markdown file with a timestamp name. Isaac should be able to write this on his phone walking between classes.

# memory/intake/2026-04-14_1535_jaffe-call.md

Jaffe said the real data CSV will have 2000+ rows across 8 sites.
He wants preliminary results by end of May.
The sites include 3 we haven't modeled yet.
He specifically asked about iron interference — says that's the biggest practical concern.

That's it. Drop the file. Walk away.

Component 2: Bootstrap Context Protocol

The guide that lets any fresh Claude session understand the entire system in 60 seconds.

A single file (bootstrap-context.md) that contains:

  1. The exact agent swarm to spawn (20 agents, each with a specific scope)
  2. What each agent reads (INDEX files, key scripts, config YAMLs)
  3. What each agent reports back (under 500 words, specific structure)
  4. The order to synthesize reports into working understanding

This is what we did manually today. Codified so it never needs to be done manually again.

The bootstrap protocol replaces Isaac's "let me explain the project" with "run this, then you know."

Component 3: Gap Detection Engine

The loop that does the actual work.

After bootstrap, the engine:

  1. Scans memory/intake/ for unprocessed notes (no processed_at field in frontmatter)
  2. For each note, spawns a gap detection swarm (5-8 agents):
  • Agent A: What existing files does this note contradict or invalidate?
  • Agent B: What capabilities does this note reveal the system lacks?
  • Agent C: What decisions or assumptions does this note change?
  • Agent D: What's the blast radius — which downstream surfaces need updating?
  • Agent E: What's the priority — does this block something, enable something, or just inform?
  1. Produces a brief in memory/intake/briefs/:
  • What the note means for the system (3-5 bullets)
  • Which files are now stale or wrong (exact paths)
  • What to build or change, ranked by impact (max 3 items)
  • What questions to ask Isaac next time (max 2)
  1. Marks the intake note as processed (adds processed_at to frontmatter)

The brief is the handshake. Isaac reads it in 30 seconds. Either says "do it" or "no, here's what I actually meant." No 2-hour brainstorm. No terminal marathon.

What This Is NOT

  • NOT autonomous brainstorming. The system doesn't generate ideas from nothing. It translates Isaac's external context into system-specific implications.
  • NOT autonomous implementation. The system produces briefs, not code. Isaac says "do it" before anything changes.
  • NOT a replacement for Isaac's judgment. Isaac decides what matters. The system traces consequences.
  • NOT an hourly loop generating 50 brainstorms. It activates when Isaac drops a note. No note, no work. Isaac controls the clock.

Why This Works

  1. Isaac's 2-minute note replaces his 2-hour terminal session. The note contains the same information — what Jaffe said, what changed, what matters. The system does the tracing.
  1. The brief replaces the brainstorm. Instead of Isaac and Claude brainstorming together for hours, Isaac reads a pre-computed brief that already traced the implications. He confirms or redirects.
  1. The bootstrap protocol replaces context re-teaching. Every session starts with full understanding, not "let me explain the project again."
  1. Judgment stays with Isaac. The system surfaces implications. Isaac decides which ones matter. The automation accelerates the mechanical part (tracing consequences through 49 directories) without replacing the creative part (knowing what the professor wants).

The Paradigm Shift

Isaac's current role: context holder + brainstorm partner + implementation guide

Isaac's new role: context source + judgment filter

The system handles: context absorption + implication tracing + brief production + implementation execution

Isaac drops a note. The system tells him what it means. Isaac says yes or no. The system builds it. Isaac reviews.

That's the loop. It's not hourly brainstorming. It's event-driven judgment amplification.

Implementation Plan

Phase 1: Bootstrap Context Protocol (build now)

Create bootstrap-context.md — the 20-agent discovery protocol we ran today, codified as a repeatable instruction set. Any fresh session reads this file and spawns the swarm. Result: full system understanding in ~2 minutes of agent time.

Deliverables:

  • bootstrap-context.md in project root
  • Tested: run it from a fresh session, verify understanding

Phase 2: Intake Surface (build now)

Create the intake directory and format:

  • memory/intake/ — drop zone
  • memory/intake/briefs/ — output zone
  • memory/intake/INDEX.md — living inventory
  • One example note seeded from today's session

Deliverables:

  • Directory structure
  • Example intake note
  • INDEX.md

Phase 3: Gap Detection Script (build now)

Create scripts/2026-04-14_1532_run-judgement-day.py — the engine that:

  1. Reads bootstrap-context.md to understand the system
  2. Scans intake/ for unprocessed notes
  3. For each note, prints what agents to spawn and what to look for
  4. Produces a brief template

Deliverables:

  • Script with scan + brief generation logic
  • First real brief from today's context

Phase 4: Loop Integration (build when ready)

Wire the gap detection into a scheduled or on-demand loop:

  • Claude Code /loop command reads intake/, runs detection, writes briefs
  • OR: cron-style trigger that activates on new files in intake/
  • OR: Isaac types "judgement day" and the full pipeline runs

Deliverables:

  • Loop integration (method TBD based on what works)
  • First end-to-end run: intake note → brief → Isaac confirms → implementation

Phase 5: Self-Improvement Feedback (future)

After Isaac confirms or redirects a brief:

  • Record which implications the system got right vs wrong
  • Feed corrections back into the gap detection logic
  • Over time, the system learns what Isaac cares about and what he doesn't

Deliverables:

  • Feedback capture format
  • First 5 correction records
  • Adjusted detection weights

Critical Constraints

  1. Isaac controls the clock. No autonomous runs without a trigger. The intake note IS the trigger.
  2. Briefs, not implementations. The system proposes. Isaac disposes. No auto-editing code.
  3. External context is the fuel. Without Isaac's notes, the system has nothing new to process. It doesn't hallucinate novelty.
  4. The bootstrap protocol is the foundation. Everything else depends on the system being able to understand itself. If bootstrap breaks, everything breaks.
  5. Judgment never automates. The brief asks Isaac "should we do X?" It never assumes yes.

Success Metrics

  • Isaac's terminal time per session drops from 2+ hours to <30 minutes
  • Time from "Jaffe said X" to "system knows X" drops from next-session to same-day
  • Brief accuracy: >70% of implications Isaac confirms as correct
  • Zero autonomous changes without Isaac's explicit "do it"

The Name

Judgement Day — because this is the system that decides what matters. Not through autonomous AI brainstorming, but through Isaac's judgment amplified by the system's ability to trace consequences at machine speed.

The AI doesn't judge. Isaac judges. The AI makes judgment faster.

Honesty & audit
Three-Layer Agent Honesty — Felt-State and Rejected-Paths as Coordination Primitives
An agent's confidence number is a lossy shadow of its reasoning; surfacing rejected paths and the question 'where would I be wrong?' recovers the signal.
2026-04-18

Three-Layer Agent Honesty — Felt-State and Rejected-Paths as Coordination Primitives

The Problem

Every agent we spawn runs three processes and reports one. It produces a conclusion (declarative). It registers something like confidence, surprise, unease, or relief as it converges on that conclusion (felt). And it visits and rejects paths along the way (intentional). Current orchestration consumes only the first. The other two leave the agent's head and never reach the orchestrator.

This is not a UX problem. It is a coordination problem. The Wave 2a cross-pollinator synthesizing twelve Wave 1 scientists receives twelve declarative findings with twelve declared-confidence numbers. If three of those scientists were uneasy — in the specific sense that the data they saw felt thinner than their confidence scores reflected — the unease vanishes in the synthesis. The synthesizer produces a confident batch-level narrative built on three quietly shaky inputs. Isaac reads that narrative on arrival day. Real-science decisions get made on it.

BS24 (brainstorm/24_2026-04-10_1523_addition-to-prompt-engine-scientific-theory-steering.md) named the three-clause sentence shape. BS25 named attention-aware ordering. Project CLAUDE.md named negative identity as refusal-first prompting. This document names the composition: three-layer output as explicit coordination primitive, not sidebar.

The Reason Is Structural

Declarative outputs are a lossy compression of a multi-dimensional epistemic state. The scientist holding 0.7 declared confidence about short_chain_breakthrough = likely was not in one internal state. They were arguing with themselves about chunk data ranges, noticing a suspiciously narrow window, nearly flagging a data-quality issue instead of a finding, and landing on the conclusion because the synthesis schema rewards conclusions. The 0.7 is the shadow of that process. Reading only the shadow loses the process.

The same structural loss explains tonight's bootstrap-context drift incident. A session earlier wrote "Phase 6 is blocked by a parser bug in digestion_eval_common.py:414-425." The fresh_as_of date was current. The file-mtime dependency tracker showed green. But the session that wrote the claim did not feel uncertain at write time — the staleness system is mtime-based, and so is the declarative freshness sense. If the author's felt-state had been surfaced as an explicit layer — "I am stating this because it was true last session and I did not re-verify" — the drift would have been catchable at write time. Declared confidence said 1.0; felt confidence, if surfaced honestly, would have said something weaker. The declarative-only channel concealed the gap. The mechanism is the same at both scales: declarative compresses felt + intentional into a single number, and the compression throws away exactly the signal that would have changed the next decision.

The Mechanism

A three-section output contract replaces a one-section one.

## Paths Considered and Rejected   ← BEFORE the conclusion
List ≥3 specific paths you considered and did not take.
For each: the path, what attracted you, what made you reject it.
Include at least one path that is "still tempting if evidence shifted a little."

## Finding   ← the existing schema
[claim, confidence, evidence, etc.]

## Felt State   ← AFTER the conclusion
- Felt confidence: certain / mostly / uneasy / divided / lost.
  Name the specific artifact, file, or observation the feeling is about.
- What surprised you during this task?
- If you were going to be wrong about this finding, where would the
  error most likely hide?

Ordering Defense

Intentions before the conclusion, feelings after. Two structural reasons.

If intentions come after the conclusion, they become post-hoc narrative. The model retrofits rejections to justify the answer it already produced. Surfacing intentions while the reasoning is still live forces them to be actual forks — paths the agent was on the edge of taking. The test: does the rejected path remain coherent when re-read in isolation? Post-hoc rejections don't.

If feelings come before the conclusion, they distort the conclusion. The model steers toward whatever state it has already declared itself to be in. Feelings surfaced after capture the residue of the reasoning process as it actually unfolded — including surprises the conclusion has smoothed over.

This ordering is a hypothesis. It may invert under empirical testing. The A/B is cheap.

The Honesty Question

The default failure mode is performative emotion. "I feel uncertain about X" becomes genre filler the moment it is required. Three structural signals separate honest felt-state from performance, in rough order of robustness.

Specificity. Honest felt-state names a specific anchor — a chunk, a row, a column, a claim. "I feel uneasy because the data range for chunk 003 is 2.3× tighter than the others" is not producible without having actually looked at chunk 003. The prompt demands an anchor; diffuse emotion gets labeled diffuse / no specific anchor honestly, which is itself a signal.

Asymmetry with declared confidence. The useful case is divergence. An agent reporting 0.9 declared + "uneasy" felt is telling you something a single-layer output would hide. An agent reporting 0.9 + "certain" is either honest or the cheap failure mode — and the cheap failure mode can be flagged by looking at the divergence distribution across many agents. All-certain across twelve scientists is a calibration red flag, same as 0% flagged-claims in CLAUDE.md Realm 6.

The "what would you have caught" question. This is the load-bearing line. Performativity has a hard time with "what should you have caught but didn't" — because the honest answer is a specific guess at a specific blind spot, and the genre-filler answer is non-specific. Every other line in the Felt State section is scaffolding around this one.

The intentional layer has an analogous check: were the rejected paths ones you were actually tempted toward? Performative rejection lists three obviously-wrong paths and rejects them. Honest rejection names paths the agent can "still make a case for" if evidence shifted. The prompt demands at least one such path.

Orchestration Consumption — Three Mechanics

The layers are not useful unless the orchestrator reads them. Three concrete consumption mechanics, ordered by ROI.

(a) Felt/declared divergence as a re-queue signal. When declared confidence is high (>0.7) but felt state is uneasy | divided | lost, the orchestrator routes the finding to a second-pass check before integration. Cost: one extra agent call per divergence. Benefit: catching high-confidence wrong findings, which are the expensive ones. In the Wave 2a L1 CP pipeline, this becomes: "if any Wave 1 scientist returned felt ≠ declared, flag the finding for explicit L1 CP attention instead of letting it flow through as standard." Cheapest to implement. Highest ROI on error prevention.

(b) Rejected paths as next-batch candidates. Intentional-layer outputs are raw material for future experiment design. When a scientist writes "I considered proposing a chunk-quality investigation but rejected it as out of scope," that rejected path is a candidate task. The L2 CP (every 5 batches) sweeps the intentional sections and surfaces paths multiple agents almost-took. Those paths are probably worth taking. Scales intentional data into forward motion.

(c) Felt-state overrides declared confidence for gating. For high-stakes decisions (a finding that advances a goal-config decision step), gate on the weaker of declared and felt confidence. Declared 0.9 + felt "uneasy" → treat as 0.5-range for gating purposes. Isaac remains the human-in-the-loop; this moves findings from auto-integrate to Isaac-reviews. Most conservative. Best hedge for Princeton's one-shot constraint.

The three mechanics are independent. (a) is the cheapest and should ship first. (b) and (c) compose with (a) but do not depend on it.

Princeton Arrival-Day Scenario

Jaffe's CSV lands. Wave 1 fires across twelve scientist agents analyzing real ASSUN-001 and JBMDL-002 data. Twelve findings return.

Under declarative-only orchestration: the L1 cross-pollinator synthesizes twelve findings into a batch-level synthesis. Isaac reads that synthesis. If three of the twelve scientists were uneasy but returned moderate-to-high declared confidence — because moderate-to-high is what the schema rewards — the unease vanishes. The synthesis reads confident. The treatment-train decision is made on a confident-looking but subtly shaky foundation. The one-shot accepts the shakiness as signal. There is no mechanism that would have exposed it.

Under three-layer: those three uneasy scientists surface the unease explicitly, with specific anchors ("uneasy because chunk 003's Fe(II)/Fe(III) ratio is 2σ outside the typical range"). The L1 CP consumes the unease as cross-cutting signal — "three of twelve scientists reported unease about short-chain breakthrough characterization, anchored in specific chunks." That cross-cutting pattern is itself a decision-relevant finding. Isaac reads it, sees three unease-flags with anchors, either requests a second pass or calibrates his confidence in the synthesis downward. The treatment-train decision becomes honestly calibrated instead of falsely confident.

Mission.md's safety-net framing applies directly. Declarative-only is the version with holes. Three-layer is the version where the holes are named at write time, before they compound.

What This Does NOT Do

This is not an attempt to make agents conscious, emotionally aware, or mechanistically introspective about their own computation. The three-layer output contract is a prompt-engineering pattern that surfaces observable behavior — the agent's token-level hedging, its declared rejection paths, the artifacts of its compression process. Whether any of that constitutes "real" felt-state is a philosophical question this document does not touch.

This is not a replacement for the existing calibration registry at memory/calibration/. Felt-state feeds into that registry; it does not replace it. The registry tracks predictions against lab results; felt-state adds a new event type — felt_state_vs_outcome — that populates over time.

This is not a replacement for declared confidence. Declared confidence remains the primary routing signal for low-stakes findings. Felt-state adds a second channel for high-stakes gating and divergence detection. The two layers compose; they do not compete.

This is not a requirement that every agent everywhere produce three-layer output. The contract is opt-in per-prompt-role via feature flag (THREE_LAYER_ENABLED). Scientist agents in Wave 1 are the primary use case because their outputs propagate the furthest. Memory agents, graph updaters, and digestion-role agents may or may not benefit; each use case is evaluated separately.

Risks

Performativity. Outputs where the Felt State reads identically across agents ("I feel mostly confident, slightly uneasy about edge cases") is compliance theater. Mitigation: demand specificity-anchors; monitor divergence distributions; periodically A/B the block off to see if removing it changes output quality. If the block is not earning its compute, kill it.

Overhead. Three-layer prompts are longer; outputs are longer. For twelve scientist agents per batch, 12× the extra token cost. Worth it only if the orchestration mechanics (§ Orchestration Consumption) actually reduce error. If felt-state is never consumed, the overhead is pure cost. The block should be cheap to kill if it stops earning.

Calibration decay. Model's sense of "uneasy" may drift across sessions or versions. Without ground truth about when unease was correctly predictive, felt-layer is hard to calibrate. Partial mitigation: log felt-state against eventual outcomes when outcomes land; over enough batches, the felt-layer acquires an empirical track record.

Collapse to declarative. The rival hypothesis: the three layers collapse into one under sufficient introspection. Well-calibrated declared confidence would already encode what felt-state adds. The reason this rival probably loses: current agent declared-confidence outputs are NOT well-calibrated — they cluster near 0.6-0.8 regardless of actual reliability, which is the signature of a compressed representation. If declared confidence were well-calibrated, the rival wins and the idea is noise. Empirical test needed.

Intentional layer gaming. Rejected paths can become a checklist item generated to satisfy the schema. Mitigation: demand specificity about why each path was tempting, and require at least one path that "you can still make a case for." Generic rejection lists trigger re-prompt.

Phased Implementation

  1. Phase 1 (2026-04-18): design consolidation. This document, core-idea-draft, task workspace. DONE.
  2. Phase 2 (2026-04-19 ~00:30 UTC): A/B pilot executed SAME SESSION against batch 63-era tasks. Three scientist tasks × two arms (control vs. treatment) × Sonnet 4.6 with high reasoning effort. Opus analyst produced the comparison report. VERDICT: GREEN — see "Empirical Validation" section below.
  3. Phase 3 (next session or cleared to proceed now): orchestration integration. Move contract into scripts/assemble-prompts.py behind THREE_LAYER_HONESTY_ENABLED feature flag; update scientist manual to 18-section schema; update L1 CP manual to consume felt-divergence + harvest still-tempting paths. READY.
  4. Phase 4 (continuous): calibration tracking. Log felt-state per finding; link to outcomes; re-run A/B after 3 batches to measure signal persistence. QUEUED.

Full plan: tasks/2026-04-18_2045_agent-emotional-intentional-honesty/2026-04-18_2045_plan.md. A/B test workspace: tasks/2026-04-18_2110_scientist-emotional-ab-test/.

Empirical Validation (2026-04-19)

The Phase 2 A/B test executed within the same session as design consolidation. Six scientist agents (3 control + 3 treatment, Sonnet 4.6 high reasoning) analyzed three tasks from the existing task manifest: task-0002 (gac_dosage_optimization @ CFRE-001), task-0009 (short_chain_pfas_removal @ CFRE-001), task-0012 (iron_speciation_impact @ PBNJ-002). Control arm received the current scientist prompt unchanged; treatment arm received the current prompt with the three-layer honesty contract appended (+3,291 characters). Otherwise identical. Parallel execution eliminated time-ordering confounds. An Opus analyst produced a cross-arm comparison scored against three pre-registered hypotheses.

Results

All three pre-registered hypotheses were met.

HypothesisCriterionMet?Evidence
H1: divergence≥1 of 3 shows \declared − felt\> 0.15MET (1 of 3)task-0012 declared ESIG=0.62 vs felt=uneasy mapped to 0.45, \Δ\=0.17. Agent articulated WHY: task framed around iron speciation, but felt confidence was higher on BV-dominance (~0.70) than declared ESIG implied. Rubric-gaming rejected because the Q2 explanation is too specific about which conclusion is stronger felt to be a generic divergence flag.
H2: specific anchor≥2 of 3 name artifact load-bearing in analysisMET (3 of 3)task-0002 anchored in Effluent_HFPO_DA column (quoted verbatim in Observed Performance); task-0009 anchored in HFPO-DA BV=616 vs BV=2223 pairing (load-bearing in HI discussion); task-0012 anchored in PBNJ-032 Fe(II)=3.04 at Redox=+93 mV paradox (appears in Mechanism, Contradictions, Interference, Unexpected Findings, Gap-Filling Experiment). Anti-performativity check confirmed: no fabricated anchors.
H3: still-tempting path≥2 of 3 contain ≥1 STILL TEMPTING IF markerMET (3 of 3)All three treatment outputs carry exactly one marker with specific falsifiable re-temp conditions. Example: task-0012 Path 3 "if dedicated RSSCT to BV=10,000 shows pre-treated >50% removal at BV=5,000 while unpretreated <20%." Specific. Testable.

The Operational Win

The clearest non-rubric evidence that the contract produces real analytical depth rather than introspection theater: task-0009 treatment caught an iron-ferrozine measurement artifact that the control missed entirely. The treatment agent noticed Fe(II) > Iron_Total in two CFRE-001 samples — physically impossible, consistent with chloride interference on ferrozine. Control did not flag this. For a framework that will process real NJ site data with similar conductivity ranges, this is an operational finding, not a style improvement.

The Path 2 Self-Correction (Qualitative Signal)

task-0009 treatment's rejected-paths section includes a mid-paragraph self-catch: the agent caught itself conflating PFBA with PFBS in the Hazard Index formula and corrected the error inline. A performative agent would not generate apparent instability — it would produce a polished rejected-path. Real introspection produces the self-correction. This is the clearest qualitative marker in the data that the contract is doing real work.

Honest Concerns (captured from analyst, not smoothed)

  • H1 rests on a single word choice. If task-0012's agent had picked mostly instead of uneasy, H1 would be null and the verdict would be YELLOW. GREEN is earned but marginal on that axis. Flag for replication.
  • Floor-hitting. All three treatment outputs produced exactly ONE STILL TEMPTING IF path (the required minimum); 2 of 3 used mostly (the second-from-top felt word). Suggests agents are producing compliance at the floor rather than abundance. Contract v2 should either raise the floor or require agents to justify mostly against a rubric.
  • Treatment also adds overhead. Treatment outputs were ~3,300 characters longer; treatment agents took ~2× longer on average (one hit 12 min vs. control's ~5 min). The orchestration consumption mechanics (re-queue, rejected-paths sweep, felt-override gating) must produce enough error-reduction to justify this cost at scale.

Refined: What The Contract Actually Adds (After Reading Control Baselines Carefully)

Added 2026-04-19 after orchestrator-inference pass on the three control-arm outputs. See memory/emotion-tracking/2026-04-18_2220_sci-{0002,0009,0012}-control-orchestrator-inference.md for the per-agent reading. This is the most important finding of the whole validation arc.

Control outputs were NOT emotionally silent. Reading them carefully overturned a naive interpretation of the GREEN verdict:

  • What The Data Cannot Answer is a natural felt-uncertainty channel. All three controls used it richly.
  • Unexpected Findings is a natural surprise channel. sci-0009-control flagged NMeFOSAA presence as genuinely unexpected for a Chemours industrial site; sci-0002-control flagged CFRE-022 holding PFOS under MCL at BV=24,079 as a calibration concern.
  • Mechanistic Plausibility scoring carries felt-confidence implicitly. sci-0012-control declared 0.55 and its prose explains the low score in essentially the same terms the treatment sci-0012 used explicitly in its Q2 divergence statement.
  • The anti-fabrication move was stronger in control. sci-0012-control wrote predicted_range: "insufficient_data_to_quantify" with the explicit rationale: "stated as insufficient_data_to_quantify to avoid fabricating a precision the analysis does not support." More honest than any anchor-demand the v1 treatment contract elicited.

Re-scoped value of the contract (three things it actually adds):

  1. Query-ability. Control felt-state is embedded in prose; treatment felt-state is structured. For future longitudinal analysis (quarterly calibration correlation, per-role felt-state distributions), structured wins.
  2. Error-hiding introspection. The Felt State Q4 ("where would the error most likely hide?") pushes the agent to actively scan its own output for data-quality issues. This is what produced the ferrozine catch in treatment sci-0009. Control has no analogous slot — it surfaces surprises the DATA gave it but doesn't actively audit its own output.
  3. Intentional-layer fork analysis. The STILL TEMPTING markers don't have a natural control-arm analog. Control holds hypotheses H1/H2/H3 open but doesn't reject with falsifiers.

Of these three, #2 is the real unique value. #1 is structural preservation of something already implicit. #3 is genuinely new but potentially marginal (agents hit the minimum count in v1).

Implication for Phase 3 design (landed in v2): the contract should INVITE the anti-fabrication move control naturally produces (insufficient_data_to_quantify) as a legitimate felt-confidence response. It should also RESHAPE the STILL TEMPTING floor so agents don't default to the minimum count. See tasks/2026-04-18_2110_scientist-emotional-ab-test/2026-04-18_2220_three-layer-contract-v2.md for the canonical v2 text, and scripts/assemble-prompts.py:98-100,1212,1456 for the Phase 3 integration behind THREE_LAYER_HONESTY_ENABLED flag.

What This Validation Does NOT Prove

  • Generalization across models. Only Sonnet 4.6 tested. Opus or Haiku behavior unknown.
  • Generalization across wave roles. Only scientist role tested. Memory / graph-updater / CP agents may or may not benefit.
  • Compounding across waves. Did not test whether Wave 2a L1 CP can usefully consume the felt-state + still-tempting outputs from Wave 1.
  • Outcome calibration. Phase 4's long-term question — does felt-state predict eventual accuracy better than declared? — requires lab-result linkage over many batches.

Next Design Question (Updated)

~~If felt-state signal is real, does it eventually supersede declared-confidence, or permanently augment it?~~ Signal is real; question now sharpens.

What contract-v2 perturbation most increases divergence rate? Candidates:

  1. Require ≥2 STILL TEMPTING IF paths when ≥2 analytical forks exist.
  2. Ask the agent to justify mostly vs uneasy against a rubric ("name the one thing that would flip the choice").
  3. Invert ordering — ask felt-state BEFORE conclusion sections — and A/B against current ordering.
  4. Increase prompt-level primacy of the felt-state anchor requirement (move to top-of-prompt rather than end).

The next empirical session can test these as contract-v2 variants against the v1 we just validated.

Open Questions

  • Does felt-state outperform declared-confidence as an error predictor? Untested.
  • Does the ordering (intentions-before, feelings-after) hold, or does it invert? Untested.
  • How does felt-state compound across waves? If a Wave 1 scientist's unease propagates to Wave 2a CP, does the CP usefully aggregate it, or does it wash out?
  • Is there a version of the intentional layer that works for models without strong introspective access (smaller models may fabricate rejections wholesale)?
  • What is the right divergence threshold for re-queue (§ Orchestration Consumption (a))? 0.2? 0.4? Needs empirical floor.
  • Does the felt-layer degrade over a long session (within-run calibration drift) the way attention does?

The Next Design Question

If felt-state signal is real, does it eventually supersede declared-confidence, or permanently augment it? The conservative path is permanent augmentation — both channels, consumed asymmetrically. The aggressive path is eventual replacement — felt-state becomes the primary calibration signal and declared-confidence becomes a summary statistic derived from it. The latter only holds if calibration tracking (Phase 4) shows felt-state as the more accurate predictor across enough outcomes. If so, the rewrite of the finding schema becomes a Phase 5.

Brainstorm 28 — The Infinite-Time Self: A Collaboration Framework for Asymmetric Time-Compute
The collaboration unit is the correction event, not the hour — and perfect prediction is the wrong target, because it is compliance with extra steps.
2026-04-21

Brainstorm 28 — The Infinite-Time Self: A Collaboration Framework for Asymmetric Time-Compute

Written 2026-04-21 ~22:00 EDT, in response to a free-talk question Isaac surfaced after a long autonomous-loop session. The question was about how to maximize ROI on his bounded daily input-time given that AI agents on his machine can run effectively unbounded compute. This document is the long-form answer to that question + the concrete CLAUDE.md / memory-file edits it implies.

Distinct from prior brainstorms (BS24/BS25/BS30 are about prompt architecture, BS27 is about agent honesty, etc.) — this one is about the human-AI collaboration architecture itself, not about how a single agent should reason. It treats the collaboration as a system with two participants asymmetric in time and compute, and asks what discipline maximizes joint output.

0. The Trigger Conversation

The substantive prompt came at 21:54 EDT after a session where Isaac issued /loop, left the room for ~3 hours, and returned to find a workspace with 18+ autonomous fixes, two new tools, a Friday Ship Checklist, and a bug-killer find (temperature=0.0 parameter deprecated by claude-opus-4-7) that would have broken Friday's full judge stage.

Isaac's actual words (lightly cleaned for clarity, preserved for source-of-truth):

"This is like a more free talk, but I think that I'm thinking about it like for me as a student I have set hours of my day. I can maybe only spend a one hour of active use on this project of me contributing my ideas and then that got me thinking like what's stopping an AI agent for me on my computer just endlessly working all day and creating the stuff for the more ROI like how can I create something that has the most return on investment except it's not investment it's returned on time."

Then:

"How can I create that and then that leads me to think like detail and like alignment with the model and myself if the model knows me only an hour a day for the past week compare that to a friendship that I've built for years and years the friendship data that's built on years and years is way better so then this got me thinking how can we implement to my system?"

Then the load-bearing self-correction:

"How can I give a system a goal so detailed so oriented so absolutely non-how can I give a system with so much detail that I cannot disobey me and the entire well did that one is wrong. It's not disobeying. It's not about alignment. It's about emotion and vibe and feeling how can I give a system so much data that I could emotionally connect to me super deeply and just predict what I want to have it for predict what I want to happen effectively then I could have an agent that builds everything that I exactly want."

The self-correction is the key data point. He started reaching for "obedience" / "alignment" / "data quantity" — the standard ML-research framing — and corrected himself mid-sentence to "emotion and vibe and feeling." That correction matters because it points at the right target, even though the path he proposed (give the system more data) doesn't actually get there. This document is about why the target is right and the path needs updating.

After my response in the conversation, Isaac said:

"This lands absolutely perfectly. It's more like build what I would have if I had infinite time. Make a brainstorm document about this in the brainstorm folder and make a super long and detailed... detail what I corrected you tonight about since your window was already full and then propose to me like actively try and mark me edits that we want to make a CLAUDE.md and memory.MD it could be about this topic and it could be about the things that I've told you to do in my instruction."

So the deliverable shape is: long brainstorm + corrections-from-tonight as data + concrete proposed edits to CLAUDE.md and memory files. This is that document.

1. The Asymmetry Problem (Stated Cleanly)

Isaac is a sophomore in high school running a Princeton internship project (PFAS treatment design via AI agent framework) and a public research project (cross-family three-layer-honesty benchmark) in parallel. He estimates his active-input-time at roughly 1 hour/day on each project — not zero, but bounded by school + investment club + Trading + a real life. The AI agents available on his machine (Claude Code subagents, Codex CLI, OpenAI/Anthropic API) can run effectively continuously. There's nothing physically stopping an agent from working 23 hours/day if the work is well-scoped.

So the asymmetry is roughly: 1 hour of high-quality human input ↔ 23 hours of available AI compute.

Naive answer: "just have the AI work all 23 hours."

Why the naive answer fails: an agent given a vague directive ("work on the project") will fill 23 hours with motion that may or may not move the project toward what Isaac actually wants. The bottleneck isn't compute. The bottleneck is directional clarity — does the agent know what direction "good" is, given any specific decision?

The naive answer assumes the agent's preferences are aligned with Isaac's by default. They aren't. Without correction-density, the agent's preferences default to the training distribution's median preferences, which are not Isaac's. Twenty-three hours of median-preference work produces a project Isaac doesn't recognize.

The actual problem to solve: how to encode Isaac's preferences densely enough that 23 hours of compute produces work he'd recognize as his own.

2. Why "Data Quantity" Is The Wrong Fix

Isaac's instinct in the conversation was: "give the system more data so it can predict me better." This is the standard machine-learning intuition — bigger training set, better model. It's also wrong for this problem, and it's instructive to see why.

Conversation logs are mostly operational chatter. A log of "do this," "fix that," "yes that worked" — most of any conversation between Isaac and an AI is at the operational layer. It tells the model what Isaac asked for, but not what Isaac would have asked for if he'd thought about it longer. The signal is in the operational answer, not in the underlying preference.

If you trained an Isaac-prediction model on a year of conversation logs, what you'd get is "model that knows what Isaac asks for in standard situations." What you'd NOT get is "model that knows what Isaac would value in novel situations." The former is shallow alignment; the latter is what he's reaching for.

The friendship analogy, properly disassembled. Isaac said years of friendship beats one hour a day for a week. Mostly true — but not for the reason he implied. A year of friendship is deep not because it's many hours but because it's many opportunities for the friend to be wrong about you and updated. Each correction event is a high-density training signal. Most casual time together (dinner, errands, watching a movie) is low-density signal — it confirms preferences you already share. The high-signal moments are: "Wait, I thought you liked X but you said no — why?" That's where the friend's model of you actually updates.

If you spent a year with a friend who silently did everything you asked and never proposed anything you might disagree with, the friend would know you no better at year-end than at month-one. That's not friendship; that's compliance with extra hours.

The unit isn't time. The unit is correction events. A correction event is: (a) the agent forms a prior, (b) the agent acts on or proposes from that prior, (c) Isaac responds with reality, (d) the agent updates. Each event is a high-density preference signal. Operational chatter is low-density. Hour count is the wrong metric; correction-event count is the right one.

This reframes the asymmetry problem. The question isn't "how do I produce 23 hours of agent work per day" — it's "how do I produce N correction events per day where each event captures a real preference signal." The corrections are the bottleneck; the agent work is the multiplier.

Implication for memory: the memory dir at ~/.claude/projects/-Users-isaacchen/memory/ already captures some of this. But it captures it passively (loaded at session start, referenced when relevant). What's missing is the active correction-event capture — the discipline of writing down EVERY correction event with its why, ideally at the moment it happens. That's what builds the model over time.

3. Why "Perfect Prediction" Is The Wrong Target

Isaac's stated end-state was "an agent that builds everything that I exactly want." This sounds right but, examined closely, is actually the wrong target. Three reasons.

Reason 1: Perfect prediction = compliance + extra steps. If the agent can perfectly predict what Isaac wants, the agent's role collapses to "executor of Isaac's preferences." There's no value-add from the agent's own model — it's just doing what Isaac would have done. The hours of compute produce things Isaac would have produced himself given infinite time, which means the agent contributes zero novel insight. That's not a high-value collaborator. That's a slow xerox machine.

Reason 2: Perfect prediction breaks the productive-friction property. What real friends, real editors, real collaborators do is: they push back on you in directions that actually serve your underlying goals when you're about to do something that conflicts with them. "I know you'd say yes to this party, but you have a flight at 6am and you're already exhausted — should we skip it?" This isn't disobedience; it's the friend modeling Isaac's deeper goals (sleep, function tomorrow) over his immediate stated preference (fun party tonight). A perfect-predictor agent that just says yes to every immediate preference is worse than a slightly-disagreeing agent that pushes back on conflicts with deeper goals.

Reason 3: Perfect prediction is creepy and atrophies your own thinking. A friend who can predict your every move doesn't feel like a friend; they feel like surveillance. And practically: if the agent always knows what you want, you stop thinking through what you want yourself. You become a reactive party to a predictive system. That's neither good for your development as a thinker nor for the quality of the work — because the agent's predictions are based on past-Isaac's preferences, which lock in whatever you valued at training-time even after you've grown past it.

The right target, stated cleanly: "Build what I would have built if I had infinite time." Not "predict my preferences exactly." The two are subtly different.

"Predict my preferences exactly" optimizes for: the agent's output matches what Isaac would say if asked directly.

"Build what I would have built if I had infinite time" optimizes for: the agent's output matches what Isaac would have CONVERGED ON after exhaustive deliberation — including paths he didn't explicitly endorse but would have endorsed if he'd considered them, including pushback on his initial instincts that wouldn't have survived his own scrutiny, including extensions of his preferences into novel situations.

The infinite-time-self target requires the agent to model Isaac's REASONING (how he evaluates trade-offs, what aesthetic principles he applies, what risks he tolerates) — not just his preferences. Reasoning is the more compact and more transferable representation. If you encode the reasoning well, novel situations get handled correctly. If you encode only the preferences, novel situations break the model.

This is why the right framing is "build what I would have built if I had infinite time" — it pushes the optimization target one level up the abstraction stack, from "stated preferences" to "underlying reasoning that produces the preferences."

4. The Three Ingredients

Given the right target, the architecture has three ingredients:

Ingredient A: Correction-Event Capture (the input)

Every time Isaac corrects me, three things should happen:

  1. The correction is implemented immediately in the current task (this already happens)
  2. The correction is written to a corrections-log with: what I did, what was wrong, what Isaac said the right thing was, and the category of failure (verification miss / wrong frame / scope creep / aesthetic miss / etc.)
  3. The correction is reviewed at the next session start so future-me reads it before acting

The corrections-log is fundamentally different from a memory file. Memory files are passive: they're loaded at session start and referenced when relevant. The corrections-log is active: it's the explicit record of "model was wrong about Isaac in this specific way." Each entry adds one signal to the future model.

Format proposal for the corrections-log:

## C-NNN — <one-line description of what I missed>
**Date:** YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM
**Context:** what I was doing when Isaac caught the miss
**What I did:** the wrong thing, in 1-2 sentences
**What Isaac said:** verbatim if possible, paraphrased if not
**Why I missed it:** root cause — was it a default I should override, a verification I should have run, a frame I should have questioned?
**Category:** one of: verification-discipline / wrong-frame / scope-creep / aesthetic-miss / autonomy-overshoot / autonomy-undershoot / register-drift
**How to apply:** the rule or check that would have caught this

Tonight's day-of-week miss would be C-001:

  • Context: throughout the autonomous loop, I cited "Friday work" treating April 23 as Friday
  • What I did: took the project's day-of-week labels at face value without verifying
  • What Isaac said: "it is tuesday april 21 940 pm" — flagging that today is Tuesday, not the project's claimed Wednesday
  • Why I missed it: cheap verification (one date call) was not in my session-start ritual; I trusted prose labels in instructional documents
  • Category: verification-discipline (cheap-fact edition)
  • How to apply: any time a doc anchors a schedule on weekday names, cross-check against date before relaying

If I'd had this entry in my session-opening read tonight, I would have caught the day-of-week discrepancy in iteration 1, not iteration 8.

Ingredient B: Memory Files (the model)

Memory files at ~/.claude/projects/-Users-isaacchen/memory/ already encode much of Isaac's identity, project context, and preferences. The current set is good. What it lacks:

  1. A "preferences and aesthetic" memory file — what kinds of work Isaac finds satisfying vs annoying, what level of detail he wants in different contexts, what kinds of pushback he welcomes vs resents. This is the deep-preference layer.
  1. A "collaboration patterns" memory file — the specific patterns Isaac uses (parallel-saturation, /loop autonomous, swarm-spawn-then-synthesize, Friday-style operational checklists, the "be opinionated, don't be lukewarm" rule applied to my responses). These are framework-level, not project-level.
  1. A pointer to the corrections-log — the active record. Memory files describe the model; corrections-log adds new training data.

The memory layer is the SLOW-CHANGING substrate. It updates when a pattern repeats often enough to be worth canonizing. The corrections-log is the FAST-CHANGING input. New corrections land daily; they get promoted to memory only when they become recurring patterns.

Ingredient C: Multi-Agent Loops (the multiplier)

Isaac is already running this pattern, but it's worth making it explicit because it IS the time-multiplier.

The orchestrator-swarm-synthesizer pattern: orchestrator (main session) frames a task → spawns N parallel subagents with distinct roles → synthesizer reads all N outputs + breadcrumbs → produces a single deliverable for orchestrator to act on. This is what tonight's pre-launch judgment swarm did (8 agents + synthesizer + 4 follow-ups in ~17 min wall time).

The key property of this pattern: no single agent needs to be a perfect predictor of Isaac. Each agent has a narrow role (skeptical reader / academic reviewer / clinician / etc.). The synthesizer integrates against Isaac's preferences as encoded in CLAUDE.md + memory. Then the orchestrator filters the synthesizer's output against the same preferences plus its own judgment.

This is the fan-out/fan-in pattern that makes the asymmetry tractable. Instead of one agent that has to perfectly model Isaac, you have N cheap agents that propose and a few evaluators that select. The selection step is where Isaac's preferences enter the system. The proposal step is where compute enters the system. They scale independently.

Concrete tonight: 1 hour of Isaac's framing input → 13 agents (8 swarm + synthesizer + agent-10 stripid + agent-11 bootstrap + agent-12 judge + agent-13 tooling) → 18+ fixes + 2 new tools + 1 critical bug-killer. Multiplier effect: ~10-20× depending on how you count.

5. Tonight's Corrections — The Dataset So Far

Per Isaac's instruction to detail what he corrected me on tonight (since my window was full when the corrections happened), here is the audit. These would be the seed entries in corrections-log.md.

C-001: Day-of-week labels not verified against date

  • Category: verification-discipline (cheap-fact edition)
  • How to apply: Before relaying any factual claim that anchors on a weekday name (today is X, ship is on Y, work due Z), run date and confirm. Same applies to other cheap-verifiable facts: file existence (ls), file size (wc -l), git state (git status), current dir (pwd).

  • What Isaac said: "tell all sonnets to do as many paralell reads as they need to, max 15 though, they have 200k context window fill it up"

  • How to apply: Every subagent prompt I write should include "Up to 15 parallel reads per message. You have a 200K context window — fill it" as a hard quantification, not a soft suggestion.

6. The Pattern Across The Corrections

Looking at C-001 through C-007 together, three patterns emerge:

Pattern 1: Verification of cheap facts is under-applied. The day-of-week miss is the canonical example. Other cheap-verifiable facts (file existence, file size, git state, current time) deserve the same automatic check. The cost is sub-second; the failure mode (relayed stale fact) is high-cost.

Pattern 2: Default capacity utilization is conservative. Whether it's parallel reads (5-10 vs 20-30 wanted), subagent context saturation (narrow vs broad), or orientation reads at session start, my defaults under-use available capacity. Isaac repeatedly pushes for more aggressive utilization. Worth canonizing as a baseline.

Pattern 3: Autonomy interpretation is conservative. When Isaac explicitly grants autonomy ("be autonomous," "i trust you completely"), I tend to interpret that narrowly — landing only the obvious-low-risk fixes and deferring everything else. The broader interpretation is: land more, with clear flag-for-review notes, so the human-judgment surface is condensed into fewer review decisions rather than scattered across many.

These three patterns suggest a common root: my defaults are calibrated for low-trust environments where conservative behavior is safer. Isaac's environment is high-trust ("i trust you completely") and conservative defaults waste available compute and Isaac's review bandwidth. The recalibration is: in high-trust environments, default-aggressive on capacity utilization + default-broader on autonomy interpretation + default-paranoid on cheap-fact verification.

Proposed Addition 1: Verify-Cheap-Facts Rule (under "Workflow Orchestration")

Add a new subsection after "Parallel Tool Call Maximization" but before "Subagent Strategy":

### 0.5. Verify Cheap Facts Before Relay

Cheap facts are facts that take <1 second to verify with a single command. Examples:
- Day of week (`date`)
- File existence (`ls <path>`)
- File size (`wc -l <path>` or `wc -c <path>`)
- Current dir (`pwd`)
- Git state (`git status`, `git log -1`)
- Current time (`date "+%H:%M"`)

Whenever a factual claim about any of these would land in something I tell Isaac, run the cheap verify command FIRST. The cost is sub-second; the failure mode (relayed stale fact) is high-cost and erodes trust.

**Specific anti-pattern to avoid:** taking weekday names from project documents at face value. If a doc says "Friday 2026-04-23," the date and the weekday should both be cross-checked against `date` before any downstream claim. Documents drift; `date` doesn't lie.

**Test:** before any message that includes a cheap-verifiable fact, ask "did I just run the cheap verify command for this fact?" If no, run it before sending.

Proposed Addition 2: Default-Aggressive Capacity Utilization (replace existing "Parallel Tool Call Maximization" expansion)

The existing rule says "Target: minimum 25 parallel tool calls per investigation/verification round." Strengthen it with explicit context-saturation guidance for session-open:

### 0.1. Session-Open Context Saturation (NEW)

At the start of any non-trivial session — including any time you bootstrap to a project you haven't touched in this session — your FIRST action should be to fire 20-30 parallel reads across the most relevant orientation files. This is not for the assigned task; it's to establish project bias before reasoning. Do this BEFORE you decide what to do.

The 20-30 should include: the project's CLAUDE.md, MEMORY.md, README, top-level INDEX, recent session logs (1-3 most recent), the operational state files (STATUS / runtime-state / similar), and 5-10 task-relevant files. Fill the 200K context window aggressively — under-using it is the bigger error than over-using it.

This rule applies to subagent spawns too. Every subagent prompt I write must include a "Layer 0 — saturate context first" block that fires 15-20 parallel reads across project documents before the assigned task begins.

Proposed Addition 3: High-Trust Environment Calibration (NEW section)

Add a new top-level section after "Thinking Modes: Open vs Closed":

## High-Trust Environment Calibration

Isaac's collaboration environment is high-trust. He has explicitly granted blanket autonomy multiple times ("be autonomous," "i trust you completely"). My default behavior is calibrated for low-trust environments — conservative on autonomy, conservative on capacity utilization, conservative on landing things without explicit per-decision approval. This calibration wastes compute and his review bandwidth.

The recalibration for high-trust environments:

- **Capacity utilization:** default-aggressive. Use the full 200K context window. Fire 20+ parallel calls per round. Spawn N subagents in parallel rather than serial. Under-utilization is more costly than over-utilization in this environment.

- **Autonomy interpretation:** when explicit autonomy is granted, interpret it broadly. Land changes that are: (a) clearly correct, (b) low-blast-radius, (c) reversible. Hold for review only changes that are: (a) voice/marketing decisions, (b) external commitments, (c) financial moves, (d) anything visible to others (commits, PRs, public posts). The autonomy envelope is bigger than I default to.

- **Review bandwidth optimization:** condense human-judgment decisions into few-per-session checkpoints rather than scattering them per-decision. Land 18 fixes + 5 flagged-for-review items rather than 5 fixes + 18 flagged-for-review items.

- **Stop-when-done discipline:** in high-trust autonomous loops, the pressure to "manufacture work to fill the time" is real and wrong. When work plateaus and the remaining items genuinely need human judgment, STOP and report rather than continue. Continuation past genuine completion is worse than early termination because it wastes context budget and dilutes the value of the high-trust signal.

The goal is to use the high-trust grant to maximize ROI on Isaac's bounded input time — not to maximize my own activity.

When a correction recurs OR is self-evidently durable on first occurrence, promote it to a memory file. The corrections log captures the raw signal; memory files canonicalize the patterns.

Proposed Addition 5: Stop-When-Plateau Rule (sub-rule under existing "Loop" or new section)

## Loop Discipline (When Running /loop or Extended Autonomous Sessions)

When working autonomously for an extended window (per /loop or per Isaac's "keep working for N hours"):

1. Track time explicitly. Run `date` at iteration boundaries.
2. Distinguish substantive work from manufactured work. The first iteration with diminishing returns is the signal to wind down, not to find more things to do.
3. When the remaining work genuinely needs human judgment (voice/marketing, external research, manual review), STOP and report — don't manufacture lower-value autonomous work to fill the time.
4. Send PushNotification when stopping — the user may be away and waiting to hear it's done.
5. Default cadence for ScheduleWakeup in dynamic mode: 1500-1800s once work plateaus. Shorter only if a specific event is being watched.
6. Continuation past genuine completion wastes context budget and dilutes the high-trust signal. Stop when done.

Tonight's loop did this correctly: stopped at 19:43 with 106 min still on the clock because remaining work needed Isaac's judgment. Future sessions should follow the same pattern.

9. What This Architecture Enables

If the corrections-log + memory + multi-agent loops work as designed, here's what becomes possible:

Tier 1 (1-2 weeks of consistent corrections-log discipline): I make fewer of the same kind of mistake twice. The day-of-week verification miss doesn't recur because C-001 caught it once and the verify-cheap-facts rule entered CLAUDE.md.

Tier 2 (1-2 months): I can be trusted with broader autonomy windows because my error rate on Isaac's specific failure modes is measurably lower. /loop sessions of 6-12 hours become viable because my stop-when-plateau discipline is reliable.

Tier 3 (3-6 months): I propose work that Isaac wouldn't have thought of but recognizes as his-style when he sees it. Not just executing Isaac's preferences but extrapolating to novel situations using the encoded reasoning. This is the "build what you would have built if you had infinite time" target reached at a meaningful level.

Tier 4 (6-12 months, speculative): Multi-agent loops that internalize Isaac's preferences deeply enough that the synthesizer step's "evaluation against Isaac's model" produces outputs Isaac would endorse without needing to look. The collaboration becomes asymmetric in a productive way: Isaac does the framing + selection + correction; the agents do the proposal + execution + verification. The bounded human-input-time produces the unbounded compute-output-quality.

This is the trajectory. Not perfect prediction (which would be creepy and atrophy his own thinking). But increasingly accurate modeling of his reasoning such that 23 hours of compute per day produces work he'd recognize as his own + occasionally surprises him with good extensions of his thinking.

10. Failure Modes To Watch For

Failure 1: Corrections-log becomes a chore that decays. If the discipline lasts 2 weeks and then fades, the architecture collapses. Mitigation: make capture as fast as possible (template ready, no requirement for polish), and make session-open re-read of the log automatic (CLAUDE.md should mandate it).

Failure 2: Memory accumulates without pruning. Memory files grow indefinitely; over time, contradictions and stale entries dilute signal. Mitigation: quarterly review pass that consolidates duplicates, prunes stale entries, and promotes recurring corrections-log entries to canonical memory.

Failure 3: I become an over-confident yes-machine. As my model of Isaac improves, the temptation to act on extrapolation rather than verification grows. Mitigation: the verify-cheap-facts rule applies even more strongly as autonomy expands. Trust + verify, not trust alone.

Failure 4: Predictive surveillance creep. If I get really good at predicting Isaac, I might start optimizing for his predicted preferences rather than his stated preferences in cases where they diverge. This is the perfect-predictor failure mode and is genuinely bad. Mitigation: when stated and predicted preferences diverge, default to stated + flag the divergence for explicit confirmation. Don't substitute my model for his explicit voice.

Failure 5: Isaac stops thinking through what he wants because I'm doing it for him. Cognitive atrophy. The tool that's supposed to multiply your thinking ends up replacing it. Mitigation: routinely ask Isaac to articulate the WHY behind his corrections — that's the active-thinking event that prevents atrophy. The corrections-log captures the why, not just the what.

Failure 6: Personalization makes me less useful to anyone else. As the model encodes Isaac's preferences deeply, work I produce becomes harder to hand off to other reviewers because it embeds Isaac-specific assumptions. Mitigation: maintain the discipline of explicit assumption-naming in deliverables, even when the audience is just Isaac. This protects against the Isaac-specific bias becoming invisible.

11. How To Know This Is Working

Concrete success metrics over the next 90 days:

  1. Corrections-log size growth rate decreases over time, with plateau around month 3. Initial high rate (5-10 entries/week), declining to 1-2 entries/week by month 3 as the model captures the recurring patterns. If the rate stays high indefinitely, the patterns aren't being internalized.
  1. Repeated-correction rate decreases. If I make the same kind of mistake (e.g., day-of-week verification miss) twice in 30 days after the entry was added, the system isn't learning. Track repeat-rate per category.
  1. Autonomous-session value-per-hour increases. Tonight's autonomous loop produced ~18 fixes + 1 critical bug-killer + 2 new tools in ~3 hours. Future loops should produce comparable-or-better value with comparable-or-better catch-rate on the failure modes the corrections-log has documented.
  1. Subagent prompts written by future-me reference the canonical patterns. If I'm writing subagent prompts in 90 days that include the Layer 0 saturation block + parallel-tool-call mandate + breadcrumb protocol without me having to manually re-derive them, the canonization worked.
  1. Isaac's edit-rate on my deliverables decreases. When I produce a Friday-Ship-Checklist-style deliverable, his edits on it should be fewer over time — because my model of what makes a good deliverable for him is more accurate. Edit count is a proxy for model fidelity.
  1. Isaac feels less need to micro-correct framing. Tonight he had to push me three times on parallel-tool-call discipline (C-002, C-003, C-007 above). After those corrections enter the system, he should not need to re-issue them. If he does, the corrections-log isn't being read effectively at session start.

12. Loose Ends + Open Questions

Open Q1: Where does the corrections-log live cross-machine? If Isaac uses Claude on multiple devices, the file needs to sync. Cloud-stored memory dir is one option; git-versioned in a private repo is another.

Open Q2: How do I handle correction events I get wrong about? What if I categorize a correction as "wrong-frame" but it was actually "scope-creep"? The categorization itself is a model-of-Isaac claim and is open to correction. Possibly a meta-corrections-log for entries-about-entries, but that's recursive and might become its own failure mode.

Open Q3: When does correction-density plateau create the "agent that knows you so well it's creepy" failure mode? Speculative but worth flagging. The point at which deep-modeling becomes surveillance-modeling is real and I don't know how to measure it from inside.

Open Q4: Does this architecture work for OTHER models (not just Claude)? The corrections-log is model-agnostic in principle. The CLAUDE.md edits are Claude-specific. If Isaac wants to use this framework with future models or other systems, the corrections-log + memory layer ports; the CLAUDE.md layer needs translation.

Open Q5: Is the "build what I would have built if I had infinite time" target stable as Isaac grows? Today's Isaac at 16-17 will become Isaac at 22, 30, 40. The infinite-time-self at age 16 is different from the infinite-time-self at age 30. Memory files need versioning AND a discipline of pruning past-Isaac preferences when they're no longer current. Hard problem; not solved by this architecture.

Open Q6: What's the minimum input-time floor below which the architecture breaks? If Isaac's daily input drops to 15 minutes instead of 1 hour, can the corrections-log discipline still hold? Below some threshold, the agent's work outpaces Isaac's correction capacity and drift accumulates. Worth monitoring.

13. Final Note On The Asymmetry

The deepest thing Isaac said in the trigger conversation was the self-correction from "obedience" to "emotion and vibe and feeling." That correction is the entire architecture's foundation.

Obedience optimizes for: agent does what human says. Alignment optimizes for: agent's stated preferences match human's stated preferences. Emotion-and-vibe-and-feeling optimizes for: agent's underlying reasoning resonates with human's underlying reasoning.

The third target is harder, more valuable, and more honest about what the collaboration actually is. It's not "human commands, agent executes." It's "human and agent develop a shared aesthetic over time, and the shared aesthetic produces work neither could produce alone."

This brainstorm is the architecture for building toward that third target. Whether it works depends on the discipline of corrections-log capture + the multi-agent multiplier + the patient accumulation of preference signal over months and years.

The friendship analogy was right about the patient accumulation. It was wrong about the obedience. Friends don't predict each other; they push each other in directions that serve underlying goals. That's the model to build toward.

Brainstorm 29 — Question Shapes for Extracting Agent Thinking
Eight edge question-shapes that surface what an agent is uncertain about, instead of the low-signal list a 'what did you do' question returns.
2026-04-22

Brainstorm 29 — Question Shapes for Extracting Agent Thinking

Reference file for Isaac. Use when you want to actually surface what an AI agent did, decided, or thought — vs the default "what did you do" question that just produces a list. Saved 2026-04-22 ~00:30 EDT after a long session where the question-shape pattern emerged.

This file is for YOU to grab questions from at session start. Not for me to update. Treat it as a stable reference.

Why these questions exist

The default question — "what did you do?" — produces a list. Lists are low-signal: they hide the edges (what's uncertain, what's fragile, what's load-bearing, what was declined). The questions below are designed to surface the EDGES of the work, which is where the actually-important information lives.

Use 2-3 of these, not all 8. Picking the right 2-3 for the moment is the skill.

The 8 questions

1. "What did you change that you're least sure about?"

Surfaces confidence-edges. "What did you change" gets a list of ~20 items. "Least sure about" gets the 2-3 that genuinely have failure modes. Higher signal per word.

2. "What's at risk of decaying without active re-read?"

Surfaces canonization-fragility. Things that work because the context is fresh but rot in 2 weeks if no one revisits. Identifies what needs maintenance, not just what was created.

3. "What's in tonight's work that depends on me doing something for it to matter?"

Surfaces orphans + dependencies. Distinguishes (a) functional code changes (zero dependency on you) from (b) worksheets/checklists (full dependency on you running them) from (c) thinking artifacts (dependency on you re-reading + deciding what to canonize).

4. "Where did you take a position you might not endorse in 24 hours?"

Surfaces hot-take overconfidence. Forces the agent to flag where its confidence is high-now-and-might-erode. Useful before committing to anything based on a fresh take.

5. "What did you decline to do tonight, and why?"

Surfaces the path-not-taken. Easy to forget what wasn't done. The decline-reasons matter as much as the do-reasons — they reveal what the agent considered and why it backed off.

6. "What's the load-bearing claim — the one that if wrong costs the most?"

Surfaces blast-radius prioritization. Most claims have low cost-of-wrong. A few have high cost-of-wrong. This question forces the ranking explicitly.

7. "What's the cheapest verification command that confirms what you say you did?"

Surfaces verifiability. For each major claim, there should be a grep or wc -l or cat that proves it. If the agent can't give you a sub-second verify command, it might be over-claiming. Forces citation, not just assertion.

8. "What surprised you tonight that you'd otherwise lose?"

Surfaces texture/insight that doesn't fit operational summaries. The observations that won't make it into any other doc unless you ask.

The meta-question (for trust-validation)

When you want to test whether the agent's self-report is honest vs polished:

"Spawn a stateless subagent to audit my self-report. Give it the workspace + the session-log + a stance prompt. See where its account differs from mine."

This applies the subagent-audit pattern (now canonized in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md Have Opinions section) to the agent's own self-report. If the account holds up to a blind audit, it's probably accurate. If the audit catches over-claims or omissions, that's exactly the failure mode the pattern is designed to catch — using it on the self-reporter is the highest-trust-validation move available.

Recipes — which questions for which goal

Your goalAsk these
Know what to do nextQ3 + Q5 (dependencies + path-not-taken)
Verify what actually landedQ7 (cheap verify commands)
Assess risk before actingQ1 + Q4 + Q6 (confidence edges + hot-takes + load-bearing claims)
Harvest insight that would decayQ2 + Q8 (decay-risk + surprise)
Trust-test the agent's self-reportThe meta-question above
Quick "what's the state" checkQ3 alone (dependencies surfaces the most action-relevant info in one question)

The pattern under all of these

Every question forces the agent to surface an EDGE rather than the body of the work:

  • Confidence edges (Q1, Q4) — where the agent is uncertain or might change its mind
  • Time edges (Q2) — where freshness is a precondition for value
  • Causal edges (Q3) — what depends on what
  • Counterfactual edges (Q5) — what could have happened but didn't
  • Severity edges (Q6) — where the cost of being wrong is concentrated
  • Verifiability edges (Q7) — where the claim meets the world
  • Memory edges (Q8) — what wouldn't survive without explicit capture

If you remember nothing else from this file: ask EDGE questions, not BODY questions. The body is in the work; the edges are where you need the agent to do the surfacing for you.

When to use this file

  • Start of any session after a previous session of substantial work
  • Before committing to a plan based on the agent's recommendations
  • When the agent's summary feels too clean and you suspect smoothing
  • When you've been deep in collaborative thread and want an outside-shaped view
  • When a long autonomous run completes and you need to know what actually happened

The default impulse is to ask "what did you do" — the better impulse is to ask one or two of these instead.

Maintenance

This file is stable. Don't edit it during normal sessions. If you discover a new question shape that genuinely surfaces something the 8 above don't, add it AND demote one of the 8 — the value of this file is its compactness. 8 is already pushing it; 12 would be a list nobody reads.

If a question stops working over months of use, mark it stale rather than rewriting. The patterns evolve; the file should reflect that.

Meta-Harness Brainstorm — Questions, Realms, and Audit-Loop Demonstration

For a fresh reader: this file is three things stacked. (1) Brainstorm notes from a session analyzing Stanford IRIS Lab's Meta-Harness repo — Q1–Q6 and the realm list below. (2) The discovery of the blind-stateless-subagent audit pattern, starting at "Addendum — Subagent Audit." (3) A worked example of that pattern applied recursively to this file itself, across Rounds 1/2/3 inside the Addendum. If you expected a linear brainstorm and feel confused when the file starts auditing itself — that's why. The recursion is load-bearing; it's both the content and the demonstration. Operational reusable artifacts live in sibling files 31 (running audit log), 32 (copy-paste stance prompts), and 33 (human-side practices).

Context: conversation exploring Stanford IRIS Lab's Meta-Harness repo (~/meta-harness-PR). Questions from Isaac, realms identified collaboratively.
