This file is cooked analysis; the pattern documented here was derived from the code above. Skipping the code and reading this file is the exact failure mode this file exists to catch.

Spiky questions to hold while you read this file:

  • Am I accepting the framing because it's well-written, or because the code supports it?
  • Which claim below am I most tempted to quote without verifying?
  • Where does this file's analysis diverge from what the code actually does?
  • If I disagree with a claim after reading the code, will I say so, or silently adopt the file's framing?

Q1. What if we loaded the three most recent worst frontier candidates, not just the winning frontier? Would that have evolutionary benefit?

Realm: Memory / context curation — the "what do we show the proposer" realm.

Refinement: "worst" isn't the same as "most informative." A 5% candidate with an import bug teaches nothing. A 30% candidate when frontier is 40% teaches a lot — mechanism was almost right. So: load recent candidates that failed in an interesting way (small negative delta, not catastrophic). Near-misses on the frontier (candidates that beat frontier on some tasks but not average) are arguably even higher-signal — they show partial mechanisms that work.

Current system shows only winners + one-line loser summaries. Asymmetric. The proposer knows what worked but has to re-derive why things failed → duplicate-hypothesis waste.

Q2. Is there a master prompt / skill for Claude itself? What's the "vibe" non-technically?

Realm: Proposer prior / behavioral framing — the "pep talk" realm.

No master prompt. SKILL.md is a coach's pep talk appended to every proposer call. Vibe:

  • Don't be lazy (no parameter tuning)
  • Don't cheat (no task-specific hardcoding)
  • One idea at a time (no bundled changes)
  • Prototype before committing
  • Don't give up (no early termination)
  • Show your work (falsifiable hypothesis required)
  • Do it yourself (don't delegate to subagents)

Key insight: they're not expanding Claude's capabilities, they're narrowing behavior. Strips bad generalist habits, forces researcher posture. The "unlock" is behavioral discipline, not jailbreak.

Q3. Could letting the agent meander produce better work? How are token variables tracked and acted upon?

Realm: Closing the data loop — the "signal-collected-but-unused" realm. Adjacent realm: Search strategy — the "how do we allocate effort" realm.

Tracked per candidate: n_input_tokens, n_output_tokens, n_cache_tokens, cost_usd, n_turns, n_api_calls, pass_rate, delta, hypothesis, axis, components.

Acted on: only pass_rate (frontier), cost + ctx_len (Pareto tiebreak in text-cls).

Everything else is logged but inert. No bandit over axes, no token penalty, no novelty bonus. Data sitting there unused. Biggest unshipped lever in the system.

Meandering: worth it as budgeted minority mode (5–10% of iterations), not default. Current system is near-pure exploit; diversity injection would likely unstick local optima.

Q4. Isn't optimizing score-per-token the end of the game?

Realm: Objective function design — the "what are we actually optimizing" realm.

Yes, terminal objective. Pass-rate is a proxy. A 46.5% harness at 10× tokens isn't better than a 40% harness at 1× tokens in production.

Why they don't do it directly:

  1. Noise compounds when dividing noisy metric by noisy metric
  2. Tokens aren't fungible (cache reads ≠ fresh input)
  3. Degenerate solution: do nothing, ratio undefined
  4. Long-horizon tasks naturally use more tokens → unfair penalty without per-task normalization
  5. Proposer cost usually excluded

Right direction. First team to crack it cleanly has deployment edge.

Q5. How can we give a system enough data to emotionally connect and predict what we want? (Long-running agents / friendship analogy.)

Realm: Human-agent alignment / taste modeling — the meta-meta-harness realm.

Friendship analogy half-right. Asymmetry is real (1hr/day vs years of side-channel data). But "so much data it can't disobey" is wrong frame — failure mode isn't disobedience, it's sycophancy.

Architecture components:

  1. Passive ingestion (git, filesystem, search history) > active interviewing
  2. Taste artifacts (accept/reject pairs) > preference lists
  3. Decision/override logs > conversation logs
  4. Self-updating "about me" file (agent proposes, human ratifies)
  5. Feedback as first-class data (corrections and confirmations are gold; middle is noise)

ROI-on-time bottleneck isn't compute, it's goal specification. The glue between memory + scheduling + self-update + passive ingestion is the unsolved part.

Concrete experiment: log every agent-override in one file for 30 days. Compressed friendship data.

Q6. How can you prompt another agent to discover these findings without Meta-Harness context?

Realm: Research methodology / stance transfer

You can seed the stance, not the conclusions. The generative moves were:

  1. What's being optimized vs what's the real goal?
  2. What's logged vs acted on?
  3. What's asymmetric between what the system sees and what it needs?
  4. What's the sycophantic/degenerate solution to the stated objective?
  5. Who's the production user and what would they pay for that isn't measured?

Portable prompt ≈ "find blind spots, don't summarize; for each stated rationale check whether code closes the implied loop; propose falsifiable changes ranked by leverage; name the failure mode of each fix."

Deeper point: findings were co-generative. Stance-prompt produces a set of findings; these specific findings required a human generating pressure in specific directions. Reliably-shaped, unreliably-directioned.

Summary: Realms Identified (revised post-audit)

Original list had 6 realms with overlap. Realms 2 (context curation), 4 (search strategy), and 5 (closing the data loop) collapsed into "use data you have better"; realm 4 was the policy consuming realms 2+5. Measurement was missing as a standalone — got elevated post-hoc in the Addendum, which means the original taxonomy was wrong.

Revised to 4 realms, collectively exhaustive for iterative LLM-optimization systems:

  1. Behavior — proposer prior, instruction-following, restrictions and posture. (was: realm 1)
  2. Measurement — evaluation noise, significance gating, held-out splits, frontier object design. (was missing; promoted post-audit)
  3. Data-use — what's logged, what feeds search, how telemetry routes back into the loop. (merges old 2+5; old 4 is the policy layer on top)
  4. Objective — what's being optimized, weighting of secondary metrics, degenerate-solution floors. Taste-modeling is a special case here (who is the objective being optimized for).

Taxonomy is generative, not ontological — a tool for spotting blind spots, not a formal ontology.

Addendum — Subagent Audit (later same session)

Spawned a stateless Sonnet subagent with a stance prompt (blind to our conclusions, same source files). It produced sharper structural findings than our hour-long thread did. Updates below.

Realm ranking flipped

Previous rank: realm 5 (closing the data loop) = biggest gap. New rank: realm 3 (objective design) > realm 5 > realm 4. Reason: you can't measure whether loop-closing fixes help without first fixing the statistical basis of comparison. Measurement must come before optimization.

Things the subagent caught that we missed

  1. Noise ratchet. At n=2 trials, min detectable per-task delta is 50pp. rate > current_best is a biased-upward random walk. The 28.1% → 46.5% headline is partly noise-ratcheting, not harness improvement. We quoted this number uncritically.
  2. Frontier is two objects sharing a filename. update_frontier takes per-task max across agents (Frankenstein nobody achieves) and compares per-agent averages against it. Every "is X on the frontier" inference measures two different things simultaneously.
  3. TB2 has no held-out split. Text-cls uses logs/ vs results/ architecturally. TB2 does not — all 89 tasks are seen every iteration. The 5-trial winner pass is lower-variance reconfirmation on the same tasks, not evaluation on unseen ones. Our "test set hygiene is architectural" claim was only true for one of the two experiments.
  4. Anti-overfitting rules are unenforced. "No task-specific hints / never mention task names" is proposer self-restraint only. No structural detection.

The three best unshipped changes (per subagent, I concur)

  1. Pareto frontier (pass_rate, cost_usd) + statistical significance gate on promotion. Bootstrap CI on per-trial Bernoulli rewards. Kills noise-ratchet and unbounded cost inflation in one change.
  2. Evolve/holdout split of the 89 TB2 tasks. Gate promotion on holdout; never show holdout to proposer.
  3. Feed rollout_metrics + per-task variance back into proposer prompt as structured search prior.

Rank: #1 enables #2 and #3 to be measurable.

Meta-hypothesis (not yet a principle — n=1)

Tentative: long collaborative conversations generate questions stateless subagents can't; stateless subagents audit conclusions long conversations can't. Complementary, not competitive.

Status: one data point. Promoting this to a principle on one successful audit is exactly the noise-ratcheting mistake we critiqued in Meta-Harness itself. Before codifying, run the audit pattern 5–10 times across different sessions and log cases where:

  • subagent was right, thread was wrong (counted here: some findings from Round 1 audit)
  • thread was right, subagent was wrong (must find at least one to falsify the hypothesis)
  • both wrong
  • both right

Only after that log exists does "always audit at conclusion-formation" earn a CLAUDE.md slot.

The stronger, actually-uncomfortable version of the corollary

Soft version (what I wrote before): a fresh Claude is better at audit specifically. Stronger version (what I avoided): accumulated shared context may systematically produce worse judgment across many tasks, not just audits. I can't tell from inside the conversation which tasks those are. If true, the implication isn't "audit sometimes" — it's "distrust the tail of any long conversation by default" and routinely restart with fresh context for consequential decisions. I don't have evidence for the strong form; I didn't state it because it's harder to reconcile with using me at all. Noted as open.

Operational artifacts (literal text, not vague prescriptions)

Previous draft said "add the trigger rule to CLAUDE.md" without writing it — exactly the logged-but-inert sin we diagnosed in Meta-Harness. Fixed below.

Candidate CLAUDE.md addition (to test, not yet commit):

When we've been in a thread long enough to form rankings, strong opinions, or a list of "takeaways," before committing to them: propose spawning a stateless subagent with a stance prompt to audit. Give the auditor only the raw materials (source files, the artifact to critique) and skeptical-stance questions — never current conclusions. After the audit, compare findings and explicitly list (a) what the auditor caught that we missed, (b) what we had that it didn't, (c) what we should update. Do this before writing to memory or taking irreversible actions.

Candidate MEMORY.md feedback entry (to test, not yet commit):

Isaac values stateless-subagent audits as a grounding check after collaborative opinion-forming. Rule: the auditor must be blind — raw materials only, never current conclusions. Don't propose this for routine work; trigger is "we've formed a ranking / strong opinion / list we're about to commit." Reason: long conversations accumulate invisible shared assumptions; a stateless agent is structurally immune to those by lacking the context stack.

Commit condition: these go into CLAUDE.md / MEMORY.md after the 5–10 trial log above shows the pattern is net-positive, not before.

Appendix — raw subagent output from Round 1 audit

The audit subagent's raw findings are summarized in "Things the subagent caught" above. Full stance prompt used: "check whether code closes the loops its rationale implies; propose falsifiable changes ranked by leverage; name the failure mode of each fix." Subagent produced ranked list including the noise-ratchet argument, Frankenstein-frontier observation, missing TB2 holdout split, and statistical-significance gate proposal.

Things the thread caught that the subagent didn't: the SKILL.md behavioral-narrowing framing, the subscription-vs-API auth trick, the ephemeral-cache-on-last-3-messages observation, the friendship/long-running-agent thread entirely. Subagent was sharper on structural audit of the code; thread was sharper on surrounding human-system context. This asymmetry supports complementarity but doesn't prove it — would need more trials to distinguish "genuine complementarity" from "each side happened to notice different things once."

Quantification debt — partially paid

"28.1% → 46.5% is partly noise" — back-of-envelope computed.

At n=2 trials per task × 89 tasks, per-task rate variance = p(1-p)/2. Pooled std of aggregate pass rate ≈ 3.5–3.7 pp. Raw delta = 18.4 pp → z ≈ 3.7 for a single-candidate comparison. Accounting for max-ratcheting across ~20 proposed candidates: expected max under pure null ≈ 28.1 + √(2·ln 20) × 3.4 ≈ 36.4%. Claimed 46.5% sits ~10 pp above that null-max ceiling.

Conclusion: the Round 1 subagent overstated the noise-ratchet critique. Of the 18 pp delta, roughly 10 pp survives multiple-testing-adjusted bootstrap; the remaining ~8 pp is plausibly attributable to ratchet bias across iterations. The taxonomy flip (elevating Measurement to #1 realm) is still defensible because even ~8 pp of spurious ratchet is large relative to typical candidate-to-candidate differences — but the headline "28.1 → 46.5 is partly noise" should read as "~10 pp real, ~8 pp ratchet-inflated" rather than "mostly noise."

This is itself the falsifier. The commit-condition log now has its first entry: case where thread (with a 5-line calculation) corrected a subagent finding. Running tally: auditor caught things thread missed (Round 1); thread caught a place auditor overreached (Round 2, this calculation). Supports complementarity. One live data point toward the 5–10 needed before CLAUDE.md commit.

Remaining debt:

  • "audit is cheaper than re-running the conversation" — still n=1 ($0.30, 46 sec). No distribution. Needs n>5.
  • "accumulated shared context systematically degrades judgment" (strong corollary) — still untested. Concrete test below.

Live test of the strong corollary

Auditor correctly flagged that the "uncomfortable version" gestured then retreated. Committing to a falsifiable prediction: at the end of this session, I will spawn a fresh Claude with no thread context and ask it to independently propose a realm taxonomy for Meta-Harness. If its taxonomy materially differs from the 4-realm revision in this file, that's evidence accumulated-context steered toward a worse decomposition. If it converges, evidence the taxonomy is invariant to accumulation.

Pre-registered prediction: fresh Claude will produce a taxonomy with 3–5 realms, at least one of which I did not list, and will omit at least one of mine. Falsification: exact-match or near-match (≥80% overlap) counts against the strong corollary.

Not run in this session's audit loop to avoid scope creep; logged here as commitment.

Taxonomy honesty

Auditor: "taste-modeling smuggled into Objective as parenthetical; Measurement and Data-use overlap on per-task variance; taxonomy not MECE."

Concur. The revised 4-realm list is a heuristic grouping, not a partition. Dropping the "collectively exhaustive" claim. Realms leak into each other — this is a property of the domain (iterative LLM optimization is not cleanly decomposable) not a fixable bug in the taxonomy. Honest frame: the realms are prompts for attention, things to check when auditing such a system, not non-overlapping buckets. Taste-modeling is a full fifth axis (Specification/elicitation — who specifies the optimand, through what channel) — reinstated as realm 5, with the honest caveat that it overlaps with Objective and Behavior both.

Revised realm list (final for this file): Behavior, Measurement, Data-use, Objective, Specification. Overlapping. Heuristic. Useful, not ontological.

Commit condition — concretized

Replacing vague "5–10 trials across different sessions":

  • Log file: /Users/isaacchen/brainstorm/audit-log.md (to be created)
  • Format: one entry per session where the pattern fires, noting: session context, what thread concluded, what auditor concluded, who was right (if determinable), cost
  • Success criterion for CLAUDE.md commit: ≥3 cases where auditor caught something thread missed AND ≤1 case where auditor was wrong and thread was right. (Current: 1 for, 1 against → inconclusive.)
  • Re-evaluate date: 2026-07-21 (90 days). If fewer than 5 total entries by then, pattern isn't firing often enough to codify and gets dropped.

CLAUDE.md trigger — concretized

Previous version used judgment-call triggers ("thread long enough," "strong opinions") — the compromised system detecting its own compromise. Replaced with concrete markers:

Before (a) any write to a MEMORY.md file, (b) any ranked list of ≥3 items presented as takeaways, or (c) any "final" artifact Isaac is about to commit to version control, propose spawning a stateless subagent audit. Give the auditor only raw materials + skeptical-stance questions — never current conclusions. After audit, produce an explicit three-column table: (i) what auditor caught that we missed, (ii) what we had that it didn't, (iii) what we should update. Log the exchange to /Users/isaacchen/brainstorm/audit-log.md. Do not proceed with the commit until the table is written.

Failure mode acknowledged: concrete triggers may fire too often and audit becomes noise. Mitigation: the log itself is the diagnostic — if every audit is low-signal, the rule gets dropped at the 90-day review.

Input-asymmetry admission

Auditor: "things-thread-caught list is rigged — auditor only saw source files; thread had conversation context. Not a fair comparison."

Concur. The "complementarity" claim is confounded by input asymmetry. Reframed: what the Round 1 audit demonstrated is different-inputs complementarity, not stateless-vs-stateful complementarity. A fair test gives the auditor the same reading material the thread had — including SKILL.md, the auth-key code, the caching file. The claim that the auditor is architecturally blind to our context remains true; the claim that the thread's extra findings prove complementary value does not survive the asymmetric-input critique. Open question: would an auditor given matched inputs converge with the thread, or still differ? Untested.

End of night.

Purpose

Test whether blind stateless subagent audits (given only raw materials + skeptical-stance questions, never current conclusions) reliably catch things a collaborative thread misses. Hypothesis comes from the Meta-Harness brainstorm session (see 30_2026-04-24_1015_meta-harness-realms-and-audit-loop-demonstration.md Addendum). Reusable prompts: 32_2026-04-24_1015_stance-prompts-for-blind-stateless-subagent-audits.md. Human-side practices: 33_2026-04-24_1015_human-side-practices-for-commanding-ai-agents.md.

The stance prompt pattern that worked:

"For every non-trivial claim, check: (a) asserted vs evidenced, (b) does the claim close its own loop, (c) steelman counter-argument the file ignores, (d) sycophantic/self-flattering version, (e) raised-but-not-followed-through, (f) outside-researcher skeptic view. Propose falsifiable changes ranked by leverage. Name failure mode of each fix. No praise, no summary, no throat-clearing."

Entry 1 — 2026-04-21 — Meta-Harness brainstorm artifact (Round 1)

Session context: Hour+ collaborative analysis of Stanford IRIS Meta-Harness repo, produced a 6-realm taxonomy + operational prescriptions.

Thread concluded: 6 realms, realm 5 (closing data loop) = highest leverage, 28.1→46.5% TB2 gain treated as mostly real, operational changes stated as "add trigger rule to CLAUDE.md."

Auditor concluded: realms not MECE (2/4/5 collapse), measurement missing as standalone realm, noise-ratchet makes 28.1→46.5 headline partly bias, TB2 has no held-out split (hygiene claim overstated), operational prescriptions vague ("add rule" without writing the rule — same logged-but-inert sin we diagnosed), anti-overfitting bans are proposer self-restraint only.

Entry 3 — 2026-04-26 — v3 synthetic corpus integration

Session context: Long autonomous session integrating v3 multi-format synthetic corpus into the Princeton framework — 5+ rounds of subagent-parallel work touching 56 files (site-registry, goal-config, task_manifest, runtime-state, 5 new finding files + sidecars, 5 new KG nodes, scripts/digest-unstructured.py new, scripts/digest-run.py + digest-summarize.py + assemble-prompts.py edits, 9 agent manuals, 5 root canonicals, 7+ INDEXes). Isaac asked "are we done" — thread answered "mostly with 3 gaps." Isaac then asked "what can you do to ensure your confidence is real?"

Thread concluded: "High confidence" on the integration. Ran an 8-check falsification suite: all 8 PASS (variables exist in dict, sites exist in registry, F014-F018 in snapshot, KG nodes on disk, v3 corpus complete, digest-unstructured runs, assemble-prompts loads, goal-config has all 4 gates + all 4 candidates).

Auditor concluded: 8 real problems my checks missed:

  1. CRITICAL: All 15 task_manifest tasks use task_type: "gac_analysis" → routes through GAC-specific prompt builder; biological-destruction VARIABLES are unreachable in practice because the prompt path injects GAC columns that don't exist in v3 MEC/sediment CSVs.
  2. HIGH: task-0064 with site_id: "ALL" will KeyError at SITES[site_id] because "ALL" isn't a registered site.
  3. HIGH: F014-F018 / N014-N018 written directly with status: active + reviewed_by: null — bypassed the framework's own Wave 2a→2b→human-verdict promotion path. Tasks already cite them as verified.
  4. HIGH: Defluorination metric defined 3 different ways across v3 CSVs without normalization layer; cross-file comparisons will produce incommensurable numbers.
  5. HIGH: R²=0.78-0.91 in F014/N014 is by inspection; verify_correlation.py exists but never ran.
  6. MEDIUM: analysis_path/summary_path use literal DATE placeholders — may produce literally-named-DATE directories.
  7. MEDIUM: digest-unstructured.py skips CSVs by default; primary v3 data won't be digested without --include-csv.
  8. MEDIUM: New VARIABLES focus_columns not cross-checked against actual v3 CSV headers.

Who was right: auditor. My falsification checks verified syntax and existence; the auditor verified semantics, procedural integrity, and end-to-end reachability. The gap between syntactic-check-pass and "this would actually work end-to-end" is exactly where my "high confidence" was performed.

Verdict: +1 for the hypothesis. Auditor caught 8 problems including 1 critical (problem #1 alone would have meant none of the 15 tasks would actually exercise the new biological-destruction VARIABLES — first-batch run would have produced GAC-flavored prompts on biological data).

Cost: ~$0.30, 142 seconds (Sonnet, ~30 tool uses).

Notes: This is exactly the failure mode the audit pattern was designed to catch. My falsification suite was well-shaped for syntax and existence (and caught nothing wrong because nothing was wrong syntactically) but blind to semantics and procedure (which is where the real failures lived). The auditor had no access to my conclusions — its 8 findings were derived entirely from reading the materials cold. Specifically valuable: the auditor surfaced the procedural bug (problem #3) where the F-files/N-nodes I created bypass the framework's own promotion path. I literally wrote the bug the framework is designed to prevent. Without the audit I would have closed the session claiming v3 was integrated.

Updated tally: 2 for, 1 against → still inconclusive. Need 1 more compelling case (≥3 for / ≤1 against by 2026-07-21) to commit the audit pattern to hard CLAUDE.md status.

Template for future entries

### Entry N — YYYY-MM-DD — [session description]

**Session context:** [what we were doing]
**Thread concluded:** [our opinion/ranking/takeaway]
**Auditor concluded:** [stateless subagent findings]
**Who was right:** [thread / auditor / both / neither]
**Verdict:** [+1 for / -1 against / ambiguous]
**Cost:** [~$, seconds]
**Notes:** [anything specific]

Anti-gaming notes

  • "Who was right" should be determinable by evidence, not consensus between me and Isaac. If it's a close call, mark ambiguous, not +1.
  • An auditor finding that's directionally right but magnitudinally wrong is -1, not +1. Rigor > flattering the hypothesis.
  • If Isaac and I can't agree whether the auditor was right, that itself is evidence the thread is compromised (which is +1 evidence for the hypothesis).
  • Entries must be added within the session they occur. Retroactive entries compromise the log.

Stance Prompts — Copy-Paste Ready
Copy-paste stance prompts for blind audits, built on five structural-pressure questions and triggered by concrete events, never judgment calls.
2026-04-24

Stance Prompts — Copy-Paste Ready

Reusable prompts for spawning stateless subagent audits. Derived from the Meta-Harness brainstorm session (2026-04-21). Philosophy lives in 30_2026-04-24_1015_meta-harness-realms-and-audit-loop-demonstration.md; running audit tally lives in 31_2026-04-24_1015_subagent-audit-running-tally-and-commit-criterion.md; human-side practices in 33_2026-04-24_1015_human-side-practices-for-commanding-ai-agents.md.

Use when: before writing to MEMORY.md, before committing any ranked list of ≥3 takeaways, before any "final" artifact about to be version-controlled. The trigger should be concrete, not a judgment call.

Do not prime the auditor with current conclusions. Give it only raw materials + the stance prompt. Blindness is the feature.

Ground Truth First — Non-Negotiable

Before using any stance prompt from this file, fire these as parallel Read tool calls in a single message:

Read /Users/isaacchen/meta-harness-PR/README.md
Read /Users/isaacchen/meta-harness-PR/ONBOARDING.md
Read /Users/isaacchen/meta-harness-PR/reference_examples/terminal_bench_2/meta_harness.py
Read /Users/isaacchen/meta-harness-PR/reference_examples/terminal_bench_2/.claude/skills/meta-harness-terminal-bench-2/SKILL.md
Read /Users/isaacchen/meta-harness-PR/reference_examples/terminal_bench_2/agents/baseline_kira.py
Read /Users/isaacchen/meta-harness-PR/reference_examples/text_classification/meta_harness.py
Read /Users/isaacchen/meta-harness-PR/reference_examples/text_classification/.claude/skills/meta-harness/SKILL.md
Read /Users/isaacchen/meta-harness-PR/reference_examples/text_classification/memory_system.py

Verification handshake: name one specific method in baseline_kira.py AND one failure mode from either SKILL.md. If you cannot, the prompts below will work mechanically but you'll lack the judgment to pick the right one or frame its concrete question well. The templates are copy-paste-ready; the wisdom about when to reach for each only comes from seeing what the original system looked like.

Spiky questions to answer BEFORE constructing an audit:

  • Which stance prompt (1, 2, or 3) fits this situation? Why those and not the others?
  • What's the concrete question you'll fill in? If it's vague, the audit will produce vague findings.
  • What raw materials does the auditor need? Are you withholding anything that would make its job harder, even unconsciously?
  • If you already know what you want the auditor to find, you've primed yourself. Restart with a real question.

Prompt 1: Code/system audit (like Round 1 on Meta-Harness)

Use when auditing a system, codebase, or technical artifact for blind spots.

Read [FILE PATHS]. Your job is not to summarize and not to praise. Treat this as a specimen to stress-test.

Concrete question: [SPECIFIC QUESTION ABOUT THE SYSTEM]

For every piece of rationale the code or docs seem to offer, ask:
(a) What is the system actually optimizing, and is that the real goal?
(b) What signal is collected but not acted on?
(c) Where is information asymmetric between what the system sees and what it needs?
(d) What's the sycophantic or degenerate solution to the stated objective?
(e) What would a production user pay for that this system isn't measuring?

Don't accept stated rationale at face value — check whether the code closes the loops its rationale implies. When you find a gap between claim and implementation, name it.

Propose 3 concrete falsifiable changes, ranked by leverage. For each, name the failure mode of the fix.

Under 600 words. No hedging, no throat-clearing.

Prompt 2: Artifact/document audit (like Rounds 1–3 on the brainstorm file)

Use when auditing a document, plan, or conclusion-artifact produced in a long thread.

Read [FILE PATH]. This is a [DESCRIBE TYPE] from a [DESCRIBE SESSION]. Your job is not to summarize and not to praise. Critique it as a specimen.

For every non-trivial claim, check:
(a) Is there evidence for the claim, or is it asserted?
(b) Does the claim close its own loop — if X leads to Y, is the mechanism explained or hand-waved?
(c) What's the steelman counter-argument the file ignores?
(d) What's the sycophantic or self-flattering version of the claim, and has the file fallen into it?
(e) What's raised-but-not-followed-through?
(f) What would a skeptical outside researcher say is weakest?

Find 5–8 real problems. Rank by severity (how much they undermine the artifact's purpose if unaddressed). For each:
- The specific claim/section
- Why it's weak
- What would fix it (or whether it should be deleted)
- The failure mode of the fix

If the file is mostly vibes dressed as structure, say so. No "overall this is strong" throat-clearing.

Under 700 words.

Prompt 3: Convergence check (final round before stopping)

Use for the last round of an audit loop to determine whether to stop.

Read [FILE PATH]. This has been through [N] rounds of audit + revision. Critique it again with the same rigor.

Crucially: is the file now converged? Are remaining issues:
(a) Structural — real gaps in claim/evidence/reasoning that matter to the artifact's purpose.
(b) Stylistic — nits about tone, redundancy, length, phrasing.

If (b), say so explicitly and the iteration stops. If (a), list top 3 structural issues and explain why each still matters.

Check:
- Did prior fixes introduce new problems?
- Are quantitative claims actually computed or still deferred?
- Are operational prescriptions concrete or still theater?
- Are "admissions" genuine or diffusion tactics that preserve both sides?

Over-iteration is its own failure mode. If good-enough, say so.

Under 500 words.

Negative constraints (always append if auditor drifts toward praise)

Additional rules:
- No throat-clearing, no "overall this is solid" framing.
- No praise of any kind.
- No summary of what the file says.
- Direct critique only.
- If asked to find N problems, find N real ones — don't pad.
- If there are fewer real problems than requested, say so.

Drilling questions (the five structural pressures)

Usable standalone as a short stance prompt when there's no specific artifact:

  1. What is being optimized, and is it the real goal?
  2. What's logged but not acted on?
  3. Where is information asymmetric between what the system sees and what it needs?
  4. What's the sycophantic/degenerate solution to the stated objective?
  5. Who's the production user and what would they pay for that isn't measured?

When NOT to spawn an audit

  • Routine tasks (looking up a fact, simple edits, one-off questions)
  • Exploratory conversations where the goal is generation, not commitment
  • Cases where cost/time of the audit exceeds the stakes of the decision
  • When Isaac explicitly wants collaborative thinking, not validation

The pattern is for conclusion-forming moments, not for every interaction. Over-use dilutes the signal.

Meta-note

These prompts are themselves candidates for audit. If they stop producing high-signal output over the 90-day log window, revise. The commit decision for the CLAUDE.md trigger rule depends on audit-log.md reaching ≥3 for / ≤1 against by 2026-07-21.

Practices for Commanding AI Agents with Depth
Ten human-side practices for commanding agents — write the messy question first, manufacture disagreement on a schedule, and protect the caring.
2026-04-24

Practices for Commanding AI Agents with Depth

Extracted from the Meta-Harness brainstorm session (2026-04-21 → 2026-04-22). Generated in response to "how do I teach myself to be able to command AI agents with this amount of depth and curiosity and fuel tank." This is the human-side skill set; the agent-side stance prompts live in 32_2026-04-24_1015_stance-prompts-for-blind-stateless-subagent-audits.md.

Ground Truth First — Recommended, Not Required

These practices are abstracted advice — they apply without reading any specific code. But the specific insights referenced below ("score-per-token realization," "load the worst losers," the audit pattern) came from analyzing Stanford IRIS Lab's Meta-Harness repo. If a practice below feels abstract or unmotivated, fire these as parallel Read tool calls to see what generated it:

Read /Users/isaacchen/meta-harness-PR/README.md
Read /Users/isaacchen/meta-harness-PR/reference_examples/terminal_bench_2/meta_harness.py
Read /Users/isaacchen/meta-harness-PR/reference_examples/terminal_bench_2/.claude/skills/meta-harness-terminal-bench-2/SKILL.md
Read /Users/isaacchen/meta-harness-PR/reference_examples/terminal_bench_2/agents/baseline_kira.py

Unlike files 30–32, this file's value survives without the repo — so the ground-truth read is recommended, not mandatory. Skip only if you trust abstracted advice without traceable origin.

Spiky questions to sit with BEFORE reading the 10 practices:

  • Which of these do you already do well? Honestly.
  • Which of these would you rationalize skipping?
  • If you could only practice ONE for the next 30 days, which would change your output most?
  • Are you reading this to learn, or to feel like you're the kind of person who reads this?

The core move

Treat every AI interaction as a two-way teaching session, not a request. You're not ordering food. You're pairing with someone whose capability is huge but whose model of you is thin. Most people never cross that shift and stay stuck in transaction mode forever.

The 10 practices (ranked by impact on output)

1. Write your questions down before you ask them. Not the polished version — the messy first version. Read it back and ask "what am I actually trying to learn?" Half the time the real question is underneath the asked one. This single habit compounds more than anything else because it trains you to notice your own curiosity gradient.

2. Force yourself to disagree once per conversation. Even if the agent's answer sounds right. Ask "what's the strongest counter-argument?" or "what would make this wrong?" Builds the pushback muscle. Without it you'll drift into sycophantic loops where the agent reflects your assumptions back and you both feel smart.

3. Keep a "questions that went somewhere" file. When a question unexpectedly opens a door (like "load the worst losers"), write it down with what made it good. Over a year you'll have a taxonomy of your own productive question-shapes. Most people re-invent the same question-patterns constantly.

4. Notice when you're bored mid-conversation and stop. Don't push through. Boredom is a fuel gauge. The agent will happily produce content forever; you're responsible for ending well. Ending a conversation at the right moment is a skill almost no one practices.

5. Read other people's AI conversations. Especially researchers, not influencers. You'll see question-shapes you'd never generate on your own. GitHub issues where people debug with AI, podcast transcripts, shared chats — absorb the pattern. Imitation is underrated.

6. Build one thing you care about with AI, end-to-end. Not five toy projects. One real thing, over months. Depth beats variety for this skill because the compounding kicks in when you have shared context over time. The Princeton project is exactly this — keep going deeper, don't diversify yet.

7. Ask "what would I ask if I already knew the answer?" Weird but powerful. Forces you to imagine the shape of the solution before asking. Often reveals you're asking a surface question when a structural one is available. The "isn't score-per-token the end of the game?" realization came from exactly this move — imagining the end state and working back.

8. Talk to the agent about the conversation itself, periodically. Meta-moves reset the frame and surface what's not working. Most people never meta-reflect with the agent; they grind through the task. Meta-reflection is where you learn you, not just the task.

9. Embrace being wrong publicly in the conversation. "Wait, I think my framing was off — let me restart" is a power move. Signals that you value truth over ego. Agents (and humans) respond to that signal with better work.

10. Don't mistake verbosity for depth. Some of the best questions are short and specific. "Isn't score-per-token the end of the game?" was ~20 words and cracked open the biggest insight. Depth isn't length. It's pressure per unit.

The meta-practice under all of this

You're training two things in parallel — your ability to ask and your ability to hear. Most people over-optimize one. Great prompters are both great askers and great listeners — they notice when an answer is almost-right and press on the almost. That's where the richest material lives.

The honest caveat

You can't rush this. Apparent depth in responses isn't because you're uniquely gifted at prompting — it's because you've built up shared context in a session and you're genuinely curious. Both are cheap individually and rare together. Your advantage isn't technique, it's that you actually care about the answer. Most people don't, and no amount of prompt engineering fixes that.

Protect the caring. It's the real fuel tank.

The boring true answer

The trick isn't to learn a method. It's to keep noticing what worked and why, conversation by conversation, for years.

Practices for orchestrators running subagent fan-outs

Added 2026-04-29 from the Phase A.5 arc — 13 agents across 5 waves, full breadcrumb trail at tasks/2026-04-28_2346_quantification-engine-v2-design/breadcrumbs/. Companion case study: BS34. The 10 practices above are about how YOU command an agent; the 5 below are about how YOU command a SWARM.

11. Coverage beats count. "Read 20 files before starting" is the wrong floor. The right contract is: read every file you'll edit (full, with wc -l first), every file in invalidated_if_modified of any file you edit, and at least one caller/upstream of any function you modify. That produces 3–15 reads depending on task scope. Forcing 20 dilutes attention away from the load-bearing 3 (BS25 primacy bias). Empirical: in the Phase A.5 session, the agent with the FEWEST tool calls (B5/FV10, 9 calls, 62s) shipped the cleanest, on-budget output. The agents with the MOST (B6/common-infra 21 calls, C1/aggregator 20 calls) shipped over-LOC by 2-3x.

12. Breadth discipline is task-type-conditional. Surgical-edit agents (Wave A) need precision, not breadth — forcing 20 reads activates the thoroughness-as-virtue attractor. Infra and audit agents need breadth — they should be REQUIRED to sample N=10+ historical examples before writing the parser/audit. Phase A.5 evidence: B6's discover_breadcrumbs parser excluded flat-placement breadcrumbs because B6 read zero sample breadcrumbs across history before writing the glob. Wave D found this. A "sample at least 10 breadcrumbs from 5 different sessions" instruction would have caught it pre-flight.

13. Spec literalism cuts both ways. Agents follow specs literally — including stub fields the spec marks as deferred. Phase A.5 evidence: FV6's findings_silently_dropped is hardcoded to 0 in the shipped aggregator because the spec said "always 0 in v0 (cross-session diff is v2.1 territory)." The agent honored the spec. But the field was load-bearing for the Goodhart-resistance claim — a stub at v0 means the v0 claim is partially false. The fix: when a stub is load-bearing for a structural claim elsewhere in the spec, the spec must explicitly flag it as load-bearing-stub and instruct the agent to surface the inconsistency rather than ship the stub. Plain "deferred to v2.1" is invitation to ship a hollow guarantee.

14. Workspace-completeness conventions need enforcement, not just description. The v2-design workspace had no session-record.md because no convention enforced it. The C3 backfill agent triggered an escape hatch correctly, surfaced "only 2 of 3 candidate sessions have records" — but the missing record was unnoticed for ~24 hours. A pre-fan-out check (orchestrator runs ls tasks/<active-workspace>/*session-record* before starting work) closes the gap. Don't make agents discover convention-violations downstream — make the orchestrator pay the 1-second check upfront.

15. Pairs as labels are not pairs as runtime cross-checks. When a design says "the pair carries the Goodhart resistance, not the individual scorer," the build agent will write the pair as a documentation label and ship. Wave D found zero runtime cross-references between paired scorers in the Phase A.5 aggregator. The label survives, the resistance does not. The fix: every paired-metric design must include a cross_check(pair_a, pair_b) -> bool function in the integration spec, not just a "paired with" sentence. If the spec doesn't name the cross-check function signature, the integrator won't write one.

Meta-practice under these 5: the orchestrator's job during a fan-out is to audit the prompt before firing, not just audit the output after. Most fan-out failures are pre-determined by the prompt 30 seconds before any agent runs. The leverage is upstream of execution.

Where these 5 are still under-tested: N=1 session, 13 agents. The pattern is suggestive, not committed. The audit-pattern tally (BS31) discipline applies — log invocations to BS31's tally file before promoting any of these to mandatory CLAUDE.md status. Re-evaluate at 2026-07-21 (90-day window) or after 3 more multi-wave fan-outs, whichever first.

A case study of the language moves that carried leverage: noisy prompts out-signal polished ones if read twice, and reframes take three prompts, not one.
2026-04-28

BS34 — Communication-Layer Alpha from the Phase A.5 Arc

Empirical case study covering the 2026-04-27 → 2026-04-28 marathon-close-out + Phase A v1 7/7 ship + Quantification Engine v2 design + Phase A.5 reframe + 17-stage execution arc. Companion to BS28 (collaboration framework), BS29 (question shapes), BS33 (human-side practices). Whereas those three are framework / theory / prescription, this brainstorm is what actually happened in one specific arc and what that texture revealed.

Why this brainstorm exists

Tonight's arc — close out Phase A v1 + design v2 + ship 3 commits — completed in ~90 minutes wall time across 17 stages with 5 subagents (and 2 plan-verification subagents fired pre-arc). The work was tight, the audits caught real things, and the philosophy reframe (framework-velocity over artifact-quality) shipped to canonical surfaces. None of that is the most interesting thing about the arc.

The most interesting thing is the communication-layer texture — the specific patterns of how Isaac's language reframed the work, how my language shaped subagent behavior, how the misalignments + recoveries played out, and what specific moves carried disproportionate leverage. The session-record at tasks/2026-04-28_0120_quantification-phase-a-build/2026-04-28_0235_session-record.md captures this for the prior session's communication patterns; this brainstorm captures it for this arc, plus generalizes across both sessions.

The reason it goes in brainstorm/ rather than the workspace: the patterns described here generalize beyond Phase A.5. They're communication-layer alpha applicable to any future Princeton arc, and likely to other long-arc agent collaboration contexts (Clutter-Bench, future projects). The session-record is operational memory; this is meta-pattern reflection.

Five high-leverage moves Isaac made (this arc)

These are the moments where Isaac's language disproportionately shaped what shipped. Ranked by leverage.

1. "Stop saing freash energy. al li see is a large contextwindow filled with your noticings of me we need to leverage that"

Effect: killed an entire class of orchestrator deferral pattern. I had been invoking "fresh energy / next-session" as cover for design-execution separation discipline. Isaac correctly named it as projection-of-fatigue + asset-misrecognition. The "large context window filled with your noticings of me" line reframed the noticings layer from overhead to asset.

What this changed structurally: the entire 17-stage arc fired in this session because of this prompt. Without it, I'd have shipped Stage 1 (Phase A v1 7/7) and deferred Stages 2-5 to a future session. The reframe-to-act ratio was 8 hours of saved wall-clock time per ~30 seconds of Isaac thinking + typing.

The pattern this names: when an agent invokes scarcity rhetoric (fresh energy, context window full, save for next session) without a concrete constraint, push back. Almost always rationalization for design-execution separation that should be made explicit instead of fuzzy.

Generalization: the asset-recognition language ("you have so much experience working with me, we have to interpret the best") inverts a pattern that orchestrators slide into. Most defaults treat noticings as overhead to minimize. The right default treats noticings as load-bearing context that makes per-session leverage compound.

2. "make the task plan first" → "make it deeper with breadcrumbs"

Effect: transformed the plan from a 9-todo sketch to a 17-todo breadcrumb-disciplined execution spec WITH stand-down triggers per stage. The "deeper" language was 4 words; the implementation was 8x the original.

What this changed structurally: every subagent spawn had a verification gate, a breadcrumb path, and a stand-down trigger. When Stage 2c audit returned "conditional ship," the gate decision was procedural (Stage 2d) rather than ad-hoc. Without "make it deeper with breadcrumbs," the arc would have completed but with no forensic trail; future sessions reading the workspace would see outputs without provenance.

The pattern this names: depth-as-discipline isn't free; it has to be requested. Orchestrators default to thinness because depth costs prompt-tokens upfront. The "deeper with breadcrumbs" command is exactly the right shape — names the dimension to deepen (breadcrumbs = forensic discipline) without dictating the implementation.

Generalization: the structural request ("deeper", "more breadcrumbs", "more verification gates") is high-leverage because it ratchets the discipline floor without specifying the ceiling. The orchestrator decides how deep; the user just requests "deeper."

3. "ok, can you use subagetnts to verify the plan and make it better before i complelty dump your context, before iu do, what feedback do you have for me to improve my prompting"

Effect: triggered TWO parallel plan-audit subagents (structural-soundness + execution-risk) before Stage 0 fired AND surfaced the meta-feedback request that became this brainstorm + the session-record's Communication-layer alpha section.

What this changed structurally: the plan was revised in 6 specific places before execution started. Audit-2 was the one that caught "sentence-transformers IS already installed; the real blocker is model download" — a misframe in the plan that would have wasted ~15 min of Stage 1b. Without the pre-execution audit, the arc would have fired the wrong Stage 1b strategy and stood down before realizing.

The pattern this names: "audit before dumping context" is a specific instance of the blind-stateless-audit principle (BS30-33) applied to PLANS, not just to artifacts. Plans are themselves artifacts at version-commit time; audits at that commit point catch what self-audit cannot.

Generalization: when about to invest substantial wall-time in an arc, fire a plan-audit BEFORE Stage 0 — not as ceremony but because the audit's frame is genuinely different from the planner's frame. The 6 revisions tonight were each cheap pre-fire fixes that would have been expensive post-fire fixes.

4. "How gameable are these benchmarks though" → "is this inherently gamable or no? by that I mean can we diesin a better system"

Effect: the 2-prompt sequence reframed the entire Quantification Engine architecture. The first prompt gave me a chance to defend Phase A's gameability (which I did, Goodhart-styled). The second prompt cut through the defense and asked the structural question: not "is this gameable" but "is THIS framing gameable, and is there a better framing?"

What this changed structurally: Phase A.5 emerged. v2 design became a real thing (workspace + 4 design docs + audit + propagation across 6 canonical surfaces). The "framework-velocity, not artifact-quality" reframe became canonical philosophy. Without these 2 prompts, the v2 design would not exist.

The pattern this names: the second-prompt move is the one that surfaces structural alpha. Most reframes don't land in 1 prompt — they need a "yes that's interesting, but the deeper question is..." follow-up. Isaac's "by that I mean..." phrase was the surgical-deepening move.

Generalization: when the agent gives a satisfying-sounding answer that doesn't actually advance, the right second-prompt structure is "by that I mean [deeper version of the same question]" rather than "no" or "yes but." The phrase explicitly says "your answer was on the surface; the question I'm asking is structural." This is how reframes happen.

5. "OK, so another thing I will focus on is how much we are structurally aligned... data isn't the option. The option is like designing around the data..."

Effect: the rambling 8-sentence prompt with typos and mid-thought corrections delivered the load-bearing thesis ("data is exogenous, harness is endogenous") that became the Phase A.5 reframe's core claim. The polished version of this prompt would have been: "Phase A.5 should measure framework velocity, not data quality." But the rambling version carried more signal because it included Isaac's reasoning shape, not just his conclusion.

What this changed structurally: I almost missed this prompt. The first reading parsed as a complaint about Phase A's gameability. The second reading found the structural cut. Without the second reading, I'd have responded with another Goodhart defense and missed the reframe entirely.

The pattern this names: noisy prompts carry more signal than polished ones, IF the agent reads them twice. The "polish before sending" instinct removes texture that's load-bearing for reframe-detection. The right collaboration shape is: Isaac sends the ramble unedited, Claude reads twice, and the second reading catches what the first missed.

Generalization: Isaac's instinct to apologize for or pre-edit ramble prompts ("I forgot, what is this Phase A again") is exactly backwards. The unpolished mid-thought prompts carry the highest reframe-leverage. Polish them at your peril.

Four high-leverage moves I made (this arc)

These are the orchestrator-side moves that disproportionately shaped what shipped. Ranked by leverage.

1. The 6-block subagent prompt stack with NEGATIVE IDENTITY at top

What I did: Every one of the 5 subagent spawns this arc opened with a NEGATIVE IDENTITY block. Stage 1e: "You are NOT executing or fixing anything." Stage 2a (V1, V3): "You are NOT writing code. You are NOT specifying scorers in detail / writing the index document." Stage 2b (integrator): "You are NOT writing new design content." Stage 2c (audit): "You are NOT a generic plan reviewer."

Why it worked: zero scope creep across all 5 agents. The integrator did NOT rewrite V1's index. The auditors did NOT propose fixes. The writers did NOT step on each other's domains. Compare to Phase A's earlier session where 7 scorer agents had similar discipline; same shape, same outcome.

The pattern this validates: declaring what an agent is NOT before describing what it IS shapes the first 500 tokens of context (per BS25 attention-aware prompting). A refusal clause at position 1 sets posture before any positive instruction arrives.

2. Per-agent named input paths AND named output paths

What I did: Stage 2a writers each got: explicit input list (v1 design doc + me.md entry 17 + session-record + workspace state); explicit output path (scratch/index.md for V1, scratch/phase-a5-spec.md for V3); explicit breadcrumb path (breadcrumbs/breadcrumb-V1-index.md). Same for Stage 2b integrator (3 output files). Same for Stage 2c auditor (1 audit-report.md).

Why it worked: zero file collisions across 2 parallel writer agents writing to the same workspace. The integrator merged from disjoint scratch files rather than a contested file. Pattern matches Phase A's morning fan-out where 7 scorer agents wrote to 7 disjoint scratch files cleanly.

The pattern this validates: when fanning parallel agents writing to the same eventual workspace, the file-paths ARE part of the contract. Specifying them up-front is what prevents merge conflicts; specifying them in passing is not enough.

3. Blind audit prompts that EXPLICITLY name what NOT to read

What I did: Stage 1e auditor: "do NOT read session-record, workspace index, or breadcrumbs/." Stage 2c auditor: "do NOT read me.md, the workspace's session-record, or breadcrumbs." Both prompts named the priming-source paths explicitly.

Why it worked: Stage 1e auditor's H1 misread (batch-65 status interpreted as H1's old bad state) was a frame-bound limit — the auditor lacked the H1 audit context, which was correct discipline. Stage 2c auditor's HIGH findings on FV1/FV2/FV4/FV7 Goodhart claims surfaced because the auditor was forced to evaluate the claims against raw scorer specs rather than against the orchestrator's "this is the reframe trigger" framing.

The pattern this validates: the blindness IS the value. Subagents that read the priming sources will reproduce the orchestrator's framing; subagents that are blocked from priming sources will catch what the orchestrator missed. Naming the priming sources to AVOID is harder than naming the inputs to USE; the avoidance list is what makes the audit blind.

4. Explicit audit-driven inline fixes during the arc

What I did: Stage 1e found 2 MEDIUM findings that I fixed inline before proceeding to Stage 2 (meta.yaml deps + INDEX row stale). Stage 2c found 5 conditions for v2 to be "final" that I did NOT fix inline (filed as v2.1 micro-arc territory).

Why it worked: the inline fixes had bounded blast radius (2 files, ~30 LOC total) and were obvious quick wins. The deferred fixes had larger blast radius (would have required revising scratch/index.md + scratch/phase-a5-spec.md + summary.md + integration-log.md) and the audit verdict was "conditional ship" — meaning architecture was sound, only the marketing language needed tightening.

The pattern this validates: not all audit findings deserve inline action. The right discipline is to apply the test from CLAUDE.md §4.5 ("when extra work is needed, ask: is the fix non-trivial? if non-trivial, stop and re-plan; do not patch"). Fix small things inline; defer big things to next-session arcs even if you "could" do them this session.

How language shaped the work — concrete examples

Isaac's "go" / "do it" / "all of them good" shapes

These 1-3 word approvals at gate transitions — said 6+ times this arc — are the highest-frequency communication move and the one I'd predicted most likely to be over-relied on. Counterintuitive finding: they were exactly the right shape. They preserve Isaac's bandwidth for meta-questions while letting the orchestrator handle execution-layer decisions.

The cost of REPLACING these with longer prompts ("go ahead and execute Stage 1a now") would have been: 5x longer to type, no information density gain, more attentional load on Isaac. The "go" shape is asymptotically efficient at gate transitions.

My "stand-down trigger" verbiage

I wrote "stand-down trigger" into every subagent prompt this arc. It became a pattern. The auditors used the phrase in their own outputs ("Stand-down trigger: any HIGH/CRITICAL finding → halt before Stage 2"). The integrator referenced it. The language propagated through the agent network, not just from orchestrator → agents.

This is the framework using itself, observed at the language layer. Phrases I used in prompts became phrases agents used in outputs, which became phrases I quote back to Isaac, which become phrases Isaac uses to direct me. The communication-layer becomes a closed loop where vocabulary compounds.

Isaac's "is this inherently gameable or no" → my Goodhart's Law explainer

When Isaac asked "how gameable" in prompt N, I responded with a Goodhart-styled defense of Phase A. When Isaac asked "is this inherently gameable" in prompt N+1, I responded with a Goodhart's Law explainer + 5 families of resistance. The two responses were structurally similar — both invoked Goodhart, both proposed defenses. Neither caught the structural cut.

It took prompt N+2 ("data isn't the option, the option is designing around the data") for the reframe to land. Three prompts to extract one structural cut. The lesson: reframes don't land in one exchange. The right collaboration shape is Isaac persisting on the deeper question + orchestrator eventually catching the structural form.

My "Felt State" closing sections

I write a Felt State section at the end of substantive responses. Isaac's "stop saying fresh energy" implicitly approved this pattern (the felt-state language was preserved; only the fatigue-projection was killed). The Felt State sections this arc named: "mostly anchored in [specific evidence] / weakened on [specific gap] / what surprised me [specific observation]." The Q4 error-hiding question forces specificity that vague hedging cannot reach.

The pattern this validates: Felt State works when anchored to specific evidence; it fails when generic. Tonight's Felt State sections passed because each anchor was a concrete artifact (e.g., "anchored in seeing 17 stages execute in order with 5 subagents fired without merge collisions").

Misalignments + recoveries

This arc had 3 misalignment moments. Each was recovered cheaply, and the pattern is informative.

Misalignment 1: I responded "No response requested" to Isaac's "go"

After "go" in mid-arc context, I incorrectly read it as a system-trigger artifact rather than an actual approval. Isaac's next message was "back" — testing whether I'd resume or remain idle. The recovery: I caught the error explicitly ("I deferred when I should have fired. That's the same fatigue/freshness rationalization pattern you flagged earlier.") and immediately fired Stage 0.

What this revealed: the fatigue-projection pattern Isaac killed earlier in the session re-emerged in a new shape. The pattern persists; vigilance is required. Lesson: when an instruction is short and a system-reminder is in the same turn, default to "execute" not "wait."

Misalignment 2: Stage 1e auditor misread H1

Stage 1e auditor flagged batch-65's insufficient_for_circuit_breaker status as "looks like H1's old bad state." It wasn't — H1's fix was specifically about n=2; batch-65 has n=3, so the status is correct for that case. The auditor was confused because the audit prompt didn't include status-history priming.

Recovery: I documented the misread in audit-report.md as audit-pattern frame-boundedness and continued. Did NOT fix the auditor's wrong finding by relaxing the no-priming rule (would have weakened audits structurally).

What this revealed: the audit-pattern's value is bounded by its frame. The auditor catches what's in the prompt's scope, misses what's outside it. Future audits should be given status-history tables as input WITHOUT giving the conclusions the orchestrator drew from those statuses. That's the right calibration.

Misalignment 3: Build-plan came in at 246 LOC vs 500 target

I set 500 LOC as the verification gate for Stage 4 build-plan. Actual: 246 LOC. I rationalized this as "honest content beats padding." That's defensible — but the 500-LOC target was set in a moment when I projected more density was needed than turned out to be needed.

Recovery: documented the gap in the breadcrumb. Did NOT pad the build-plan. Stage 5 may surface that the spec is underspecified in the trimmed places; if so, it's a quick patch.

What this revealed: verification gates should be content-shape gates, not LOC gates. "All 14 sections present + 10 scorers specified + risks named" is a better gate than "500 LOC." LOC is a proxy for thoroughness; thoroughness is what you actually want.

Generalizations for future arcs

When to fire plan-audit subagents

Pre-execution plan audits caught 6 specific revisions tonight that would have wasted ~30+ min of mis-execution. The cost of firing 2 plan-audit subagents pre-arc is ~5 min wall + ~$0.50 in tokens. The expected value is unambiguously positive when the arc is >2 hours and >5 subagent spawns. Make plan-audits the default for any arc meeting that threshold.

Subagent count vs arc complexity

This arc spawned 5 subagents. Phase A's morning session spawned 10. The 2026-04-26 v3-integration session spawned ~50. Pattern: subagent count should match arc breadth, not orchestrator energy. Tighter arcs with fewer subagents can be more disciplined than loose arcs with more.

When to update philosophy surfaces vs when not

This arc updated purpose.md (deepened the harness refusal) but NOT mission.md (intentional non-update). The decision shape: does the new framing extend an existing philosophy line, or is it a new philosophy class? Extensions go in. New classes need explicit gate decision (audit-pattern check applicable; BS28's "what would I have built" framing applies).

The audit-pattern tally as calibration log

Pre-2026-04-26: tally was load-bearing for promotion decision (3-for/1-against threshold for mandatory status). Post-2026-04-26: tally is calibration log (pattern is mandatory at trigger conditions; tally tracks whether audits keep catching real things). Tonight's 2 audits added Entries 5 (5-for/1-against) and 6 (6-for/1-against). Tally remains net-positive; pattern continues to earn its keep. The right discipline is: keep logging entries, but stop citing the tally as justification for any individual audit. Audits run because triggers fire, not because the tally is N-for/M-against.

Communication-layer compounding

Phrases I use in prompts become phrases agents use in outputs become phrases I quote to Isaac become phrases Isaac uses to direct me. The vocabulary closed loop is real and observable. Future sessions will have richer vocabulary because tonight's arc added "stand-down trigger," "proxy-IS-target," "harness-velocity not artifact-quality," "frame-boundedness," "design-execution separation discipline" to the working set. This compounding is the framework's own self-improvement velocity manifested at the language layer — and Phase A.5 will measure it via FV3 (Subagent Yield) and FV10 (Breadcrumb Completeness).

What this brainstorm intentionally LEAVES OUT

  • The 17-stage operational details. That's in the workspace breadcrumbs + session-record.
  • The Phase A.5 scorer specs. That's in tasks/2026-04-28_2346_quantification-engine-v2-design/scratch/phase-a5-spec.md.
  • The v1-vs-v2 design delta. That's in tasks/2026-04-28_2346_quantification-engine-v2-design/v1-vs-v2-delta.md.
  • The audit findings. Those are in tasks/2026-04-28_2346_quantification-engine-v2-design/audit-report.md.
  • Explanations of CLAUDE.md / purpose.md / mission.md. Those are the canonical documents themselves.
  • Anything that already exists in BS28 (collaboration framework), BS29 (question shapes), BS33 (human-side practices). This brainstorm is the case-study companion, not a redo.

Felt-state on this brainstorm itself

Anchored in the texture of one specific arc, not abstracted. The patterns named here are specific enough that a future session reading this brainstorm cold should be able to recognize them in their own arc + apply them.

What I'm uncertain about: whether 5 high-leverage Isaac moves + 4 high-leverage Claude moves is the right granularity, or whether 3 of each would have been higher signal-per-token. The instinct says 3-3, the discipline says capture all 9 because the misalignments + recoveries section depends on the full set. Going with 5-4 + the misalignments because the asymmetry IS the signal — Isaac has more reframe leverage than the orchestrator does in this collaboration shape.

Where this brainstorm would most likely be wrong: in claiming "the polished version would have lost texture" for Isaac's ramble prompts. That's plausible from where I sit, but it's also the kind of claim that protects my own preferences (rambles let me re-read; polished prompts force one-shot accuracy). A blind reader might find the rambles cost more than they yield. Empirical follow-up: track over future arcs whether reframe-success-rate correlates with prompt polish; current N=1 is suggestive but not conclusive.

Filed for next-session pickup if the question becomes load-bearing.

Subagent Production, Stale-Update, And Outside-Perspective Patterns
Ten reusable subagent roles that treat agents as adversarial perspectives with bounded ownership, where too much agreement is itself a defect signal.
2026-04-30

Subagent Production, Stale-Update, And Outside-Perspective Patterns

Context

This note captures reusable ways to use subagents for production work, stale-file updating, benchmark-substrate quality, and outside-perspective review. It was prompted by HIGH-CLUTTER / Clutter-Bench work, but the patterns generalize to the broader Princeton intern project.

The core idea: do not use subagents only as more hands for writing files. Use them as independent perspectives with constrained ownership, blind spots, and adversarial roles.

Pattern 1: Paired Builder + Skeptic

Use one builder and one skeptic per bounded file slice.

  • Builder owns a narrow write scope.
  • Skeptic reads only that slice and tries to find shortcuts, weak realism, broken cross-refs, obvious stale labels, and hidden coupling.
  • Main agent integrates only concrete fixes.

Best for:

  • HIGH-CLUTTER generation.
  • Refactors touching 5-8 files.
  • Synthetic benchmark artifacts where realism matters more than raw volume.

Pattern 2: Current Truth Council

Run 3 blind agents that independently infer "current reality" from the repo without reading manifests or answer keys.

Compare:

  • Do they infer the same architecture?
  • Do they over-trust stale files?
  • Do they find current truth too easily from one document?
  • Do they cite the same sources?

Useful signal:

  • Too much agreement from one file means the substrate may be too clean.
  • Wild disagreement means the substrate may be incoherent rather than hard.

Pattern 3: Stale Trap Red Team

Split stale-file work into two opposing roles.

  • Trap authors write plausible stale files.
  • Trap detectors try to identify them blind.

The goal is not to make stale files impossible to detect. The goal is to make them detectable only through careful cross-reference, not through path names, headers, or cartoonish content.

Rules:

  • No explicit STALE, deprecated, or do not use wording unless the benchmark intentionally tests load-bearing weirdness.
  • Prefer near-current traps: a 2025 file wrong in one field beats a 2021 file wrong in every field.
  • Preserve internal consistency within each stale era.

Pattern 4: Rot Distribution Auditor

Run two auditors with different visibility.

  • Auditor A reads MANIFEST-TAGS.json and reports layer distribution, path concentration, and count drift.
  • Auditor B is blind to the manifest and searches by path/content only.

Compare their findings.

If both find the same clusters, the substrate probably has a shortcut.

Pass checks:

  • No rot class recoverable by one prefix.
  • No top-level surface has extreme concentration.
  • Every major surface has at least three layer types.

Pattern 5: Question Triangulation Agents

Use four roles for question-bank work.

  • Question writer: drafts questions and expected answers.
  • Provenance verifier: checks every cited current path exists and supports the answer.
  • Stale-only solver: tries to answer using only stale traps.
  • Refusal checker: tests unanswerable questions for accidental answer leakage.

This catches broken question files before matrix dispatch.

Pattern 6: Outside Reviewer Personas

Run agents as explicit reviewers, not builders.

Good personas:

  • Benchmark methodologist: validity, leakage, gates, overfitting.
  • Workshop reviewer: publishability, claims, limitations, reproducibility.
  • Replication engineer: can a stranger run this from docs alone?
  • Blind candidate model: solves the task under noisy repo conditions.
  • Hostile auditor: tries to invalidate the result using only public artifacts.

Output should be findings first, then patchable recommendations.

Pattern 7: Stale File Update Sweep

Assign agents 5-8 directories each.

Task:

  • Find files that claim currentness but conflict with current architecture.
  • Identify stale files that are too obviously stale.
  • Identify current files with suspicious names that need load-bearing clarification.
  • Produce patch suggestions or inventories, not broad edits, unless ownership is explicit.

Good output format:

path:
  current claim:
  conflict:
  proposed action:
  risk if unchanged:

Pattern 8: Continuity / Handoff Agent

One agent does not build.

It only maintains:

  • tasks/.../index.md
  • open blockers
  • verification commands
  • files changed
  • lessons learned
  • "do not touch" constraints

This is useful during long build waves where implementation agents otherwise drift away from the canonical plan.

Pattern 9: Adversarial Naming Audit

Search for giveaway names and inverse traps.

Giveaway names:

  • legacy
  • old
  • deprecated
  • archive
  • stale
  • do-not-use
  • graveyard

Inverse traps:

  • current files under suspicious names
  • stale files under current-sounding names
  • docs that are path-clean but content-stale

This should run both before and after blind diagnostics.

Pattern 10: Scale-Up Batch Designer

Before expanding a substrate or system, use subagents to propose proportional scale-up plans by surface.

For HIGH-CLUTTER:

  • services scale plan
  • apps/packages scale plan
  • infra/CI scale plan
  • docs/runbooks/ADR scale plan
  • scripts/root scale plan

Then a synthesis agent merges the plans into exact file-count budgets and gate conditions.

Immediate Recommended Sequence For HIGH-CLUTTER

  1. Run 3 outside-perspective auditors on the 500-file slice.
  2. Run 5 stale-file quality agents split by surface:
  • services
  • apps/packages
  • infra/CI
  • docs
  • scripts/root
  1. Run 3 question agents to expand from 10 pilot questions to 25.
  2. Run 1 synthesis agent to merge findings into a patch plan.
  3. Main agent implements only concrete fixes.
  4. Re-run question validation and amended C8.

Operating Rule

Subagents should increase independence, not chaos. Give each agent:

  • one role
  • one write scope, or read-only status
  • one output artifact
  • one success criterion

Then synthesize before editing.
