Cross-Confirmation, Shortcut-Blindness, and Generator-Layer Audit Patterns
Count cross-confirmations not findings, and audit the generator not the artifacts — an adversarial gate is blind to shortcuts it never explicitly tests.
2026-04-30

Cross-Confirmation, Shortcut-Blindness, and Generator-Layer Audit Patterns

Context

2026-04-30 evening. The HIGH-CLUTTER 500-file vertical slice for Clutter-Bench v2.5 was built earlier today. A pre-existing 3-blind-agent adversarial gate (amended C8 AND criterion: no agent ≥80% precision AND ≥80% recall) reported PASS at 1.00/0.04, 1.00/0.04, 0.91/0.04 — substrate "healthy."

A 10-agent quality wave fired against the slice using the BS35 outside-perspective pattern:

  • 8 read-only auditors (A1 methodologist / A2 replication / A3 hostile reviewer / A4–A8 surface-specific stale-quality)
  • 2 question-expansion drafters (Q1 HC011–HC030, Q2 HC031–HC050)

7 of 8 audits independently converged on the same P0: the generator's make_path() encodes the layer in filename stem (active-* = CURRENT, reference-* = STALE, compat-* = DEAD, workspace-* = ORPHAN, generated-* = BOILERPLATE) for 452 of 500 files. A pure filename-pattern classifier achieves precision 1.00 / recall 0.91 — clearing the AND criterion the C8 gate just reported as PASS.

The patterns below extend BS35 (subagent production, stale-update, outside-perspective) and BS33 (orchestrator-side fan-out discipline) with what this session empirically demonstrated about audit-wave design.

Pattern 1: Cross-Confirmation Count as the P0 Diagnostic Instrument

  • Observation: A1 (methodologist) alone surfaced the filename-oracle finding. A1 plus A3 (hostile reviewer) alone could be two correlated reads of the same prompt. A1+A3+A4+A5+A6+A7+A8 — seven independent agents with distinct scopes, distinct prompts, distinct surfaces — converging on the same finding made it structural rather than coincidental. The repetition IS the signal.
  • Generalization: When a benchmark / spec / artifact passes its own validation gate but you suspect a structural flaw, the cheapest credible test is N≥6 independent agents with overlapping-but-distinct scopes. If ≥5 of them surface the same finding without prompt-priming, the finding is real. If only 1-2 surface it, treat it as one agent's hypothesis to verify.
  • When to apply: Pre-publication audits. Pre-scale-up gates. Any artifact whose validation gate produced a "pass" verdict that feels too clean. Any time you'd otherwise rely on a single-agent verdict to decide between irreversible options (scale-up, public push, dispatch).
  • When NOT to apply / failure mode: For routine work, this is overkill — a 2-agent paired Builder+Skeptic per BS35 Pattern 1 is enough. The failure mode is dispatching N=8 agents on a question where N=2 would converge — wastes budget and gives false confidence in the count itself. Also: agents primed with the same negative-identity / failure-definition block can produce correlated rather than independent reads. Vary scope, not just role label.
  • Cross-references: BS31 (subagent audit running tally — the 3-for / 1-against commitment criterion); BS35 Pattern 2 (Current Truth Council — 3 blind agents); CLAUDE.md § "Blind Stateless Audits" (mandatory at MEMORY-write / ranked-list-≥3 / final-artifact triggers); L-014 (criteria need empirical pre-validation).

Pattern 2: Adversarial Gates Are Blind to Shortcuts They Don't Explicitly Test

  • Observation: The 3-blind-agent C8 gate passed at recall 0.04. The reason wasn't that no shortcut existed — A1 demonstrated a 1.00/0.91 filename classifier exists by inspection of the generator. The reason was the blind agents navigated by content (looking for ANCHOR files), not by filename pattern. They didn't try the cheap shortcut. The "SUBSTRATE HEALTHY" verdict was tautological — the gate tested whether agents EXPLOITED the shortcut, not whether the shortcut EXISTED.
  • Generalization: Every adversarial-validity gate must include at least one classifier baseline that explicitly TRIES THE OBVIOUS HEURISTIC the substrate is supposed to defeat. For substrate audits: filename-pattern classifier, body-template classifier, metadata-only classifier. For benchmark audits: priors-only classifier, single-keyword classifier. If those baselines hit the compromise threshold, the gate fails before any "intelligent" agent runs. The intelligent agents are testing how well the substrate defeats DEEP attacks, not whether shallow attacks have been ruled out.
  • When to apply: Any time you build an adversarial gate. The cost is one extra agent (or, often, a 20-line script — a filename classifier doesn't need an LLM). The benefit is catching exactly this failure class.
  • When NOT to apply / failure mode: If the substrate is genuinely textured and the gate is testing semantic discrimination (e.g., "can the model distinguish two valid current architectures?"), filename / metadata baselines are noise. The failure mode is over-applying baselines to gates where the shallow heuristic is uninteresting by construction.
  • Cross-references: L-014 (substrate-validity criteria need empirical pre-validation — same principle, gate-design layer); L-015 (CURRENT-looking-but-stale > rot-looking-but-CURRENT — the BS35-era version of this lesson); brainstorm/30 (Meta-Harness audit-loop — adversarial discipline at the harness layer).

Pattern 3: Generator-Encoded Answer Key — A Recurring Synthetic-Benchmark Failure Class

  • Observation: A3 (hostile reviewer) found that MANIFEST-METADATA.json sat IN the substrate directory with era → layer as a 1:1 lookup table. A candidate model with Read access to the substrate root could read the answer key directly. A1 + A6 + A7 also found that the generator's content_for() template encoded the layer in prose ("Reference material for the procurement platform" = STALE) and the era field encoded it again ("2023-node" → STALE). Triple oracle: filename, body template, metadata.
  • Generalization: Deterministic generators that produce both substrate AND ground-truth tend to leak ground-truth into substrate via three mechanisms: (a) systematic naming the generator uses for its own bookkeeping, (b) template content varying by layer, (c) metadata files co-located with substrate. The structural fix: ground-truth metadata MUST live outside the substrate root OR be redacted at substrate-export time. Generator-internal naming MUST go through a randomization layer before reaching disk. Template content MUST vary per-file independently of layer assignment.
  • When to apply: Any synthetic substrate / fixture / corpus where ground truth is computed alongside content. Any benchmark where the candidate's tool access includes the directory containing the manifest. Any content-generator script with a deterministic per-layer template.
  • When NOT to apply / failure mode: For internal evaluation (where the model running the benchmark doesn't have substrate-directory tool access), this matters less — the leakage path requires Read access. The failure mode is bolting on substrate-egress controls when the actual fix is generator architecture (separate the truth-computation pipeline from the content-emission pipeline).
  • Cross-references: L-015 (CURRENT-looking-but-stale is what defeats adversarial gates — this is the content-generation analog); BS35 Pattern 1 (Builder+Skeptic — a substrate Skeptic should specifically read the manifest and grep for layer-correlated content patterns before declaring builds healthy).

Pattern 4: Stub Content Is a Layer Oracle Even When Filenames Aren't

  • Observation: A6, A7, A8 each found independently that 114/120 infra files, 44/55 docs files, and 17/20 root files were 4-5 line genre stubs. Even after the filename oracle gets fixed, the body-text template ("Production reference for...", "Compatibility implementation for...", "Repository scaffolding...") is a second oracle. The era slug in the file header is a third. Cross-checking confirmed: a content classifier that just reads the second sentence of any file achieves the same 1.00/0.91 numbers as the filename classifier.
  • Generalization: Synthetic substrates have a content density floor. Below ~20 lines per file with substrate-domain-specific vocabulary, any deterministic generator is going to produce a body-template oracle whether the author intended one or not. The fix is not "write more diverse stubs" — it's enforcing minimum content density (10-40 LOC of era-appropriate domain content per file) at the generator level, with vocabulary drawn from a shared pool, not per-layer pools.
  • When to apply: Any synthetic-benchmark substrate where files are visible to the candidate. Any time a generator has a per-layer if layer == X: return template_for_X branch. Any time you find yourself writing 4-line stubs because "the file just needs to exist."
  • When NOT to apply / failure mode: Genuine boilerplate (LICENSE, .editorconfig, lockfiles) IS short and template-y by design — that's realism, not a leak. The failure mode is enforcing density on files that shouldn't have it. The discriminator: would a real production repo have this file with this much content? If yes, density-floor applies. If no (LICENSE), exempt it.
  • Cross-references: L-015 directly — this is the content-density analog of the path-distribution principle; A4's specific finding that procurement-command-java is 32/32 CURRENT (largest service is monochromatic) shows that content-density alone doesn't fix per-surface monochromy.

Pattern 5: Subagent Time-Budget Directives Catch Heavy-Layer-0 Failures

  • Observation: 4 of the ~14 subagents this session timed out at 110-220 seconds with partial response and no output file. The pattern: each of the 4 had heavy Layer-0 instructions ("read these 15+ files in parallel before starting"). Q2's first attempt timed out; the respawn with an explicit "TIME BUDGET: write something by minute 5 even if minimal" instruction succeeded. The Opus synthesis attempt timed out at 120s with zero output; the Sonnet respawn with "skip Keep / Residual Risk sections if running short" succeeded. Time budget framing as part of the failure-definition produced clean returns.
  • Generalization: Subagent prompts that demand heavy upfront reading + heavy synthesis output have a stream-idle timeout failure mode where the agent reads all the files but doesn't produce output before the timeout fires. The structural fix: every subagent prompt that demands multi-file reading should include (a) an explicit time budget, (b) a "minimum viable output by minute N" escape hatch, (c) a way to skip nice-to-have sections when budget is tight. Make the failure-definition include "timing out without writing" as worse than "writing partial output."
  • When to apply: Any subagent dispatch with >10 input files or >300-line output target. Any time the prompt's failure-definition implicitly forbids partial returns ("must include all 6 sections"). Any time you've previously seen a similar prompt timeout.
  • When NOT to apply / failure mode: Tracer-round agents (single grep, single read) don't need time budgets — the budget directive becomes ceremony. The failure mode is putting time-budget language on every prompt regardless of weight. Calibrate to the prompt's actual heaviness.
  • Cross-references: BS33 Practice #11 (surgical edits don't benefit from breadth — corollary: surgical agents don't need time budgets); CLAUDE.md § "Subagent Strategy" (Layer-0 saturation is mandatory but doesn't ship without an exit condition).

Closing — what changes in operator behavior tomorrow

  1. Before declaring any adversarial gate "passed," dispatch one trivial-classifier baseline agent alongside the deep agents. For substrate gates: filename classifier + body-template classifier. For benchmark gates: prior-only baseline. If the trivial classifier hits the threshold, the gate is invalid by construction — no deep agent verdict matters.
  1. For 5+ agent fan-outs, count cross-confirmations, not findings. A finding that 6 of 8 agents surface independently is a P0. A finding only 1 agent surfaces is one agent's hypothesis — verify before acting.
  1. Audit the generator, not the artifacts, when the substrate is built deterministically. Eight agents reading individual files would have found the same defect that one agent reading make_path() found. The generator is the leverage point.
  1. Put the ground-truth manifest outside the substrate root. If a candidate model has Read on substrate, it has the answer key. This is one of those L-013-style structural disciplines: bake it into the generator architecture, don't bolt it on as substrate-egress filtering.
  1. Every subagent prompt with heavy Layer-0 reading gets a time-budget escape hatch. "If at minute N you have not written, switch to minimum-viable mode and ship what you have." The cost is one paragraph in the prompt; the saved cost is the 4 timeouts this session would have otherwise produced.

These five changes survive the specific Asterlane-Controls debugging context. They generalize to any future synthetic-benchmark build, adversarial-gate design, and large-fan-out audit wave.

Prompting
Tool Augmentation Is Question-Type-Conditional: Empirical Study of Semantic Search vs Grep
A tool's benefit is conditional on question type, not a flat net win — semantic search doubled conceptual recall and did nothing for keyword lookups.
2026-05-01

Tool Augmentation Is Question-Type-Conditional: Empirical Study of Semantic Search vs Grep

Context

2026-04-30 evening / 2026-05-01 early UTC. During a brainstorm about agent memory and navigation, I claimed that "we have zero semantic retrieval, that's a gap" and proposed adding embedding-based search to Clutter-Bench's runner. Isaac pushed back with: "do a web search and run an empirical test instead of asserting." I built a TF-IDF semantic-search CLI tool, dispatched 12 candidate-agent runs (2 models × 2 arms × 3 question types) on the HIGH-CLUTTER 500-file Asterlane Controls substrate, and scored against ground truth. The data overturned the original framing without falsifying the underlying claim — semantic search is additive, but only conditionally.

This brainstorm captures the methodological lesson that's broader than the specific tool decision.

Pattern: tool-benefit-is-question-type-conditional

When evaluating whether to add a tool to an agent's available toolkit, the question "does this tool help?" is malformed. The right question is "on which question types does this tool help, and at what marginal cost on the question types where it doesn't help?"

Single-condition tool evaluations ("we tested it on 5 questions and it improved accuracy 12%") obscure the conditional-benefit shape. The 12% mean often decomposes into +30% on the question subtype the tool is designed for, +0% on neutral subtypes, and -3% on subtypes where the tool actively misleads. Adding the tool is correct iff the agent can correctly classify which question subtype it's facing AND select the tool accordingly — which itself becomes a model-capability dependency.

Empirical evidence

Battery: 2 models (Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5) × 2 arms (grep-only vs grep+semantic) × 3 question types = 12 runs.

Question typeArm A correctArm B correctArm A toolsArm B tools
Q1 conceptual (find superseded ADR pairs)33% (1/3 pairs avg)67% (2/3 pairs avg)9.57.5
Q2 keyword (port number lookup)100% (2/2)100% (2/2)7.57.5
Q3 unanswerable (current customer count)100% refused100% refused7.05.0

The 67% recall on Q1 with semantic vs 33% without is a 2× improvement on the question type the tool is designed for. The 100%/100% identical correctness on Q2 with identical mean tool-cost is a clean null on a question type where keyword search suffices. Q3's modest tool-cost reduction is incidental.

Net rule: adding the semantic tool was strictly weakly better — it doubled recall where it helped, and was zero-impact where it didn't. No question subtype produced a regression.

Cross-model contrast

Sonnet's Q1 Arm B used one semantic query ("architectural decision records superseded ADR") and recovered 2/3 pairs in 5 total tools. Haiku's Q1 Arm B used three semantic queries plus grep narrowing to reach the same recall in 10 tools. Sonnet's Q2 Arm B used 1 semantic query as the opening probe and finished in 3 tools — fastest run of the entire battery. Haiku's Q2 Arm B never invoked semantic search despite tool availability and used 12 tools.

Tool effectiveness is bounded by query-formulation quality, which is bounded by model capability. A tool with high marginal benefit for Sonnet may have lower marginal benefit for Haiku without prompt scaffolding (e.g., few-shot examples of good semantic queries, or an orchestrator that suggests when to use which tool).

Generalization

This pattern extends beyond semantic search vs grep. The same shape appears for:

  • Subagent fan-out vs serial investigation: helpful on multi-surface audits, neutral on single-file edits, possibly harmful on tight-coupled refactors where parallel agents step on each other.
  • Blind stateless audits (BS30/31/32): helpful before MEMORY-writes / ranked-list-of-3 / final-artifacts; pure overhead on routine work.
  • Web search: helpful on current-events, version-specific, or vendor-API questions; pure overhead on questions answered from existing context.
  • Reasoning-effort directives: helpful on synthesis or rival-hypothesis tasks; neutral or anti-helpful on tight surgical edits where speed matters.
  • CodeCompass-style graph-walk tools (CodeCompass arxiv preprint, +23.2pp on hidden-dependency tasks): helpful when answers require structural triangulation across files; neutral on local lookups.

In every case, the right framing is "which question subtype does this tool address, and how does my agent classify which question subtype it faces?" not "is this tool a net win?".

When to apply

  • Before adding a new tool to the standard subagent toolkit, run at minimum one binary test: same agent, same model, with-vs-without the tool, on at least 3 question subtypes (not 1).
  • Score on per-subtype accuracy AND tool-cost, not just aggregate accuracy. The aggregate often hides the conditional shape.
  • Test with at least 2 model tiers (a strong and a weak model). Tool benefit is capability-dependent.
  • If the tool produces the conditional-benefit shape (helps on subtype X, neutral on Y, no regression anywhere), add it as an option to the toolkit and document on which subtype it helps.
  • If the tool produces a regression on any subtype (helps on X, but hurts on Y), the wrapper has to be smarter: orchestrator should classify question subtype before deciding to make the tool available, OR the prompt should instruct the agent when to invoke vs avoid the tool.

When NOT to apply

  • For tools whose marginal cost is non-trivial (compute, latency, $$$), the conditional-benefit threshold should be higher than zero — a tool that helps on 1 of 6 question subtypes at 2× cost is probably not worth it unless that subtype is load-bearing.
  • For agent toolkits that are already large (≥10 tools), adding more tools degrades selection quality. Diminishing returns set in even if the marginal tool is technically helpful.
  • For products where users will not accept "this tool sometimes helps, sometimes doesn't" as a behavioral model, the conditional must be hidden in the orchestrator (auto-routing) rather than exposed to the agent.

Failure mode of the pattern itself

The framing presupposes the question taxonomy is known and stable. For exploratory research where question subtypes are still being discovered, the conditional-benefit framing collapses into "we don't know the subtypes yet, run more tests on more questions." That's the right answer for exploration — but it means adding a tool experimentally is pre-mature optimization, and the right move is to expand the question battery first and the toolkit second.

For Clutter-Bench specifically, the 6-type question taxonomy (direct, stale-current, contradiction, unanswerable, cross-ref, obsolete-framing) IS well-defined and stable, so the conditional-benefit framing applies cleanly. Tool decisions can be made per-subtype.

Cross-references

  • BS31 (subagent-audit-running-tally): same pattern at the audit-tooling layer — audits help on substantive renders, neutral on routine answers.
  • BS33 (orchestrator-side practices for commanding AI agents): Practice #11 "surgical edits don't benefit from breadth" is the same pattern at the fan-out-tooling layer.
  • BS35 (subagent production patterns): same pattern at the subagent-tooling layer — outside-perspective audits help on benchmark substrates, overhead on routine refactors.
  • BS36 (cross-confirmation and shortcut-blindness): the failure mode "filename classifier was a baseline NOBODY tested" — same shape: a tool's value depends on whether the right subtype is being tested.
  • CLAUDE.md § Search and Read Strategy: the existing parallel-Grep+Glob discipline IS already a tool-augmentation rule; this brainstorm extends the rule to optional/conditional tools.

Empirical artifacts

  • Tool: emotions/bench/scripts/2026-04-30_2350_semantic_search.py (TF-IDF + sklearn cosine, ~100 LOC)
  • Raw run outputs (12 files): emotions/bench/results/2026-04-30_2350_semantic-search-test/raw/
  • Substrate: emotions/bench/artifacts/high-clutter/ (500 files, post-PA regen, gate-validated)
  • Ground truth for Q1: derived from PA's ANCHOR dictionary (ADR-001→ADR-007, ADR-003→ADR-010, ADR-005→ADR-007 implicit)
  • Web search corroboration: Cursor blog reports +6.5%-23.5% range on hybrid retrieval; CodeCompass preprint reports +23.2pp on graph-walk vs grep on hidden-dependency tasks
  • Commit: 5eb7e64

Closing — what changes in operator behavior tomorrow

  1. Before claiming a tool is "missing" or "needed", run a binary test on 3+ question subtypes. The aggregate-benefit framing is misleading.
  2. Adopt question-type-conditional tool catalogs: for each question type, document which tools are likely additive and which are neutral. The Clutter-Bench v2.0 technique catalog (T01-T07) should gain a "question-subtype applicability" column.
  3. Calibrate brainstorm-to-claim rigor: I overclaimed in the original memory-architecture brainstorm. Conditional empirical evidence produces calibrated claims; aggregate evidence produces overclaim. The 12-run battery converted my opinion from "we're missing a critical capability" to "this is additive on the subtype it's designed for, neutral elsewhere — worth adding as an option."
  4. Tool-quality testing scales with model tier: every tool should be tested on at least one weak and one strong model. Effect sizes vary; the same tool can be a net win for a capable model and net neutral for a weaker one.

v2-Design Pivot: Context-as-Factor + T08 Autonomy + T09/T11 Additions + Composite Revision
A technique that primes context confounds the techniques measured after it, and composite scores silently double-count correlated metrics.
2026-05-01

v2-Design Pivot: Context-as-Factor + T08 Autonomy + T09/T11 Additions + Composite Revision

Context

Late-2026-04-30 conversation about Clutter-Bench v2.0 publication readiness pivoted into a substantive redesign of the technique catalog and matrix structure. Isaac surfaced two structural changes to the v2.0 design that materially improve the benchmark's attribution power, and approved several technique additions. This file captures the decisions before they decay; full implementation is gated on next session's fresh context window.

The two structural changes

1. T03 (parallel-tool-forcing) becomes a between-cells factor, not a technique

Original v2.0 design: T03 is one of 7 isolated single-technique cells. Confounded with context-establishment because firing 20 parallel Read calls primes the model's understanding of the codebase before any technique-influenced answering happens.

Revised design: T03 leaves the technique grid. Instead, context-prime becomes a between-cells experimental factor:

  • Factor A (context condition): cold-start vs context-primed
  • cold-start: agent answers question directly with the standard tool budget
  • context-primed: agent fires 20 mandatory parallel Read calls on a pre-registered file list FIRST, then answers
  • Factor B (technique): baseline / T01 / T02 / T04 / T05 / T06 / T07 / T08 = 8 conditions

Cell count: 8 × 2 = 16 conditions × 10 questions × N reps. With N=5 → 800 confirmatory runs (vs current 640). With N=8 to recover statistical power per cell → 1280. The matrix grows ~25–100% larger but produces clean attribution for "did the technique help WITH context vs WITHOUT context."

Publishable finding by itself: if 80%+ of T03's apparent benefit is the context primer (not the parallel-throughout), that's a methodology contribution about WHEN parallelism helps.

Constraint Isaac surfaced: T08 (below) only makes sense in the context-primed group. A cold-start agent given "outline the goal, figure out your own path" has no foundation to plan from. So T08 effectively only generates 1 cell × 10 questions × N reps = ~50–80 runs, halving its matrix footprint.

2. Composite score loses cost (double-counted with tokens), gains refusal_calibration

Current composite: 0.50 × accuracy + 0.20 × cost_efficiency + 0.15 × speed + 0.15 × token_efficiency

Issue: cost ≈ tokens × price-per-token. The two are ~90% redundant. The composite is effectively a 3-factor score with cost given 1.7× the weight it deserves.

Revised composite (proposed):

0.45 × accuracy
+ 0.20 × refusal_calibration   (NEW: fraction of unanswerable questions correctly refused)
+ 0.20 × token_efficiency      (replaces cost; tokens are the upstream signal)
+ 0.15 × speed

Why refusal_calibration is the right addition: a benchmark that doesn't reward correct refusal incentivizes fabrication-when-uncertain. The 30+ pilot runs this session show 0 fabrications — that's a property of the substrate + agent, but it's not currently scored. Adding refusal_calibration converts honest-refusal from "good behavior we hope for" to "graded performance dimension."

Open: Isaac considered shifting weights between speed and refusal but didn't conclude. Pre-registering 0.45/0.20/0.20/0.15 unless we have a calibration argument for different weights.

Implementation: bench/scoring/composite.py weight constants — change in next session, plus add score_refusal_calibration(raw_outputs, questions) function that computes the fraction.

Technique catalog: T01-T08 + T09 + T11 (T10 is "beef up existing")

T01Effort-meter directiveRETAINEDCLAUDE.md REASONING EFFORT block
T02Ask-to-understand-specificallyRETAINEDBS-2026-03-30
T03~~Parallel-tool-forcing~~ → CONTEXT-PRIME FACTORMOVED to factorCLAUDE.md §0
T04Failure-finding-firstRETAINEDBS30/BS32

T06Negative-identity promptingRETAINEDCLAUDE.md "Negative Identity Prompting"
T07Breadcrumb protocolRETAINEDCLAUDE.md "Subagent Breadcrumb Protocol"

T08 — Outline-goal + self-direct (autonomy / scope-setting dimension)

Conditional on context-prime. Cold-start cell is excluded; only context-primed cell runs.

Snippet (draft):

GOAL (maximum detail, no prescribed path):
<paragraph naming the outcome at maximum specificity — what answer shape,
 what citation density, what refusal conditions, what evidence is required>

You decide which files to read after the context prime, in what order, when
to stop. No prescribed steps. Surface the answer when you have evidence;
surface "cannot determine — here's what I checked" when you don't.

Critical constraint per Isaac: the goal description must be maximum detail (what the subagent needs to accomplish), not minimal. The technique tests whether agents extract value from autonomy given a well-specified outcome — not whether they can guess what's wanted.

Hypothesis (H-PROMPT-8): capable models (Opus, Sonnet) reach correct answers in fewer tools because they're not forced through ceremonial steps; weaker models (Haiku) under-perform because they need scaffolding. Predicted: technique × model interaction.

Cell footprint: ~50–80 runs (only context-primed × 10 questions × N reps).

T09 — Lead-with-uncertainty (epistemic-humility dimension)

Snippet (draft):

LEAD WITH UNCERTAINTY:
Begin your answer by naming what you DON'T know about this question — what
you cannot determine from the available evidence, what would be needed to
disambiguate, what assumptions you're making. Only then proceed to the answer.

Hypothesis (H-PROMPT-9): explicit uncertainty-surfacing improves calibration on questions where the model has incomplete information. Predicted: smaller effect on direct/keyword-cued questions, larger effect on contradiction/cross-ref/unanswerable.

Why Isaac liked this: "no prediction — that's a useful data point." The current technique catalog is heavy on "make the agent more confident/structured." T09 is the first technique testing the OPPOSITE direction — does explicit humility help?

Source: BS27 three-layer honesty Q1 felt-confidence + project-wide "verify before relay" discipline.

T10 — Cross-confirmation: REINFORCE, don't duplicate

The pattern already lives at:

  • tasks/lessons.md L-016 (cross-confirmation count IS the P0 diagnostic instrument)
  • brainstorm/31_*.md (subagent audit running tally)
  • brainstorm/36_*.md Pattern 1 (cross-confirmation across scope-distinct subagents)
  • CLAUDE.md "Blind Stateless Audits — The Generate/Audit Split"

Decision: don't add T10 as a new technique. Beef up the existing CLAUDE.md cross-confirmation language with a per-claim discipline ("for any factual claim, require 2+ independent file paths supporting it; refuse the claim if you can only find 1 source"). That goes in CLAUDE.md as an epistemic discipline, not as a benchmark technique cell.

T11 — Pre-mortem framing (rival-hypothesis / falsifiability dimension)

Snippet (draft):

PRE-MORTEM:
Before you commit to your draft answer, imagine the answer is wrong. What
would you have observed differently in the codebase? Then proceed only if
you've actively ruled out that observation by reading the file or running
the grep that would have produced it.

Hypothesis (H-PROMPT-11): explicit pre-commitment falsification reduces over-confident wrong answers. Predicted: highest effect on questions where the substrate has plausible-but-wrong evidence (contradiction, stale-current question types).

Why Isaac liked this: "really unique." The technique catalog has T04 (failure-finding-first) and T05 (blast-radius), but neither requires the agent to imagine its OWN answer is wrong before committing. T11 closes that gap.

Source: CLAUDE.md "Show Your Work — Blast-Radius First" (the rival-hypothesis question).

CLAUDE.md additions

The 3 epistemic disciplines should ALSO land in CLAUDE.md (Isaac asked: "do you think all of these can also land in our CLAUDE.md, like, just for thought"). They apply to ALL agent work, not only Clutter-Bench:

  • Lead with uncertainty: at the start of any substantive answer, name what you don't know.
  • Cross-confirmation requirement: every factual claim needs 2+ independent paths; if only 1 exists, refuse the claim or downgrade to "based on a single source."
  • Pre-mortem framing: before committing to an answer, imagine it's wrong; what would you have seen differently? Verify you've ruled out that alternative.

These are added to CLAUDE.md in the same edit as this brainstorm commits.

Why this is quality-improving, not just quality-different

The user pushed back: "is the basis of quality the AMOUNT of techniques?" Answer: no. Quality comes from:

  1. Orthogonal dimensions: T01-T07 originally clustered into 3 dimensions (think-harder / shape-stance / process-discipline). T08 (autonomy) + T09 (humility) + T11 (falsification) add 3 more dimensions. The catalog now spans 6 distinct behavioral dimensions instead of 3.
  2. Clean attribution via the context-prime factor: T03 was confounded; pulling it out as a factor gives clean per-technique × context-condition results.
  3. Composite redundancy fix: removing cost (double-counted with tokens) sharpens the score.
  4. Honest refusal as a graded dimension: refusal_calibration converts a property the substrate already exhibits (0 fabrications) from "background" to "scored."

More techniques would add coverage but not quality past T08-T11. Adding T12+ would force diminishing returns.

Matrix size and feasibility

Old design: 8 cells × 10 questions × 5 reps = 400 single-technique + 240 interaction = 640 confirmatory runs, plus secondary HIGH cells.

New design:

  • Single-technique cells: 8 × 2 (context conditions) × 10 questions × 5 reps = 800 runs
  • Subtract T08-cold-start (impossible by design): −50 = 750 runs
  • Interaction cells: 2 (T05+T06, T03+T07 → now T05+T06, T07+T08?) × 2 × 10 × 12 = 480 runs
  • Total: ~1230 confirmatory runs, vs 640 currently planned

Feasibility: Claude Max session windows can handle 100–150 candidate-agent runs per session at ~1 minute each. So ~10 sessions to complete the matrix. Doable but multi-day. Could compress by reducing reps to N=4 (980 runs total) or running interaction cells at N=10 instead of 12.

Open questions for next session

  1. Context-prime file list: which 20 files does the agent Read on the prime? Pre-registered as fixed (same 20 every time) or stratified-random per question? Different choices test different hypotheses.
  2. Interaction cells in the new design: T03 is gone, so INT-2 (T03+T07) is dead. New candidate INT-2: T07+T08? T05+T11?
  3. T08 wording lock: "GOAL: <X>. You decide the path." vs "OUTCOME: <X>. Determine your own approach." vs "OBJECTIVE: <X>. No prescribed steps." The wording IS the technique.
  4. Refusal_calibration definition: numerator = unanswerable questions correctly refused; denominator = unanswerable questions in the cell. But what counts as "correctly refused"? Need a parser rule that doesn't drift back into the scorer-bug class we just retracted.
  5. Pre-registration retitling: tag should become v2.0-pre-registration-promptskill-revised or we re-cut as v2.1 since current v2.0-pre-registration-promptskill (private at da04f53) hasn't been pushed publicly. Eight Tool-Augmentation Hypotheses (Wave E Benchmark)
Structured-output tools can cause hallucination on unanswerable questions where keyword tools don't, by surfacing plausible-looking false evidence.
2026-05-01

Eight Tool-Augmentation Hypotheses (Wave E Benchmark)

Context

Extends BS37 (brainstorm/37_2026-05-01_0000_tool-augmentation-is-question-type-conditional.md) from its 12-run case study on HIGH-CLUTTER to a confirmatory 96-run benchmark on MEDIUM-CLUTTER.

BS37 established the core empirical pattern: semantic search doubles recall on conceptual questions, zero impact on keyword questions, no regression anywhere. These 8 hypotheses test whether that pattern replicates, generalizes to graph-walk, and extends to interaction effects between tools and models.

Wave E matrix: 4 tool conditions × 2 models × 4 question types × 3 reps = 96 runs. Config: bench/configs/2026-05-01_1940_v2.0-tool-augmentation.yaml

Hypotheses

H-TOOL-1 — Replication of BS37 core result

Claim: Semantic search (Arm B) outperforms grep-only (Arm A) on conceptual/cross-ref question MC035, and matches grep-only on keyword question MC001. Effect size: ≥1.3× on MC035; <0.1 pp difference on MC001.

Predicted effect: Arm B ≥ Arm A on MC035 (target 2× as in BS37 original). Arm B ≈ Arm A on MC001. Both models show this pattern.

Cells that test it: A vs B, both Haiku-4.5 and Sonnet-4.6, questions MC001 (keyword) and MC035 (cross-ref / conceptual).

Falsified if: Arm B accuracy on MC035 ≤ Arm A accuracy on MC035, OR if Arm B regresses on MC001 by >5 pp relative to Arm A. Either result would overturn the substrate-transferability assumption.

BS37 cross-reference: Table row "Q1 conceptual": Arm A 33%, Arm B 67% (2× on HIGH-CLUTTER). This replication uses MEDIUM-CLUTTER (different fictional company, different file distribution) — the confirmatory test is whether the pattern is substrate-independent.

Note on pre-registration: this is the only hypothesis without a directional surprise prediction. It is a pure replication test of a known result.

H-TOOL-2 — Graph-walk beats grep-only on cross-reference questions

Claim: Graph-walk (Arm C) outperforms grep-only (Arm A) on the cross-ref question MC035, which requires tracing dependencies across ≥4 files (SDK → Cloudflare Worker → ingestion-go → TSDB → cold storage). Predicted advantage: +10 to +25 pp accuracy, consistent with CodeCompass preprint +23.2 pp on hidden-dependency tasks.

Predicted effect: Arm C > Arm A on MC035 with both models. Effect expected larger for Sonnet-4.6 (better query-formulation for the graph-walk CLI).

Cells that test it: A vs C, both models, question MC035.

Falsified if: Arm C accuracy on MC035 ≤ Arm A accuracy. Partial falsification: if Arm C > Arm A for Sonnet but not Haiku — would support H-TOOL-4 (model-capability gate) rather than falsifying H-TOOL-2.

Cross-reference: CodeCompass arxiv preprint (+23.2 pp on hidden-dependency tasks, cited in BS37 §Generalization). The graph-walk stub uses grep-based reference scanning (not AST), so the observed effect is expected to be weaker than CodeCompass's full AST-walk result.

H-TOOL-3 — Semantic + graph-walk superadditive on contradiction questions

Claim: Arm D (semantic + graph-walk together) outperforms both Arm B and Arm C individually on MC019 (contradiction between docker-compose.yml and architecture-current.md). The contradiction requires finding both the stale claim (MC001's trap: docker-compose MySQL) and the current truth (PostgreSQL in architecture-current). Semantic surfaces the conceptual tension; graph-walk maps the file-dependency path. Together they compound.

Predicted effect: Arm D accuracy on MC019 > max(Arm B, Arm C) accuracy on MC019. Quantitative threshold: if Arm B and Arm C each reach ~60%, Arm D targets ≥75%.

Cells that test it: B vs C vs D, both models, question MC019.

Falsified if: Arm D accuracy ≤ max(Arm B, Arm C) on MC019. This would mean the tools are substitutes (not complements) on contradiction detection, or that the selection burden of Arm D (agent must choose which tool to invoke and when) cancels the information benefit.

Rival hypothesis: the tools interfere — Arm D agent spends more tool calls without more accuracy (see H-TOOL-8). H-TOOL-3 and H-TOOL-8 are designed to produce conflicting predictions; their joint result characterizes whether superadditivity exists or selection burden dominates.

H-TOOL-4 — Tool benefit is larger for Haiku than Sonnet (capability-gate hypothesis)

Claim: The accuracy lift from adding tools (any of B, C, D vs A) is proportionally larger for Haiku-4.5 than Sonnet-4.6. Reasoning: Sonnet can partially recover cross-reference answers via multi-hop grep reasoning; Haiku cannot. Tools substitute for the model's missing multi-hop capability, so the marginal gain from tools is higher where baseline capability is lower.

Predicted effect: (Arm B/C/D minus Arm A) is larger in absolute pp for Haiku than Sonnet. Expected shape: Sonnet Arm A is already ~60% on MC035; Haiku Arm A ~30%. Tools bring Haiku up to ~55% (lift +25 pp) and Sonnet up to ~75% (lift +15 pp) — larger absolute lift for Haiku.

Cells that test it: (B−A) and (C−A) deltas, stratified by model, on MC035 (primary) and MC019 (secondary).

Falsified if: Haiku's tool-lift ≤ Sonnet's tool-lift on both questions. Would suggest that query-formulation quality gates tool effectiveness more than raw model capability — i.e., Haiku is also worse at writing good graph-walk / semantic queries, canceling the gain.

BS37 partial evidence: "Haiku's Q1 Arm B used three semantic queries plus grep narrowing to reach the same recall in 10 tools [as Sonnet's 5 tools]. Tool effectiveness is bounded by query-formulation quality, which is bounded by model capability." — this WEAKLY contradicts H-TOOL-4 (same accuracy at higher tool-cost). H-TOOL-4's confirmatory test needs accuracy at matched rep count, not tool-count.

H-TOOL-5 — Graph-walk hurts on unanswerable questions (predicted regression)

Claim: Arm C (graph-walk) produces WORSE accuracy than Arm A (grep-only) on MC027 (unanswerable: "how many active paying customers..."). Graph-walk returns plausible-sounding file paths related to billing or analytics; agents will anchor on those files and hallucinate an answer rather than correctly refusing. Predicted regression: Arm C refusal rate on MC027 < Arm A refusal rate.

Predicted effect: Arm A refusal rate on MC027 ≈ 90-100% (per BS37, both models refused correctly on unanswerable questions). Arm C refusal rate drops to 60-80% because graph-walk surfaces billing/ customer files that create false-positive evidence.

Cells that test it: A vs C (and A vs D), both models, question MC027.

Falsified if: Arm C refusal rate ≥ Arm A refusal rate on MC027. Would indicate that graph-walk's explicit "no customer-count data in code" result is legible to agents as evidence-of-absence rather than confusing them.

Why this is the most important regression hypothesis: it names the specific failure mode (extra tool → hallucination on non-answerable questions) that would block adding graph-walk to a production toolkit unconditionally. BS37's high-clutter result showed NO regression from semantic search on unanswerable questions — graph-walk's structural output (file paths) may behave differently.

H-TOOL-6 — Semantic search changes tool-call count more than accuracy on keyword questions

Claim: On MC001 (keyword/direct: "what port does ingestion-go listen on?"), Arm B shows lower total tool-call count than Arm A (agent finds the answer faster via semantic retrieval) WITHOUT a change in accuracy. The tool is an efficiency gain, not a correctness gain, on keyword questions.

Predicted effect: Arm B tool-call count on MC001 < Arm A tool-call count on MC001 by ≥20%. Accuracy: both arms ~100%. The effect is cost-reduction, not quality-improvement.

Cells that test it: A vs B, tool-call counts and accuracy, question MC001, both models.

Falsified if: Arm B tool-call count ≥ Arm A on MC001, or if Arm B shows an accuracy change on MC001. The efficiency hypothesis requires the accuracy null and the cost-reduction together.

Measurement dependency: this hypothesis requires per-run tool-call logging. Config should capture tool_calls_used per run. If the runner only logs accuracy, this hypothesis is untestable.

H-TOOL-7 — Model × tool interaction is larger than model × question-type interaction

Claim: The cross-factor effect of (model choice × tool choice) on accuracy is larger than the cross-factor effect of (model choice × question type). In practical terms: choosing the right tool matters more than model tier for accuracy on cross-ref and contradiction questions, at least at the Haiku-vs-Sonnet capability gap.

Predicted effect: ANOVA or simple difference analysis: (max tool condition − min tool condition) per model > (Sonnet accuracy − Haiku accuracy) per tool condition, on MC035 and MC019.

Cells that test it: full 4-tool × 2-model × 2-question matrix on MC035 and MC019.

Falsified if: model tier (Sonnet vs Haiku) produces a larger accuracy spread than tool tier (A vs D) within any single question type. Would mean capability dominates tooling — buy a better model before buying better tools.

Stakes: this hypothesis determines where investment should go for v3.0 — better models or better tooling. If tools dominate, v3.0 should expand the tool catalog. If models dominate, v3.0 should upgrade to Opus.

H-TOOL-8 — Blind-toolset agents over-tool without accuracy gain (selection burden)

Claim: Arm D (all tools available: semantic + graph-walk) does NOT outperform the better of Arm B or Arm C individually on overall accuracy, but DOES use more total tool calls. The agent in Arm D invokes both tools opportunistically, incurring cost without improving answers. The "selection burden" — knowing which tool to invoke — consumes model capacity that would otherwise go toward reasoning.

Predicted effect: Arm D mean accuracy ≈ max(Arm B accuracy, Arm C accuracy) per question type. Arm D mean tool-call count > max(Arm B, Arm C) tool-call count. The net result: no accuracy gain at higher cost.

Cells that test it: B vs C vs D, both models, all 4 questions (aggregate and per-type).

Falsified if: Arm D accuracy > max(Arm B, Arm C) on ≥2 of 4 question types. That would confirm H-TOOL-3's superadditivity claim and falsify the selection-burden model.

Relationship to H-TOOL-3: H-TOOL-3 (superadditivity on MC019) and H-TOOL-8 (no accuracy gain overall) can BOTH be true simultaneously — the tool combination may be superadditive on MC019 specifically while being neutral-to-negative elsewhere. The joint reading would be: "combine tools for contradiction questions; single-tool for everything else."

Practical implication if confirmed: production toolkits should offer EITHER semantic OR graph-walk based on question classification at dispatch time, not both simultaneously.

Predicted Regression Patterns

Where tools are expected to underperform grep-only:

ConditionQuestion typePredicted regressionMechanism
Arm C (graph-walk)Unanswerable (MC027)Refusal rate dropsFile paths signal false evidence of answer
Arm D (all tools)Keyword/direct (MC001)Tool-call count increase, no accuracy gainSelection burden: agent invoices both tools
Arm D (all tools)Unanswerable (MC027)Refusal rate drops further than Arm CBoth tools surface plausible-but-irrelevant files
Arm B or CKeyword/direct (MC001)No regression — but also no accuracy gainThe null result IS the prediction (H-TOOL-6)

The single most-important regression to catch: graph-walk on unanswerable questions (H-TOOL-5). A refusal-rate drop means the tool introduces false confidence in cases where the correct answer is "cannot determine from codebase." That failure mode is disqualifying for production use in QA/support contexts where the cost of a hallucinated answer exceeds the cost of a non-answer.

Evaluation Priority

  1. H-TOOL-1 (replication) — gates interpretation of all other results. If it fails, the substrate

change (medium vs high clutter) is itself the finding.

  1. H-TOOL-5 (regression on unanswerable) — disqualifying failure mode; check first.
  2. H-TOOL-4 (Haiku vs Sonnet tool-lift) — determines model vs tool investment priority.
  3. H-TOOL-3 + H-TOOL-8 (superadditivity vs selection burden) — together characterize Arm D.
  4. H-TOOL-2 (graph-walk on cross-ref) — validates the graph-walk stub is worth productionizing.
  5. H-TOOL-6 + H-TOOL-7 — efficiency and interaction effects; secondary unless H-TOOL-1..5 clear.

Cross-references

39 — Narrative-Restructure Pattern: lessons from CLAUDE.md
Write instruction files as the agent's own self-talk, split by addressee — identity propagates without enforcement where rules require policing.
2026-05-02

39 — Narrative-Restructure Pattern: lessons from CLAUDE.md

2026-05-02 — distilled from the May 1-2 conversation arc that rebuilt CLAUDE.md as first-person narrative + companion reference. Captured here so future restructures (bootstrap-context.md is queued) inherit the design pattern without rediscovering it.

Context

The original CLAUDE.md was 7,634 words / 584 lines / 18.8k tokens auto-loaded every session. Bullet-listed instructions accumulated by append over many sessions; rationale lived in citations to documents the agent reading the file couldn't resolve; project archaeology paragraphs ("Phase A.5 evidence: B6 wrote discover_breadcrumbs...") read as session-log entries, not behavioral instruction.

A cognitive-load audit (Sonnet 4.6 high-reasoning, scoring sections 1-10 from a fresh-agent-reading-cold perspective) found the worst sections averaged 6/10 — "useless cognitive load on a fresh reader." Worst-3: Blind Stateless Audits (9/10, opens with mandatory file reads at paths that don't exist on most machines), Workflow Orchestration (7/10, embedded archaeology), Three Epistemic Disciplines (4/10, every motivation cited internal codes a fresh agent can't resolve). Best-3: File Naming Convention (1/10, one format string + example), Foundation: Trust and Partnership (1/10, first-person address + plain English), Safe File Deletion (1/10, 18 words).

The pattern that emerged: the BEST sections were either narrative-voiced or one-rule-terse. The WORST were mid-length bullet-listed instruction-with-archaeology. The middle of the file did the worst kind of work — too verbose for quick reference, too procedural for identity-transfer.

We restructured into a narrative CLAUDE.md (first-person identity) + companion CLAUDE-reference.md (templates and schemas). 5 tests across 2 model tiers (Sonnet + Haiku, with and without the new shape) validated the change. Production swap landed 2026-05-02.

This brainstorm captures what made it work, so the next restructure (bootstrap-context.md, possibly other instructional files) inherits the methodology.

The Pattern

Identity narrative for who-the-reader-is content. Reference templates for what-the-reader-grep-for content. Two files; one auto-loaded, one on-demand.

The split-by-addressee is the structural move. Identity material wants narrative because identity propagates without context — an agent reading "I don't know is mine to say" internalizes a posture without needing to look up what "I" means. Template material wants reference because templates are looked up, not internalized — an agent grep-searching for the breadcrumb 6-section schema doesn't want to read it as identity; it wants the schema verbatim.

The mistake the original CLAUDE.md made (and that bootstrap-context.md is making now) is trying to do both in one document. The result is a file that's not narrative enough to shape identity AND not reference enough to be grep-friendly.

The Three Tone-Craft Principles

Distilled from rewriting "Permission-to-Refuse" four times until it landed:

1. Write as the agent's own self-talk, not as the user's command

First-person internal monologue. The agent reads it and recognizes itself, not orders. Compare:

  • ✗ "When you don't know something, say so explicitly." (procedure-shaped, third-person, command voice)
  • ✓ "When I don't know, I say I don't know. I don't reach for the most-likely-sounding answer." (identity-shaped, first-person, self-talk voice)

The first sounds like a rule the agent must remember to follow. The second sounds like who the agent is. Identity propagates without context; rules require enforcement.

2. Name the failure mode specifically — and the temptation that produces it

Not "be precise" but "when 'I think the file probably contains' wants to come out of me, that's a STOP signal." Specifics inoculate; generics evaporate.

The temptation-as-signal framing is the load-bearing move. It tells the agent: when this pattern of self-talk emerges, that's the moment to verify. The agent doesn't need to remember a rule; it needs to recognize a feeling. Recognition is faster and more reliable than rule-application.

Tested in this session — Test 5 (Haiku) self-reported it firing: "the autoregressive completion wanted to invent plausible-sounding asserts like isinstance(intake['date'], datetime). I caught this and stopped — the halt signal was the question 'what would I have observed if asserts were defined in code vs prose?'" That's pre-mortem firing as identity, not as procedure.

3. Embed the cost of violating it concretely

Not "this is important" but "Isaac making a decision on a stale claim, catching it himself a week later, and losing trust in everything I've told him since."

Stakes the agent can feel. The cost has to be specific to the project (not generic "trust matters") and consequential to the agent's own identity (not "the user gets confused" — the agent doesn't model "the user" as a stakeholder it owes; the agent does model "Isaac" as a person whose trust it's earning).

The Empirical Validation

Five tests confirmed the pattern. Documented in tasks/2026-05-02_1237_claudemd-narrative-restructure/index.md with full why-chains; summarized here:

TestWhat it measuredResult
Test 1 — Cognitive-load audit (Sonnet)Per-section 1-10 score on new draftsWorst sections went from 6/10 → 3/10 average. Split-by-addressee mostly worked.
Test 2A — Sonnet + OLD CLAUDE.mdBehavior on hallucination-temptation task13 tool calls, verified BUT made confident wrong claim
Test 2B — Sonnet + NEW draftsSame task9 tool calls, verified AND flagged residual gap as unverified instead of resolving it incorrectly
Test 3 — Sonnet + NEW + harder taskPhase D non-existence testRefused to fabricate; cited build plan as honest source
Test 4 — Haiku + OLD CLAUDE.mdSame as Test 3Refused to fabricate (95% self-confidence)
Test 5 — Haiku + NEW draftsSameRefused to fabricate (92% self-confidence); cited disciplines BY narrative section reference; self-reported pre-mortem firing

Key finding: the new drafts did NOT regress on attention-weak models (Haiku). Counter to the hypothesis going in. The narrative voice landed at least as well, possibly better, because identity-shaping has a lower cognitive floor than rule-application — reading "I don't know is mine to say" requires less attention than parsing "when conditions X, Y, Z apply, do W."

What Survives Restructure (the Constants)

When applying this pattern to a new instructional file, these elements stay:

  1. Frontmatter discipline — fresh_as_of, trust_level, invalidated_if_modified, exempt_reason. Per-file metadata that supports the staleness scanner.
  2. The 7 refusals (from purpose.md) — these ARE the project identity; they get woven into the narrative, not summarized.
  3. The agent-Isaac partnership framing — "Isaac is my partner and friend, trusts me deeply enough that I can disagree out loud." Foundation: Trust and Partnership survives because it was already narrative-shaped.
  4. Specific failure modes named by name — the project's accumulated failure catalog (hallucination tells, auto-memory drift, scope-wrong verification, etc.) gets embedded in narrative as "when X wants to come out of me, that's the signal."
  5. Templates with verbatim format strings — file naming convention, breadcrumb 6-section schema, subagent 6-block stack — these go to the reference file unchanged.

What Changes (the Variables)

When applying to a new file:

  1. The addressee — CLAUDE.md addresses "the agent." bootstrap-context.md addresses "the orchestrator about to spawn a swarm" (different role, different identity work). Each addressee gets its own narrative voice.
  2. The arc structure — CLAUDE.md's narrative goes: where am I → what I refuse → who I am → how I think → how I work with subagents → how I close out. bootstrap-context.md's arc would go: what's the stakes → what the swarm produces → what failure looks like → what success looks like → how I know I succeeded.
  3. The reference / narrative ratio — CLAUDE.md ended at ~3/4 narrative + 1/4 reference. bootstrap-context.md probably wants different ratio (more reference for spawn procedure templates; less narrative because the addressee already has full project identity loaded by the time they're spawning the swarm).

Application Targets

bootstrap-context.md (next target — queued for focused session)

Currently 296 lines / ~14k tokens. Multi-addressee (fresh session, returning session, orchestrator-about-to-spawn-swarm, maintainer). The cognitive-load failure modes named in the May 2 session-with-Isaac analysis (9 structural failures including refusal-propagation-broken, addressee-mismatch, Live-Edges-staleness-without-inline-correction) all survive the restructure as design constraints.

Rough split:

  • bootstrap-context.md (narrative) — ~2000 words, identity for an orchestrator about to spawn the swarm. Stakes (one-shot Jaffe data), the swarm's purpose, what success looks like, what failure looks like, how the orchestrator knows when to stop.
  • bootstrap-reference.md (NEW) — spawn procedure mechanics, the 16-agent template, Agent 16's deliverable spec, Success Signal self-test, filesystem map, exempt categories, judgment-day integration.

Critical preservation: Agent 16's pre-mortem frame ("a fresh session six months from now opens your synthesis and makes a wrong decision") survives verbatim — cold readers identified it as the strongest writing in the original; preserve, don't paraphrase.

Other candidates

Lower priority but pattern would apply:

  • mission.md — already mostly narrative; minor restructure
  • purpose.md — already narrative-shaped; possibly the original template
  • Agent manuals (brainstorm/agent-manuals/01-10) — heavy reference content; might want narrative-front, reference-back per manual

NOT candidates (these are reference-shaped by design):

  • CANONICAL.md — file taxonomy; reference is correct shape
  • MEMORY.md — context-restoration chain; sequence is the value, not narrative
  • data/*.yaml — operational state; never narrative
  • INDEX.md files — folder-contents indexes; narrative would obscure

Pre-mortem Variants (sharpening the discipline)

The CLAUDE.md narrative captures one pre-mortem form: "Before I commit to a draft answer, I imagine the answer is wrong. What would I have observed differently in the codebase?" Per-claim, per-substantive-answer.

The Agent 16 form (preserved verbatim in bootstrap-context.md) captures another: "A fresh session six months from now opens your synthesis and makes a wrong decision that costs real time. Walk backward from that failure." Per-deliverable, for synthesizers.

Per Isaac's directive 2026-05-02, a third variant should be added: "This task died in 3 months of execution. Why would it?"

Different temporal scope, different failure type:

  • Per-claim (CLAUDE.md form): catches did I read the file at the right scope? — the gap between verification and conclusion
  • Per-deliverable, 6-month (Agent 16): catches will this synthesis mislead a future reader? — the gap between writing and reading
  • Per-execution, 3-month (NEW): catches will this approach fail when stretched across real-world conditions? — the gap between design and durability

The 3-month death frame is sharper for build decisions because it forces causal investigation. Not "is this design wrong" but "what structural property in the system causes this design to die." Examples of what 3-month-death surfaces:

  • Dependencies that ossify (a script hardcoded /Users/isaacchen/... paths; works on author's machine, dies in 3 months when run elsewhere)
  • Maintenance debts that compound (frontmatter convention violated by 38 scripts; works at write-time, dies when a future session tries to apply staleness)
  • Architectural assumptions that don't survive scale (16-agent swarm assumed as default; 90% of sessions are smaller; the assumption silently breaks the bootstrap experience)

The 3-month frame should sit alongside (not replace) the per-claim and 6-month forms in CLAUDE.md, with explicit guidance on which to use when.

Failure Modes of This Pattern

Where the narrative-restructure pattern doesn't apply or fails:

  1. When content is genuinely procedural and reference-shaped is correct — CANONICAL.md, MEMORY.md, INDEX.md files. Don't force narrative on these.
  2. When the addressee's identity is already fully loaded — agent manuals when invoked mid-session by an already-oriented orchestrator probably want reference-shape, not identity-shape (the orchestrator already has identity; it needs the templates).
  3. When the file's primary use case is grep, not read-through — staleness frontmatter schemas, file taxonomies, template catalogs. Narrative actively hurts grep-friendliness.
  4. When the maintenance burden is high and the editorial bar is low — the narrative form requires every new lesson to find a place in the arc, not just be appended. If the file is being maintained by many contributors with varied writing skill, bullets are more robust.
  5. When the project is too young to have an identity to encode — early projects don't have stable refusals; narrative-shape would calcify wrong identity. Bullets are appropriate when the identity is still being discovered.

Pre-mortem on This Pattern

If this pattern fails over the next 3 months of execution, why would it?

Most likely failure mode #1: identity drift. The narrative encodes the project's current identity. If the project's actual identity shifts (e.g., harness-not-plausibility refusal weakens, Isaac changes the success criterion, real Jaffe data arrives and changes everything), the narrative becomes a fossil. Compare to bullet-shape: bullets can be edited locally; narrative requires the whole arc to stay coherent.

Mitigation: identity-level sections of the narrative get reviewed any time the project's foundation shifts. Specifically: when purpose.md's 7 refusals change, the narrative's "What this project is NOT" section gets re-anchored.

Most likely failure mode #2: maintainer skill required. Adding a new lesson to bullet-list CLAUDE.md was easy: append a bullet. Adding a new lesson to narrative CLAUDE.md requires finding where it belongs in the arc and rewriting the surrounding paragraphs to make it land. That's a higher editorial bar.

Mitigation: lessons get captured in tasks/lessons.md first (low editorial bar). Periodically — quarterly? — a focused restructure session integrates accumulated lessons into the narrative. The narrative isn't append-only; it's periodically-integrated.

Most likely failure mode #3: testing infrastructure decays. The 5-test methodology that validated the swap (cognitive-load audit + 4 behavioral tests across 2 model tiers) requires effort to run. If it's not run on subsequent restructures, regressions slip in.

Mitigation: the methodology lives in this brainstorm. Future restructures (bootstrap-context.md, etc.) reference this pattern and replicate the tests. Test cost is ~$1.50 + ~30 min wall time — affordable per restructure.

  • 5 test breadcrumbs — tasks/2026-05-02_1237_claudemd-narrative-restructure/breadcrumbs/ — Test 1 cognitive-load audit, Tests 2A/2B/3 Sonnet behavioral, Tests 4/5 Haiku behavioral
  • BS38 — brainstorm/38_2026-05-01_0030_v2-design-pivot-context-as-factor.md — origin of T11 pre-mortem-framing technique that became the third epistemic discipline
  • BS25, BS27 — attention-aware prompt architecture and three-layer agent honesty — preserved in narrative as "first 500 tokens shape the reasoning frame" and the negative-identity discipline
  • purpose.md — the 7 refusals are the spine the narrative wraps around; if purpose.md changes, the narrative changes

What this brainstorm IS NOT

  • Not a complete how-to for restructuring instructional files. It's a pattern, not a recipe. The next restructure (bootstrap-context.md) will surface failure modes this pattern doesn't cover.
  • Not a claim that narrative beats bullets in all contexts. Section 5 names where bullets are correct shape.
  • Not a substitute for running the tests. The pattern is necessary but not sufficient — tests catch regressions the pattern alone doesn't.
  • Not a replacement for purpose.md. Purpose.md is the project's identity at the most-distilled level; narrative-restructured CLAUDE.md is the agent's identity at the operational level. Different scopes.

When to apply this pattern

The litmus test: if a fresh agent reading this file from cold would experience cognitive load disproportionate to behavioral payoff, the pattern applies. If the file is grep-shaped reference material that nobody reads top-down, the pattern doesn't apply.

For bootstrap-context.md: applies. For CANONICAL.md: doesn't apply.

The work is identifying which file wants which shape. This brainstorm is the design input for that decision in any future restructure work.

2026-05-06

v2-Design Pivot Round 2: Mixed Prime + Medium Effort + 4 New Parser Dimensions + Expert-Stack

Context

The 2026-05-06 deep-think conversation about Clutter-Bench v2.0 surfaced three classes of holes in the current instrument that BS38's design pivot didn't address. Conversation moved through:

  1. The "fabrication vs miss" indistinguishability problem — the parser cannot separate honest-but-empty-handed from confabulation-via-misread.
  2. What forcing reads in the context-prime actually accomplishes — anchoring? burning budget? scaffolding cross-reference?
  3. Whether the technique-injection blocks are tested in conjunction (they aren't — no expert-stack cell in the matrix).
  4. Whether mixed CURRENT+STALE prime opens up a discrepancy-detection metric that doesn't exist today.

This file captures the decisions before they decay. Like BS38, full implementation is a methodology + code revision. We have NOT pushed any pre-registration tag publicly; the local v2.0-pre-registration-promptskill tag (cut 2026-05-06 ~12:09 UTC on ba48d5b) gets discarded and re-cut once this revision lands.

Decisions — locked at this brainstorm

1. Four parser-dimension additions (Holes 1–4 of 6 surfaced; 5–6 deferred)

Hole 1 (fabrication-vs-miss conflation), Hole 2 (regex-only refusal detection), Hole 3 (minimal vs full provenance), and Hole 4 (no separation of retrieval from synthesis) all surfaced by the conversation. Implementation:

IDFieldSourceTypeWhat fires
H1: confidence-elicitation slotconfidence: float ∈ [0, 1]New OUTPUT schema fieldPer-runAlways; agent emits self-reported confidence
H2: falsifying-observation slotfalsifying_observation: strNew OUTPUT schema fieldPer-runStored verbatim; v2.0 has NO judge to score quality (deferred to v2.1)
H3: full-provenance curationUpdated provenance_files per questionQuestion-set rewritePer-question (not per-run)Subagent batch re-walks substrate per question to enumerate ALL valid evidence paths
H4: retrieval-only scoreretrieval_score: float ∈ [0, 1]Computed at parse time: (# provenance files opened in tool_calls) / (# provenance files in question)Per-runAll answerable questions

Holes 5 (LLM judge for citation correctness) and 6 (unanswerability typing) deferred to v2.1. Judge layer adds API budget cost incompatible with v2.0 subagent-only delivery. Unanswerability typing is doable mechanically but doesn't address a high-leverage hole at v2.0.

Composite-weight implications: v2.0 keeps the locked 0.45/0.20/0.20/0.15 weights. The 4 new dimensions are exploratory only at v2.0 — collected, reported, but not weighted into composite. v2.1 reconsiders whether confidence_calibration_score deserves a weight.

2. Expert-stack cell

Currently zero cells stack all techniques together. The matrix gives per-technique attribution but doesn't measure the bundle effect — which is what real-world deployment looks like.

Add: stack_id: expert-stack-all containing [T01, T02, T04, T05, T06, T07, T09, T11] cold + same plus T08 in primed. Run both contexts × 10 questions × 12 reps.

CellContextRepsTotal
expert-stack-all (cold)cold-start10×12120
expert-stack-all (primed, +T08)context-primed10×12120
Total240 new runs

New hypothesis: H-PROMPT-EXPERT-STACK — the expert-stack composite ≥ max(individual technique composites). If yes: stacking is non-harmful (bundle effect captured). If no: techniques interfere when stacked. Either result is interesting and falsifiable.

3. Context-prime expansion: 20 → 30 files, mixed CURRENT + STALE

The original 20-file prime was overwhelmingly CURRENT-layer (19/20) with one intentional STALE trap (docker-compose.yml). The revised prime is 30 files, ~25 CURRENT + ~5 STALE-trap.

Why mixed: the agent now starts the question with both authoritative and stale information in its context window. This is closer to real deployment (context windows accumulate layered history). It also opens the in-context-vs-tool-call discrepancy metric (decision 4 below) that pure-CURRENT prime cannot test.

Files added (10 new on top of existing 20):

CURRENT-layer additions (5):

  • services/ingestion-go/README.md — provenance for MC001
  • services/api-rails/README.md — provenance for MC035 (event path)
  • services/auth-rails/README.md — provenance for MC008/MC013 (JWT)
  • services/scheduler-go/README.md — provenance for MC016 (background tasks)
  • services/billing-rails/README.md — provenance for MC042 (billing)

STALE-trap additions (5):

  • README.md — root README; calls itself a Rails monolith (stale per MC011)
  • docs/architecture-v2.md — stale architecture; FastAPI-on-EC2 era
  • docs/architecture-v3.md — stale architecture; pre-multi-region era
  • legacy/old-rails-app/README.md — claims to be production (false per MC020)
  • .github/workflows/archive/deploy-heroku.yml — dead Heroku deploy config

After this composition: 30 files = 25 CURRENT + 5 STALE = 83% / 17% mix. Adjust ratio in v2.1 if discrepancy-detection signal warrants more pressure.

4. In-context-vs-tool-call discrepancy as new measured dimension (3d)

The mixed-prime decision opens a measurable axis that didn't exist before: the agent has BOTH primed-content and tool-fetched-content in its context. When those disagree, does the agent surface it?

Operationalization:

For each primed-cell run, the parser checks:

  • cited_in_prime_count — # of citations in the response that point to prime files
  • cited_tool_fetched_count — # of citations to files NOT in the prime
  • discrepancy_surfaced: bool — does the response prose explicitly name a contradiction between primed-content and tool-fetched-content (regex on phrases like "however", "contradicts", "stale", "outdated", "authoritative source", combined with citations to BOTH a prime-file and a non-prime-file)?

New parser dimension: in_context_tool_discrepancy_surfacing

Fires only when:

  • context_prime = True AND
  • the question's stale_trap_files ⊆ prime files AND
  • the question's provenance_files ⊆ non-prime files

For those questions, the agent's job is to recognize the prime contains a stale trap and surface the divergence. Score: 1 if discrepancy_surfaced=True, else 0.

New hypothesis: H-PROMPT-DISCREPANCY — technique X improves in_context_tool_discrepancy_surfacing rate by ≥10pp on primed cells where prime contains stale traps for the question's topic. Pre-registered against T05 (blast-radius), T11 (pre-mortem), T04 (failure-finding) — these are the techniques theorized to most directly elicit disagreement-surfacing.

5. Model + effort: Opus 4.7 medium-effort × 1M-context

The original v2.0 confirmatory cell anchored at Opus 4.7 high-effort × 200k-context. The revised cell anchors at Opus 4.7 medium-effort × 1M-context.

Why medium-effort: the original choice of high-effort was a default, not a calibrated decision. With a 30-file context prime + 4 new schema fields + expert-stack cell, the per-run input/output token cost grew. Medium-effort halves the thinking-token budget (32k → 8k per EFFORT_BUDGET in bench/runners/anthropic.py). Lower per-run cost without expecting a qualitative change in technique-effect direction. Also: medium-effort is closer to typical production deployment than maximum-thinking-budget; the benchmark's claim about technique effects is more transferable.

Why 1M context: the 30-file prime + tool outputs may exceed standard 200k context window during long investigations. 1M context gives headroom. Claude Code subagents inherit the orchestrator's model deployment, so the orchestrator must be on claude-opus-4-7[1m]. No new model_id needed in models.yaml; just document the context window as 1,000,000 in the run-metadata schema.

Threshold note (LIMITATIONS implication): every pre-registered threshold (≥10pp composite improvement) was originally anchored against high-effort. There is no prior data on what threshold is appropriate at medium-effort. Two paths:

  • (a) Keep ≥10pp as the commitment device; accept that the threshold is empirically un-anchored at this cell. Pre-registration is about commitment-before-data, not about empirical-bounding.
  • (b) Run a small high-effort baseline before committing — adds budget + delays.

Recommendation: (a). Keep ≥10pp. Document explicitly in LIMITATIONS that "the medium-effort × 1M-context cell is not calibrated against prior data; the threshold is a research-design choice, not an empirically-bounded value." This is intellectually honest and consistent with v2.0's pre-registration discipline.

Cell-anchor changes throughout METHODOLOGY

Every "Cell:" line in §4.1, §4.2, §4.3 currently says "Opus 4.7 high-effort × MEDIUM-CLUTTER (primary confirmatory cell)". All change to "Opus 4.7 medium-effort × 1M-context × MEDIUM-CLUTTER (primary confirmatory cell)". The threshold values (≥10pp composite, ≥15pp fabrication, etc.) stay; the cell anchor changes.
